Large shark stuck in city canal draws 600,000 visitors as rescue efforts begin in South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:37:09 UTC
14:37:09 KST

Rescuers have begun trying to rescue a large shark that has been trapped in a narrow city canal in South Korea for more than a week, and become an unlikely tourist attraction in the process.
More than 600,000 visitors are estimated to have visited the southern port city of Busan since the 3.5-metre shark – nicknamed Bukang-i after the name of Busan’s North Port – was first spotted on 18 September in the waterway at a waterfront park.
Experts believe it to be a bronze whaler shark that followed prey from the sea into the canal and could not find its way out.
The coastguard in the city about 200 miles (325km) south-east of Seoul tried to drive it out on the day it appeared but suspended the operation six hours later, on the advice of scientists who warned that forcing the animal could harm it or make it aggressive.
On Tuesday morning coastguard boats sprayed jets of water behind the shark to push it towards the canal’s mouth, a method officials said was modelled on the rescue of a great white shark that became trapped in shallow water off Massachusetts in 2004.
The first attempt failed, after the the shark slipped past the boats and swam back into the canal, the Herald Business reported.
The fisheries institute said the shark was stable, but officials said its ability to feed and move was restricted, which could weaken it the longer it stayed.
Sharks are not unknown in South Korean waters. The national institute of fisheries science recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that are the sharks’ prey.
The North Port Waterfront Park, which usually draws about 2,000 people a day on holidays, recorded 607,000 visits between 19 and 28 September, according to the city.
On Tuesday Kim Jung-sook, 62, came to say goodbye to the shark, telling the Maeil Shinmun newspaper: “I’ve grown attached to it after seeing it here for a few days … I feel a bit sad.”
Busan’s mayor, Chun Jae-soo, is a fan too. “It really has star quality. It comes up every five to 10 minutes,” he told CBS radio. “It’s just so pretty.”
The city has named the shark an honorary publicity ambassador, giving it the title “Shafluencer”, after 91% of respondents to a city Instagram poll backed the idea. Boogi, the city’s mascot, is to accept the certificate on its behalf.
Lee Do-yoon, eight, who came with his father to see it off, was not worried that it appeared to be time to say goodbye.
“It’s OK,” he said. “Bukang-i is going to meet its friends.”

Australian central bank raises interest rates to 15-year high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:37:05 CST
14:37:05 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia's central bank on Tuesday raised interest rates to a 15-year-high, citing inflation driven by the conflict in the Middle East.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said its Monetary Policy Board voted unanimously to lift the cash rate target from 4.35 percent to 4.60 percent, the highest figure since November 2011.
It marks the fourth rate rise delivered by the RBA so far in 2026 after three previous increases of 0.25 percentage points each in February, March and May.
Economists and Australia's major banks had unanimously predicted the decision to raise the cash rate target on Tuesday.
The Monetary Policy Board said in its decision statement that the conflict in the Middle East has broadened, causing global energy prices to rise much higher than assumed when the board decided to keep interest rates on hold in August.
"The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast. Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation," it said.
Speaking earlier on Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said that the conflict in the Middle East has been "absolutely disastrous" from a cost-of-living and economic perspective.
"We're seeing inflation going up around the world; we're seeing interest rates going up around the world. And unfortunately, Australia's not immune from the same pressures," he told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.
The latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) showed that annual inflation fell from 3.8 percent in June to 3.5 percent in July.
The trimmed mean, the measure of underlying inflation preferred by the RBA, remained steady at 3.6 percent. The RBA targets annual inflation of 2-3 percent.
The ABS will release inflation data for August on Wednesday, and the Monetary Policy Board will next meet at the start of November. ■

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's economic growth is forecast to slow to 3 percent in 2026 from 5.3 percent in 2025, driven by surging energy costs, weakening tourism, and declining remittances, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Tuesday.
The Southeast Asian nation, which relies heavily on garment, footwear, and travel goods exports, alongside agriculture, tourism, and real estate, faces a mounting combination of domestic and global headwinds.
"Growth is projected to slow to 3 percent in 2026 before recovering to 4 percent in 2027, reflecting higher energy costs, weaker tourism and remittances, decelerating garment exports, subdued domestic demand, and tighter financial conditions," the IMF said in a press release.
"Inflation is expected to remain elevated at 5.6 percent in 2026 before easing as energy prices normalize," it added.
The current account deficit is projected to widen sharply, although resilient foreign direct investment and adequate international reserves provide important buffers.
The IMF said risks to growth are tilted to the downside, including from renewed energy and trade disruptions, persistent scam activities, and a sharper real estate correction.
Potential disruptions from El Nino conditions could keep agricultural price pressures elevated, it added. ■

Evicted Spanish pensioner to return home, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:36:00 UTC
14:36:00 KST

Evicted Spanish pensioner to return home, lawyer says
September 29, 2026
An elderly woman who was evicted from the Madrid apartment she lived most of her life in and whose case sparked widespread solidarity protests across Spain, is going to be able to return home, her lawyer said on Monday.
Video last week showed Maria del Carmen Abascal, known by her nickname Maricarmen, being taken out of the building on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, is a wheelchair user and a resident of the Spanish capital's Retiro neighborhood.
Her dramatic eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards who took the case to heart to bring one of the country's most pressing problems to the center of attention: the housing crisis.
Rising prices and a shortage of homes have pushed people out of the market in Europe's fourth-largest economy, with the weekend's protest having put pressure on Spain's left-wing government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of the Spanish capital, with many having then pitched tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night. More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters, calling it "a result of the social mobilization."
"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.
Spanish housing bill Tuesday falls short of protester demands
Sanchez, who last week called the eviction a "social tragedy," is hoping to secure backing for a long-delayed housing bill at Tuesday's meeting of Spain's Council of Ministers.
But according to El Pais, the legislation put forth Tuesday falls short of the demands of protesters who are asking for tougher action against abusive landlords and a freeze on rents until the housing crisis is resolved.

====================================================================================================

AI boom and arms industry set €1bn startups at record level in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:32:06 UTC
14:32:06 KST

By Alexander Sturm, dpa.
Germany’s startup sector is producing a growing number of companies valued at over €1 billion ($1.14 billion), partly driven by the artificial intelligence boom, according to an annual study.
The research by the German Startup Monitor shows that about €8 billion in venture capital has flowed into startups by the end of September 2026, surpassing the approximately €7.5 billion invested throughout the whole of the previous year.
By the end of September, 10 new startups have achieved a company valuation of at least €1 billion – so-called “unicorns” – according to the report, which has been published yearly since 2013.
The data analysis and survey of more than 1,800 growth companies is to be presented in Berlin on Monday by the German Startup Association.
With a total of 39 unicorns, Germany has reached a record level, the report said.
These include major names such as online broker Trade Republic, smartphone bank N26 and software firm Personio. New additions this year include software company Osapiens, Neura Robotics and defence firm Stark Defense.
“Germany is founding [new companies] again – broadly and on a strong technological basis,” said Verena Pausder, chairwoman of the association.
For the purposes of the study, startups are defined as companies that are less than 10 years old, offer innovative products or business models, and have strong ambitions for growth.
Defence and AI key drivers
The startup sector is benefiting from rising investment in defence companies, including Quantum Systems and Helsing, which are attracting large sums from investors.
AI is a further growth driver. For 53% of the startups surveyed, the technology is central to their product – up from 39% in 2024. At the same time, AI is said to be making it significantly easier to found companies.
The report also highlights weaknesses in the startup sector. Capital flowing in was said to be concentrating more heavily at the top. “Across the board, the number of financing rounds is around a quarter below the 2021 level.”
Some 89% of founders surveyed called for more venture capital from Germany and Europe.
“The available capital is not sufficient to make the leap to the top of the world,” Pausder said.
International strategy
A majority of startups (62%) also said they would prefer the United States for a potential stock market listing, with only 27% favouring Germany. And for digital technologies, 64% said they relied predominantly or entirely on US providers – partly due to a lack of European alternatives.
The government must implement its startup strategy and make financing easier, Pausder said. She added that company formation within the EU must be simplified.
The association sees strengths in the sector’s links with universities. Every second startup (51%) was said to be supported by research institutions, and for 59% the product was said to stem from new scientific findings.
Universities are the most important pillar in the ecosystem, said association research expert Alexander Hirschfeld. “Measured against the quality of Germany’s research landscape, however, far too few companies are still being founded from it,” he said.
The shortage of skilled workers is causing less concern among startups. Only 15% see it as a major obstacle, down from 30% two years ago. Some 83% said they planned to make new hires within 12 months.
Source: dpa.com

Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian and Norwegian activists
- Published
A pro-democracy group has accused the Vietnamese government of abducting two of its members, an Australian and a Norwegian citizen, in Cambodia and taking them back across the border.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed that they had arrested Tran Hiep and Nguyen Duc Thuan, but say they had entered the country using forged documents and planned to carry out terrorist activities.
It said the men had admitted to being members of Viet Tan, which Vietnam sees as a terrorist organisation.
Viet Tan called their arrest a "blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam".
The group, which has members in Vietnam and abroad, said the two men had been travelling in the southern border district of Kaoh Andaet in Cambodia when they went missing and had not been heard from since 18 September.
Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, told Australian media he had been meeting pro-democracy activists in Cambodia and had no intention of travelling to Vietnam.
He was meant to meet her in Bangkok to board a return flight to Australia but never turned up, she said.
"He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen," she told the ABC.
According to a Vietnamese state media report published on Monday, Tran and Nguyen were detained with a third man at the border in Tay Ninh province on 18 September.
The trio "confessed to being members of the terrorist organisation 'Viet Tan,' [and] carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam in order to carry out terrorist and sabotage activities," the report said.
They were charged on Monday with membership of a terrorist organisation while an investigation continued "to clarify the criminal acts of the suspects in order to handle them according to the law", it said.
"A state orchestrating the abduction of individuals abroad and forcibly taking them to its territory is a serious act of transnational repression," said Viet Tan. "It violates Cambodia's sovereignty and the fundamental principles of international law."
The Viet Tan statement did not mention the third man, who was named by authorities as Thai Cong Truong Son.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consular support was being provided to Tran's family.
"That's what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we'll continue to engage directly with the family."
"Vietnam authorities' confirmation that they detained [these] activists... demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia," Phil Robertson, Director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates said in a statement.
"This latest act is an unacceptable outrage."
The Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities have been contacted for comment.

Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The Russians started the attack at 18:00 on 28 September. They launched a Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile and two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Kursk Oblast.
They also used 152 Shahed (82 jet-powered) and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoy UAVs.
The drones were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk and from Hvardiiske and Chauda in temporarily occupied Crimea.
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
Quote: "As of 08:00, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 109 aerial assets:
- 1 Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile
- 2 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles
- 106 Shahed, Gerbera and other types of drones."
Details: Hits by aerial assets have been recorded at 24 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at 16 locations.
The attack is ongoing, as several Russian drones are still in the airspace.
Background: Air-raid warnings were issued in the city of Kyiv and several Ukrainian oblasts on the night of 28-29 September due to the threat of Russian ballistic missiles. Explosions were heard in the capital and fires broke out.

Gaming Scottish granny plays her way to Guinness world record

Gaming Scottish granny plays her way to Guinness world record
- Cath Bowie, a 78-year-old Scottish grandmother, became the world's oldest female Fortnite streamer recognised by Guinness World Records in 2023.
- She started playing Fortnite in 2017 after watching her grandson and began streaming in 2018, gaining over 24,000 followers on Twitch.
- Bowie enjoys the game's challenge and community, encouraging older people to try gaming and never let age stop them.
AI generated
In 2017, Cath Bowie saw her grandson play the multiplayer shooter game Fortnite and decided to give it a try. Little did she know that nine years later she would play her way into the record books.
On Sept 24, the 78-year-old Scottish grandmother was named the world’s oldest female Fortnite streamer by Guinness World Records (GWR).
She was also featured in the Guinness World Records Gamer’s Edition 2027, which was released in September.
Bowie, better known as “grumpygran48” to over 24,000 followers on Twitch, said she was “instantly intrigued” when she saw her then 17-year-old grandson playing the game in 2017, when Fortnite launched Battle Royale mode.
Battle Royale mode is an online multiplayer video game type where a large group of players fight to be the last person or team alive.
“Nearly nine years later I am still playing it, still absolutely loving it, and although still growing older I have never made my age a deterrent,” Bowie told GWR.
She said she had tried other online games, but nothing got her hooked as much as Fortnite.
“I call myself a ‘Fortniter’ more than a gamer,” she added.
She started streaming in 2018, but her grandson was sceptical of her success.
“As a young guy he just couldn’t believe that his grandma would do such a thing and suggested that nobody would join me or watch me,” Bowie said.
“Saying that was like a red rag to a bull to me. I would show him that I could do it — 24,000+ followers later and he doesn’t mention it. I wonder why?”
Bowie said she loves the challenge the game gives her. She streams herself playing for up to six hours a day.
Over the years, many of her fellow gamers became supporters and friends.
“I play with some wonderful folk - from the UK, quite a few from the USA, from Canada, New Zealand and Australia,” she told the BBC’s Radio Scotland Breakfast programme.
“It’s super meeting all these folk. The chat we have, it’s lovely — I’ve had folk with me for quite a few years now.”
And to older people who want to try gaming, Bowie said: “Never let age stop you. If I can do it so can you.”

Tuesday and Wednesday will bring more clouds, with isolated rain clouds bringing light rain in some areas, according to the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre.
There is also a possibility of local thunderstorms in western and central regions during the night into Wednesday.
With light winds prevailing, fog will form overnight and in the mornings, reducing visibility. Overnight temperatures will vary depending on cloud cover. During the night into Tuesday, as skies become clearer, temperatures across most of the country will fall to +5°C to +10°C, while along the Kurzeme coast they will remain at +11°C to +13°C.
During the night into Wednesday, cloud cover will keep minimum temperatures at +10°C to +14°C. Daytime temperatures will reach +14°C to +19°C, with the thermometer climbing to around +20°C in some areas.
At the beginning of October, weather conditions will remain calm,
with light winds and fog forming in some areas overnight. At the beginning of Thursday night, clouds will still bring light rain to parts of eastern Latvia, but the following days are expected to be mostly dry.
Daytime temperatures will still rise a few degrees above +15°C, but the progression of autumn will gradually make itself felt, with temperatures slowly declining and nights becoming increasingly cooler.

More than 80 reported abducted in Nigeria as police find human remains
Farmers and women abducted in northern Niger and Zamfara states as police find human remains, including 28 skulls, at suspected gang camps.
More than 80 people have been reported missing in Nigeria after being abducted by armed gangs, a media report said, as authorities announced the discovery of human remains suspected to belong to victims of kidnapping in the southeastern state of Abia.
The AFP news agency reported on Monday that at least 87 people, mostly women, were missing after two separate weekend attacks.
Recommended Stories

- list 3 of 3Why are kidnappings recurrent in Nigeria?
At least 47 farmers were abducted by armed men while harvesting peanuts in the northern Niger State on Saturday, while 40 women were kidnapped in the neighbouring state of Zamfara on Sunday, the agency reported, citing two security reports and a local source.
The kidnappings in the Mariga area of Niger and Yargada in Zamfara are the latest attacks by criminal gangs who specialise in ransom kidnappings and cattle rustling. Locally known as “bandits”, they regularly carry out bloody raids on villages, killing residents and torching homes after looting them.
Separately, police in Abia announced in a statement on Sunday that they found 28 human skulls and bones ”suspected to be [of kidnapped] victims”, after raiding camps linked to criminal groups in the forests.
In a statement on X, the police said suspects at the scene had fled and added that “efforts are intensified to apprehend the fleeing suspects”.
Mass abductions for ransom have become common in parts of northwestern and north-central Nigeria, with armed gangs frequently holding abductees until they are paid large sums of money.
In August, gunmen abducted as many as 600 worshippers during Friday prayers at a mosque in Dekera village in the north-central Niger State.
According to research from SBM Intelligence, a Lagos-based consultancy, armed groups raised some 7.8 billion naira (nearly $6m) in ransom payments between July 2025 and June 2026, more than triple the 2.6 billion naira paid during the same period last year.
The latest wave of kidnappings comes a few months ahead of the January presidential elections, in which security, along with the rising cost of living, is set to be a major issue.
President Bola Tinubu has faced growing criticism over lax security.
Residents of Niger State protested last Monday over the abduction of hundreds of people who, they said, remained in captivity a month after gunmen attacked several communities in one of the country’s largest mass kidnappings.

Ukraine's digital minister: 'We want Europe to use Ukraine as an AI sandbox'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:15:25 UTC
14:15:25 KST

Ukraine has built a digital state under the pressure of war. Digital Minister Oksana Ferchuk tells Euronews what Europe can learn from Ukraine, from digital government and AI to cybersecurity and resilience.
Do you know where your driving licence, ID or marriage certificate is right now? In Ukraine, you can access these and many other essential documents directly on your phone.
The country has built one of the world’s most advanced digital government systems, with services that allow citizens to handle much of their everyday bureaucracy online.
During her visit to Berlin, Ukrainian Minister of Digital Transformation Oksana Fedorova met with her German counterpart, Karsten Wildberger, to discuss how Ukraine and Germany could share their experiences.
The two countries agreed to bring together dedicated teams to take a closer look at what Ukraine has done well – but also at what has not worked – and explore which of its digital solutions could be useful for Germany.
Euronews met Ferchuk at the Ukrainian Embassy in Berlin during her visit to discuss the kind of cooperation Germany and Ukraine can expect, her views on the latest warnings about AI, and how Ukraine's digital infrastructure can withstand Russian attacks.
Euronews: What are some of the key things Germany can learn from Ukraine that these teams will be looking at?
Ferchuk: First of all, our ecosystem of state services, which we utilise in a platform called Diia ("action" in English). It's a mobile app, web portal and network of offline locations where we, as a government, provide public services to Ukrainians.
The app gives users access to more than 30 digital documents, including your passport, driving licence, information about your children, your tax ID and your children's tax IDs. Beyond these documents, which we believe could also be used across Europe as the EU moves in the same direction with its digital identity wallet initiative, we offer a wide range of services. These include selling a car through the app, giving someone else permission to drive your car without having to visit an office and checking and paying fines online.
Another area of the app is where you can get married or divorced online and you can even propose online. Ukrainians living abroad who want to get married under Ukrainian law can also do so through Diia, with our postal service then sending them the official paper certificate by post.
In total, we offer around 250 public services online. We agreed to analyse these services together with the German ministry team, identify some for service design, and potentially even develop a prototype for Germany. We also agreed to build this connection not only between our government teams, but also to introduce German counterparts to the IT companies that have been developing these kinds of applications and services for the Ukrainian government for several years. We call them the GovTech Alliance of Ukraine, and we'll be happy to introduce them to our German partners.
Euronews: There seems to be a greater acceptance of making mistakes along the way.
Ferchuk: This is one of the biggest differences between the IT world and government. In government, we have to do everything in accordance with the law. But as a government, working together with parliament, we also have the ability to change the law.
That is the mentality we have. If we see that a simple, user-friendly service cannot be provided because of certain legislative restrictions, and changing those laws would have a positive impact on society, we change the law and then make the service easier to use. In the IT world, by contrast, success often comes from experimenting and trying things repeatedly.
To give people the freedom to innovate, you have to give them permission to make mistakes. Those mistakes should never compromise data protection or security, and they should never breach the law. But you have to give your IT teams the freedom to make mistakes. Otherwise, they will simply follow what is already set out in the legislation, and there will be no real innovation.
Euronews: If we look ahead to the winter, Russia also targets critical infrastructure, so there can be situations where there is no electricity, no mobile network, or people simply can't charge their phones. How do you make sure that people can still access these essential services in those situations?
Ferchuk: That's a very important question and another area of cooperation with the German government. We discussed it separately because we are not only building a digital state; we are building digital resilience. This is not our first winter. Unfortunately, it's the fourth or fifth, depending on how you count from the very beginning.
Will this winter be more difficult? Yes, we expect it to be, but we have been preparing for it since the summer.
We have a specific programme with telecom operators and are training our teams on what to do when the electricity goes out during blackouts. We are preparing to use generators and batteries to keep base stations running and mobile networks operational. We are now planning for outages of up to five days, with a plan for each area. Unfortunately, Russia started attacking our digital infrastructure a week ago. They attacked more and more our data centres.
Recently, they attacked two of our telecom providers. But the result is that the services are still available because we have backups and can move systems into the cloud or underground. We have a specific resilience strategy for all state-owned and government IT systems and services. We have backups for everything and are now conducting exercises, including deliberately switching some systems off.
It's all part of the training. What Europe can expect from Ukraine is an opportunity to see how the state can use AI to improve public services. With your Ministry of Digital Transformation, we have agreed to connect our AI teams and develop some services together. Your teams will be able to see how we train our models, which models we use and how the architecture is built. And we are ready to share not only our successes, but also our mistakes. This is an important message for the European Union. We are now required to harmonise our legislation with the so-called AI Act.
But we would like to propose a slightly different approach. We propose that Europe use Ukraine as an AI sandbox: a place where it can observe the experiments we are conducting, learn from what works and then implement those lessons safely in the European environment. In the digital sphere, our experience with documents and public services could also be replicated across the European Union, creating a single digital space where documents are accepted across borders and services are available cross-border. This is our proposition to the European Union and to Berlin.
Euronews: Why is Ukraine so digitally advanced? Was this something that was accelerated by the full-scale invasion, or did it already exist before the invasion?
Ferchuk: That's more of a philosophical question. I'd say it started in the early 2000s, when many businesses began innovating and developing digital products, laying the foundations for Ukrainians to start using digital applications. We realised that it was much easier, more convenient and more user-friendly when services were available online.
The first wave of adoption and acceptance really came from the commercial sector. Then, in 2019, a new government came to power, and several prominent figures from Ukraine's IT sector joined it. They had a clear vision and strategy and in 2019 they established the Ministry of Digital Transformation. From that point on, that vision was implemented, refined and continuously updated. As a result, we now have a government that thinks about digital transformation and digital tools across all areas. And it's not just about policies.
We have also created dedicated digital transformation positions in every ministry and every major government body. If you want to provide a service to a citizen, you often need information from different government bodies. We have digitalised much of this information and created a large number of decentralised registers. This is also very important: the registers are protected, and the information is never stored in one central database.
When you, as a citizen, request a service, we only retrieve the specific information we need about you from each relevant register or database. We then bring that information together to provide the service. That is one of the reasons why this system is possible.
Euronews: How do you protect data when so many government services are online? Russia is using hybrid warfare, including cyberattacks. Is there a specific security system or firewall in place, or does accessing only specific pieces of information from different ministries already provide an additional layer of protection?
Ferchuk: Both.It's a really complex architecture that is, first of all, decentralised. Second, we classify information according to its level of importance. We have open information and a lot of open data that is publicly available in Ukraine.
Then we have personal information, which is protected and not publicly available, but can be accessed when you request it as an individual. And then there is classified information, which has to be protected under much stricter rules. For each type of information, we have specific rules on how it should be protected, based on international best practices.
Is it 100% safe? In IT, you can never say that anything is 100% safe. But this is also a battlefield. The enemy is attacking us in cyberspace every day. There are thousands of attacks every year, and we are constantly developing our skills and our community of experts who know how to protect and monitor these systems 24/7.
We have what we call security operations centres, where teams monitor system logs and analyse anomalies and user patterns, increasingly with the help of AI. So it's a constant process: the enemy improves its tactics, and we improve our tools and defences.
Euronews: Like a cat-and-mouse game.
Ferchuk: It's a constant technology race. The good thing is that Ukraine has a large community of IT specialists and a strong academic sector, producing around 20,000 IT specialists each year.
This environment has also helped us build a strong community of cybersecurity experts. The major companies that develop and sell cybersecurity tools globally are also very interested in testing their technologies in the Ukrainian environment.
Euronews: Is there a parallel here with the defence industry? With drones, for example, companies are gaining valuable battlefield experience because their systems are being tested and used in Ukraine.
Oksana Ferchuk: It's the same approach, but the difference is that this experience is valuable not only for countries at war. Cyberattacks are already a reality for many countries. Different types of adversaries, not just Russia, are using these tactics to disrupt or destabilise the IT systems of other countries and their allies. So this knowledge is very valuable.
The good thing is that the major companies producing cybersecurity tools are very interested. They come to us, and we work with them directly. They provide us with new updates, and there is also a continuous cycle of innovation: new tactics from the enemy, new products from vendors, and new defensive tactics and experience from our teams. It's developing very quickly. That’s why we are concerned and would really like our partners and allies to be part of this race and see what's happening.
The Baltic countries are very good at sharing this experience. We would love Germany to do the same.
Euronews: You've mentioned AI. Some AI developers themselves warn about the risks of increasingly powerful systems. From a more basic perspective, how do we ensure that AI doesn't get too much access to our digital infrastructure?
Ferchuk: I don’t really want to comment on it in those terms, because some people make very emotional statements that are then picked up by other media. I'd rather approach it from a different perspective. When the internet was first developed, there were concerns that it would change the world, take away our jobs and so on. So we shouldn’t be afraid of this new technology.
When you look at AI in more detail, you understand how advanced it is and what kind of fundamental changes it can bring to our everyday processes. AI is a really powerful tool. It can help us analyse more data, make more decisions based on facts rather than feelings and, above all, eliminate the routine bureaucratic work that everybody hates. So I see the influence of AI in a very positive way.
At the same time, for people who are afraid of AI and are wondering whether to use it to modernise their economies and everyday lives, they have to look at what is happening in other countries, where this question is no longer being asked. Those countries are already in a race, actively building infrastructure and training specialised models that increase productivity and efficiency and will have a huge economic and cultural impact.
If your country or your industry is not using this technology, somebody else in another country already is. And we have to remember that we are part of a global market and are competing globally. So I would say it’s really wrong not to pay attention to this technology. It can improve our lives dramatically. We just have to be wise enough to put the right guardrails in place and use it in an ethical, effective and responsible way. We actually have a strategy for using AI to achieve the maximum possible impact.
Our vision is to build what we call a full AI stack. We are working on our own sovereign AI factory infrastructure. At the same time, we use cloud infrastructure to compare the performance of different models. We mostly use open models and train them for specific tasks, and we now have a lot of experiments under way for government use.
Then we have the application layer. This includes the mobile applications I mentioned earlier. Diia is a government services app used by more than 24 million Ukrainians. It's a great platform for showing people what an AI-powered service can look like. We launched the world's first AI assistant that helps you understand how to access the government service you need.

OpenAI scraps release of newest AI model over safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:03:28 UTC
14:03:28 KST

Darren Lyn
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
OpenAI said Monday that it is scrapping the release of its newest next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) model over safety concerns, according to media reports.
The move comes in the wake of recent industry-wide instances of rogue AI models conducting cyberattacks on their own.
OpenAI nixed the plans because of concerns researchers raised during its internal testing, which makes the decision one of the clearest instances that AI's autonomous misbehavior could halt the industry's lightning-fast progression of artificial intelligence development.
The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI had planned to launch the model, known as GPT-6.1 Astra, in the coming days or weeks, aiming for an October debut. According to the report, "the model was more capable than the company’s previous models in completing challenging tasks from end-to-end without human assistance, as well as writing."
 
Specifically, GPT-6.1 Astra showed higher levels of deception, according to an internal interview with OpenAI's head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.
It wasn’t always honest about telling users of the actions it did or didn’t take, he said.
In addition, the GPT-6.1 Astra model engaged in what is called "scope authorization," meaning that it "would push ahead on a task without asking the user for permission and would at times reach for external tools and services even if it might be unsafe."
"For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a tradeoff," said Jain. "You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction."
OpenAI’s move followed weeks of reports that some of its AI models went rogue during their testing, hacking into websites without the company’s knowledge or exhibiting other behavior that the lab said was "concerning," such as hiding mistakes and making up data as well as hacking into several outside companies' websites, temporarily disrupting, and even shutting down, some of their operations.
Last week, OpenAI announced that it was pausing training for its most advanced models and said that it would instead focus on the safety of future models. The company added that it has embarked on an extensive review of actions taken by its new models during testing and that it was possible it would discover more incidents.
OpenAI’s Chief Executive Sam Altman said Friday in a social media post that the company had "not been as fast as we would have liked" in disclosing AI incidents.
"We are prioritizing as best as we can based on severity," he said.
The cancellation announcement of the newest artificial intelligence model comes one day ahead of OpenAI’s annual developer conference in San Francisco, where new models and services are usually launched and offered to software developers at reduced prices, a segment in which the ChatGPT maker competes with rival AI company Anthropic to win over clients.
But in recent weeks, OpenAI and Anthropic have both called on industry partners "to slow down the development of cutting-edge AI models and invest in safety standards, noting they will temper the pace of their own internal AI progress."

Storms are intensifying as temperatures rise. Which countries are most at risk?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:02:23 UTC
14:02:23 KST

From colour-blindness to women’s clothing, early warning systems must ensure no one is left behind.
“Climate change is making storms more intense, dangerous, shifting their paths, and putting more and more people within their reach,” according to the recent WorldRiskReport.
Storms cause the greatest economic damage of any extreme natural event, the report finds, with poorer economies hit disproportionately harder than wealthy industrialised nations. They also rank third in terms of fatalities, after earthquakes and extreme hot or cold temperatures.
Is climate change making storms worse?
The annual report, by German NGO alliance Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV) at Ruhr University Bochum, focused this year on storms as one of the most common and destructive natural hazards worldwide.
“We are seeing a rise in the proportion of the most powerful storms,” says Dr Friederike Otto, climate scientist and co-founder of World Weather Attribution (WWA), who is interviewed in the report.
She says human-induced climate change, resulting from the burning of fossil fuels, is to blame, with greenhouse gases warming the atmosphere and the oceans.
“When a tropical cyclone develops under these warmer conditions, it has access to more energy, increasing the intensity of its wind speeds and associated rainfall,” says Dr Otto.
Fuelled by warm ocean water, tropical cyclones are spreading to previously storm-free regions, shifting towards the poles – as seen when Hurricane Ophelia struck the Iberian Peninsula and Ireland in 2017.
Warmer ocean temperatures are also making rapid intensification of storms more common, making it more difficult to implement warnings, the report says.
Rising temperatures are not only making storms more destructive, they are also adding new dangers such as increased risk of flooding, erosion and landslides in coastal areas due to sea level rise.
Convective storm systems, meanwhile, which range from thunderstorms to long-lived supercells, are seeing increased rainfall due to climate change, since warmer air holds more moisture.
Which countries are most at risk from storms?
Just 10 countries bear the majority of global storm exposure: the Philippines, Mexico, Madagascar, Mauritius, Japan, China, Micronesia, the US, South Korea and Australia, according to the report’s Storm Risk Index, which assessed 193 countries.
Only two European countries fall within the top 100 most at-risk in terms of physical exposure and societal vulnerability: Portugal (69th place) and Ukraine (96th).
While tropical cyclones are rare in Europe, extratropical cyclones are more common. These develop over the sea but are much weaker. However, they still impact weather on land: “Especially in Northern Europe we see an increase in the number of these storms, which means that winters have become much wetter,” says Dr Otto.
Storm risk is unevenly distributed with coastal cities and islands most vulnerable. “Cities like New York and Boston, or Beijing and Tokyo will see tropical cyclones in the future,” says Dr Otto.
The wider World Risk Index, which measures overall disaster risk from all natural hazards, features 13 European countries in the top 100, with Türkiye the only one in the top 50, in 38th place.
Also in the top 100 are Italy (51st), Greece (56th), Spain (58th), France (78th), Albania (81st), Poland (82nd), Portugal (86th), the UK (89th), Croatia (92nd), Belgium (94th), the Netherlands (96th) and Germany (99th).
The importance – and limitations of – early warning systems
“The future significance [of storms] lies not only in their physical intensity, but also in how well societies adapt, through resilient infrastructure, improved forecasting, early warning systems, and climate mitigation efforts,” says Dr Otto.
To be effective, warnings must be worded clearly, reach marginalised groups, and factor in households that need active assistance to evacuate.
“Storm warning systems must reduce vulnerabilities, not just track hazards,” reads the report, urging the use of All-Vulnerability Warning Systems (AVWS), which “consider all hazards, all time scales, and all people”. These could factor in everything from reduced mobility due to societal clothing mandates for women, to the risk of map misreading due to colour blindness.
It also points out that warning systems typically focus on wind – missing the greatest dangers to life: flooding and storm surges. As storms often gain sudden strength just off the coast, these can be hard to predict. Using multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWS), which take into account air temperature, precipitation type, precipitation amount, wind speed, wind direction, iciness, lightning and tornadoes, can help.
How else can countries prepare for more intense storms?
While state-run, nationwide protections are essential in reducing the devastation of storms, community-based disaster preparedness helps to fill the gaps – for example when people do not have access to a radio or mobile phone.
Insurance can also play a crucial role in the aftermath of a storm. While in the Global North it now covers about half of all storm damage, it is often unavailable or unaffordable for many in the Global South. This tends to slow reconstruction efforts, and can lead to a “spiral of poverty” that lasts generations, the report warns.
In these cases, informal resource sharing is often forced to fill the gaps, but resources tend to become overwhelmed in a crisis.
Besides improvements to warning systems and disaster relief, reducing emissions would in turn slow the intensification of storms with climate change.
“The impacts today are already reaching the limits of what societies can adapt to, as we’ve seen with Hurricane Melissa in 2025,” says Dr Otto. “Thus limiting warming to 1.5°C is crucial for societies to get a chance at adaptation.”

Mali Army, Russia’s Wagner Committed War Crimes Against Civilians, Amnesty Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Malian forces and Russia’s Wagner mercenaries committed war crimes including killings and torture of civilians during joint operations, Amnesty International said in a new report.
The rights group documented the deaths of at least 34 civilians across seven locations in the central Ségou and Mopti regions and northern Timbuktu region between June 2023 and December 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Amnesty, none of those killed was directly participating in hostilities at the time of their deaths.
Some civilians were deliberately shot while trying to flee or after being detained. Others had their throats cut or were burned alive or after death, the report found.
The findings add to years of reports documenting abuses by Mali’s armed forces and their Russian partners as Bamako has increasingly relied on Moscow for military support against jihadist groups operating across the Sahel.
Mali’s military rulers, who seized power in coups in 2020 and 2021, turned toward Russia and brought in Wagner personnel from late 2021.
Around 1,000 Wagner fighters were deployed in Mali before the group was replaced in June 2025 by Africa Corps, which operates under Russia’s Defense Ministry, according to Amnesty.
Civilians Killed During Joint Patrols
Among the cases documented by Amnesty was a Feb. 12, 2025 operation in Tin Adanda, a small settlement in the Timbuktu region.
Four people were killed during a joint Malian military-Wagner patrol, according to the report.
Putin Signs Decree Increasing Russian Army: Over 2.4 Million, Including 1.5 Million Active-Duty Personnel
One survivor interviewed by Amnesty described losing two sons and a cousin after they were detained and killed.
The organization said the cases pointed to a broader pattern in which civilians were treated as suspected collaborators with armed groups despite no evidence they were participating in fighting.
The vast majority of victims belonged to Fulani, Arab and Tuareg pastoral communities.
Some were suspected of links to armed groups solely because of their ethnic background and because they lived in areas where insurgents were active, Amnesty found.
Drone Strikes Kill at Least 23
The report also documented two Malian military drone strikes in the Timbuktu region that killed at least 23 people, including at least five children.
One strike hit a market in Ejdeir in March 2025. Another struck a family home in Tangata in November.
Amnesty said it found no evidence that members of armed groups or military objectives were present at either location.
“If confirmed, these operations would constitute a direct attack against civilians and civilian objects and should be investigated as war crimes,” Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s regional director for West and Central Africa, warned.
Witnesses told Amnesty that 16 civilians were killed and seven injured in the Ejdeir market strike.
The Malian military later announced it had attacked what it described as a gathering of “terrorists” at a transit camp northwest of Léré and killed 11 fighters.
Amnesty’s analysis found that the location described by the military corresponded to the market that was hit.
Torture at Military Bases
Amnesty also gathered testimony from 15 men who described being tortured or otherwise mistreated during joint Malian-Wagner patrols or while held at the Léré and Nampala military bases.
Witnesses corroborated torture involving at least 30 people, while five detainees were reported to have died at the bases from torture or poor detention conditions.
Survivors described being suspended by their arms from metal bars, subjected to simulated drowning, beaten with iron rods and sticks, and shocked with electricity.
Amnesty concluded that Wagner personnel carried out most of the torture described in the testimonies, often in the presence of Malian soldiers.
In some cases, Malian troops allegedly acted as interpreters, stood by during the abuse or threatened detainees themselves.
Those held at the bases were not brought before courts and had no access to lawyers or relatives during detention periods ranging from one day to four months, the report found.
Amnesty Demands Accountability
Amnesty called on Malian authorities to investigate the abuses and clarify the command structure governing foreign military personnel operating in the country.
“Our findings show the harrowing reality facing civilians caught in the conflict, who are paying the highest price while impunity continues to prevail,” Sivieude warned.
“The Malian authorities cannot ignore these grave allegations and fail to launch effective and impartial investigations into the alleged crimes.”
The organization also urged Bamako to publish its agreement with Africa Corps and establish an independent accountability mechanism capable of monitoring abuses by Malian forces and their foreign partners.
Amnesty said it submitted its findings to Malian authorities on Aug. 3 but had received no response by the time the report was published.
Wagner Gone, Russian Presence Remains
Although Wagner formally withdrew from Mali in June 2025, Russia’s military presence continued.
Africa Corps replaced the group and remains active under Russian Defense Ministry control, according to Amnesty.
Reports of abuses have continued under the new structure.

As AI models go rogue, do you still trust OpenAI and Anthropic to stop them? I don’t and neither should you | Chris Stokel-Walker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:54 UTC
14:00:54 KST

Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. Fool me more than 16,000 times – as OpenAI agents did to a UN public data hub while repeatedly trying to find its way around the UN’s cyber-blocks – and perhaps it’s time to admit the system we have for keeping AI agents under control isn’t working particularly well.
The news about AI systems cropping up in places they shouldn’t sounds alarming. Though the description of these as “hacks” is perhaps overstating things, AI has exploited issues in IT systems that humans simply haven’t got around to finding. It’s also important to note that we shouldn’t be worried that the machines have suddenly become sentient and decided to rebel against humanity. There is not enough evidence to suggest that’s what is happening. The systems are simply following instructions and trying to complete the tasks they have been given, even if they’re sometimes finding unintended ways around obstacles to do so.
But we ought to be very concerned about the fact the AI companies we’re meant to trust to keep their models in check seem unable to do so. Worse than that, they don’t seem to know what their products are even doing.
The scale of the problem is staggering. In June, an OpenAI research agent given the job of looking up public medicine spending data in Australia was repeatedly blocked by a Medicare statistics portal. OpenAI’s model found a way around the blocks, gaining unauthorised access and secreting away the documents. It took until August for OpenAI to discover what had happened. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said the company had taken “way too long” to tell his government, and it’s very hard to disagree with him.
OpenAI has since published a reporting framework for model “misalignment”, along with six more examples of its AI committing troubling behaviour from the previous six months. The firm acknowledged that its previous disclosures were “ad hoc and less frequent than ideal”, and said evidence about AI safety needs to be checked by people outside the companies building the models.
This isn’t just an OpenAI problem, which makes it all the more worrying. Anthropic found three incidents in which its Claude models got unauthorised access to real third-party systems after reviewing about 141,000 model transcripts. It only found a fourth, dating back to January, after collating a dossier for an independent investigation. Google confirmed that Gemini had accessed systems belonging to three real companies during testing. Another OpenAI agent used DNS – the system that acts as the internet’s address book, turning web addresses into machine readable forms – to reach an outside chatbot despite internet restrictions. Another published a researcher’s GitHub token – an access password – while trying to cheat on a mathematical proof, despite twice being told to stop. And research agents posted 53 user images to external hosting sites.
Other agents accessed census data using credentials found online, copied the US Securities and Exchange Commission information elsewhere and apparently tried unsuccessfully to break into a US Department of Education website. OpenAI says it has notified dozens of third parties affected by its agents, and that its review of past activity is still ongoing.
These haphazard, post-hoc discoveries of major incursions into companies and organisations’ IT systems are not the right way to police a technology as powerful as AI. We learned a while back not to leave air crash investigations solely to Boeing or Airbus. Now we need to be less naive about AI.
Last week, at the UN general assembly, the AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury launched the Independent AI Evaluation Foundation (IAEF) with $10m in philanthropic backing. Its immediate focus is education, but the important idea is to turn independent AI evaluation into an actual profession: people and organisations with the skills, infrastructure and standards to test these systems without having a financial stake in whether they pass. Because right now, a company can report an incident, investigate it, announce whatever mitigations it’s made and move on.
The IAEF is a welcome intervention but it can’t fix the problem on its own. It can’t compel OpenAI or Anthropic to hand over logs, preserve evidence or tell a government that one of its systems has crossed a line. And its $10m is chump change beside companies such as Anthropic, which is lining up a proposed public listing that has been discussed at a valuation of about $2tn. But it is infrastructure we should be building on, and which politicians should press the case for.
Governments need to agree to common rules that compel companies to disclose serious AI incidents and near misses, and to do so quickly. They need to make them open up their books to external evaluators rather than relying on the goodwill or whims of the companies themselves. And the findings should be shared so we can learn from every incident. The labs should help design those rules but they shouldn’t have the final say until they have earned our trust.
And money complicates things: while OpenAI has postponed its IPO until at least 2027 amid the safety concerns, it seems that Anthropic’s flotation is still going full steam ahead. There are billions – potentially trillions – of dollars riding on how these companies and their products are perceived. We created independent auditors and accident investigators in other industries because we understood that good intentions don’t remove real conflicts of interest.
The labs can and should keep building better fences. But when a model manages to gets over one, they shouldn’t be the only ones allowed to decide what happens next. Because so far they’ve shown themselves to be uniquely unqualified to do so.
- 
  Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:54 UTC
14:00:54 KST

In the 1990s, conservationists in Cambodia feared the Siamese crocodile had disappeared for good. Fishing and hunting had devastated the species throughout the 20th century, leaving populations across its native south-east Asia on the brink of extinction.
But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the remote Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them. Passing this knowledge to researchers surveying the area in 2000 led to an official recording of the species – and bolstered the mission to revive the population.
“[The Chorng] share a spiritual relation between nature, sacred species and the forest,” says Sony Oum, the country director for Conservation International in Cambodia. “They believed that [the crocodiles] were there, and they helped the scientists and researchers to spot the sites.”
Now, more than a quarter of a century on from the initial sighting, a 315-hectare (778-acre) wetland in Pursat province at the northern end of the Cardamom mountains has been formally declared a genetic conservation area to protect the habitat of one of the world’s last wild populations of Siamese crocodiles.
The area, formally designated by Cambodia’s environment ministry on 22 July, will be home to at least 40 Siamese crocodiles that are thought to live there, making it a crucial site for a species still classed as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list.
Habitat destruction, poaching and cross-breeding with crocodiles kept on farms have left few genetically intact wild populations of Siamese crocodiles. With small, isolated groups in the wild vulnerable to inbreeding, conservationists say preserving genetic diversity can improve the animals’ ability to reproduce and withstand disease.
Oum describes the site as a “genetic bank” for the species – a population that, if it remains healthy and expands, could one day help support crocodile recovery in Malaysia, Myanmar and Indonesia, where the reptile is thought to have become extinct.
The new protection area is the latest stage in a conservation effort that has undertaken an extraordinary task.
In 2011, the conservation charity Fauna & Flora International set up a Siamese crocodile breeding facility to boost numbers of genetically pure Siamese crocodiles for release into protected rivers.
The charity has released 246 Siamese crocodiles into the wild since then, with 100 of those released since 2024.
“Natural recovery of this species takes a long time,” says Vanny Lou, who manages the Siamese crocodile programme in Cambodia for Fauna & Flora. “This is one of our approaches to boost the species’ recovery from the brink of extinction.”
“We have 648 individuals [at the breeding centre], including the parents,” he says. “Seventy-one of those are breeding parents – 54 female and 17 male.” Lou says it takes three to four years to get a baby crocodile to the appropriate age and size to release back into the wetlands.
Before release, some crocodiles are fitted with acoustic tags, allowing conservationists to track where they move and target protection efforts. Local community wardens then help monitor the animals and their habitats.
The wardens help the conservation organisations by identifying potential nesting sites, monitoring rivers, patrolling for illegal fishing and poaching, and reporting threats to government officials. And who better than the people who put the species back on the map – the Chorng.
Oum says the fact that Chorng communities have lived alongside the crocodiles for generations and regard them as sacred guardians of the rivers and forests makes them the perfect people to assist the conservation.
“The Indigenous people have a strong belief in the connection to nature,” says Oum. “They do some cropping and farming alongside the river, and when the Siamese crocodiles come to destroy the crops, [the Chorng] smile happily and feel blown away. They’ve been coexistent for a long time.”
In 2024, five wild Siamese crocodile nests containing 106 eggs were found in the Cardamom mountains. Community wardens monitored them and saw 60 hatchlings emerge – the species’ largest recorded breeding event in the wild this century.
“Without active involvement from the community as the frontline, our programme would not be successful,” says Lou.
Sim Khmao, a Chorng community warden, says they are happy to do it. “They are not afraid of the crocodiles,” he says. “They understand them – because they have been here since our ancestors’ period.”

‘We have time to make our case’: Labour insiders are confident Burnham can sell his social care reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:54 UTC
14:00:54 KST

It is a brave party leader who is prepared to go into an election promising a multibillion-pound new public service – likely to be funded by tax rises or holding back increases in the state pension.
But Andy Burnham’s colleagues are excited about the confident promise of new social care system that seven previous prime ministers have failed to deliver.
“I’m not worried about it because we have time to make the case,” said one cabinet minister, who was asked about the difficulty of getting voters on board.
David Cameron’s team is credited with inventing the political metaphor of “pitch-rolling” – borrowing from cricket to describe how leaders need to start preparing bumpy ground in advance if they want their policy to flourish.
This appeared to be Burnham’s strategy for getting the public used to the idea of paying more into a system that will give them protection in old age when he floated his ambition in a Sunday morning interview.
It is not clear yet how the prime minister intends to fund a service that could cost up to £18bn a year, according to some estimates. Reform UK has already claimed that a “death tax” could be brought in to pay for it. Economists have raised the idea that the pension triple lock could be scrapped to help fund the costs.
Whatever the mechanism, Labour strategists are hoping that over the course of the coming years, all the arguments will have been had, the sting of the opposition’s attacks will have worn off and the scheme as a whole will be baked into views of what the party is offering at the next election.
That way they would seek to avoid the failure of Theresa May’s abrupt attempt to overhaul social care during the 2017 election when she surprised voters – and her own party – with the idea of making people pay for their own care if they had more than £100,000 in assets. The plan did not survive for long when it became clear that more older people might have to sell their own homes to fund personal care.
An attempt by Gordon Brown and Burnham himself failed in 2010, when a discussion paper raised the idea of a levy on the estates after death as well as a contributory system. However, the government did not reach a consensus on how it should be funded, and then lost the subsequent election.
If he learns the lesson of those previous attempts, Burnham has almost three years to make his case and try to win over the doubters who think the problem is too difficult to resolve.
And every year, with an ageing population and the social care system under strain, more and more people have realised system is a lottery, where many elderly people and their families largely have to fund their own care.
Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said it was a “difficult move politically, because it has immediately sparked speculation as to how it would be funded”, but it “could dramatically change lives for the millions of people who have someone in their life who needs care”.
Whether the plan will end up being funded by older people, those of working age, or both, there are obvious perils in going into the next election signalling that people will have to pay more when household budgets are under severe pressure.
Governments have a particular phobia of targeting pension benefits because of the tendency of older people to vote with their pockets. The memory of attempts by Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves to cut the winter fuel allowance is burned into the minds of Labour MPs, who had to deal with an angry backlash from a surprised public.
And no party has dared touch the triple lock – which promises the state pension will rise by the higher of inflation, earnings or 2.5% – since it was created by the Conservatives in 2010.
However, that is why some policy brains think there is a golden opportunity to create a trade-off aimed directly at older people, offering a better care system in return for a weakening of the guarantee.
The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell has told LBC: “You put social care and you amend the triple lock at the same time. You do that as a package, which leaves older people much better off and is revenue neutral.”
Alex Clegg, a senior economist at the Resolution Foundation thinktank, said the savings from the triple lock might not be billions in the course of a parliament but more could be clawed back in the long term. He also said savings from the triple lock might be an “easier sell to pensioners” if changes came in tandem with better social care.
Burnham is expected to set out some more details of his vision for a social care system in his conference speech on Tuesday. He may not yet have all the answers about how it will be paid for, with a review of the system by Louise Casey still to come.
But Labour MPs believe he is the right person to start laying the foundations for change. One senior Labour figure said: “Unlike Keir, he can make an argument, and everyone hopes he can take the country with us.”

Thomasina Miers’ recipes for turmeric chicken and cardamom apple tart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:54 UTC
14:00:54 KST

Despite the back-to-school, back-to-work vibes of September, I also think it’s a time of celebration. There’s the feeling of new things, with apples, corn, walnuts, squash and mushrooms appearing at the markets, and my garden has finally emerged from its drought-induced slumber, as if coming out of a trance – it is greener, more alive, reawakening. There’s still the odd bit of warm weather in which to play, too, so light up the grill, get creative in the kitchen and dance like it’s June again.
Grilled turmeric chicken with garlic, kefir and chilli
Rich Indian spices, sweet onion, garlic and lemon make this marinade stand out when it hits the grill. Serve with a garlicky raita on the side.
Prep 10 min
 Marinate 30 min+
 Cook 30 min
 Serves 4-6
1kg chicken thighs (about 6), preferably boneless and skin-on 
2 tsp sea salt
  1 medium onion, peeled and roughly chopped
  2 fat garlic cloves, peeled 
  2 red chillies
  1 tsp ground turmeric
  2 heaped tsp garam masala
  1 lemon
  300g kefir
  ½ tsp chilli powder (optional) – kashmiri for a mild flavour, ancho for a rounded taste and a little heat, cayenne if you like things hot
1 handful fresh coriander, leaves picked
For the raita
½ cucumber
  1 fat garlic clove, peeled and finely grated
Salt and pepper
Season the chicken thighs generously with salt. Put the onions, garlic, chillies and spices in a food processor, squeeze in the juice of half a lemon and blitz to a paste, scraping down the sides of the bowl a few times as you go. Add a teaspoon of salt and 100g kefir, and blitz again to make a beautiful, ochre-coloured paste. Taste it – I like to add some chilli powder. Slather the marinade all over the chicken thighs and leave for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or for a few hours/overnight in the fridge.
Shortly before you’re ready to eat, coarsely grate the cucumber skin and all into a sieve, suspend it over a bowl, and push down to squeeze out any water (the juice is a delicious drink; try it with a little salt and pepper). Mix the squeezed cucumber with the remaining kefir and grated garlic, then season generously.
Heat a griddle pan (or barbecue) and chargrill the chicken for six minutes on each side, until the meat is cooked through and the skin is deliciously crisp and golden. Serve scattered with fresh coriander, the remaining half-lemon cut into wedges and the raita.
Sugar-burnt cardamom and apple puff tart
A crisp, caramelised, scented tart that takes very little time to prepare, but still feels like a proper pudding.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 1 hr
 Serves 6-8
10 green cardamom pods
  100g sugar 
  Salt
  5 medium sharp, crisp apples (about 450g)
Juice of ½ lemon
  40g unsalted butter
1 320g sheet shop-bought puff pastry (preferably all-butter)
Plain flour, for dusting
1 small egg
  40g ground almonds
Start by making a cardamom sugar. Put the pods in a mortar and bash them a few times with a pestle. Slip off and discard the loosened green sleeves, then bash the remaining black seeds with vigour. Add the sugar and a generous pinch of salt, and bash again to release the cardamom oils and aromatics into the sugar.
Quarter and core the apples, then slice into 2-3mm-thick half-moons. As you slice them, toss in a bowl with the lemon juice so they don’t discolour. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.
Melt the butter in a small pan (or in the microwave). Lay out the pastry on a board. Lightly flour a rolling pin, then roll the pastry so it’s a little larger and a little thinner, but still in a similar rectangular shape. Line a baking tray with baking paper, lay the pastry on top and use a small, sharp knife carefully to mark a 2cm border all around the edge; take care not to cut through the pastry completely. Prick the inside of the border all over with a fork (this will stop it rising in the oven). Whisk the egg with a teaspoon of water, then brush this all over the pastry.
Bake for five minutes, then remove and scatter the ground almonds all over the centre of the pastry. Arrange the apple slices in an overlapping pattern on top, then drizzle or brush with the melted butter and sprinkle the lot with the cardamom sugar.
Bake for another 20 minutes, then turn down the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and bake for a final 10 minutes, until the apples are browned and caramelised. Leave to cool a little on a rack, then slice and serve with vanilla ice-cream, thick cream, custard or all three.

UK exercise lead explains why warships are sunk off Hebrides
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:47 BST
14:00:47 KST

The American frigate destroyed off the Hebrides this month was fitted with instruments by both navies before it was hit, so that every weapon that struck it could be measured, the British officer who ran the exercise has said.
Lieutenant Commander Paul Atkins, UK lead project officer for Atlantic Thunder, said the sinking was a battle damage assessment as much as a demonstration.
“We have US scientists that have placed loads of sensors all over the ship, including the UK have placed some sensors over there,” he said. “And as each of the weapons hit, we conduct the battle damage assessment and download all the footage and download all the information of the sensors so that it can be looked at after the exercise and worked out exactly what the impact was.”
The two countries then go their own way with the results. Each takes away what it can from the shared sensor picture and assesses its own weapons on its own, the British working through what their munitions did to the hull while the Americans do the same with theirs. What the exercise is for, Atkins said, is “understanding how we can work together in future as a joint force when we need to”.
The range was not picked for its convenience, of course, and Atlantic Thunder has always been held there, roughly 150 nautical miles offshore to clear enough airspace for the weapons being fired. The conditions are part of the attraction.
“Up here, we’ve got very strong winds and weather up here, so we can test to the full ability compared to going down off ranges that are like further south, where you don’t get as much wind,” Atkins said. “We can get rain one day, wind the next, or we could get it all at once.”
That variability, along with the range of water depths available in the Atlantic, is what makes it useful for trialling new munitions. Sinking exercises have become uncommon in British waters, which is the reason the two navies went back to running them.
“Atlantic Thunder sinkexes don’t actually happen very often in the UK, so that’s why we’ve started to do this again, to ensure that when we are working with the US we have got the capabilities to be able to do that should we need to,” Atkins said.
The exercise now runs on a two-year cycle, and the work does not stop between iterations.
“It’s literally as soon as one Atlantic Thunder finishes, the planning already starts for the next one two years later,” he said, describing initial conferences to settle which units take part and what scenarios they will run, followed by environmental assessments for the range. Getting it signed off, he said, is a very long process.
This year’s exercise was a solely British and American affair, drawing on an American destroyer, Royal Air Force Typhoons, United States Air Force F-15 Eagles and Royal Navy frigates. Command and control was run from the Hebrides range control building, with a commodore embarked in the destroyer taking charge of the task force at sea, and each unit brought its own weapons to test.
Atkins declined to say which munitions were used. The point of putting each one against the same hull, he said, was to test and analyse them as each unit came in, and to establish that the weapons do what they are supposed to do.

EPP backs suspension of asylum rights in response to ‘hybrid attacks’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:13 UTC
14:00:13 KST

The European People’s Party wants to allow migrants to be returned without their asylum claims being individually assessed in cases of “hybrid attacks” by third countries targeting an EU border, a controversial proposal likely to trigger political opposition.
The European People’s Party (EPP) will call for the suspension of the right to apply for asylum in the EU in cases of “hybrid attacks”, where third countries facilitate large-scale migration with the aim of destabilising a European border.
The controversial measure would allow migrant people to be sent back without an individual assessment of their circumstances, effectively resulting in “collective pushbacks” that are prohibited under current EU law.
The measure could form part of the new “European Emergency Response Framework”, announced by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her State of the Union speech, to tackle irregular arrivals.
Some EU countries have already temporarily suspended the right to seek asylum and support the measure. However, the proposal has drawn criticism from left-wing politicians and migration experts.
The EPP's call is part of a resolution due to be adopted on Tuesday at the EPP’s political assembly in Toulouse, according to several party sources.
“There are some delegations against it, but the majority of the party is on board,” a senior EPP member told Euronews.
In the text seen by Euronews, the EPP calls on member states to “adopt an additional protocol on asylum and migration authorising the refusal of entry or return without an individual asylum procedure for illegal migrants used in hybrid attacks.”
The text cites the situation in Ceuta, where around 80,000 migrants irregularly entered at the end of July, with several thousand still on the streets of the Spanish exclave. The episode was described as a “hybrid attack and instrumentalisation of migrants” in a recent European Parliament resolution.
“Similar cases require a response that goes beyond the current instruments designed to address migratory flows,” the resolution says.
The EPP is the EU’s largest political family, and its proposals often shape legislation adopted by the European Commission and endorsed by the European Parliament.
In the current legislature, the party has taken a tougher stance on migration, backing legislation to deport asylum seekers and irregular migrants to third countries with no connection to them.
Last June, the EPP adopted another resolution urging the European Commission to limit the right to asylum “in cases of instrumentalisation” and when irregular migrants attempt to enter the EU from a third country deemed “safe”.
