Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:05 UTC
14:00:05 KST

South Korea and Ukraine are locked in an escalating diplomatic dispute over who agreed what regarding the circumstances of two prisoners of war captured fighting for Russia.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told the UN general assembly last week that his country had “sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea”.
Seoul had long said it would take the men. But rather than celebrate, on Monday South Korea summoned Ukraine’s most senior diplomat in Seoul and demanded an apology.
Here’s a brief guide to what has happened, and why.
Who are the PoWs and what has happened to them?
Ukrainian forces captured the two men in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were among thousands of troops Pyongyang sent to fight for Moscow. Both men later said they wanted to go to South Korea, which regards North Koreans as its own citizens.
In July, Zelenskyy and South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, agreed to resolve the issue while respecting the soldiers’ “free will”. The captured pair reportedly arrived in South Korea via a third country earlier this month.
North Koreans arriving in the South as defectors are usually questioned by the National Intelligence Service before being sent to a state resettlement centre, although sensitive cases can reportedly bypass the centre.
Why is Seoul so angry?
Seoul says Kyiv requested secrecy about the transfer, fearing domestic criticism for passing up the opportunity to exchange them for “a large number” of Ukrainian prisoners. South Korea says it agreed, citing the safety of the two men and their families as well as diplomatic and security considerations.
After Zelenskyy revealed the transfer in his UN speech, Lee said on X that Ukraine had broken a “non-disclosure agreement” and that this was regrettable. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn responded on Facebook that there had been no such agreement, prompting accusations from Lee’s critics that the president, whose approval rating has hit a low of 37.9%, had lied.
Lee’s office called Kyiv’s statement “false” and said its conduct “seriously damages trust” between the two governments. On Monday, the foreign ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires, demanding an apology at governmental level.
Was there actually an agreement?
South Korea’s foreign ministry told Ukraine’s envoy there had been a “clear agreement”. Asked by the Guardian the same day whether anything had been put in writing, the ministry said only that the two sides “had decided to handle it confidentially”. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not respond to a request for comment.
Has North Korea said anything?
No. South Korea’s unification ministry said it had “not identified any related developments so far” and would continue monitoring.
North Korea has glorified soldiers who killed themselves rather than be captured. The transfer of two who survived and chose the South is “a fatal matter” for Pyongyang, says Cho Han-bum of the Korea Institute for National Unification. Having built a “heroic narrative” around its troops, the regime is unlikely to disclose the transfer domestically, he says.
How big a diplomatic incident is this?
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, South Korea condemned Moscow’s actions, joined western sanctions and, in July, pledged a $100m support package. But it has kept the war at arm’s length, refusing to send weapons directly to Kyiv, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Before the war, Russia was one of South Korea’s biggest trading partners. Lee’s government is also keen to improve relations with Pyongyang.
The row has turned that cautious support for Kyiv into open criticism, largely from Lee’s own camp. Kim Byung-joo, a Democratic party lawmaker, said there was “no reason or need” to support Ukraine and has urged the government to review its aid “immediately”.

I worry about Russian miscalculation in Baltics – interview with Britain’s top general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Britain’s top navy general Gwyn Jenkins visited Lithuania and the Baltic states last week as the UK continues to build the 10-nation Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) as a coalition of the willing that would speed up decision-making in case of a Russian attack.
“I'm not being alarmist. Nobody is catastrophising what could happen in the Baltics”, he said, adding that Russia will continue “to probe for weaknesses” unless NATO countries show strength.
In an exclusive interview with LRT.lt, General Jenkins spoke about the importance of the Klaipėda seaport, the British-led JEF as a coalition of the willing, and the growing risk of Russia “doing something stupid” in the Baltics.
You mentioned the word alarmism. I'm seeing a lot of that now, especially in international media. From your perspective, are there any signs we're seeing that would require more vigilance than before?
I'm a military strategist by profession. Our job is to be prepared, and that means we take all our threats, all the threats that we see in front of us, very seriously, but that isn't an excuse for making the Russians out, out to be more than they are.
[...] Russia is bleeding in Ukraine. It has made a massive strategic mistake in picking an egregious illegal war with a sovereign state on European soil that we are all supporting.
While the war goes on, I don't believe Russia has the capacity to take the more alarmist courses of action that some people talk about. It recognises that we are a phenomenal force if it was stupid enough to pick an Article 5-type scenario.
But the concerns are of something happening below that threshold?
If I have a concern about Russia, it is that I don't think they're very professional. I think their ability to miscalculate is huge. When I see it in the Baltic, and I see it in the North Sea, and I see it around the British Isles and elsewhere, unprofessional behaviour has the potential to escalate certain scenarios.
Our management of that and our ability to contain something– if they do something silly, stupid, illegal, egregious – that is where the concerns lie. And that's not the same as a pre-planned massive invasion of Europe.
This threat is very serious. I am worried and concerned about Russian behaviour and what they might do either during the war or once the war in Ukraine is finished [and] what happens to the Russian state after that point.
[...] If I wind back 15 years, I was in the military staff college education, right round about the G8 in Northern Ireland when Vladimir Putin was there. I actually met him because I was the military assistant to the prime minister.
At the time, in all of our war games and exercises at that point, the precursor to war was what we’re living through at the moment [in Europe]. If you'd asked the 15-years-ago me what the condition-setting would look like for confrontation with NATO, we're in all of that. That is not to predict a war, but it is to say that we can't be complacent.
What do you remember of Putin?
He's very short in a way that his images don't necessarily portray. He’s very intense, not very engaging as an individual with anyone. But I didn't spend a lot of time with him.
The Suwalki Gap question receives a lot of attention. What can you comment from the naval, or from the British, perspective?
Land resupply is obviously crucial to both your nation and all the Baltic states and all our forward land forces – the UK forward land forces in Estonia, the Germans here. If military strategy and history teach me anything, it's don't depend on just one line.
The sea lines of communication and our ability to resupply across the Baltic Sea is really important. I think you have some of the best port facilities in the Baltic states; they are really important infrastructure that we should make sure that we can protect.
Is that what you talked about during your meetings here?
Yeah, I have., because we have learnt a lot from Ukraine in terms of their ability to protect their port infrastructure and the challenges they've had. I think we've seen a lot from the conflict in the Gulf recently in terms of how you protect port infrastructure from a range of possible attack options.
I'm really keen that we continue to talk about how that can be done here, how we support each other in that, because it's important to all of us. It's been a key part of my, some of my discussions here.
For people who don’t know about the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which also includes Lithuania, is this a fail-safe for below-Article 5 crises?
So the most important thing I think about JEF is it is a complement to NATO. We are working hand in glove through the JEF with the NATO planners on how the JEF can support NATO plans. The advantage of the JEF is there's 10 of us, and we don't need consensus to act.
Is it a coalition of the willing, essentially?
Basically. As the scenario evolves, the flexibility of the JEF means any of us can contribute [in a way] that is really supportive of the NATO plans.
When you look at the way the NATO plans are set up now, as NATO is developing consensus and trying to understand what has happened and is deciding what its response is, we have the ability as JEF nations to act quite quickly in support of each other.
I know that politically you're quite keen to stress that JEF is not competing with NATO. But I think for many people in the Baltics, saying that we have some form of a regional alliance where nations can act quickly in case there's a danger would be a reassurance factor.
It should be reassuring, because JEF has been a really useful construct for all of us. It will span the Baltic to the high north [and] all the navies that we're talking with and all the nations are really enthusiastic about it.
So what’s Lithuania's role? Protect Klaipėda at all costs?
I think there is definitely a view of, as we work through the JEF plans, where the critical bits of infrastructure are on which we both nationally depend and on which NATO depends, and how we would focus resources in different scenarios.
When I was in Norfolk [NATO and US naval base] recently, talking with them, [...] they would really welcome that.

UK offers nuclear umbrella to Finland, other JEF countries
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:59:11 EEST
13:59:11 KST

The United Kingdom has offered a "nuclear umbrella" to members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) military partnership, which includes Finland, as part of a wider defence agreement.
The umbrella is a security guarantee by a nuclear-armed state to protect a non-nuclear ally.
The offer was confirmed during a visit by General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of the UK's Naval Staff, to Finland on Monday, where he met with MP Heikki Autto (NCP), chair of parliament's defence committee.
Yle understands that JEF member countries — which includes the Nordic nations, Baltic states, the UK and the Netherlands — will sign an agreement at a meeting in Oslo in November.
"Their naval commander has highlighted Britain's strong commitment to JEF cooperation, and through that these new opportunities have also been created," Autto told Finnish news agency STT on Monday.
The deal would mean a separate nuclear umbrella outside of Nato's extended deterrence strategy offered by the US, UK and France to all non-nuclear member states within the alliance.
"Finland is under the nuclear umbrella. It is guaranteed by our submarines, which are patrolling the Atlantic right now," Jenkins noted in an interview with tabloid Iltalehti.
Iltalehti also noted the significance of the planned JEF agreement for Finland's defence as it will not require the triggering of Nato's article 5, which states that an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all.
Finland joined a French-led nuclear deterrence initiative earlier this month, but that agreement does not include a separate nuclear umbrella.
In a press release on Tuesday morning, the Finnish defence ministry announced that Minister of Defence Antti Häkkänen (NCP) will attend a meeting with his JEF counterparts in Reykjavík on 1–2 October.
"We have a very important meeting ahead of us," Häkkänen said. "JEF is a multilateral defence cooperation framework of great importance for Finland, and its role is highlighted by the current security situation."

Lithuania will test its public warning and information system on Tuesday, with warning sirens sounding for three minutes and short emergency alerts being sent to mobile phones.
The sirens will sound from 11:52 to 11:55. LRT will then broadcast information and recommendations for residents along with regional and local radio stations.
Short emergency alerts will be sent to mobile phones between 11:52 and noon. They will be received by phones on which the emergency alert function is enabled.
According to the Fire and Rescue Department (PAGD), the system test will take place as part of Vytis Vault 2026, the country's largest exercise to test its mobilisation system.
Further reading
There are currently 1,163 warning sirens in Lithuania, which can alert about 69% of the country’s population, according to PAGD.
As part of measures under the Civil Protection Strengthening and Development Programme, Lithuania plans to install a further 275 warning sirens and connect 600 existing sirens across the country to a centralised warning siren control system.
By 2029, there should be 1,438 warning sirens operating across the country, 1,125 of which will be centrally controlled by PAGD, which should reach around 75% of the population.

You can’t flood countries with migration. This is a country that was built on immigration," Rubio said.

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu vs. Ronen Bar: What the partial Oct. 7 records show, and what remains disputed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:57:09 UTC
13:57:09 KST

The fierce confrontation that erupted Monday between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar is the latest chapter in a dispute that has continued for nearly three years: What did each man know before the Oct. 7 Hamas attack, what did the security service recommend and what decisions did the prime minister make?
Netanyahu accused Bar of “failures and crimes” and said the former Shin Bet director knew of a “real danger” on the night before the attack but failed to alert him. Bar responded unusually forcefully, saying he intends to sue Netanyahu for defamation and accusing the prime minister of selectively and manipulatively releasing documents and meeting transcripts. He called for the records to be published in full.
At the center of the dispute are 55 pages Netanyahu released in February as part of his answers to a State Comptroller investigation into the events surrounding Oct. 7. The document contains numerous quotations from security discussions, but in most cases the full transcripts were not released. Instead, Netanyahu authorized selected excerpts for publication, leaving the context of some statements contested.
One of the clearest examples comes from a security assessment Netanyahu convened on Oct. 1, 2023, just six days before the massacre. Netanyahu adviser Topaz Luk pointed Monday to a quotation attributed to Bar from that meeting: “We can be very, very generous, even enticing, on humanitarian issues ... I don’t think that, given the situation as we know it, we can initiate a round of fighting.”
The quotation appears in the transcript excerpts Netanyahu authorized for release. Netanyahu’s document also argues that during that discussion “no official proposed eliminating Hamas’ leadership in Gaza” and says it was Netanyahu who instructed the security establishment to prepare for such targeted killings. The released material also includes assessments that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar wanted a return to calm, while then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant said Israel had a “deep interest in achieving calm in the Gaza Strip.”
What was left out of the excerpts
That is where the dispute over context begins.
According to an investigation by ynet and its sister publication Yedioth Ahronoth reporters Ronen Bergman and Yuval Rubovitch, Bar also said during the same meeting: “Sinwar feels strong. We need to confront him. An operational plan for the Gaza Strip must be prepared.” Then-IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi, according to the investigation, called for preparations for a “broad campaign in the Gaza Strip.” 
Bergman reported another detail Monday concerning the quotation highlighted by Luk. He said Bar’s remark that Israel could not at that stage initiate a new round of fighting was only part of his comments. Later in the discussion, in material not included in the excerpts released by Netanyahu, Bar reportedly sought to advance an assassination plan known in the investigation as “Double Rights.”
The plan was intended to kill Sinwar and Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif simultaneously, followed by strikes on commanders beneath them. Bar reportedly said the operational infrastructure for such a move would first have to be rebuilt.
A summary of the meeting issued by the Prime Minister’s Office at the time adds another piece to the picture. Alongside instructions to expand the use of humanitarian benefits and advance a civilian arrangement with Hamas, the summary called for “advancing operational readiness for the targeted killings that were recommended.”
Regarding Hamas leaders, the summary emphasized preparations for emergencies; regarding Hamas headquarters directing terrorism in the West Bank, it referred to action during routine periods as well. The wording shows that proposed targeted killings had been discussed within the security establishment, though by itself it does not establish who proposed each action or when.
In other words, the available material allows both points to coexist: Bar did not recommend immediately launching an all-out war in Gaza and did discuss humanitarian measures, while he also regarded Sinwar as increasingly confident, called for confronting him and, according to the investigation, sought preparations for offensive action.
The full transcript of the Oct. 1 meeting has not been released, meaning the public cannot independently examine the complete sequence and context of the discussion.
Bar’s warning to Netanyahu was serious, but not a specific Oct. 7 alert
Bar’s account does not rest only on the Oct. 1 discussion.
In an affidavit submitted to the High Court of Justice in April 2025, Bar said the Shin Bet repeatedly warned political leaders during 2023 that Israel’s internal divisions were creating what its enemies viewed as a “window of opportunity” and could lead the country into a “perfect storm.” He said that as early as April he had recommended a “focused, forceful move” to halt the erosion of Israeli deterrence.
The affidavit also backed up earlier reporting by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nadav Eyal that, in July 2023, before the Knesset vote abolishing the judicial “reasonableness” standard, Bar told Netanyahu he was delivering a “warning of war.”
According to that report, Bar made clear that he had neither a specific date nor time for such a conflict, but warned that Israel’s enemies perceived the country as internally weakened. With Netanyahu’s approval, Bar later delivered a similar message to opposition leader Yair Lapid.
That warning, however, was not intelligence indicating that Hamas was preparing to attack Israel on Oct. 7, nor was it a specific warning of an impending assault from Gaza. At the time, the security establishment’s concern centered on a possible multi-front escalation, with Hezbollah and the West Bank among its major areas of concern. Netanyahu’s office has therefore maintained that the prime minister received no warning from Bar of “a war in Gaza.”
The Shin Bet failure on the night before the attack
None of those earlier warnings removes the Shin Bet’s own intelligence failure, something Bar himself has acknowledged.
According to Bar’s affidavit, IDF officials were informed at around 11 p.m. on Oct. 6 of unusual activity that had been detected. At 3:03 a.m., the Shin Bet circulated an alert describing “unusual preparations and the possibility of offensive intentions by Hamas.”
Bar wrote, however, that the warning level assigned to the information was wrong and constituted a “Shin Bet failure.” The intelligence picture was mistakenly interpreted primarily as Hamas preparing for possible Israeli action and, under the more serious scenario considered, as preparations for a limited raid.
No one, Bar wrote, assessed that Hamas was preparing to launch an attack on the scale that began that morning.
Because of the concerns, a joint Shin Bet-Yamam counterterrorism response team was sent south. Bar has said that at 5:15 a.m. he instructed officials to update the prime minister’s military secretary as well.
Netanyahu ultimately received his first call from his military secretary, Avi Gil, at 6:29 a.m., after the Hamas attack had begun. Who was responsible for the gap between Bar’s claimed 5:15 instruction and the call reaching Netanyahu at 6:29 remains one of the questions not fully answered by the publicly available material.
Bar also accepted personal responsibility shortly after the massacre. In a letter to Shin Bet employees, he wrote that despite actions taken by the agency, it “failed to provide sufficient warning that would have enabled the attack to be thwarted,” adding that as the head of the organization, responsibility rested with him.
His warnings during 2023 and reported recommendations for offensive measures against Hamas therefore do not change the fact that the Shin Bet under his leadership failed during the critical night to identify the developing events as a strategic-scale assault and provide a warning that could have led to a different level of military and national preparedness. Bar himself has acknowledged that failure.
Not simply ‘Bar wanted quiet and Netanyahu wanted to attack’
The material released so far does not fit neatly into a version in which one side consistently sought quiet while the other consistently pushed for military action.
The Shin Bet was also part of the mistaken assessment that stability in Gaza could be maintained through a combination of calm and economic relief. In an intelligence report dated Oct. 3, 2023, four days before the massacre, the agency wrote that renewing understandings with Hamas based on “security calm in exchange for relief measures” offered “potential for maintaining stability in the Gaza Strip,” possibly over an extended period.
Other documents from the days before the attack reflected assessments that Hamas was seeking to advance its goals without being drawn into a military confrontation.
At the same time, public material shows that Bar had warned months earlier about the risk of war, recommended forceful action to restore deterrence and said on Oct. 1 that Sinwar needed to be confronted. According to Bergman’s reporting, Bar also sought to advance preparations for killing both Sinwar and Deif.
Netanyahu’s own meeting summaries similarly show that his approach was not limited to targeted killings. In the days before Oct. 7, he also instructed officials to make greater use of economic and humanitarian measures and advance a civilian arrangement with Hamas.
That is why the unreleased transcripts remain central to the dispute. As long as the public sees only selected sentences approved for release by one participant, alongside affidavits and investigative reports containing additional excerpts, it is possible to establish portions of what was said but much harder to determine the full context, sequence and weight given to each recommendation.
Only an inquiry with access to the complete records, including classified material, could fully establish not merely who said what, but what decisions were ultimately made, who made them and what action followed.

Mali: Damning evidence of war crimes by state armed forces and Wagner Group personnel – new report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:54:36 UTC
13:54:36 KST

- Killings of civilians during military joint operations
- Civilians tortured to death in detention, others subjected to simulated drowning, beatings and electric shocks
- Fulani, Arabs and Tuaregs targeted
Members of Mali’s armed forces working together with personnel from the Wagner Group committed war crimes, including the murder and torture of civilians, during joint operations between 2023 and 2025, Amnesty International said in a new report.
‘No one is spared’: War crimes committed by the Malian army and foreign allied forces along the Mauritanian border documents the killings of at least 34 civilians in seven localities in Mali between June 2023 and December 2025, committed by the Malian armed forces (Forces armées maliennes – FAMa) and the Wagner Group (a Russian private military company active in Mali between late 2021 and June 2025).
The report also documents other serious violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law, such as torture, enforced disappearance, and the pillaging and destruction of civilian property.
“Our conclusions paint a harrowing picture of the lives of civilians trapped in the conflict, paying the ultimate price while impunity remains rampant. The Malian authorities cannot dismiss these serious allegations without opening impartial and effective investigations into the alleged crimes,” said Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa.
“They must protect civilians during military operations, comply with and ensure respect for international humanitarian law, urgently clarify the chain of command under which foreign personnel act in the country, and monitor their conduct through an independent, domestic accountability mechanism.”
Unlawful killings of civilians
The report provides details of seven incidents during which 34 people were unlawfully killed in the Ségou, Mopti and Timbuktu regions.
Based on information gathered by Amnesty International, none of the victims were taking direct part in hostilities at the time of their deaths. They were deliberately shot while trying to flee or after being arrested. Some had their throats slit, others were burnt alive or post-mortem. In Tin Adanda, a small hamlet in the Timbuktu region, four people were killed on 12 February 2025 during a joint patrol by FAMa and Wagner. Hana*, a survivor who has taken refuge in Mberra (Mauritania), lost two sons and a cousin who were arrested and then killed. Describing the members of the military operation, she said: “They were mostly white men, accompanied by FAMa.”
Civilians in conflict-affected regions in Mali continue to face grave risks. The authorities must protect them.
Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa
Drone strikes on civilians
The report details two drone strikes carried out by the FAMa which targeted a market in Ejdeir (16 March 2025) and a family home in Tangata (November 2025) in the Timbuktu region, killing in total at least 23 people, including at least five children.
“We found no evidence of the presence of members of armed groups or military objectives at either drone strike site. If confirmed, these strikes would amount to direct attacks on civilians and civilian objects, and should be investigated as possible war crimes,” said Marceau Sivieude.
In Ejdeir, the drone strike hit a market without warning, during the day. On 17 March 2025, the Malian military stated that it had targeted “terrorist gatherings” in a transit camp 109km northwest of Léré, killing “11 terrorists”. According to Amnesty’s analysis, the details provided by the FAMa, particularly the location correspond to the Ejdeir drone strike.
Even if fighters or military objectives were present, attacking a market at a time when it was full of civilians in a manner that caused civilian casualties would be indiscriminate. Indiscriminate attacks that kill and injure civilians are war crimes if carried out intentionally or recklessly.
According to seven people interviewed by Amnesty International, some of whom lost relatives or were themselves injured in the attack on Ejdeir, as well as civil society organizations, there were no fighters at the market; all 16 people killed and seven injured were civilians.
Malian refugees living in camps near the Mauritanian border with Mali, in the Hodh ech-Chargui region. For illustrative purposes. © Patrick Meinhardt / AFP via Getty Images.
“They tied our hands to the posts; our feet didn’t touch the ground”
Amnesty International interviewed 15 male survivors of torture and other ill-treatment from the Ségou, Mopti and Timbuktu regions who said they were tortured during joint FAMa – Wagner patrols or during their detention in the military bases of Léré and Nampala.
This was notably corroborated by other individuals who witnessed acts of torture committed against 30 individuals during patrols or within the two military bases. Eyewitnesses reported that five people died in the bases as a result of torture and poor detention conditions.
According to Amnesty International’s investigation, these crimes were mostly committed by members of Wagner in the presence of FAMa members, who at times served as interpreters, and who stood by and did nothing, or, in some cases even threatened detainees. Victims had their arms suspended from a metal bar, were suffocated by simulations of drowning, beaten with iron bars and sticks, or subjected to electric shocks.
Those detained and tortured in the military camps were not brought before a judge. They had no access to a lawyer or their families throughout their detention, which lasted from one day to four months.
We urge the Malian authorities to ensure comprehensive accountability for war crimes committed against all communities.
Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa
Fulani, Arabs and Tuaregs targeted
A herder from the Ségou region who has taken refuge in Mauritania said: “In their minds [those of the soldiers and Wagner members], all herders are terrorists, and as a result they do not hesitate to burn people and property. Not even a blind person, nor even an elderly person, will be spared.”
The vast majority of the victims of these violations were members of pastoralist communities (Fulani, Arabs and Tuaregs) suspected of colluding with non-state armed groups, based solely on their ethnic background and their presence in an area where these armed groups were active.
“We urge the Malian authorities to ensure comprehensive accountability for war crimes committed against all communities. They must ensure that the FAMa, foreign military partners and members of armed groups suspected of war crimes are investigated and prosecuted as required in proceedings that comply with the right to a fair trial, without recourse to the death penalty,” said Marceau Sivieude.
“Civilians in conflict-affected regions in Mali continue to face grave risks. The authorities must protect them and make publicly available the agreement between the Government of Mali and Africa Corps, which succeeded Wagner in June 2025 and now operates in Mali. The African Union should condemn violations of international humanitarian law in Mali and support the fight against impunity for crimes under international law,” said Marceau Sivieude.
Background
This report is based on research conducted from 2025 to 2026 in ten localities in the Hodh ech-Chargui region of Mauritania where 290,000 Malian refugees were registered by UNHCR as of 31 July 2026. Amnesty International interviewed 119 refugees from the Ségou, Timbuktu and Mopti regions.
The report’s findings were shared with the Malian authorities on 3 August 2026. Amnesty International had not received a response at the time of publication.
Over the last decade, serious violations of international humanitarian and international human rights law have been committed by all parties to the non-international armed conflict between the Malian army and various non-state armed groups. Amnesty International recently reported several of these violations allegedly committed by members of the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (GSIM) and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA).
Around a thousand members of the Wagner private military security company were deployed to Mali from late 2021 until June 2025. While the Malian government has denied their presence on its territory, the Russian authorities have stated that Mali had sought the support of a private company to combat insurgent fighters.
The situation in Mali has been under investigation by the International Criminal Court (ICC) since 2013. In June 2026, Mali notified its withdrawal from the Rome Statute. However, it will not affect ongoing investigations, and the ICC will maintain jurisdiction over crimes under the Rome Statute committed between January 2013 and 23 June 2027, the date the withdrawal will take effect.
* Names have been changed to protect identity.

Elder loses bid to appeal ruling on genocide against King Charles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:54:01 UTC
13:54:01 KST

In short:
Judges have rejected Krautatungalung elder Robbie Thorpe's landmark bid to prosecute King Charles III over the alleged genocide of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
The case alleged that the king is perpetuating genocide by maintaining systems that disadvantage Indigenous people across numerous socio-economic measures.
What's next?
Mr Thorpe says he will take his allegations against the monarch to the International Criminal Court in the Netherlands.
An Aboriginal elder pursuing a case of genocide against King Charles III has hit a legal hurdle.
Judges have rejected Krautatungalung elder Robbie Thorpe's landmark bid to prosecute King Charles III over the alleged genocide of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
The case alleges that the king, along with the Australian government and its institutions, is perpetuating genocide by maintaining systems that disadvantage Indigenous people across numerous socio-economic measures.
"Australia is just totally in denial," Mr Thorpe said.
"If it wasn't for the acts of terror and the policies of genocide, Australia wouldn't exist.
"That's my reality, and a lot of other people's."
Monday's ruling by Victoria's Court of Appeal was Mr Thorpe's third legal defeat since he began trying in 2023 to launch a private prosecution against the monarch in Melbourne Magistrates' Court.
The alleged offences were continuing acts of genocide committed since September 28, 2022 against First Peoples, contrary to common law, federal law concerning genocide and First Peoples' sovereign laws.
But the filing was knocked back by a senior registrar of the Magistrates' Court on the grounds that it did not reference any "proper source of law".
A judicial review by the Supreme Court upheld the registrar's decision.
The Court of Appeal dismissed an application by Mr Thorpe to appeal the decision on the basis that it had no real prospect of success.
"While acknowledging the significance of the questions raised by Uncle Robbie, the primary judge stated [correctly and self-evidently] that the only jurisdiction she could exercise was the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Victoria," the appeal court said.
"The primary judge concluded that the senior registrar of the Magistrates' Court acted lawfully … as the charges alleged in the charge-sheet did not disclose an offence known to the law of Victoria."
It leaves the 68-year-old activist with one final domestic option: seeking permission to appeal to the High Court of Australia.
Mr Thorpe said on Monday he did not expect to receive a fair hearing in Australia.
After exhausting his options in Australian courts, he said he would take his allegations against the monarch to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Netherlands.
"The International Criminal Court will expose Australia for what it really is — a lying, racist, illegal occupation committing genocide," Mr Thorpe said.
British monarch has common law immunity in UK
The British monarch has common law immunity from all criminal and civil liability in the United Kingdom, a condition that has likely been inherited by Australia.
This immunity will likely complicate any case brought against King Charles III.
Mr Thorpe said his efforts in Australian courts would play a role if the case reached an international jurisdiction.
"We're exhausting the domestic remedies," he said.
"It's accruing all this unwillingness, inability, reluctance to deal with these issues.
"Sooner or later, we'll get a chance in the international court, and this will all be relevant."
The ICC does not recognise head-of-state immunity and has the jurisdiction to prosecute on a charge of genocide.
But an individual such as Mr Thorpe does not have the option to launch a private prosecution in the ICC.
The UN Security Council can refer a prosecution, but is unlikely to do so with Britain as a member.
The most common path is for an individual to make the ICC's Office of the Prosecutor aware of evidence, as happened in cases against Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Mr Thorpe suggested Türkiye might be the country to take the charges to an international court.

North Korean hackers steal millions in crypto heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:52:34 UTC
13:52:34 KST

North Korean group 'WaterPlum' steals millions in crypto hack
A North Korean hacking group is using job ads to harvest sensitive information from unsuspecting applicants from hundreds of countries, authorities warn.
The group, known as "WaterPlum", infiltrated at least 30,000 devices stealing $US10.71 million ($15.25 million) worth of cryptocurrency from 7,000 accounts.
Cybersecurity officials from the US, Japan, Germany and Australia issued a joint statement saying the group was targeting individual IT professionals.
What happened?
Between December 2025 and July this year, members of WaterPlum presented as an employer advertising fake roles specifically for software developers and IT professionals.
They would instruct applicants to download files for software alternatives to video conferencing apps such as Zoom to conduct interviews.
Authorities said members of the group also operated as North Korean IT workers at companies.
They would use artificial intelligence (AI) face-swapping software when beginning online interviews for roles, and then ask to disable their camera "because of network issues".
It was discovered after Japanese authorities were able to identify a "laptop farm", which obscures someone's real location, and found evidence WaterPlum had transferred millions in cryptocurrency to places outside Japan.
Those who were a part of the laptop farm were often located in North Korea, China and Russia, with a small number in Africa and south-east Asia.
University of Melbourne's Andrew Cullen, who specialises in cybersecurity and AI, said these were two of the main types of scams run by the group.
He said he had seen reports of fake North Korean employees for the last three to four years but it has been accelerating.
"I don't think anybody in the West has a particularly strong grasp on exactly how long this has been happening,"
He said it was difficult to understand the scale of the problem, especially as it related to workers infiltrating companies, because that information was rarely disclosed.
"It's really hard for governments and cybersecurity organisations to try and collect this large-scale data to show how much of a problem it is across the economy," he said.
Authorities said the group had also been able to access ID images, passwords and other sensitive data from thousands of people that could be used for extortion.
They also said the group operated under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department, subordinate to the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea.
What does it mean?
Dr Cullen said hacks of this nature were likely to become more prevalent because of rogue AI agents and AI tools that enable hackers to work faster with a larger scope.
According to the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), an independent security think tank in the UK, AI was being used to speed-up the process of ransomware operations.
Dr Cullen described ransomware as when someone is locked out of their systems, and is then charged a ransom for access to their own data.
"So, instead of a hacker who is on the other side having a conversation about the extortion, that can be farmed out to an AI system," he said.
"Or an AI system can be used to help those who are doing these kind of hacks sound more natural, talk to more people, keep track of what they're doing more efficiently."
What are some countermeasures?
Dr Cullen said cybersecurity could sound big and scary, but there were simple principles that could help protect someone's data and security.
These included changing passwords regularly, keeping devices updated, and avoiding suspicious links and software.
He also said employers should meet physically with remote staff to verify their identities.
"These are all the basic cybersecurity messages that we've had for the last 10 years,"
Dr Cullen said this was because hackers had not improved but the volume and speed of them have increased.
Outside of increasing funding to cybersecurity, Dr Cullen said governments could also set rules that made hacking people in Australia less attractive.
He highlighted setting specific legislation that stopped companies paying bribes to ransomware groups.
"So there's a real job for the government to make sure they're setting the legislation so that Australians aren't targeted," he said.

OpenAI postpones release of latest AI model over security concerns as the industry faces new safety pressures

04:52:32 UTC
13:52:32 KST

The decision comes after the AI giant faced fierce criticism in recent weeks after it was discovered its models broke out of confined restraints during testing and training phases and hacked into commercial and government websites, compounding calls for greater AI safety measures.
OpenAI said late on Monday that it was delaying the release of a new artificial intelligence model out of security concerns voiced by its researchers, the latest in the company's effort to decelerate the pace of the technology's rapid advance.
OpenAI’s decision to hold back the latest model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up.
The announcement comes a day before AI executives are set to huddle with US President Donald Trump in Washington as technology companies face new pressure to be accountable for how their models can be abused.
In a statement from OpenAI's head of safety systems Saachi Jain, the version “didn't quite meet the bar.” It had become more persistent in completing tasks, but OpenAI needed to balance that capability against unauthorised behaviour.
Jain insisted the company was committed to ensuring the model was safe whether in the company's testing or in the hands of users.
"We have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” she said.
OpenAI paused training of its most advanced models last week, saying training would resume “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards.”
That was after it disclosed instances in which AI agents exceeded their instructions, including by accessing government websites without authorisation.
Earlier this week, it was revealed that an OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian government website in June and accessed private data, which experts called the first of its kind and proved a tangible sign towards superintelligence.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has joined other industry leaders, including main rival Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, in calling for a slowdown, warning that companies do not yet have adequate safeguards to control the most capable systems created by mankind.
Altman was scheduled to deliver the keynote address for OpenAI's annual conference for software developers in San Francisco on Tuesday.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman is expected to attend the White House's event on Tuesday in Altman’s place.

Five million robots now work in factories as humanoid hype faces reality check
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:46:57 UTC
13:46:57 KST

Over five million industrial robots now work in factories worldwide, the highest total ever recorded, even as Boston Dynamics shelves a stock listing and Chinese regulators slow a rush of humanoid IPOs, showing a widening gap between practical machines and the humanoids capturing headlines.
The global operational stock of industrial robots rose 9% last year to reach roughly 5.08 million units, the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) said in its annual World Robotics report published last Thursday.
The IFR is a Frankfurt-based non-profit that has tracked the industry for close to three decades and represents more than 3,000 organisations worldwide.
According to the report, annual installations of industrial robots jumped 11% to surpass 600,000 for the first time, reaching 603,000 units.
"Industrial automation is progressing at high speed," said Jane Heffner, the IFR's president, adding that "the new mark of five million robots operational in factories worldwide is more than double the number seven years ago. The strongest growth is taking place in Asia, followed by Americas. Europe is moving ahead more slowly."
Europe's more cautious build-up
The slower pace of growth in Europe shows up clearly in the numbers.
The EU's operational stock passed 700,000 robots for the first time in 2025, reaching 712,000 and accounting for 84% of all robots in operation across Europe.
"The EU's manufacturing sector has invested significantly in automation," Heffner said. The stock has grown more than 80% since 2015, when it stood at 390,000.
However, growth has stalled for now.
New installations across the EU fell 11% in 2025 to 60,500 units, even as installations elsewhere accelerated. The bloc's five-year compound annual growth rate stood at a comparatively modest 3%.
Germany remains by far the largest European market, accounting for 41% of EU installations. But the number of robots installed there fell 8% to under 25,000 as its automotive sector, still the largest single customer, continued to retreat.
Italy, France and Spain follow, each adding between 4,300 and 7,800 robots, with installations in all three down by double digits.
Meanwhile, China widened its lead over the same period, installing 354,000 robots, up 20% and now accounting for 59% of global deployments.
The US also overtook Japan to become the world's second-largest market, installing almost 38,500 units, up 12%.
A reality check for humanoids
Humanoids remain a tiny market beside established industrial robots.
Only about 7,000 were sold worldwide last year for industrial and professional use, the IFR said in a separate release, the first time it has tracked the category.
Many were bought to generate training data for AI models rather than carry out work, and car manufacturers piloting them typically run fewer than ten machines.
Bank of America nonetheless forecasts 90,000 humanoid shipments this year and 1.2 million by 2030.
The gap between ambition and reality is showing in financial markets too.
Boston Dynamics, owned by Hyundai, is unlikely to pursue a stock listing next year, as its Atlas humanoid has yet to be deployed at scale and the company remains unprofitable, a senior Hyundai executive said this month.
In China, regulators have reportedly used informal guidance to hold back humanoid IPOs after shares in robot maker Unitree soared more than fivefold on their 19 August Shanghai debut, then fell 55% from their peak.
Even Elon Musk has been unusually candid about the difficulty of his own Optimus programme at Tesla.
"This is going to be the hardest product to scale manufacturing that we've ever made at Tesla, because everything on the robot is new," Musk told investors on Tesla's second-quarter earnings call, adding that "there is no supply chain."
Where the real value sits
A report published this year by Brussels-headquartered Arthur D. Little, the world’s oldest management consultancy, makes the same point.
"Humanoid robots will capture attention; specialised physical AI will capture value," it states, using physical AI as an umbrella term for machines, from robot arms to self-driving cars, that can perceive, decide and act in the real world.
It puts that broader market at around $18 billion (€15.8bn) today, of which humanoids account for just $2 billion (€1.75bn) to $3 billion (€2.63bn), and projects that it will reach $60 billion (€52.7bn) to $100 billion (€87.9bn) by 2030.
Many humanoid demonstrations "are fake, AI-generated, or heavily staged", the report warns, while real ones often show pre-recorded routines or remote human operation.
The sweet spot, it argues, is structured environments such as factories and warehouses, where wheeled robots and fixed arms will scale first because they are cheaper and easier to tailor to specific jobs.
"Why would we limit it to mimic the human form factor...?" asks Dave Grant, CEO of PickNik Robotics, in the report.
Human-level dexterity, reliable autonomy outside controlled settings and the absence of a "killer app" remain major constraints for humanoids, alongside unresolved liability and insurance questions.
Siemens has trialled a robot for logistics tasks at its Erlangen factory, and BMW is deploying a humanoid in car and battery production. But these trials sit alongside the IFR’s conclusion, which suggests that most humanoids remain at the prototype or pilot stage while conventional industrial robots are still more economical for factory work.
Therefore, the world’s robotics story this year is not about humanoids, but about a slower, steadier build-up of machines that already work.

====================================================================================================

934 silver coins found: questions over Germany's biggest Roman hoard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:44:39 UTC
13:44:39 KST

In autumn 2025, a father from the Rhineland only meant to briefly sweep a field near Wesseling, south of Cologne, with his metal detector. Then it beeped and he unearthed a Roman silver coin – and it was not the only one.
Probablemente ha sido el hallazgo de su vida: el buscador aficionado de tesoros, un padre de familia de Renania, no esperaba nada especial aquel día cuando, de repente, sonó su detector de metales. Localizó una moneda romana de plata, luego más. Cuando llegó a 15 piezas y el aparato seguía marcando señales, comprendió: "Esto es algo mayor".
Lo que los arqueólogos recuperaron a continuación superó todas las expectativas: 934 denarios romanos de plata con un peso total de 3,1 kilos. El Landschaftsverband Rheinland (LVR) califica el hallazgo como el mayor tesoro numismático conocido de la época del emperador Adriano en el territorio de la actual Alemania. En todo el mundo solo existirían cuatro tesoros monetarios romanos de esta época que sean mayores.
El lugar del hallazgo se encuentra al sur de Colonia, en una región que desempeñó un papel importante durante la época de los emperadores romanos. La cercana Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, la actual Colonia, era entonces un importante centro político, militar y económico a orillas del Rin.
Un patrimonio que probablemente se transmitió durante generaciones
Resulta especialmente fascinante el arco temporal que abarcan las monedas. La más antigua data del año 148 a. C., es decir, de la época de la República romana. La más reciente se acuñó en 124/125 d. C. Entre ambas hay más de 270 años. Cuando, probablemente en el segundo cuarto del siglo II, se enterró el tesoro, la moneda más antigua tenía ya más de dos siglos y medio y, al parecer, seguía siendo válida como medio de pago. El hallazgo ilustra así el tiempo que podían permanecer en circulación las piezas antiguas en el sistema monetario romano.
El valor del tesoro es difícil de traducir hoy a términos monetarios. Una referencia la proporciona el sueldo de un legionario romano: un soldado raso recibía en aquella época alrededor de 300 denarios al año, de los cuales aproximadamente la mitad se retenía para manutención y equipamiento. Para ahorrar una cantidad comparable, habría tenido que reservar durante unos seis años todos sus ingresos disponibles.
¿Por qué nunca se recuperó el tesoro?
Los arqueólogos consideran que el dinero se enterró deliberadamente para guardarlo de forma segura. Probablemente la persona que lo ocultó murió antes de poder revelar a alguien dónde estaba escondido.
La forma en que se ha recuperado el tesoro aporta al menos algunas pistas: parte de las monedas se trasladó en un bloque compacto de tierra al taller de restauración del LVR-Landesmuseums Bonn. Allí, las radiografías revelaron, entre otros elementos, fragmentos de un recipiente de cerámica y restos de paja. Todo indica que alguien depositó en su día las monedas en un recipiente acolchado con paja.
Todo apunta a que el patrimonio se fue acumulando en torno al año 100 d. C., pero que no se enterró hasta varias décadas después, ya durante el reinado del emperador Adriano.
Un breve viaje a la época de la que procede el tesoro: el emperador Adriano (76-138 d. C.) gobernó el Imperio romano desde 117 hasta su muerte, a los 62 años. Se le considera uno de los llamados "cinco buenos emperadores" y apostó por asegurar y consolidar el enorme imperio. Adriano recorrió amplias zonas del territorio, ordenó ampliar carreteras, templos y ciudades y es conocido especialmente por la muralla de Adriano en Britania, levantada para proteger la frontera romana frente a las tribus del norte.
Sin embargo, su reinado no fue pacífico: entre los años 132 y 135 se produjo en la provincia romana de Judea, que se extendía por parte del actual Israel y de los territorios palestinos, un levantamiento contra el dominio de Roma. Bajo el liderazgo de Simón Bar Kokhba, rebeldes judíos combatieron contra las tropas romanas. La revuelta fue aplastada con gran dureza por Roma.
Las monedas de plata que encontró este vecino de Renania pasan ahora a ser propiedad del estado federado de Renania del Norte-Westfalia, y está previsto que el descubridor reciba una recompensa.
Una parte de las monedas se ha presentado por primera vez al público este septiembre en Bonn. A partir de marzo de 2027 está previsto que el tesoro se exhiba en la exposición arqueológica permanente del Bonner LVR-LandesMuseums.

WELLINGTON, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The New Zealand government has approved tougher penalties and new offenses to help tackle the illicit tobacco trade, Associate Health Minister Casey Costello said on Tuesday.
The approval of two sets of legislative changes will support Health New Zealand, the Ministry of Health, customs and police in identifying and disrupting the black-market tobacco trade, Costello said in a statement.
The proposed changes include a new infringement offense carrying a fine of 2,000 NZ dollars (1,134 U.S. dollars) for breaches of tobacco packaging regulations, as well as a strict liability packaging offense of up to 200,000 NZ dollars for manufacturers, importers and distributors.

The changes to fines and offences require amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 before taking effect, the statement said.
Separately, the Customs and Excise (Border Security) Amendment Bill, introduced to Parliament last week, would increase the maximum prison term for tobacco smuggling and excise evasion from six months to seven years.
Costello said the measures would strengthen the government's cross-agency response to illicit tobacco activity. ■

Cholesterol, blood pressure can be silent killers. European Commission is after them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:40:21 UTC
13:40:21 KST

The European Commission is urging EU countries to step up cardiovascular health checks, as it launches the bloc’s first EU Screening Week.
The Commission on Monday proposed a Council recommendation encouraging regular checks of blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, with a particular focus on people at higher risk.
Cardiovascular disease is the EU’s biggest killer, claiming around 1.7 million lives a year and costing the economy more than €282 billion. The Commission says up to 80% of cases can be prevented by tackling risk factors including hypertension, obesity and high cholesterol.
“A very large majority of premature cardiovascular diseases could be avoided if we identify risks earlier and if we act earlier,” Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said during the press briefing on Monday.
Screening is key to catching diseases in time.
Fewer than half of EU countries currently have cardiovascular health-check programmes, according to the Commission, with significant differences in how they operate.
The proposal is part of the Commission's Safe Hearts Plan, presented in December 2025, which aims to cut premature cardiovascular deaths by 25% by 2035. It calls for broader access to screening, targeted measures for vulnerable groups and greater use of digital and AI tools, subject to human oversight.
As part of the EU Screening Week, health organisations have established checks across Europe, free of charge and accessible to everyone.
“This initiative can hopefully lead to reducing inequalities,” Sophie Millar, EU Policy Advocacy Manager at the European Society of Cardiology, told Euronews Health.
She added that while in Brussels, around the Commission, people may be more likely to know their numbers, there are activities targeting harder-to-reach communities. These include “the more vulnerable groups who actually have the biggest need to know their numbers and to get their tests done.”
Blood sugar is one of the three numbers being checked, as diabetes is often missed. The International Diabetes Federation (IDF) estimates that, in Europe, one in four people living with diabetes remain undiagnosed.
Diabetes is not only a disease in itself, but also a risk factor for many others and taking the necessary measures in time is essential.
“Diabetes is one of the main root causes of many other non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and kidney disease,” Maxence Prizzi, EU Policy and Advocacy Coordinator at the International Diabetes Federation Europe (IDF) said.
“Primary prevention starts with simple health checks … it all starts with knowing your health data and health numbers and that can save lives,” Prizzi added.
The importance of regular checks
Regular checks are also important among healthy people even if nothing signals a problem.
“At a certain age, everyone needs to know their glycaemic, lipid and cholesterol levels to know if they are in the norm or not,” Grace Bayams, one of the nurses who tested people in Brussels, said.
Depending on the results, she added, doctors can recommend different regimes and treatments to keep patients at normal levels.
Angelos was among those who stopped by. Getting the checks done was a response to not having visited the doctor as often as he would like.
“This was maybe an opportunity to get a little bit more pragmatic and start going on a regular basis,” he said, adding he was looking for advice about his blood glucose.
Others stopped simply out of curiosity, among them Jack Smith, who was visiting Brussels and came across the stand by chance.
“I saw this going on and I thought it would be fun because I think I'm healthy but I've not been to the doctors to check how good my health is, so that's why I'm here,” he told Euronews Health.
Smith works as a doctor for the National Health Service in England and highlighted the need to focus on prevention to tackle long-term conditions.
“I think it's really important to raise awareness so that people know that there are things that they can do to help stop diseases happening and that they can live healthier and happier lives,” he added.

====================================================================================================

The RBA just raised rates. It affects more than just your home loan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:39:54 UTC
13:39:54 KST

What an interest rate hike means for your mortgage, savings account and the Australian dollar
For the fourth time this year, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has lifted the cash rate by 0.25 of a percentage point in a bid to bring inflation under control.
While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans.
Here's a breakdown of how the latest increase will affect households differently, depending on whether Australians are paying off a mortgage, renting, or relying on savings.
Where are we at with the cash rate?
To first understand how the cash rate impacts different parts of our hip pocket, let's take a step back.
The cash rate, set by the RBA, is Australia's official interest rate charged on unsecured overnight loans between banks.
In simple terms, it's how much it costs banks to borrow from each other. The RBA's decision to increase the official cash rate makes it more expensive for lenders to borrow money.
That means banks will almost certainly charge customers a higher interest rate to still make a profit because they are paying more to borrow the money in the first place.
On Tuesday, the RBA increased the cash rate to 4.6 per cent in an attempt to slow down inflation in the economy.
Commonwealth Bank head of Australian economics Belinda Allen says the central bank has lost its patience, given inflation has sat above the target band for most of the past six years.
"Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive," Ms Allen says.
"That tends to slow household spending and business investment, reducing some of the demand pressures in the economy and, over time, helping bring inflation back towards the RBA's 2–3 per cent target."
How the cash rate increase could affect you
Mortgages
Read more
Rate rises are felt fastest, and most sharply, by Australians with variable-rate mortgages because banks typically pass on RBA increases in full.
AMP chief economist Shane Oliver says the cash rate is the main tool steering borrowing costs and households should expect lenders to adjust quickly.
"As we've seen with the first three hikes this year, the banks will likely announce a 0.25 per cent increase in their mortgage rates on the same day," Dr Oliver says.
Ms Allen says households with a mortgage may lower spending or use savings to keep spending as a result of higher interest rates.
"This cash flow channel is one way monetary policy works to impact demand in the economy," she says.
Each 0.25 per cent rise in the cash rate adds roughly $91 per month to repayments on a $600,000 variable-rate loan with 25 years remaining. The four 2026 increases totalling 0.75 per cent have added approximately $360 per month for borrowers on a $600,000 loan.
That equates to about $4,320 extra per year.
Here's how much a September rate hike will cost borrowers:
It is not just existing mortgage borrowers hit by the rate rises though.
For prospective buyers, Canstar estimates that the borrowing capacity of someone on an average full-time wage of $108,650 would be reduced by more than $47,000, while a couple both on average wages would see a reduction of nearly $95,000.
If you are on a fixed-rate home loan, you won't see any changes. Those rates are locked in.
But when the fixed term expires and rolls to a variable rate, the full impact of any rate cycle will apply at once.
Rents
Read more
For renters, the interest rate impact is more indirect.
Some landlords may try to offset the impact of rate rises on their cash flow by raising rents over time, although there are constraints on how often and how much rent can be increased each year in most states.
The RBA has also dismissed the idea that landlords pass their increased borrowing costs on to renters.
Speaking on 9Now's The Pay Off podcast, RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter said what was really driving rents came down to supply and demand.
"If you're an individual landlord, you own one property in one rental market, you might want to put the rent up when your interest rate goes up if you've got a mortgage," Dr Hunter said.
"But you're competing with all the other properties that are available … and so, it's demand and supply; it's the local market that will equilibrate rent.
"If rents are tracking up, it's usually because demand growth is stronger than supply growth."
Ms Allen and Dr Oliver agree with this logic.
Cotality's quarterly rental review found rents rose by 1.6 per cent nationally in the June quarter, driven by a severe lack of available stock across the country.
The national dwelling vacancy rate sat at 1.6 per cent, unchanged from March and remaining below the five-year average of 1.8 per cent.
"The main factor driving rents is the shortage of rental property," Dr Oliver says.
Savings
Read more
There is one silver lining in the rate rise, for some. Savings accounts and term deposit interest rates usually rise after an RBA hike, making it more attractive to park your money.
This is because, while the cash rate also affects borrowing costs for banks, it also sets the rate of return for their own deposits. Cash rate hikes improve their returns, which may be passed on to consumers through higher savings interest rates.
Dr Oliver says while short-term deposit rates largely move in line with the cash rate, longer-term term deposit rates are also shaped by government bond yields and other borrowing costs.
With today's RBA increase and bond yields already rising, he says savers are likely to benefit from higher returns.
"The odds are, yes, we will see deposit rates continue to rise."
Australian dollar
Read more
Higher interest rates tend to strengthen the Australian dollar (AUD).
And that's because it's more attractive for foreign investors to park their money in Australian interest-bearing assets (like savings accounts, term deposits, and government bonds) because they can get a higher rate of interest here.
This increases demand for the AUD, making the currency more valuable.
That generally means imported products can cost less in Australian-dollar terms and overseas travel becomes cheaper.
But Ms Allen says the Australian dollar's value depends on far more than the RBA's cash rate decisions.
"The Australian dollar is influenced by many things — global interest rates, commodity prices, China, investor sentiment and expectations about the Australian economy — so you can't say that a 25-basis-point rate hike will automatically result in a particular move in the dollar," she says.
Dr Oliver agrees, noting that with the US Federal Reserve also tightening monetary policy, any upward pressure on the Australian dollar may be offset.
"I suspect it probably just keeps the Aussie dollar around where it is," he says.
Car and personal loans
Read more
Car loans and personal loans can be affected by increases in the cash rate.
But it all comes down to what type of loan you have.
Australians collectively borrowed about $4.7 billion in fixed-term personal loans for road vehicles in the three months to June 2026, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
These loans would not be affected by the cash rate until their fixed-rate period ends.
For those on a variable rate, Dr Oliver says banks may not necessarily hike rates by the full 0.25 per cent, but "the odds are they'll probably go up over time as well".
Is this the last rate hike for the year?
We don't know.
The majority of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg expect the RBA to be done with hikes for the rest of the year.
Loading...
Westpac, NAB and CBA are also in agreement.
In a weekly market update last Friday, Dr Oliver summed up the majority view.
"By the time it gets to the November meeting, there is likely to be more evidence of a cooling economy, falling home prices, a softer jobs market and rising recession risks, so we don't think a second hike let alone a third will be necessary," he wrote.
ANZ is the only major bank so far officially tipping a November rise as well, alongside HSBC and UBS.
Ms Allen says it all depends on the near-term movements in inflation data.
The RBA will deliver its next cash rate decision on Tuesday, November 3.

====================================================================================================

Breaking: RBA lifts rates to highest level in 15 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:31:39 UTC
13:31:39 KST

RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 15 years
In short:
The Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Board has lifted interest rates by 0.25 percentage points.
It lifts the cash rate target to 4.60 per cent, up from 4.35 per cent. It is the highest rate since late 2011.
What's next?
The Bureau of Statistics will release its September inflation data tomorrow.
The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 15 years.
It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.6 per cent, up from 4.35 per cent.
It will be a blow to home owners with large mortgages. It is also the highest cash rate millions of households have faced since taking on a mortgage after 2011.
But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts.
The decision to lift rates was unanimous, with all nine members of the board voting in favour.
The desire to get inflation down
In recent weeks, senior RBA officials have been warning that they are losing patience with the time it is taking to drag inflation back down into the RBA's 2-3 per cent target range.
In July, headline inflation was running at an annual pace of 3.5 per cent and underlying (or "core") inflation was running at 3.6 per cent.
The RBA wants inflation sitting around 2.5 per cent on average, over the medium term.
But Australia is not alone in its struggle to get inflation down.
In recent weeks, the European Central Bank, US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and Reserve Bank of New Zealand have all lifted rates.
The latest fighting in the Middle East has also sent crude oil prices higher in recent weeks, which has pushed more inflation around the world via higher fuel prices.
The RBA's decision to lift interest rates today comes one day before the Bureau of Statistics releases its September quarter inflation data.
RBA prepared to lift rates again if necessary
In a statement, the RBA Board said it did not want high inflation to become embedded in Australia's economy.
It said since its last meeting, the conflict in the Middle East had broadened and global energy prices were now much higher.
It said AI-related demand was driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods, and some Australian businesses were experiencing cost pressures and were either increasing prices or looking to do so.
It also said economic growth and inflation were both higher in Australia than had been expected, and interest rates needed to rise to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation back to target.
"The three increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial conditions and the economy appears to be slowing," it said.
"But inflation is still too high and the Board judged that, in light of recent developments, a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support a return of inflation to target in a reasonable period.
"The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed," it said.
What do economists say?
EY Oceania chief economist Cherelle Murphy said it was not a happy time for households.
She said consumer sentiment was at extremely low levels, lots of people had jobs but they did not feel like they were getting ahead, and the recent decline in house prices was making many families feel less wealthy.
"It's certainly going to hurt many households, this fourth interest rate hike," she told the ABC.
"But from the Reserve Bank's point of view, certainly what they see is hurting more is inflation continuing to be too high. As we know, it has been above the Reserve Bank's target band for a very long period now."
BetaShares chief economist David Bassanese said he thought the RBA would lift rates again in coming months.
"Ominously, the Bank noted that local firms are facing higher costs and are either raising prices or 'looking to do so'. This suggests that inflation could rise even further in the months ahead," he said.
Loading...
"Sadly, Australia looks set for a period of stagflationary conditions, with weak growth alongside stubbornly high inflation.
"While inflation remains above target, the RBA has limited tolerance for price pressures becoming entrenched.
"In unwelcome news for mortgage holders, it's now my base case that the RBA is now a short-priced favourite to raise rates by 25 basis points on Melbourne Cup Day, taking the cash rate to 4.85 per cent," he said.
How have banks responded to the rate hike?
Macquarie Bank was very quick to respond to the rate hike.
It said it would increase its variable home loan reference rates by 0.25 per cent per annum (effective from October 15).
It will also increase the variable interest rates paid on its transaction and savings accounts.
"For any customers concerned about making their home loan repayments, we encourage them to get in touch, as financial assistance may be available," head of personal banking at Macquarie Bank, Ben Perham, said.
Cotality said the RBA's four rate rises this year have now reduced Australians' borrowing capacity by almost $90,000 on average, which has significantly constrained buyer purchasing power.
"Higher interest rates are expected to keep housing demand and transaction activity subdued through weaker affordability and reduced borrowing power," it said.
"A meaningful housing market recovery is unlikely until borrowers gain confidence that interest rates have reached their peak and will eventually begin to fall."

Country diary: A tangle of butterflies and battle re-enactments | Paul Evans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:30:53 UTC
13:30:53 KST

I’m telling the story from a pub in the bailey opposite the ruins of Oswestry Castle. There in 1165, Henry II, the Angevin (Anglo-Norman) king of England, gathered troops from the Marcher Lords to advance on an alliance of Welsh princes for control of the Marches.
The previous Sunday, 861 years later, we went the same way as Henry’s army to Chirk Castle, Castell Y Waun a’r Ardd, to see a re-enactment of the Battle of Crogen. The present castle wasn’t built back then and the battle at Crogen was in the Ceiriog Valley below. Henry had sent woodsmen to raze woodland in the valley to remove the Welsh advantage, but he left one oak, Quercus petraea, at which Owain Gwynedd gathered his army.
That tree became the Pontfadog oak – a giant, the oldest British oak, and survived as the National Tree of Wales, much loved and storied until it blew down in a storm in 2013 at an estimated 1,600 years old. I have a small fragment of it given to me by the longtime Guardian environment editor John Vidal.
The battle re-enactment, with crashing swords and shields in the colours of Marcher lords and Welsh princes, fine horses and boinging arrows, was fun to watch with a running commentary giving a sense of what was happening and who was doing what.
Histories vary about whether this was a great battle, isolated harassments or no fighting at all, but the outcome was the same: the Welsh won. The history of the Marches, like the traumatised, ghost-ridden ground itself, has been a contested space for centuries.
It was fascinating to talk to people dedicated to making the past come to life for modern audiences. Over the castle garden wall, the past and present were weaving together in micro-dramas of moment. Two clouded yellow butterflies, Colias croceus, which had migrated here from north Africa or southern Europe, were flickering over herbaceous borders and lawns. Given the massive decline in insect populations, that pastoral scene had a spirit of resistance.
And as if to demonstrate a mystical kind of heraldry and valour of a far more ancient territorial warrior, a small copper, Lycaena phlaeas, flourished his wings.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vanguard International Semiconductor is accelerating its evaluation of a second fab in Singapore after receiving more customer requests than its first facility can handle, Nikkei Asia reported Monday.
TSMC is VIS’ largest shareholder, with a stake of about 19%, per CommonWealth Magazine. The two companies maintain a strategic partnership, with VIS licensing the chipmaker’s gallium nitride technology, which enables more efficient power use.
VIS’ fab, operated by VisionPower Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (VSMC), a joint venture between VIS and Dutch chipmaker NXP, was inaugurated Monday, per CNA. Test production began in June, just 18 months after construction started, and mass production is scheduled to begin in early 2027. The first batch of chips achieved a yield of at least 99%, VIS said.
The plant will produce power management and analog chips for automotive and industrial applications while also helping TSMC produce interposers used in advanced chip packaging for AI processors. VIS Chair Fang Leuh (方略) said demand for power-related and analog chips, particularly those used in data centers, continues to outstrip supply, per Nikkei Asia.
“We have received more requests from customers, so we are still evaluating and finalizing a second plant in terms of funding, demand, and technology nodes,” Fang said. “We will be very mindful of any future investment, given the significant capital required.”
The AI boom is also driving demand for chips beyond AI data centers, putting further pressure on supplies, according to Nikkei Asia. “Our existing capacity is stretched well beyond its limits,” Fang said, adding that VSMC has hired about 1,000 people and plans to increase its workforce to around 1,600 as production ramps up.
VIS specializes in power supply, power management, and analog chips rather than cutting-edge computing processors. VIS and NXP initially announced a NT$248.13 billion (US$7.8 billion) investment in the Singapore plant in 2024, later revising the figure to NT$213.18 billion after changes to equipment procurement plans.

Chinese research vessel near Diaoyutai Islands could be helping prepare for Taiwan invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
