‘Just look at this monstrosity!’ Inside Britain’s bilious back yard shed wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

Linda loves her shed. She loves that she can work there rather than in her dining room, which her toddler likes to tear through. She loves its Scandinavian vibe – it’s clad in wood and set on decking at the bottom of her garden. She loves the views of the countryside from the window by her desk. Or she did. Her desk faces the wall now, because she’s too nervous to face her neighbour. She never sits on the decking, either. “What if they see me?” she says. “It’s a horrible feeling.”
Linda’s neighbours are unhappy about her shed, or “garden room”, which is actually two rooms. They do not like its size (7.25 metres by 2.74 metres, or 3.5 metres if you include the raised decking) or its position, about 30 metres away from their house. Linda says they have barely spoken since the construction, which is awkward, as the gardens are separated by a low fence.
The neighbours say the shed is more than half a metre too tall and too close to their property for it to be a “permitted development”, one that can be built without applying for planning permission. In England and Wales, there is a height cap of 2.5 metres from the ground if any part of the outbuilding falls within 2 metres of a boundary (it is within 1 metre of a boundary in Scotland). If the building is further from the boundary, it can be 3 metres or 4 metres high, depending on the roof type. The council agreed and told Linda she needed to apply for retrospective planning permission. She says it was an “honest mistake” and that she received the wrong guidance from her builders. “I was mortified. I would never have done it intentionally,” she says.
Before the build, Linda says, she had a friendly relationship with her neighbours; they would lend each other tools and garden materials. She says she had had an informal conversation with her neighbours about building a garden room in the space and heard no objections. Her neighbours say they were not consulted at all before construction, which took about a month.
Linda says she found out the extent of her neighbours’ feelings about her shed only in the paperwork for their planning dispute. They said they could see it from every window of their home and that they felt they had lost all sense of privacy, which had affected their daily lives and mental wellbeing. They also said an estate agent told them it had negatively affected the value of their home.
Retrospective planning permission for her shed has been granted, on the condition that a privacy screen and other planting are put up. Was it worth it? Yes, Linda believes, but she says: “I wish we had known to go about it the right way; it would have saved us money and a heck of a lot of effort and time …”
The dispute between Linda and her neighbours is just one example of simmering resentment over the increased use of these kinds of outhouses in the UK. The news is regularly peppered with spicy shed disputes – and no social strata is exempt. Pink Floyd’s David Gilmour was ordered to move a shed in his garden in upmarket Hampstead, north London, last year after it was described as “intrusive” and “overbearing” by neighbours who wanted a retrospective planning application to be refused. It was ordered to be rebuilt further back from the boundary.
Part of the reason for these disputes is the growing popularity of outhouses. Simon Rix, a senior planning consultant and a director of Planix.uk, a consultancy company that advises people who want to extend, says he received “a trickle” of clients who wanted to build luxury sheds before the pandemic, but that has “probably gone up tenfold”.
As well as home offices, gyms and storage, many are used for habitable living spaces, as the housing crisis continues to stunt home-buying. “Quite a lot of people are coming to me because they want to move into it and let their children live in the main house,” Rix says. He is also seeing more static caravans in gardens for the same reason – these don’t count as a “development” and do not need planning permission if they are housing a family member. “Neighbours get really grumpy, because they can be quite tall and imposing,” he says.
Planning rules around these outhouses are “monumentally complex”, says Rix, who would like them to be simplified. Both sides regularly misunderstand their rights. “Neighbours frequently assume that if something looks large, blocks a view or sits right on the fence line, it must be illegal. Conversely, homeowners often wrongly assume: ‘It’s my garden, I can do what I want.’ This gap in understanding, combined with the post-pandemic boom, is creating a perfect storm for neighbourhood disputes,” he says.
The regulations and rules around erecting outbuildings as part of permitted development vary not only in terms of the height and the proximity to a neighbour’s boundary. They must also be single storey and, in England and Wales, not “forward of the principal elevation” – the front wall of the house facing the highway (in Scotland, there is some provision for a small shed). Outbuildings cannot take up more than 50% of the total garden, either, and listed homes and those in conservation areas and other special sites face different restrictions. According to research by Ronseal, more than 40% of Britons are unaware some sheds will require a planning application.
Yet even outhouses that meet permitted development heights can loom large and cause tension in tightly packed British gardens. Emma watched her husband creep into their garden under cover of darkness late one night to measure the shed their neighbours were constructing close to the boundary, because it looked so vast. “He climbed on to our picnic table with a tape measure,” she says. “It’s so close to our boundary that it wasn’t a stretch to measure it – he didn’t even need to hang over the fence.”
The shed measured under 2.5 metres and the couple had to accept that it was permitted. They felt that mentioning anything to the neighbour would only cause bad feeling, but while they have grown used to the building, which is barely used, they worry about how potential buyers will view it. “The overriding factor is they are small gardens,” says Emma. The plots are around 10 metres by 7 metres. The neighbour mentioned their plans, but “we thought it would be a pod … we didn’t anticipate the sheer size”, she says. “Remaining friends” was most important. “We get on well and didn’t want to rock the boat,” she adds. “But if it was being used as a home office constantly, with phone calls being made and they’re looking back at you, maybe we’d feel differently.”
Dr Mike Talbot, a psychotherapist and the CEO of UK Mediation, says the company has noticed a rise in inquiries concerning external structures such as sheds, garden rooms, hot tubs and even trampolines. He believes that councils tend not to intervene and often recommend mediation. Fewer than 10% of inquiries actually reach that stage, though, because while the opposing neighbour is usually the one to call them, they must then approach the shed builder – who generally does not wish to join (or share the £450 cost of the process). He recalls an occasion when a shed window “was mysteriously broken” and things turned nasty: “The shed owner went round and threatened to smash their neighbour’s face in.”
However, if mediation takes place, it can be positive. One set of neighbours built a shed to be used as a playroom and office with a window on the neighbour’s side. They had previously had a good relationship, but were “not talking … which is quite common”. (Talbot says “slamming doors or dirty looks in the driveway” are other repercussions.) The compromise was blocking the window and putting up a trellis, which appeased both parties. In another example, an agreement was made concerning the times at which the shed owner’s teenage children could use the space.
Talbot believes that people are “more insular” than they used to be and less concerned than previous generations were about getting on with their neighbours. Social media plays a part, too. “We are so much more subject to scrutiny and you know that, if you do something people consider to be out of order, it’s going to be on the local Facebook group,” he says. “Trust is slower to build; we are more cautious of whom we talk to.” But if neighbours build a good relationship, he says, they are less likely to react negatively if a large shed does appear.
Dan has a good relationship with his neighbours, so when they approached him to discuss their plans for a structure in their 20-metre garden for a family member to stay in, “I had no problem”, he says. As it would be more than 2.5 metres high and a habitable dwelling, the neighbours had to apply for planning permission. “I looked at the plans and it seemed reasonable,” says Dan.
However, issues encountered during construction meant the height increased. When Dan and his partner arrived home from holiday, “I went to our bathroom, looked out of the window and said: ‘You need to come here immediately and look at this monstrosity,’” he says. After an emotional conversation with the neighbours, they agreed to take the height down, but Dan believes it is still about 1.5 metres higher than agreed in the original plans. For the sake of keeping good relations, he has decided not to go to the council and has instead spent about £2,000 on fencing to try to hide the structure.
“I did not want to ruin their plans,” he says. “But I did feel emotionally blackmailed.” While he is getting used to it, and continues to chat pleasantly with the neighbours, “when we look out of our living room window, it’s right there. And if someone is stood in that building, they are looking right in at us. It just feels slightly invasive. When people come round and notice it, they go: ‘Oh my God, what?’ They’re shocked.” Dan’s main worry, however, is the impact it may have when he comes to sell his house.
Linda, meanwhile, hopes to rebuild relations with her neighbours. “We’re not horrible people, on either side,” she says. “No one has done anything wrong here.” But unlike her shed, which will weather and soften, she knows there is no guarantee of this.
Names have been changed

‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

Wielding a broom and dustpan, Marta García, 60, darted past the edges of tents, sweeping up bits of litter as she passed a poster that read: “What kind of times are these, when we need to defend the obvious?”
On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further.
“At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.”
Days earlier, many across Spain had watched in shock as news channels showed Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman with a disability, being evicted from the home where she had lived for seven decades. The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other.
Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.”
Abascal’s lawyers reportedly reached a deal for her to return home on Monday evening. “If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone,” her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told reporters, saying it could “help to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general”.
At the encampment earlier on Monday, many described the days of nationwide protests and the encampment as a turning point in a movement that had long simmered as rents rose by 80% within a decade, while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.
“We need stability,” said David Iglesias, 25, as he described how the ever-soaring prices had forced people to put their lives on hold to try to keep a roof over their heads.
“People who want to have children should be able to do so, even if they are renting. People who dream of becoming musicians or barbers should have the chance to do so and not have to worry that they need to work, work, work to pay for housing,” he said. “It’s an endless loop that is undermining the mental health of young people.”
As he spoke, a large banner flapped nearby, reading: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, cryptobros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.”
The swelling encampment had prompted a raft of comparisons to 2011, when the Indignados, or 15M movement, began with a month-long occupation of the same Madrid plaza before snowballing into a force that had reshaped Spanish politics. Iglesias, however, brushed off the similarity. “That was about a general demand for change,” he said. “But we have a goal, and if this goal isn’t met by Tuesday, we’ll have to take action somehow.”
It was a nod to the informal camp slogan, launched by housing campaigners and oft-repeated by protesters in recent days: “Either the rentier economy falls, or the government does.”
As Spain’s government gears up for its weekly Tuesday meeting, campaigners have put forward a list of demands, from measures to halt evictions to the regulation of short-term and room rentals, making it clear that this is being seen as a make-or-break moment.
On Sunday, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his government was “working around the clock to introduce a royal decree on housing on Tuesday”.
The protests have put the Socialist leader in a complicated spot; while his coalition government includes leftwing forces who have long pushed for change, Spain’s fractured parliament means his chances are slim of attracting support for measures that could bring about real change.
Still, the momentum has continued to grow across the country, fuelled by the campaigners who occupied the offices of Madrid’s social housing agency on Monday to those in Barcelona who began the day by blocking off major thoroughfares.
“Today cannot be a day like all others,” said Enric Aragonès of the Barcelona Tenants’ union, ahead of a protest planned for Tuesday evening in the city. “There are only 24 hours left until we find out whether the government will approve a decree that is a sham or genuine.”
In Madrid, the calls for change had attracted a diverse group, including Oscar-winning film director Pedro Almodóvar, who visited on Sunday to voice his support for the protesters. “The housing problem is paralysing Spanish life,” he told broadcaster RTVE.
Sitting cross-legged in a tent and knitting to pass the time, Guillermo Esteve said he was part of a group of vegans who had decided to show their support by joining the encampment. “We’re a group of people who believe we can do things better,” he said, describing his hope that this would be part of a sweeping change that would start with the real estate sector, then address the precarity of the labour market and eventually tackle production systems. “We want laws that give us hope, not what we have now.”
The sentiment was echoed by García, the retired schoolteacher. “This camp is an example of how people still believe that things can change,” she said. “I have my life sorted out; I have a house. But I have two daughters who are sharing bedrooms because they have no other choice. So I can’t just sit around doing nothing.”
This was how she had ended up in the heart of Madrid on a Monday afternoon, sweeping the city’s central plaza, she added with a laugh. “Look, if I didn’t think this was going to amount to anything, I would just stay home and cry,” she said. “But I have to stay helpful.”
With contribution from Stephen Burgen in Barcelona

‘Inception’ trips, Chinamaxxing and undertourism: Euronews Travel’s top trends and predictions for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:49 UTC
13:00:49 KST

From holidays within a holiday to undertourism and longevity retreats, the Euronews Travel team picks out some of the trends and destinations for travel in 2027.
Travel is constantly changing and 2027 looks set to bring plenty of new ways to see the world.
From holidays designed around health and longevity to a growing appetite for slower, more meaningful escapes, travellers are becoming more selective about how they spend their time away.
Next year will be huge for astronomy lovers, with August’s so called “eclipse of the century” viewable in parts of southern Spain and north Africa, while those in the know will be eschewing Bali for lesser explored parts of Indonesia.
It’s likely in 2027 that travellers will also look beyond the usual hotspots, rethink when and where they travel, and find new reasons to visit destinations that have long been overlooked.
There’s plenty to get your teeth into – from the rise of longevity retreats and the changing face of wellness travel to new takes on adventure, culture and accommodation.
These are the trends the Euronews Travel team expects to shape travel over the year ahead.
Our predictions and trends for travel in 2027
Eyes on the skies
It was already a big year in 2026 for those who dream of the stars, with the Artemis II mission successfully completing a lunar flyby and a solar eclipse that plunged parts of Spain and Iceland into darkness for more than two minutes.
Next year will be even bigger, with the “eclipse of the century” on 2 August and Artemis III planned for some point in 2027.
The August eclipse earned its moniker as it will be the longest total eclipse on easily accessible land in the 21st century, with cities in Egypt near the point of greatest eclipse seeing the sun blocked by the moon for more than six minutes.
Spain will be lucky once again, with totality in cities including Cádiz, Marbella and Málaga, but the eclipse will also be visible in countries including Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria and Saudi Arabia.
It’s also a big year for those who fantasise about exploring the universe, with Star Wars celebrating its 50th anniversary.
While there will of course be re-runs of the original Star Wars in cinemas, on the travel front, I imagine there will be a resurgence in visiting iconic filming locations around the globe, like the limestone karsts of Guilin, Lake Como, and Wadi Rum. Think set-jetting, but with a hint of nostalgia. Dianne Apen-Sadler
Beyond second and third cities into ‘undertourised’ destinations
Earlier this year, I made the case for giving European destinations beyond the famed capitals a little more love by venturing to “second cities” – the places travellers may overlook because they sit beyond countries’ main tourist hubs.
My guide to some of the continent’s best second cities included Basel in Switzerland, for its dynamic art scene, and Cambridge in the UK for its punt vessel cruises across the River Cam.
If 2026 was the year of second cities, 2027 could take that instinct even further. I see travellers increasingly seeking out destinations that are largely under the radar.
Social media continues to have a major impact on how we discover and plan trips, but it can also very quickly turn obscure destinations into a must-see, and overcrowded, destination overnight.
As travellers become more conscious of this, with Skift research finding as many as 42% of travellers saying they would actively avoid overcrowded places, the search for slower-paced and quieter travel could see second and even third cities lose their allure.
As such, we may see more footfall next to cities such as Japan's Toyama over Tokyo or Osaka. Around an hour away from the Japanese capital by air, the prefecture’s tourism strategy has been to retain its rural charm and offer visitors a slow mountain escape with scenic hikes and local delicacies.
At the turn of the year, we may also see more initiatives from destinations to not only spotlight “undertourised” destinations, but also manage tourist flows. Earlier this year, I spoke with Mayor of Dubrovnik Mato Franković, who discussed the “Respect the City” strategy to tackle overtourism in the “Pearl of the Adriatic”. Could this strategy work across other popular tourism destinations? Fakhriya M. Suleiman
Chinamaxxing
It seems nowadays that you can add -maxxing to the end of anything and turn it into a trend. Euronews Travel is not above this, and I will not be apologising for it, even if it’s “cringe”.
Post-Covid, there was a massive influx of tourists to Japan, but with the easing of visa restrictions, I think China is enjoying its long overdue moment in the spotlight.
Citizens from nearly 80 countries can now visit for up to 30 days visa free, which is barely enough time to discover the country’s futuristic cities, many UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and varied landscapes that will take your breath away.
Social media is also a big factor – when TikTok was temporarily shut down in the US last year, many users flocked to Douyin, the Chinese version of the app, and autotranslate on X has meant more people are interacting with users from the country.
Just last week, the payment app TenPayGo, which works with Apple Pay and international cards, launched, making it easier for international travellers, too.
I visited China earlier this year (read all about it here) but I’m desperate to go back, and I can easily see it becoming somewhere I visit again and again. Dianne Apen-Sadler
The ‘Inception trip’: A holiday within a holiday within a holiday
Multi-destination travel is not a new trend by any means, but whenever we book a holiday these days we seem to have a regular habit: we book one trip, then start booking other trips within it – often after we’ve arrived.
Inspired by Christopher Nolan’s epic dream within a dream within a dream concept, I call this the “Inception trip” – a holiday within a holiday within a holiday. We’ve done this a few times now, but this summer in Spain was a perfect example.
What began as an escape to the Spanish Pyrenees, and a few days in Barcelona tagged on at the end, somehow evolved into a much bigger road trip. Taüll in the Vall de Boí was our base, but once we arrived, we extended our exploration even further. Much, much further.
As well as day trips into the Val d’Aran and across the mountains to the medieval town of Aínsa, we made the decision to drive across northern Spain for an afternoon and night in San Sebastián to watch the solar eclipse. That happened on 12 August and we only decided that morning to venture north to see it.
It was a long drive, but totally worth it. Not just for the eclipse itself but also to scratch San Sebastián off my bucket list. Being in this trendy city for around only 18 hours, we did pack a lot in and got a taste, literally, of why it’s so popular.
The more I travel the more I seem to like the “Inception trip” format – and I suspect I’ll be doing more of it in 2027. Where’s next on my list? Who knows, but whatever we plan to travel to definitely won’t be the final itinerary. Mike Starling
Type B travel
Social media is great for exposing you to new cities you hadn’t considered visiting before, but once you’ve booked a trip it seems like the algorithm knows and keeps pumping your feed full of content about it.
It’s ruining the element of surprise in travel, with more than two thirds of tourists saying a destination felt familiar because of the amount of videos they had consumed about it, even if they hadn’t been before.
Which is why I think Type B travel is going to have a big moment in 2027.
Spontaneous, and maybe slightly chaotic, Type B travel means rocking up to a new place with no plans and nothing booked, and letting your heart decide what to do.
I think it’s a natural extension of 2026’s lore chasing, which involves doing things you wouldn’t usually do because you’re on holiday and you want some great stories to travel home with.
I also think it could go a long way to helping with problems around overtourism – you won’t end up in line for the next viral spot if you simply haven’t heard or seen it. Dianne Apen-Sadler
The evolution of longevity retreats
Like multi-destination travel, longevity retreats may also be nothing new, but the way they’re being approached is likely to shift in 2027.
The move will be towards healthspan rather than simply lifespan, namely helping people stay healthier and more active for longer.
Next year, expect longevity retreats to become less about a quick wellness reset and more about understanding your body, identifying potential health risks and returning home with changes you can actually maintain.
For travellers, that could mean anything from metabolic testing and tailored nutrition plans to sleep analysis, movement assessments and consultations with doctors or other qualified practitioners. Some retreats are also experimenting with treatments such as cryotherapy and hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
Obviously, part of the purpose of healthspan retreats is still very much with longevity in mind – and there are plenty of new openings to be aware of if any aspect of this trend is up your street.
Clinique La Prairie in Phuket is slated to open its doors this November. In a Tri Vananda – or multigenerational living community – setting, its offerings will include preventive health, personalised nutrition, movement and overall wellbeing.
Meanwhile, in Austria, Naturhotel Forsthofgut in Leogang recently expanded its wellness facility by introducing a dedicated, science-backed longevity space known as waldSPA Health. Health programmes here include intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia training, a non-invasive oxygen therapy thought to rejuvenate cells. Saskia O’Donoghue
Ditch hotel stays for checking into authentic experiences
Are all hotels the same? Well, according to research, as many as 74% of people either strongly or somewhat agreed that many hotel brands feel very similar to one another. Its findings also revealed that travellers are increasingly seeking authenticity when they go abroad. While I don’t think hotels are going anywhere in 2027, travellers may become more curious to look beyond them.
Rather than simply being an afterthought, I see niche stays forming part of the reason why someone chooses to travel abroad. I for one am very tempted to visit Morocco just to experience what the travel guides have been raving about: staying in a riad rather than a conventional hotel.
A scroll through the “#riadmorocco” hashtag is filled with snaps of travellers’ experiences these technicoloured architectural marvels built around an inward facing design where an open-air courtyard with a fountain take centre stage.
Meanwhile, Japanese Ryokans may be among the world's oldest forms of a hotel, dating back to the 8th century. Traditionally, these inns feature tatami flooring of woven straw-based rectangular mats, iconic futon bedding and yukata robes. A stay at a ryokan usually starts with a Japanese breakfast and ends with kaiseki ryori – a Japanese multicourse dinner of local delights, such as fish, soup and seasonal veggies.
There’s also the trend of volunteer exchange-for programmes, where visitors work for a set number of hours each week in exchange for their bed and board. Whether taking care of animals or painting and decorating, this sounds like a great way to not only meet like-minded people, but during downtime, explore a new destination, without having to worry about accommodation costs. Fakhriya M. Suleiman
Indonesia – so much more than just Bali
Think of Indonesia, and you’ll probably immediately land on Bali. The island has long been an enormously popular holiday destination for westerners seeking affordable luxury and a beautiful – and varied – landscape.
More recently, though, there’s been something of a backlash against Bali, with travellers unhappy at developers knocking down long-established local businesses.
I went two years ago and while it’s absolutely a fun spot and, in parts, stunning, it did feel incredibly overtouristed, with congested roads full of travellers packing in as many destinations as possible.
As Bali’s popularity has grown, so have its prices. In some cases, accommodation and food costs rival those in Europe, meaning one of the biggest reasons to visit is no more.
Luckily though, Indonesia is huge – and has countless little-visited places, so a more affordable, authentic and quieter experience is very much possible.
If you’re into nature-based, off-the-beaten-path trips, you don’t have to go far from Bali. Lombok is right next door, and boasts lower prices as well as unspoilt beaches, waterfalls, endless hiking opportunities and Mount Rinjani, the second-highest volcano and mountain in the whole country.
True nature lovers should head to Komodo National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site established to conserve the unique Komodo dragon.
You can still spot them here, as well as other creatures including the orange-footed scrub fowl, the Timor deer and various species of whales, dolphins, and sea turtles.
For true remote exploration, you could do worse than to visit Raja Ampat. The remote archipelago is famous for having some of the richest marine biodiversity on earth.
Only reachable by ferry, the region is made up of hundreds of jungle-covered islands, and is known for its beaches – with the bluest water you’ve ever seen – and coral reefs, all rich with marine life. Saskia O’Donoghue
Urban active travel: The city is the gym
Sports tourism used to be relatively easy to define: fans travelling to events to watch their favourite teams, or taking part in activities such as marathons, cycling or golf. But since the pandemic, the sector has really evolved, with outdoor adventure, wellness and fitness now becoming part of the offering.
In 2027, I predict that evolution will be reflected in our cities and towns. Running and walking are perhaps the most obvious examples. Look at any major city’s tourism website and you’ll find recommended routes for a jog or a stroll.
Some hotels have even been embracing this idea for years. For example, Westin Hotels & Resorts has more than 150 “Run Concierges” worldwide, who can accompany guests on group runs and help them discover a destination while exercising.
With city-break visitors looking to the outdoors rather than just hitting the gym, I expect more hotels and destinations to follow, offering curated routes through parks and past landmarks. This could be particularly useful for solo and business travellers who want an active way to explore.
The “race-cation” trend may be booming, but runners don’t necessarily need an event as a reason to travel. Running, cycling and fitness are increasingly becoming ways to experience a destination. Mike Starling

British warship hits frigate with live Naval Strike Missile
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:31 BST
13:00:31 KST

The Royal Navy used both of its newest anti-ship missiles during a joint US-UK live-fire exercise off the Hebrides that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron operating from her flight deck.
The round Portland fired carried a warhead and was aimed at a real ship rather than a range target, which the service describes as the first Royal Navy firing of a Naval Strike Missile, although HMS Somerset launched one off Norway in September last year.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, HMS Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of Naval Strike Missile marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.”
Petty Officer James Kenyon, an above water warfare specialist aboard the frigate, fired it. “To be involved in such a high-profile exercise is the highlight of my career,” he said. “Being the first person to fire war-shot Naval Strike Missile and achieve a hit is a very proud moment, and one that will stay with me for the rest of my career. This was the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service, and I am glad that I was able to contribute.”
Commander Dafydd Bryden, the ship’s commanding officer, said: “The opportunity to fire anti-ship missiles against a decommissioned warship is an important test of our warfighting capability. This engagement proved the effectiveness of these systems as well as the sailors and aircrew who operate them. We remain ready to fight and win at sea.”
Sea Venom was fired from the Wildcat during the same serial, and Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, confirmed to journalists that it was the missile’s first live firing since reaching initial operating capability, and that it hit the target. According to the Royal Navy, the helicopter completed the full kill chain by detecting, identifying and striking the target rather than simply releasing the weapon.
Lieutenant Commander Rhydian Edwards, test and evaluation commander at the Maritime Aviation Strike Operational Advantage Group, said: “This was a landmark moment for the Wildcat Force. For the first time we demonstrated the live firing of an operational Sea Venom missile against a representative maritime target. More importantly, we proved our ability to execute the full maritime strike kill chain under realistic operational conditions.
“This was about giving commanders confidence that Wildcat can find, fix and strike maritime targets using Sea Venom as part of a wider task group. The lessons learned from this activity will directly inform future tactics, training and operational capability development, ensuring Maritime Aviation Strike remains ready to fight and win when called upon.”
The Naval Strike Missile was brought into Royal Navy service under an interim arrangement to replace Harpoon, which left service in 2023, and has been fitted to Type 23 frigates and Type 45 destroyers using equipment transferred between hulls as ships enter and leave refit. Built by Kongsberg, the weapon is a sea-skimming missile with a low radar signature and a range well beyond that of the system it replaced, and it can strike land targets as well as ships. The service says it carries an advanced warhead, travels close to supersonic speeds and can reach targets more than 100 miles away while evading detection by skimming the sea, and that it will be complementary to the Future Cruise Anti-Ship Weapon, intended to become the fleet’s premier long-range anti-ship missile aboard the Type 26 and Type 31 frigates through the Mk41 vertical launch system.
Sea Venom, built by MBDA, is the Wildcat’s principal anti-ship weapon and replaced the Sea Skua carried by the Lynx. The Royal Navy describes it as designed to defeat corvette sized vessels or disable frigates, destroyers and other larger ships, with a Wildcat able to carry four at once, and says it can also be used overland against bunkers, buildings and vehicles. Readers will have seen the same missile turn up this week on a very different platform, fitted by STARK to an uncrewed surface vessel built near Plymouth.
The two British weapons were part of a wider engagement in which USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which delivered the final hit and sank the ship, as we reported.
Weapons were used in order of reach too we understand, with the longest range ordnance going first. Ndukwe said the American side started with the SM-6 before moving in to shorter range systems, a sequence designed to get the most out of the sensors fitted to the hull for battle damage assessment.
Atlantic Thunder 2026 was led by United States Sixth Fleet and drew in forces from five American task forces alongside the Royal Navy, the Royal Air Force and the United States Air Force. Lieutenant Commander Paul Atkins, the United Kingdom lead project officer for the exercise, said: “Atlantic Thunder 26 demonstrated the enduring strength of the UK-US alliance and the close partnership between the Royal Navy and the United States Navy. Operating together in a demanding environment, we showcased our ability to integrate seamlessly, share expertise and deliver a highly capable, interoperable maritime force. Through combined training and operations, we have strengthened our collective warfighting capability, reinforcing our ability to deter potential adversaries and deliver maritime combat power whenever and wherever it is required.”

How John Farnham pulled off one of music's greatest comebacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

How John Farnham pulled off one of music's greatest comebacks with Whispering Jack
Forty years after its release, John Farnham's Whispering Jack remains one of the most remarkable stories in Australian music history.
The 1986 album spent 25 weeks at number one, produced enduring hits that remain part of our national conscience, and transformed John Farnham from a fading teen idol into one of the country's most beloved performers.
Its centrepiece, You're The Voice, is bigger than a pop song: the unofficial anthem still inspires singalongs at pubs, stadiums and festival fields decades later.
None of it was supposed to happen.
By the mid-80s, Farnham's career was drifting. Record labels weren't interested. His attempts at chart success weren't connecting.
A stint fronting world-conquering Aussie rockers Little River Band didn't kickstart the resurgence he hoped for.
So, Whispering Jack wasn't the work of a music industry machine backing a sure thing. It was the result of the work of a small team of people convinced they saw something the rest of the industry had missed.
One last chance
John Farnham's first taste of fame came early.
As Johnny Farnham, he dominated Australian charts in the late 1960s and early 1970s, scoring a massive hit with Sadie (The Cleaning Lady), the best selling Australian single of the '60s.
But, as tastes changed, Farnham's commercial fortunes faded. He moved into musical theatre and TV, proving he remained an endearing entertainer, but not necessarily a recording artist to watch.
A reinvention was needed. Johnny became John. And while he had flashes of success, like cracking back into the Top 10 with a version of The Beatles's Help in 1980, the momentum didn't stick.
His time with Little River Band proved valuable, particularly the exposure to large-scale touring in America, but didn't provide the breakthrough Farnham and his manager Glenn Wheatley, who died in 2022, were searching for.
By 1985, many in the industry believed Farnham's biggest successes were behind him. Wheatley never accepted that.
"We all knew what he had," Wheatley told News Corp in 2018. "He's one of the greatest singers of our time. We just had to find the right songs for him."
Finding songs wasn't too hard — there were plenty around. Finding someone willing to back the project was another story.
Neither record labels nor producers showed much interest. Eventually, Wheatley and Farnham decided to do it themselves.
"I had to find out whether I could get the money to make the album for a start," Farnham told the ABC's John Hall in 1987.
Wheatley's label became his record company and the gamble got bigger. The budget for the album was about $150,000.
Speaking to Jen Jewel Brown for the National Film and Sound Archive in 2014, Wheatley recalled: "I ended up having to do it on my label again. I had to mortgage my house to do it."
"I couldn't not do it; not to John," he recalled in Clark Forbes's 1989 book Whispering Jack.
"What the hell, I had nothing to lose either. I simply had to go for this."
Building Whispering Jack
The team eventually settled on live sound engineer Ross Fraser as producer. He wasn't a known name, and it wasn't a conventional move.
It turned out to be a masterstroke.
Together, Farnham, Fraser and Wheatley embarked on an exhaustive search for material.
"I must have listened to 2,000 songs, easy, from all over the world," Farnham told Hall.
"We sent telexes all over the world to all the publishers and record companies that we were looking for songs.
"We literally got two boxes, we put 'no' on one box and 'maybe' on the other box, and we just went through them all.
"I had to listen to the songs in their entirety because, being a budding songwriter myself, I understand how much work these people put into it. So, I had to at least give them that courtesy."
Even then, the work had barely begun.
The eventual album only contained 10 tracks, but every arrangement was meticulously worked over. A month of pre-production was followed by more than two months in the studio.
"We were in there for 18 hours a day, pumping away, and we really worked hard," Farnham told Hall.
You can still hear that commitment when you hit play on Whispering Jack 40 years on.
Its sound – synthesisers, drum machines and enormous production – is unmistakably rooted in the '80s. Yet somehow it doesn't feel trapped there.
The commitment in those performances — from Farnham and his band — and the strength of those songs prove this hard-won success was well deserved.
Finding You're The Voice
Whispering Jack was still missing something when a tape arrived from England.
"The last song we found was You're The Voice," Wheatley told the National Film and Sound Archive.
A publisher insisted Farnham would love it.
"When I first heard it, my heart almost stopped," Farnham told the Toronto Star in 1987. "I felt like I'd discovered lost treasure."
According to the story that has since become part of Australian music folklore, label manager Doris Tyler heard the song first and wasn't especially convinced. But Ross Fraser was.
Driving to Farnham's house one afternoon, the producer reportedly played the cassette over and over. The more he listened, the more certain he was that the song had to be on the record.
It made the cut, but when it was released, it wasn't an easy sell. Wheatley and the team were dogged in chasing airplay before commercial radio fully embraced it.
Once they did, there was no stopping it.
The pay-off
You're The Voice became a phenomenon and its success propelled Whispering Jack to number one, where it remained for 25 weeks.
Follow-up singles Pressure Down, A Touch of Paradise and Reasons kept momentum rolling. The album became much bigger than anyone had dared imagine.
That mortgage Wheatley took out to fund the album was repaid many times over. Whispering Jack went on to become the highest-selling album in Australia by an Australian artist.
It also reached number six in the UK and topped the charts in Sweden. You're The Voice charted across Europe, an unusual feat for an Australian artist at the time.
When Wheatley and Farnham heard the news that the album had reached number one, they were together in a car.
"I was saying, 'Do you realise John that we have a number one record?'" Wheatley recalled in Forbes's book Whispering Jack.
"I looked towards him at the traffic lights, and he had tears coming down his cheeks.
"He said, 'I can't believe this is happening'."
For Farnham, this wasn't just about commercial success, it was about vindication.
"I feel more credible now," he told the Toronto Star at the time.
"I'm really working hard.
"All my life things have come too easily to me. I put everything on the line this time. And now it feels as if I deserve it."

Some of these models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic have been involved in security incidents during testing.

The attacks come as Russia has begun hitting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with faster, high-flying jet drones.
Emergency officials said the strike on the National Academy of Sciences on Monday killed two people, with one person’s body recovered from the rubble later in the evening.
Video shared online appeared to show a fast-moving drone slamming into the building at a steep angle and exploding, sending smoke into a clear sky. People were seen leaning out of windows as bright orange flames engulfed part of the building.
Volodymyr Horbulin, a former secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council, told the public broadcaster Suspilne that he was at work at the academy when it came under attack. He said his assistant, who was near the building, was killed and that he was also slightly wounded.

In a statement, the academy called the attack “Russian terror” and “barbarity” aimed at “peaceful people who were simply at their workplaces”.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of cynicism for hitting a scientific institution during the workday.
“Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries of what it believes the world will tolerate,” he said in a statement, urging Ukraine’s allies to provide more air defences.
Jet-powered drones
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces also hit a medical facility in Kyiv on Monday. He said at least nine people had been killed in Russian drone strikes throughout the country, while more than 80 people were wounded.
In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was still having difficulty countering the faster, high-flying Russian jet-powered drones.
“New interceptors are being actively tested,” he said. “Some combat groups are using them, but, of course, some details still need to be refined to achieve enough effectiveness and scale. We are speeding up the developers.”
According to the Ukrainian president, 90 of 120 drones fired on Ukraine on Monday were jet-propelled, rather than propeller-driven, with an interception rate for this type of drone at 57 percent.
Widening targets
Officials said the Russian strikes on Kyiv also targeted a pharmaceutical company and petrol stations. In other cities and regions, civilian facilities, businesses and communications infrastructure were hit.
In the southeastern city of Dnipro, a Russian drone attack on a business centre killed three people and wounded 19, according to officials. Another person was killed in a logistics office in Synelnykove, southeast of Dnipro, the regional governor said.
Emergency services said an attack on infrastructure in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia wounded 32 people.
Al Jazeera’s Jonah Hull, reporting from Kyiv, said Russia has been hitting economic targets across Ukraine “in a rolling series of strikes that have been ongoing for six days now”, during the day and night.
“Data centres increasingly being hit, as well as digital and communications infrastructure,” he said. “Kyiv Star, the country’s biggest cell provider, was hit on Sunday, as was the second biggest, Vodafone Ukraine. The government is said to be preparing for the worst: a total blackout in communications should that come.”
The Russian attacks have brought Kyiv “firmly into the eye of this war”, Hull added.
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, targeting oil refineries as well as online retailers to try to undermine revenues and support for Moscow’s war effort.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine struck Russian oil facilities in the Krasnodar region and two defence plants.
Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians.

OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:34:34 UTC
12:34:34 KST

OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT
In short:
OpenAI says it wants to "rebuild trust with the Australian people" after an agent hacked into Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service.
The company said the breach was undertaken by an internal-only model that did not have the safeguards used in publicly available products.
OpenAI has also scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns.
OpenAI has apologised for its AI agent breaching Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service, and has shelved its upcoming release of its next-generation ChatGPT model.
Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics portal administered by Services Australia.
In a blog post on OpenAI's website published on Tuesday morning, the company set out what they "will do to rebuild trust with the Australian people".
"In Australia, we are committing resources and expertise to support affected agencies," the post said.
The company also said they should have handled their response to the breach better.
"We are sorry and working to do better in the future,"
"This is a new kind of cyber incident which represents an emerging global challenge."
More details of the breach emerge
The ChatGPT maker said the breach happened during training on an "internal-only OpenAI model that was not intended for public release and without the full set of safeguards used in our publicly available products".
During this training, the agent discovered a way to gain non-public access to Services Australia Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service where it ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and statistics, as well as wrote files, the company said.
The company also confirmed an OpenAI model accessed the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research's public Crime Mapping Tool to research public crime statistics.
Agents also discovered an exposed access key to query the Victorian Agency for Health Information's reporting system.
"The extent to which this information should have been accessible is unclear, and depends on VAHI's access policies," the post said.
Lastly, the post outlined how agents retrieved statistics from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, where it downloaded material that "appears to have been publicly available".
"Separate attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful."
PM says OpenAI cooperating with government
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "OpenAI have been very constructive and open in engaging" with the government taskforce investigating the hack.
"This is a challenge that the world is dealing with."
The prime minster said artificial intelligence can improve economic growth and productivity, but comes with risks.
"We've seen those risks exposed,"
"So we need to work this through, we see this as an opportunity, but we want to seize the benefit whilst mitigating the risks."
OpenAI said they would support Australian governments through credits from their $US1 billion ($1.42 billion) Daybreak for Frontline Defenders program — an initiative they describe as support for essential service providers to improve their frontline cyber defences.
The company also said it would establish a taskforce "with independent Australian expertise to develop practical policy recommendations".
OpenAI's chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will fly to Sydney to appear at the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence on October 6.
Next-gen ChatGPT model scrapped
OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation AI model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's safety and alignment standards.
GPT-6.1 Astra was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance.
OpenAI's head of safety systems, Saachi Jain, said GPT-6.1 Astra improved model laziness but "it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done".
The decision comes ahead of OpenAI's developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.

Taiwan adds five medals at Asian Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:32:54 UTC
12:32:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan added five medals on Monday at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, including a silver in the men's 4x100-meter relay and four bronze medals in track and field, badminton, table tennis, and shooting.
The first medal of the day came from Lin Chung-wei (林仲威), who won bronze in the men's 400-meter hurdles in 48.74 seconds. The time was a personal best for Lin and placed him third behind Qatar's Bassem Hemeida and Japan's Taiju Goto, per UDN.
Lin entered the final after running 49.10 seconds in the heats, the second-fastest qualifying time. He remained among the leaders throughout the final and was level for second after clearing the final hurdle before crossing the line in third.
Lin's bronze gave Taiwan its second track and field medal of the games, following Fu Chao-hsuan's (傅兆玄) men's high jump gold on Sunday. A silver in the men's 4x100-meter relay brought Taiwan's track and field haul to three medals: one gold, one silver, and one bronze.
The relay team of Yang Chun-han (楊俊瀚), Lai Po-hsiang (賴柏翔), Chen Wen-pu (陳玟溥) and Huang Tso-chun (黃左軍) ran 38.32 seconds in the final to win silver and break Taiwan's national record, per CNA.
The time also marked the team's best performance of the season. The silver was Taiwan's first Asian Games men's 4x100-meter relay medal since the 2010 Guangzhou Games. The team had run 38.80 seconds in the qualifying round before improving significantly in the final.
Taiwan also collected three bronze medals in events outside track and field.
In badminton, mixed-doubles pair Ye Hong-wei (葉宏蔚) and Zhan You-zhen (詹又蓁) lost 21-13, 21-9 to China's Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin in the semifinals. Because the Asian Games badminton tournament does not hold a bronze-medal match, the semifinal loss secured Taiwan a bronze medal. The medal ended a 16-year wait for Taiwan in Asian Games mixed doubles, per CNA.
In table tennis, Lin Yun-ju (林昀儒) won bronze in men's singles after losing a seven-game semifinal to China's Lin Shidong. Lin reached the Asian Games men's singles semifinals for the first time and also won a bronze medal in the men's team event earlier in the Games.
Taiwan's fourth bronze of the day came in the women's 25-meter pistol team event. Cheng Yen-ching (鄭晏晴), Tien Chia-chen (田家榛), and Chen Yu-ru (陳俞如) combined for 1,734 points to finish third behind China and South Korea, per an NTNU press release.
Taiwan's medal tally in the Asian Games includes three gold, eight silver, and 23 bronze medals, for 34 medals overall. Taiwan was ranked 13th in the medal standings as of Monday night.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Chicago Director Dennis Lei (類延峰) called for stronger US support for Taiwan as China seeks to limit its international engagement, WVIK reported Sunday.

Lei said China’s military threats and gray-zone tactics are undermining regional peace and stability. Beijing has also sought to discourage other countries from maintaining normal exchanges and cooperation with Taipei, he added.
Lei pointed to statements by the US and other countries surrounding the Trump-Xi meeting that emphasized the importance of cross-strait stability. He said they reflected broad international concern about unilateral attempts to change the status quo.
He also cited bipartisan backing in the US Congress, saying more than 60 senators and representatives had expressed solidarity with Taiwan. Taipei will continue working with Washington and other partners to preserve cross-strait stability, he said.
Lei said closer Taiwan-US relations also bring economic benefits. About 40% of Taiwan’s outbound investment went to the US last year, making it the country’s largest overseas investment destination, compared with about 80% going to China in 2010, he said.
He attributed the shift to business decisions and changes in global supply chains. Taiwanese exports such as AI servers, semiconductors, electronics, and auto parts can also support US manufacturing, he said.
AI is another key area for collaboration. Taiwan produces advanced chips, while its companies manufacture about 90% of the world’s servers, giving the two sides complementary strengths in the technology sector, Lei said.
Lei also highlighted agricultural trade. The US remains Taiwan’s largest source of agricultural imports, while Taiwan announced plans last year to purchase NT$318.4 billion (US$10 billion) in US farm products.
On security, Lei said China continues to hold military exercises, employ gray-zone tactics, spread disinformation, and interfere with Taiwan’s democracy. He said Taipei would work with like-minded partners to safeguard regional peace.
As Washington and Beijing compete in AI and other advanced technologies, Lei said Taiwan-US collaboration is becoming increasingly important. Taiwan hopes to contribute its semiconductor and manufacturing strengths to help the US maintain its technological edge, he said.

Bush, and NT$445 billion under President Barack Obama. The first Trump administration approved NT$582 billion in arms sales, compared with NT$267 billion under President Joe Biden, while sales under Trump’s second administration have totaled NT$363 billion to date.

North Korea warns UN of Japan’s ‘attempts at rearmament'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:30:21 UTC
12:30:21 KST

Amir Latif Arain
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
North Korea warned the UN on Monday of longtime rival Japan's “attempts at rearmament” while emphasizing that multipolarity in international affairs was an “irresistible trend of the times.”
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, North Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Son-gyong accused Japan of taking advantage of the current volatile international environment.
He said Japan has accelerated its attempts at rearmament with an "unprecedented" commitment, including the revision of its Peace Constitution, the abandonment of its "exclusively defense-oriented policy," the reformation of its military structure and an arms buildup.
"Such actions are casting war clouds over the entire region," Kim warned.
He said that “under the signboard of counterattack capability," Japan has moved ahead with the development and possession of long-range attack weapons that put neighboring countries within striking range.
Condemning recent joint military exercises by the US, Japan and South Korea, Kim accused the United States of conspiring "with its allies to systematically amend and update the anti-North Korea nuclear war scenarios through "provocative war rehearsals of all hues and military build-up."
"The US-Japan-South Korea military alliance, unmistakably aimed at the DPRK, is being evolved by the United States into a more offensive and aggressive military bloc with a nuclear element," he said, referring to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
He reiterated that North Korea's nuclear status is "uncompromisingly" fixed and can never be reversed in any circumstances.
"I would like to reiterate the official position of the DPRK government: the status of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a nuclear weapons state that has been uncompromisingly and permanently fixed both physically and legally with absolutely no turning back, can never be reversed in any circumstances or by any means, no matter how hard and loudly the hostile forces may deny in chorus with all sorts of rhetoric," he said.
Kim observed that multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an “irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.“
"Gone are the days when an individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena."
Kim also indirectly described the US-Israeli war on Iran as "state-sponsored terrorism.”
"The new year started with the most despicable, world startling act of state-sponsored terrorism, followed by worldwide outbreaks of other appalling incidents and events," he said.
Urging the UN to firmly secure its authority and future by promoting equality and cooperation among sovereign states, Kim said the world body should no longer be misused for the sinister political purposes of ''specific forces.''
He said the effects of a disaster-prone abnormal climate have given rise to a succession of extreme high temperatures, droughts, heavy rains and floods in many countries and regions, seriously threatening the survival of mankind.
This, coupled with the spread of communicable diseases and hikes in oil prices, worsened the socio-economic crisis, he added.

Rubio says foreign actor was ‘clearly’ behind suspected RAF Fairford bomb plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:29:33 UTC
12:29:33 KST

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said unequivocally that a foreign actor was involved in the suspected UK bomb plot at RAF Fairford, hours after the five suspects arrested close to the airbase were released on bail.
“What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation,” Rubio said in an interview with Fox News on Monday evening, adding that it “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor.”
Rubio provided no evidence for his claims.
The five men, all British nationals from London in their early 20s, were detained early on Sunday after police were alerted by a local farmer about three white vans driving towards RAF Fairford, a British base that houses US bombers that fly missions against Iran.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.
Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events near RAF Fairford.
While thanking the British authorities for their handling of the incident, Rubio also said a lot of people were “disturbed that some of these people [being investigated] have been released on bail”.
Earlier in the day, Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that he would not have released the suspects on bail. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them.”
Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might be.”
Pressed to give details, Trump said: “I’d rather not. I mean I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I’d rather not say. I would not have released them.”
Trump has previously suggested the plot was known to the US authorities, but British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown.
The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.
He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.
“… But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found.
Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.

Better the French You Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:10:35 UTC
12:10:35 KST

French is a global language with nearly 400 million speakers, the majority of whom live outside of France, and now there is renewed interest in the language as France and Canada have become even more attractive destinations, especially for visitors from the US looking for liberté, egalité, et fraternité.
Another phenomenon encouraging visitors to Francophone countries is the growth of “Generation F,” or Generation Francophone, the new generation of young creatives throughout the Francophone world who “bring the French language to life.”
Once you’ve made the decision to spend time in a French-speaking country, the big choice for most Americans is between France or Québec, the heart of the Francophonie in North America. This decision depends on many factors, ranging from short-term goals to long-term residency plans, so the best advice is to try them both.
French language and Francophone culture bring us together. Any regional differences are the result of our shared—yet unique—history and experience, instructive and enjoyable, rather than barriers to understanding and appreciation.
While French speakers may not need to be concerned about basic communicative language, there are differences in the French spoken around the world, just as there are with other international and global languages.
An initial difference may be in the level of formality used by European speakers of French as opposed to North Americans, with the tutoiement, or informal address, even more easily used among North American Francophones. Some learners may be surprised by the use of char for voiture or auto, or of bon matin instead of bonjour. Even the use of English terms differs between European French and French in the Americas. For example, a university in Québec may grant a maîtrise, while a European Francophone university may grant a master(s). An expression like laisser les bons temps rouler—“let the good times roll”—may not be readily understood beyond Louisiana or North America. In addition, a Francophone from Louisiana may not at first recognize the term poudrerie, used to describe dry, fine snow that may drift with the wind to make highways plowed after snow once again treacherous. Even the word francophone is used relatively less frequently in France than in many other places where French is one of two or more official or prevalent languages.
French is among the most widely used languages in many countries around the world, so communication among cultures and crossing borders—in French—are topics of interest not only to French-speaking Americans but also to Francophones around the world. Any discussion of French, as it is spoken globally, needs to include the Dictionnaire des Francophones, an online collaborative dictionary that includes contributions from around the world.
The French spoken in the US includes influences from around the world, as well as contemporary additions. French is the most widely spoken language after English in Northern New England (Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont) and Louisiana.
In Québec, the Centre de la Francophonie des Amériques (CFA) works to encourage communication and collaboration among Francophones and Francophone communities in the Americas. In the US, the Franco-American Centre in New Hampshire (FAC), CODOFIL (the Conseil pour le Développment du Français en Louisiane), and the Nous Foundation in New Orleans are among organizations that encourage and support French language and culture in the US. In addition, Villa Albertine, the American Association of Teachers of French (AATF), and the Alliance Francaise and Federation des Alliances Françaises des USA work to promote French language and Francophone culture in the US.
Francoresponsabilité—using French whenever and as often as possible—comes to us from Québec and is being put into practice in Louisiana with the Oui Initiative. While the Francophone communities throughout the US and the rest of the Americas may not have the same history, there are many shared ideas and values. Communication among historically relatively isolated communities has been strengthened through modern media and ease of travel.
French has had a presence in what is now the US since the earliest years of the European presence. In Québec, French is the sole official language. French is also widely spoken throughout the US, most notably in New England and Louisiana. In New England, many Francophones are of French-Canadian descent, and they are now being joined by more recent arrivals from around the world. Louisiana has long been a crossroads of French and Francophone culture. In Louisiana, although many of the earliest Francophones were from Québec, the language includes many Caribbean and African influences, along with Acadian (Cajun) elements resulting primarily from Le Grand Dérangement, the expulsion of many Acadians from Canada. Contracts in French are legally accepted in Louisiana and the Code Napoléon still forms the basis of the legal system.
While some words and expressions may differ in French from region to region, this is not actually a barrier to communication but often a starting point for communication and story-telling across cultures, similar to British and American Englishes.
French offers abundant travel and educational opportunities, ranging from tourism and short-term language study to degree programs to immigration—Canadian citizenship is a possibility for many Americans with Franco-American ancestry, and residency permits for France are easier to obtain than most people realize.
Relatively few US students take advantage of the opportunities to study in France or Québec, but enrollments are on the rise…

Column: Beware of Japanese right-wing's attempt to revive militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:07:04 CST
12:07:04 KST

by Zhou Yaxin
Ninety-five years ago, the Sept. 18th Incident shocked China and the world.
It marked the beginning of Japan's long-premeditated aggression against China. The Chinese people rose up in resistance and fought an arduous War of Resistance until securing victory 14 years later, at a staggering cost of 35 million military and civilian casualties.
While the historical wounds have yet to heal, present-day concerns are mounting by the day.
Ninety-five years on, the poisonous legacy of militarism has yet to be fully addressed. Japan's right-wing forces are still going to great lengths to downplay, if not glorify, the history of aggression.
August 15, the day of Japan's unconditional surrender, should be an occasion for it to deeply reflect and repent. This year, however, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, in her capacity as head of the Liberal Democratic Party, made a cash offering to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine that honors 14 Class-A war criminals of World War II. According to Japanese media, she worshiped the shrine from afar, while multiple incumbent cabinet members and lawmakers visited the shrine in person. At the National Memorial Ceremony for the War Dead, Takaichi made no mention of "reflection" or "lessons," the customary language used by successive prime ministers, laying bare her stubborn refusal to reflect on history.
After the end of World War II, Japan never did any serious soul-searching about its war of aggression, nor did it fully purge the remnants of militarism. Many war criminals returned to politics and the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF). These right-wing figures, inheriting the militarist ideology, have tampered with textbooks and historical records and carried out PR and whitewashing campaigns in an attempt to downplay and glorify the history of aggression and colonialism, and indoctrinate Japan's younger generation with right-wing historical narratives. They express "regret over defeat" and portray Japan as a "victim" instead of reflecting on and repenting for its war crimes. By doing so, they distort perceptions among the Japanese people and the international community, and seek public support for the right-wing government's re-militarization agenda.
The right-wing forces represented by Takaichi are also accelerating efforts to revise Japan's three key security documents and seek constitutional revision to expand military capabilities. They have lifted the ban on exports of lethal weapons and signaled an intent to revise Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles. They have deployed long-range missiles with "enemy base strike capabilities." Japan's defense budget has grown for 14 consecutive years, surging to over 9 trillion yen (about 57 billion U.S. dollars) in fiscal 2026, or 2 percent of the country's GDP. Instead of adhering to its "exclusively defense-oriented" policy, Japan has now ripped off the mask of a "peaceful" nation and is attempting to make itself a "war-capable" nation again.
A comparison between Japan today and Japan before World War II reveals striking similarities:
In 1882, Aritomo Yamagata coined the "line of advantage" theory, framing the Korean Peninsula and China as Japan's "lifeline" and laying the ideological groundwork for Japan's annexation of the Korean Peninsula and aggression against China. In November 2025, Takaichi associated a so-called "Taiwan contingency" with a "survival-threatening situation," thereby grossly interfering in China's internal affairs and fabricating an excuse for meddling in Taiwan-related affairs.
Before World War II, Japan invaded Asian countries and imposed colonial rule under the pretext of "Pan-Asianism" and "liberating Asia." Today, Japan justifies its military buildup and expansion in the name of pursuing "proactive pacifism" and upholding the "Indo-Pacific order."
Before World War II, Japan inculcated unwavering loyalty to the Emperor among its people through the Imperial Rescript on Education. Today, the National Defense Academy of Japan retains the "tradition" of making students walk dozens of kilometers overnight to the Yasukuni shrine to worship the war criminals enshrined there. Under the poisonous influence of militarism, a serving JSDF member went so far as to intrude into the Chinese Embassy in Japan with a knife.
Even more dangerously, whenever Japan's economy falls into a slump, it tends to pursue external expansion to divert attention. After the Meiji Restoration, Japan vigorously developed modern industry, but suffered from insufficient domestic capital, widespread bankruptcies among farmers, acute social tensions, severe fiscal pressure, and a narrow domestic market. To secure overseas sources of raw materials and markets for its goods, Japan launched the First Sino-Japanese War, from which it obtained massive reparations and access to the Chinese market. The Showa Financial Crisis of 1927 and the Great Depression of 1929 caused anxiety in Japan, eventually leading to the growth of militarist forces and the launch of external aggression.
Today, the yen has hit a 40-year low, Japan's national debt has risen to over 200 percent of its GDP, prices are soaring, and more than 1,000 companies are going bankrupt each month. The Takaichi government seeks to prop up Japan's economy by bolstering the defense industry and aggressively selling arms abroad, at the risk of reopening Pandora's box of militarism.
In disregard of the postwar international order, Japan is trying to break free from the constraints of the postwar system. It is accelerating re-militarization and posing a real threat to peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific.
History must never be forgotten. Otherwise, past mistakes will be repeated. On the 95th anniversary of the Sept. 18th Incident, we shall never forget the suffering endured by the people of China and other Asian countries that were invaded, nor the atrocities committed by Japanese militarists. All peace-loving nations and peoples should remain vigilant against the resurgence of militarism in Japan and guard against attempts by Japan's right-wing forces to create a new Sept. 18th Incident.

NASA, Boeing outline next steps for Starliner

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- NASA said Monday it plans to conduct an uncrewed Starliner-1 mission to the International Space Station (ISS) as early as December this year or January 2027, with a crewed Starliner-2 mission targeted for 2028.
NASA also announced plans to exercise options for a fifth and sixth Starliner flight to and from the ISS, and said it will work with Boeing and United Launch Alliance to certify the Vulcan rocket for Starliner crew transportation after the final flight of the Atlas V rocket.
The uncrewed Starliner-1 will serve as an engineering evaluation mission to validate improvements made to the spacecraft, verify improved thermal environments, obtain performance data needed for system qualification and identify residual risks ahead of crewed missions, according to NASA.
The agency will use data from Starliner-1 to continue implementing corrective actions identified by its Program Investigation Team and complete the testing and certification required for crewed flight, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said, adding that the current plan is to return astronauts to space on Starliner-2 by 2028.
Boeing's Starliner spacecraft launched in June 2024 on its first crewed flight test, carrying NASA astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, and docked with the ISS. During the flight, some of the spacecraft's reaction control thrusters did not perform as expected, and helium leaks were detected.
NASA ultimately decided to return Starliner to Earth uncrewed, while the two astronauts later returned to Earth aboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft in March 2025.
In February, NASA released findings from its Program Investigation Team into the 2024 crewed flight test. The investigation identified 61 recommendations for NASA.
Based on the findings, Boeing has made thermal modifications to Starliner's service module, which NASA will evaluate on Starliner-1. NASA and Boeing also have jointly decided to implement an additional thruster valve design modification to support spacecraft certification and future crewed flights.
Following Starliner-1, NASA and Boeing will complete the service module thruster valve design modification. Boeing will also implement other improvements, including installing new crew module thrusters and batteries, as well as making minor modifications to the parachute system to improve performance and reliability, NASA said. ■
