NEW DELHI: Bangladesh's home ministry told TOI on Monday that it has launched a search for 43-year-old Assam woman Mumtaz Begum, who was sent to Bangladesh in the intervening night of June 13-14 and has been untraceable since. Top bureaucrats in Dhaka also said they were awaiting official communication from India on the case.Dr Ziauddin Ahmed, additional secretary (Political and Immigration), Bangladesh home ministry, whose office deals with border enforcement, illegal crossings and cross-border deportations, said officials were trying to locate Mumtaz but had no information as of Sunday. The matter was sent to police and other depts late on Sept 27, days after TOI reached out.Gauhati HC on Sept 3 directed MEA to "endeavour to locate Mumtaz in Bangladesh and bring her back". The HC also directed Assam govt to pay her husband Mujammel Hoque Rs 2 lakh interim compensation, observing "she was expelled without her husband or an adult family member being informed". HC found it denied her a chance to challenge it, a violation of democratic due process.
Tribunal declared Assam woman a foreigner, but Gauhati HC set it aside
Underscoring that basic human rights extend to anyone on Indian soil, the bench directed Assam Police and home dept to "ensure that declared foreign nationals are informed about tribunal orders and that their adult family members are notified before they are moved outside their district".
The court criticised the tribunal for stripping her of the "opportunity to challenge the Foreigners Tribunal's opinion before Gauhati HC".With no information in India, TOI contacted journalists, human-rights activists, officials and govt and security establishment sources across Bangladesh, focusing on Sylhet division and adjoining districts, where she could have ended up.A senior Dhaka-based businessman, who wishes to stay anonymous, joined authorities in the search and is working with govt and security contacts. An appeal with her photo and identification details, including Foreigners Identification Portal ID, was published in prominent Bengali newspapers on Sept 22. Bangla daily Manob Kantha also carried her photo and reported on the family's search.
Official efforts in Sylhet, however, have found no lead. Sylhet Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sarwar Murshed Shamim said police had "tried to locate Mumtaz within the metropolitan area but had not found her and were continuing the search."Mumtaz, from Nagaon, was declared a foreigner by a Foreigners Tribunal. The HC set aside the opinion and ordered fresh consideration, finding deficiencies in its assessment of evidence including 1965 and 1970 voter-list records of her grandfather, her father's 1977 voter-list record and voter ID, Gaonburah and Gaon Panchayat certificates, a school transfer certificate and land records.She appeared before the tribunal on May 30 with her lawyer, after which police took her into custody. She was taken to Juria and Nagaon Sadar police stations, Matia holding centre in Goalpara, then Eraligool holding centre in Sribhumi (June 4-13).Handed to BSF on June 13, she was sent to Bangladesh on June 14 from Kalaincherra, Cachar, BSF told the HC. Three months on, police, authorities and civil-society members are trying to establish where she is.

Argentina’s Milei threatens to sue UK over Falkland Islands oil project

Argentina’s Milei threatens to sue UK over Falkland Islands oil project
Argentine President Javier Milei threatened on Monday to sue Britain over the Sea Lion oil project near the disputed Falkland Islands. Argentina claims sovereignty over the British-administered territory, where a 1982 war killed 255 British and 649 Argentine troops. Developers Navitas and Rockhopper say they hold valid British-issued exploration licences.
Argentina's President Javier Milei threatened Monday to sue the United Kingdom over an oil project near the Falkland Islands, the British-administered territory over which Buenos Aires claims sovereignty.
Britain and Argentina fought a brief but bitter 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, known to Argentines as Las Malvinas, with 255 British troops and 649 Argentines killed during the conflict.
The companies developing a major oil field off the Falklands, Israel's Navitas and Britain's Rockhopper, have shrugged off Argentina's threats, insisting they have valid exploration licenses issued by the United Kingdom. The project is called Sea Lion.
"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei said in a post on X.
The Sea Lion oil field is located around 220 kilometers (137 miles) from the islands.
Read moreArgentina's poverty rate climbs to nearly one in three under Milei
"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," the libertarian president continued.
Milei's administration has already taken legal action against the project authorized by Britain, arguing it violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute is resolved.
Buenos Aires has doubled down on its claim over the Falklands since US President Donald Trump said that Washington was open to reviewing its historically neutral stance on the territory.
The British government for its part has said it stands behind the businesses operating near the Falklands, arguing it had the "right to develop their natural resources as they see fit."
Falkland business representatives on Monday also arrived in Punta Arenas, Chile, to relaunch a maritime route between the two ports.
Louise Ellis, deputy director of economic development in the Falklands, told AFP in Punto Arenas that the new shipping route "has absolutely no" relation to the transportation of critical cargo needed for the Sea Lion project.
"This project (for a new route) began before (Sea Lion) and has always had to do with what the Falkland Islands and our communities need now," she said.
The route, which aims to open later this year and had ended in the 2000s after being deemed unfeasible, will mainly involve the transport of construction materials and fresh products like food and beverages.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

KYIV - Russian strikes pummelled Ukraine on Sept 29 after hitting the National Academy of Sciences in the historic heart of Kyiv, in the latest deadly attack on the Ukrainian capital.
Kyiv has increasingly faced Russian drones and missiles as Europe’s worst conflict since World War II grinds through its fifth year.
The capital again came under fire after an air force alert warning of approaching drones.
Video footage shared online appeared to show a high-speed drone smashing into the National Academy of Sciences at a sharp angle, exploding and sending acrid smoke into the blue sky above.
People were seen leaning out of windows as bright orange flames engulfed part of the building.
Ukraine’s former national security and defence council secretary Volodymyr Gorbulin told state broadcaster Suspilne that he was at work at the academy at the time and was slightly wounded.
But he said his assistant, who was near the building, was killed.
That night, AFP journalists in Kyiv heard several explosions, as the Ukrainian Air Force warned ballistic missiles were heading towards the city.
The National Academy of Sciences is close to the German embassy, a cathedral, the national opera and government buildings.
Kyiv cultural sites, government buildings and schools have all been targeted before, according to Ukrainian authorities.
The academy called the attack “Russian terror” and “barbarity”, targeting “peaceful people who were simply at their workplaces... Ukrainian science, education and culture”.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said a separate strike in the capital hit a medical facility.
Elsewhere, Russian strikes killed four and wounded at least 19 at a business centre in the central city of Dnipro, while authorities reported an unspecified number of fatalities in a strike on a residential area in eastern Kharkiv.
Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said Russian forces damaged an ice cream factory in the Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, and residential buildings in Sumy, in the north, Rivne, in the northwest, and southern Odesa.
In Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine, strikes wounded 30 civilians, three of them seriously, the regional military administration said.
A Russian jet-powered drone also struck a Ukrainian village near the Polish border earlier on Sept 28, damaging a border checkpoint, a regional Ukrainian official said.
Winter fears
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shahed drones.
Zelensky renewed his appeal last week to Ukraine’s Western allies to step up their military support, including for US-made Patriot interceptors capable of downing powerful ballistic missiles.
Koretsky said on Sept 28 that Ukraine will postpone some spending commitments, including reconstruction work, because of delays in receiving aid from its foreign backers.
The plea for aide comes as Ukrainians consider their options with winter approaching, after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure in 2025 cut power and heating as temperatures plunged to as low as minus 20 deg C.
In an interview with Ukrainian television broadcast on Sept 27, Koretsky stopped short of saying that all residents in cities should leave before winter sets in, calling that an “extreme step”.
But he suggested that vulnerable people should relocate, to avoid overloading the hard-pressed emergency services as they deal with the aftermath of the relentless Russian strikes.
“If a person lives, for example, on the 16th floor and for instance the power gets cut, why at that moment, when the state emergency service specialists need to focus on dealing with the consequences, should we be... handling people who need extra attention?” he told TSN television.
“For such people, it’s worth finding an alternative place to stay for the winter period.” AFP

rippling glass facades and mountain-high towers shape urban district by AECOM in shaoxing
mountain-inspired towers and pebble-like podiums shape AECOM’s design in shaoxing, where offices, retail and public spaces come together around a central park.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
Mountain-inspired towers frame a central park in Shaoxing
AECOM’s Huafa Financial Vitality City in Shaoxing, China, draws on the region’s mountains and waterways to shape a mixed-use urban district. The design brings financial workplaces, hospitality, retail, and civic functions into a landscape-led framework, with a central park organizing the relationship between buildings and public space.
The architectural composition references the rhythm of local mountain ranges. Related building forms create a recognizable family of towers while allowing individual headquarters to retain their own identities. Their arrangement addresses views toward Meishan and Jinghu National Urban Wetland Park, making the surrounding landscape a reference for the district’s skyline.
Rippling glass and pebble-like forms reference waterscapes
A 168-meter International Financial Center anchors the composition by AECOM. Its orientation, rotated 45 degrees relative to the site, establishes a dialogue with the neighboring hotel tower. Subtle changes in the glass facade evoke ripples on the water, while the hotel podium takes inspiration from the rounded forms of water-worn pebbles.
At the urban scale, the proposal organizes complementary uses around the central park and a network of connections. The design seeks to bring the scale of the financial district into contact with everyday urban life, linking workplaces with shopping, leisure, and shared outdoor spaces.

Nirbhaya case
, which made registration of FIRs mandatory in offences against women, saw 
rape cases
 rise from 1,636 in 2013 to 2,166 in 2014 and peak at 2,199 in 2015. Cases fell to 1,699 in 2020 (due to Covid lockdown), the lowest level since 2013 at that point. ====================================================================================================

Want to protect yourself against cancer? Get vaccinated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:05:15 UTC
11:05:15 KST

An estimated one in eight cancer cases worldwide may be caused by infections—many of which are preventable with treatment or vaccines, according to new research.
In a study published on Monday in the Lancet Oncology, researchers estimate that infections were responsible for approximately 2.3 million cancer cases, or about 12 percent of diagnoses, worldwide in 2024.
Helicobacter pylori bacteria and human papillomavirus (HPV) combined accounted for more than an estimated 1.5 million cancer cases, the analysis found. An estimated 360,000 cancer cases were linked to hepatitis B infections, and 260,000 cases were caused by the Epstein-Barr virus.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There is good news here: millions of cancers are preventable, says Gary Clifford, the study’s senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer. “These are very actionable risk factors. We can test for them. We can vaccinate against them.”
The new estimates update older research to investigate cancer and infections that was conducted in 2018. Since then researchers have discovered that the Epstein-Barr virus, which is known to cause cancers such as nasal pharyngeal cancers and some forms of lymphoma, is also linked to some stomach cancers and some rarer lymphomas, Clifford says.
There were geographic differences in the places where cancers caused by infections occurred, too. In sub-Saharan Africa, for instance, there were higher rates of such cancers, in part because of “disparities in investment,” Clifford says, such as a lack of cervical cancer screening programs compared with those that have been available in, say, the U.S. By knowing where the infection-linked cancer burden has been highest, health officials can work to prevent those infections.
The findings serve as a reminder that infectious agents cause cancer, says Anna Giuliano, founding director of the Center for Immunization and Infection Research in Cancer at the Moffitt Cancer Center. “And there’s something we can do about it,” she says.
People can be screened and treated for hepatitis C and vaccinated against hepatitis B, both of which can cause liver cancer, for instance, she notes. Antibiotics can reduce the risk of cancer in people with H. pylori infection. And the HPV vaccine, first introduced in the U.S. in 2006, can prevent six different cancers, including cervical cancer, throat cancer and anal cancer.
In the 20 years since the HPV shot was first introduced in the U.S., in fact, rates of cervical cancer have dropped in some states by more than 50 percent among women aged 20 to 31, the first group eligible to receive the vaccine as preteens. Researchers have documented similar benefits around the globe.
“There is no question that this vaccine does what it was intended to do,” Giuliano says.
Nancy Lee, an oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, says the new findings underscore the importance of vaccination.
“HPV vaccination is critical to preventing infection and reducing the burden of HPV-related cancers,” she says, noting that, in the U.S., HPV-related throat cancer is a “growing” concern.
Ultimately, the takeaway is that “serious mortal diseases can be prevented with a simple population-based equality-driven jab in the arm,” Clifford says. “It’s really very simple and straightforward.”

Iran denounces ‘Iranophobia’ over mysterious UK airbase terror case

Iran denounces ‘Iranophobia’ over mysterious UK airbase terror case
Iran has denied any ties to a suspected terrorist plot targeting a UK airbase that houses US bombers flying missions against Iran.
On Sunday, police arrested five men they suspected of preparing a terrorist act after receiving a report of suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. However, they were unexpectedly released on bail the following day after “extensive interviews and enquiries,” according to Laurence Taylor, the head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Policing.
Without providing many details, Taylor said police were investigating whether the offense was “committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.” Reuters, citing a person familiar with the probe, reported that investigators were considering whether Iran or Russia may have been involved, as well as unspecified Islamist groups.
“The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to [the] arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” Iran’s mission in London said in a statement on X on Monday.
The embassy added that “such fabricated speculations” would only “fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”
Police cordoned off the vicinity of the base. According to the BBC, a bomb squad worked at the scene, using a remote-controlled robot to inspect white vans parked in a wooded area.
Although Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned in July that the UK would become a “definite and legitimate target” if it supported the US bombing campaign, Tehran has not claimed responsibility for any attacks outside the Middle East.
Iran has fired missiles and drones at Gulf states, which it described as legitimate targets for retaliation because they host American bases used to launch attacks against Iran.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that a suspected plot near a British military base used by the US involved "the hands of a foreign actor."
Rubio, speaking to Fox News, said the weekend incident at RAF Fairford base in Fairford, south-west England was “a very serious situation” and suggested additional information about the suspected foreign involvement could emerge in the coming days.
“There’s some things I cannot say on the air for a lot of different reasons,” he said.
"Suffice it to say that what happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."
The comments came after British counterterrorism police arrested five men near Royal Air Force Fairford in Gloucestershire on Sunday.
The men, all British nationals from London in their early 20s, were detained after authorities were alerted by a local farmer who reported seeing three white vans travelling toward the base.
Police said Monday that they were investigating whether individuals acting on behalf of a foreign state were involved. The five suspects were subsequently released on bail while the investigation continues.
RAF Fairford is used by the US military and has housed American bombers involved in operations in the region.
Rubio praised British authorities for their cooperation with the United States during the investigation.
“I do want to thank the authorities in the United Kingdom, who have been very cooperative and on top of it,” he said, adding that US officials were engaging with British authorities regarding the arrests and subsequent releases on bail.
Trump questions release
Rubio also placed the incident in the broader context of threats against US interests overseas. He specifically cited Iran, saying that Iranian actors have openly threatened American interests globally and that the United States takes such threats seriously.
“We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said. “We’re going to always take that very seriously.”
On Monday, US President Donald Trump said that British police should not have released the five men on bail.
Trump added that the case "might be" linked to Iran but declined to give details.
"I'm surprised that they released them, I wouldn't have done that," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, while adding that British authorities had worked "very closely" with the United States.
"We know everything about them. We would not have released them."

29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that a suspected plot near a British military base used by the US involved "the hands of a foreign actor."
Rubio, speaking to Fox News, said the incident over the weekend was “a very serious situation” and suggested that additional information about the suspected foreign involvement could emerge in the coming days.
“There’s some things I cannot say on the air for a lot of different reasons,” he said.
"Suffice it to say that what happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."
The comments came after British counterterrorism police arrested five men near Royal Air Force Fairford in Gloucestershire on Sunday. The men, all British nationals from London in their early 20s, were detained after authorities were alerted by a local farmer who reported seeing three white vans traveling toward the base.
Police said Monday that they were investigating whether individuals acting on behalf of a foreign state were involved. The five suspects were subsequently released on bail while the investigation continues.
RAF Fairford is used by the US military and has housed American bombers involved in operations in the region.
Rubio praised British authorities for their cooperation with the United States during the investigation.
“I do want to thank the authorities in the United Kingdom, who have been very cooperative and on top of it,” he said, adding that US officials were engaging with British authorities regarding the arrests and subsequent releases on bail.
Rubio also placed the incident in the broader context of threats against US interests overseas. He specifically cited Iran, saying that Iranian actors have openly threatened American interests globally and that the United States takes such threats seriously.
“We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said. “We’re going to always take that very seriously.”

Europe’s businesses are paying for Russia’s hybrid war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Police investigators work on the tarmac with a robot that is capable, among other things, of defusing explosives, near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Elisabeth Braw is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, author of the award-winning “Goodbye Globalization” and a regular columnist for POLITICO. Her new book, “The Undersea War,” is out Oct. 8.
Plots against defense executives, a series of arson attacks against private companies and warehouses, and explosive drones at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Had any of these worked as intended, they would have caused immense damage, not to mention claimed lives.
Advertisement
This is the situation plaguing Europe today, faced as it is with a proliferation of gray-zone attacks. And while a definitive response from the continent is yet to materialize, the bloc has finally started to name and address the hybrid war it’s been pulled into. No, summits and statements won’t thwart attacks, but acknowledgement is famously the first step to recovery.
It was only a miracle that saved workers at Leipzig airport when, on Aug. 4, an approaching drone landed poorly and lost its load of explosives. Had things gone to plan, it would have exploded next to a Ukrainian Antonov plane ready for departure, causing immense damage to a busy airport servicing the people and businesses of large parts of Germany. (Investigators later found a second drone laden with military-grade explosives right next to the airport.)
But who would want to maim and kill airport users? On Sept. 1, the German government announced it had determined Russia was behind the attack.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster arrive for a news conference at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Years ago, European governments would have preferred not to publicly attribute such reckless incidents because with attribution comes the need to respond. But this time Germany openly identified the Kremlin as the instigator, showing just how seriously Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is taking the incident.
That’s because the failed drone explosion is only the latest in a series of sinister activity of which Germany has been a particular target.
Just before the country’s national election in 2025, the exhaust pipes of hundreds of cars were sabotaged across the country, and stickers calling for people to vote for the Greens attached to their windows. While that last touch suggested environmental activists were behind the campaign, the perpetrators were later identified as agents working on Russia’s behalf.
Advertisement
A couple of months earlier, a parcel — which turned out to contain a bomb — caught fire at DHL’s depot at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The perpetrators of this event, too, were later found to be working for Russia. And a few months before that, German authorities uncovered a Russian assassination plot against arms manufacturer Rheinmetall’s CEO.
You all know about these cases, not just because I’ve written about them on these pages but because they were so brazen. And Germany is not the only country to see all manner of businesses — and even business executives — targeted by geopolitically linked strikes. The U.K. has been hit by arson, as have Poland, the Czech Republic and other European countries.
In September 2025, objects in the skies above airports in Denmark and Norway forced temporary closures. Drones keep appearing around Scottish offshore installations. Numerous Swedish communication masts have sustained suspicious damage. And in the Baltic Sea, there has been a string of suspicious cable and pipeline incidents.
The Eagle S oil tanker is escorted by a tugboat to the Port of Kilpilahti in the Gulf of Finland on Dec. 28, 2024. | Vesa Moilanen/Lehtikuva/AFP via Getty Images
So far, none of these incidents have caused devastating damage — though a 2024 arson attack subsequently attributed to Russia destroyed Poland’s largest shopping mall. But each attempt costs the affected businesses money. Each piece of sabotaged infrastructure incurs repair costs and operational losses. Each disruption causes delays and further expenses. In fact, most targeted companies have seen their operations disrupted, which means additional financial hits.
In the case of the undersea cables struck by anchors, the owners were left with significant repair bills. For power cables, repairs typically run into the tens of millions of euros. Each incident also costs personnel time. Had the Leipzig drones or parcel bombs exploded, the financial losses — and, of course, the human losses — would have been extremely painful.
Even a relatively small incident can leave the target facing significant damage: Last month WB Group, a Polish drone-component manufacturer, was subject to an arson attack and incurred losses of at least €3.5 million. Polish prosecutors believe the attack was, again, instigated by Russia.
Advertisement
But when all this happens, who foots the bill?
If the companies are lucky, their insurers will. However, standard insurance only covers standard perils. It doesn’t cover war-like acts, which is what geopolitically linked acts of harm amount to. At least that’s what many standard insurers are unsurprisingly contending. And while specialized war insurers do offer coverage for war, doing so involves having to decide what exactly constitutes war-like acts.
The most detailed discussion of this fundamental question isn’t taking place at think tanks or universities. They’re taking place in the insurance industry, as vast amounts of money are at stake. And this — rendering European companies’ operations financially unsustainable — may, in fact, be Russia’s objective.
Surveillance drone models from WB Group are displayed during MSPO International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images
Credit to the German government for convening the Baltic Sea Security Summit in August to accelerate European nations’ response to a discreditable and dangerous form of geopolitical score-settling, and for calling the Kremlin out.
Now, how will these subversive attacks on European companies continue to unfold? You will have to find out without me, as this is my farewell as a columnist for POLITICO. It has been an immense pleasure and honor to have your company. Arrivederci!
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

Mélenchon’s plan to beat the far right: Grab the first-time voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Mélenchon’s plan to beat the far right: Grab the first-time voters
The leftist veteran believes that young voters as well as those from working-class suburbs and with immigrants roots can propel him to the runoff, where he’d likely face off against Marine Le Pen.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, right, Bally Bagayoko, center, and Mathilde Panot, left, participate in a protest in Paris, on Sept. 20, 2026. | Djoudi Hamani/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — French far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is betting his blunt style and socially radical agenda will convince first-time voters to back him en masse and propel him into a runoff duel against far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen in 2027.
After embracing similar tactics in regional elections earlier this year, Mélenchon has increasingly set himself up on the campaign trail as a foil to the anti-immigration Le Pen by embracing a vision of what he calls “a new France” that celebrates diversity rooted in immigration.
The position makes him an outlier domestically — most French politicians believe the Republic should be colorblind — and in much of Europe, where leaders across the political spectrum have tried to project toughness on migration to contain the rise of nationalist forces like Le Pen’s National Rally. Mélenchon’s opponents also accuse him of playing identity politics and openly courting minority voters, Muslims in particular.
Advertisement
But polls show the plan is working at the moment.
A survey conducted by Cluster17 exclusively for POLITICO last week had Mélenchon tied for second place with center-right candidate Edouard Philippe at 19%. And a Harris Interactive poll released Monday showed the pugnacious former teacher at 18% — against 16% for Philippe. Le Pen remained well ahead of the pack in both surveys, receiving more than 30% of the vote.
The Cluster17 poll showed 47% of respondents younger than 35 backed Mélenchon. That’s more than twice the 22% that Le Pen, who placed second among that demographic, was seen receiving.
Strategists from Mélenchon’s party, France Unbowed, told POLITICO that they believe young voters, working-class citizens and those with immigrant roots will be motivated to head to the polls for the first time to back their champion given his platform.
Mélenchon is the only leading candidate accusing the French state of pushing systemic racism and Islamophobia and denouncing police brutality. He is Israel’s most vocal critic on the French political stage. And he has promised ambitious policies to tackle climate change, including shifting towards 100% renewable energy.
Road to the second round
France Unbowed points to the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis — a former home of French royalty, now one of the capital region’s poorest suburbs and home to a large working-class population, many of them of immigrant descent — as potential proof of concept.
Advertisement
Mélenchon won nearly 50% of the vote in the first round of the 2022 presidential election in the district that includes the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. Turnout was 61.2%, whereas the national average was 73.7%.
And France Unbowed scored its biggest-ever victory there when its candidate, Bally Bagayoko, scored a decisive victory in local elections earlier this year, netting more than 50% of the vote in the first round and negating the need for a runoff.
But Mélenchon remains a divisive figure. Seventy-three percent of those polled by Cluster17 earlier this month said there was little to no chance they would ever vote for the France Unbowed leader. Only 62% felt the same way about Le Pen.
Marine Le Pen speaks in the National Assembly in Paris on Dec. 4, 2024. | Alain Jocard/AFP via Getty Images
“France Unbowed has built a strong, cross-class core,” said a parliamentarian for the rival center-left Socialist Party, who was granted anonymity to discuss his opponents’ campaign. “But enlarging their base seems very difficult.”
As things stand, Mélenchon’s strategy of zooming in on voters who are most likely to vote for him appears to be tracing a path towards the runoff. On the flip side, polling indicates that he would lose by a significant margin against Le Pen in a second round — though pollsters and political scientists urge caution when it comes to polling a runoff so early in a campaign.
“You need to take things one step at a time. Running a runoff campaign before the first round is a grave mistake that has cost several favorites their election in the past,” said Antoine Léaument, a France Unbowed lawmaker and strategist.

Send rejected asylum-seekers out of EU ASAP, urges Greek minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Send rejected asylum-seekers out of EU ASAP, urges Greek minister
A pilot project to send migrants who have been denied the right to stay in the EU to designated ‘return’ countries will be in place by early next year, Greece’s migration minister told POLITICO.
Thanos Plevris talks at the plenary session of Hellenic Parliament during a discussion on the introduction of the bill of the Ministry of Migration and Asylum on legal migration in Athens on February 4, 2026. | Dimitris Kapantais/SOOC/AFP via Getty Images
ATHENS — Greece is spearheading a group of five EU countries pushing for migrants who have been denied the right to stay in the bloc to be sent to countries such as Rwanda from as early as next year.
Greece’s Migration Minister Thanos Plevris said in an interview that by the first half of 2027, the so-called Core Group of nations — Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands — aims to have a pilot project in place to send rejected asylum-seekers to designated countries outside the bloc.
He added that the project should be fully operational by the second half of the year — coinciding with Greece taking over the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU in July. The intervention comes as Europe continues to grapple with a decade-long migration crisis which has galvanized support for populist-nationalist parties across the continent.
Advertisement
Plevris emphasized that the plan does not entail establishing return facilities but rather designates return countries. “We’re not talking about centers, in the sense that someone whose asylum is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country,” he said. “If your asylum has been rejected, you will either return to your country of origin or to a third country outside the EU.”
According to two EU diplomats familiar with the issue who were granted anonymity to discuss the matter freely, the first deal will be with Rwanda. Uganda and Uzbekistan are also reportedly under discussion as possible return countries.
Plevris said the countries under consideration already have large migrant populations and camps to accommodate them, adding that the Core Group nations “are open to whatever framework the countries there want — whether they want to talk about camps, or broader integration programs.”
Rwanda has been at the center of various offshore migration plans. In 2022, the U.K. announced a controversial multimillion-pound deal with Kigali to deport asylum-seekers to the country to have their claims processed. The scheme was abandoned after years of legal challenges.
The timetable proposed by Plevris might be ambitious, given that several crucial elements of the agreement remain up in the air. The minister said members of the Core Group are currently in discussions with international organizations to establish monitoring processes that would ensure human rights are respected in third countries to which migrants will be deported.
“Obviously, we’re not going to transfer this authority elsewhere,” he added. “We want to have the expertise and the presence of international organizations, but the responsibility lies with the five countries, jointly.”
Advertisement
The financing of the plan — an issue which can be contentious with voters — would also have to come from the Core Group. “We want to have a financially realistic project,” Plevris said, adding that members of the group want the Commission to eventually have an active role in the process.
The minister acknowledged that the plan would not lead to huge numbers of migrants being outsourced to third countries. “In reality, it is another means of exerting pressure that could increase voluntary returns,” he said. “It’s an unprecedented undertaking. Even though other countries have attempted something similar in the past, this is the first time it’s being attempted since the EU regulation was passed.”
On Thursday, at a meeting of EU interior ministers, Plevris will also submit Greece’s plan to deal with emergency migratory pressures — temporarily suspending asylum applications for newly arrived people. Greece’s Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis first presented this idea in an Op-Ed published on POLITICO after tens of thousands of migrants crossed the border into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta.
“The EU migration will only work when Europe’s migration flows are managed,” Plevris said, adding that the bloc needs a mechanism to deal with emergencies.
Greece has been repeatedly accused of violating EU regulations for alleged illegal pushbacks of migrants. “Greece protects its borders in accordance with international law, and it says frankly that it will not apologize to anyone for protecting its borders,” the minister added.
Plevris, who has expressed hard-line views on migration, has expressed his support and admiration for U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach on the issue. “He gave the momentum that led to a change in migration policy, and essentially helped many groups —including us — who believed in a stricter immigration policy to see it materialize,” said Plevris.

No country for old women: Pressure builds on Spain’s Sánchez over eviction of elderly tenant
Intense protests are forcing the embattled prime minister to make a choice: Either deliver on housing or risk further alienating voters ahead of a key election year.
MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez faces renewed pressure as housing protests in Madrid escalate and his left-wing allies demand tougher action, straining his coalition ahead of a key election year.
Wheelchair-bound pensioner Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed from her home after living there since 1956, after failing to meet the new rental demands set by the investment firm that bought her building. Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday, with some protestors then pitching tents in the historic Puerto del Sol square. By Monday, hundreds of tents had been erected.
“We live in a country full of Maricarmens, and we’re saying enough is enough,” said Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenant Union, the group leading the encampment. During a speech to protesters on Sunday, thousands echoed a chant denouncing “inversores culpables, gobierno responsable,” meaning “guilty investors, responsible government”
Advertisement
Sánchez, who last week called the eviction was a “social tragedy,” is now scrambling to contain the situation by vowing to approve a long-delayed housing bill at Tuesday’s meeting of Spain’s Council of Ministers. But crafting legislation that his minority government can get through parliament is proving tricky.
The draft bill must be moderate enough to win the support of the Catalan separatist Junts party, which is conservative on landowners’ rights. But if the legislation is too lenient, Sánchez risks alienating his left-wing allies, accentuating his political isolation in a key election year. The beleaguered prime minister is already facing mounting pressure over the unresolved migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as a slew of corruption scandals involving family members and close allies.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, a version of the draft text under negotiation on Monday night proposed extending protections against evictions for vulnerable tenants through 2028, capping rent increases at 2 percent in certain cases and offering tax breaks to tenants in rent-stressed areas. Additional measures would seek to ban speculative home purchases by investment funds and potentially raise taxes on short-term tourist flats.
Those proposals fall short of the ambitious action Sumar, the smaller partner in Sánchez’s coalition, is demanding. Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz on Monday called for the public to mobilize against her own government to ensure the draft bill is “up to task.”
“In this country, rights don’t just fall from the sky,” she said.
The current draft is also unlikely to satisfy the protesters occupying the square, who are demanding the legislation include the automatic renewal of rental contracts, tougher action against abusive landlords and a freeze on rents until the housing crisis is resolved.
Advertisement
“We’re fed up with weak measures that do nothing to solve the problem,” said Jorge Collado, a 26-year-old student participating in the occupation.
Collado said he had been forced to move back to his family’s home after his former landlord dramatically raised the monthly rent when he requested a legal rental contract.
“This allegedly progressive government has spent the past eight years promising to do something about housing, but has systematically sided with the landlords who exploit us,” he said.
Pedro Sánchez delivers a speech to MPs in the lower house of parliament in Madrid on June 24, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images
With Spain due to hold national elections within the next year, Collado said the government would be making a big mistake if it didn’t take immediate steps to rectify the situation.
“When election day comes, I think many people will stay home,” he said. “And in the meantime, we’ll be staying here, for as long as it takes.”
Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Carlos III University of Madrid, called the protests “devastating” for Sánchez.
Advertisement
“These demonstrations are channelling the broad dissatisfaction of left-wing voters who feel this government has failed to deliver on its progressive promises,” he said. “They’re opening a major breach in Sánchez’s strategy for political survival: If that electorate doesn’t show up, he’s doomed.”
Marta García, a 60-year-old retired schoolteacher who was present at the anti-austerity 15-M protests in the same square about 15 years ago, said she had traveled from outside Madrid to support the protesters sleeping there.
“This is an encampment founded on rage — rage at the shameless speculative practices, at the incompetent political maneuvers, at the squandered futures — but also on the hope that things can change and be made better,” she said.
“A bill that fails, but is ambitious and courageous, will have much more of an impact than a toothless one that passes.”

Jails are hiring grounds for pro-Khalistan groups; dead drops of ISI modules also under intel lens
Unknown

10:47:33 KST

Khalistan groups target north India jails to recruit operatives, agencies flag growing threat
NEW DELHI: Intelligence agencies have flagged attempts by pro-Khalistan groups, including Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), to infiltrate jails in north India and recruit operatives. The move comes amid revelations made by a recently detained operative who disclosed having been inducted and given Gurpatwant Singh Pannun's contact while serving time in Patiala jail.Agencies are now investigating the digital footprint, dead-drop financial channels, and the broader jail recruitment network, sources said. Agencies have also noted how ISI-backed modules are increasingly relying on dead-drop methods to channel funds, supply weapons, and execute covert tasks and have largely replaced physical handovers with pre-designated drop points along isolated highway stretches and border and rural sectors.Drawn straight from the classic spycraft playbook, this method ensures that foreign masterminds or handlers remain completely insulated from the foot soldiers executing their commands on the ground. Arms, ammunition, and untraceable cash, frequently delivered across the border via drones or covert couriers, are hidden at specific coordinates, with retrieval instructions transmitted to local operatives over end-to-end encrypted messaging platforms like Signal.
The tactic of leveraging prison networks draws from a pattern highlighted by high-profile incidents like the 2016 Nabha jailbreak, which exposed the nexus between terror outfits and incarcerated criminal groups. Within these facilities, handlers and radicalised inmates target vulnerable, economically distressed prisoners - frequently first-time offenders or petty criminals lacking legal representation and financial support.
In the latest instance, agencies recently busted an SFJ-backed module and arrested operative Preetpal Singh, who, along with his associates, had spray-painted anti-Brics and pro-Khalistan graffiti across Delhi and Punjab, filmed the act and sent the video to Pannun. Singh, it turned out, had a prior history of pro-Khalistan activities, having been arrested in 2023 for a similar crime.While in prison, he was provided with a phone number to contact Pannun and execute future tasks. After his release in 2026, Singh established direct contact with Pannun and received Rs 1.5 lakh through a dead-drop location on the Faridkot-Amritsar highway. Preetpal subsequently recruited another inmate, also on bail, for the Delhi assignment.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed that more than 8,000 North Korean troops are stationed on Russian territory, warning that preparations are actively underway to deploy an additional 10,000 personnel.
Citing "new data" regarding Pyongyang's military integration with Moscow, Zelenskyy stated that additional North Korean forces are "being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia."
The statement comes after the Ukrainian leader warned in August that up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers could ultimately be deployed to fight on behalf of the Russian military, prompting Kiev to urge South Korea to provide air defence assistance.
In July, Seoul committed a $100 million non-lethal aid package to Ukraine.
Pyongyang's arsenal
Zelenskyy's remarks follow diplomatic friction between Seoul and Kiev over his public disclosure last week confirming that Ukrainian forces transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
The South Korean government expressed formal regret over the public disclosure, maintaining that both nations had mutually agreed to keep the transfer confidential.
Seoul also lodged a protest against a statement released by the Ukrainian presidential administration that denied the existence of any confidentiality pact.
North Korea has dispatched an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to bolster Russia's military campaign in Ukraine since 2024, according to assessments compiled by Ukrainian and South Korean intelligence agencies.
The vast majority of these forces have been deployed across the Kursk frontier region to help Russian forces counter a Ukrainian cross-border operation.
Beyond personnel, Pyongyang has supplied Moscow with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, alongside ballistic missiles, heavy long-range artillery systems, and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian officials and independent defence assessments.

Travel companies in southern Japan are pinning their hopes on a business revival following a planned visit by Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako to the areas hardest hit by a major earthquake this summer.

Hong Kong mustn’t miss the boat on the Pinglu Canal and Asean trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:30:11 UTC
10:30:11 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Hong Kong mustn’t miss the boat on the Pinglu Canal and Asean trade
The game-changing canal is a physical response to an economic reality: Asia’s growth is becoming more regional and more connected
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Daryl Ng is chairman of Sino Group and the founding chairman of the Hong Kong-Asean Foundation, a not-for-profit organisation promoting and deepening ties between Hong Kong and Asean to build a community of shared future to reinforce Hong Kong’s international position and support future growth. 
The official opening of the Pinglu Canal on September 16 is a milestone in modern Chinese history. More than an infrastructural feat, it signals a strategic recalibration of how China’s inland economies connect with the sea and Southeast Asia, and augurs the next phase of regional growth.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway stretches from the Xijin reservoir in Hengzhou, an emerging city in Guangxi, to the Gulf of Tonkin (known as the Beibu Gulf in China), providing southwestern inland provinces with a shorter and more cost-effective route to global markets.
Strategically, it anchors the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a rapidly growing artery that was first conceptualised under the China-Singapore (Chongqing) Connectivity Initiative endorsed in 2015 by President Xi Jinping and Lee Hsien Loong, then prime minister of Singapore.

Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:28:57 BST
10:28:57 KST

Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says
- Published
An evicted elderly disabled woman, who became symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction.
The eviction has led to widespread anger across Spain, and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has promised housing relief measures when his cabinet meets on Tuesday.
Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.
Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
Investment firm Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts.
Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.
Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation".
She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she feels better.
Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Pedro Sanchez's Socialist Party, which lacks a majority in Parliament, is hoping to pass a law to appease public outrage.

Ebola cases top 8,000 in DR Congo amid contact-tracing gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:28:52 UTC
10:28:52 KST

James Tasamba
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Failings in contact tracing as well as persistent deaths outside treatment centers have been blamed for a recent surge in Ebola transmission in the Democratic Republic of Congo, health authorities said Monday, as the number of confirmed cases topped 8,000.
Since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, the cumulative caseload stands at 8,067, including 3,901 deaths, the Health Ministry’s latest situation update showed.
The case fatality rate stands at 48.4%.
The latest epidemic has affected 63 health zones across seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi.
Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 76.4% of cumulative cases since the outbreak began.
 
The situation update indicated that of the new confirmed deaths, the majority occurred in the community, outside treatment centers in Ituri and in North Kivu due to challenges in timely case detection.
Contact tracing has fallen to 79.2%, compared to 83.4% previously.
The update showed sustained transmission in Haut-Uele province, while renewed transmission was recorded in Tshopo province.
The World Health Organization (WHO) in a report last week warned that the latest geographic expansion of the virus, including newly affected areas in South Ubangi and Haut-Uele, had increased the risk of cross-border transmission.
It also noted that the rising fatality ratio and growing number of deaths occurring in communities highlights the seriousness of the disease.
At least $2.9 billion had been mobilized for the Ebola response in the Africa region, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

Beyond manpower, Pyongyang is reportedly preparing to ship additional ballistic missile launchers to Russian forces.
Zelensky emphasized that this alliance goes far beyond the immediate war in Ukraine.
“Russia is helping North Korea learn how to wage war, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience in using them,” Zelensky stated, noting that the partnership poses a security crisis for nations across Asia that sit within range of North Korean missile systems.

Pyongyang has also supplied Moscow with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems.

Argentina’s Milei takes Falklands oil fight with UK to international court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:24:16 UTC
10:24:16 KST

Argentine President Javier Milei said Monday that his government would seek international arbitration against the United Kingdom over an oil project off the disputed, British-controlled Falkland Islands, escalating a clash over resources that could transform the economy of the sparsely populated South Atlantic archipelago.
Milei’s office said it had given the UK two weeks to halt work on Sea Lion, an offshore oilfield being developed by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and England's Rockhopper Exploration. Otherwise, Argentina would ask the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, a Hamburg-based maritime court, to order a temporary halt to the project.
“Argentina will not stand idly by,” the presidential statement said, accusing the UK of causing “irreversible and irreparable” harm.
The tribunal, an independent court established under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, can issue legally binding emergency orders. But even if it ordered the UK to halt the project, it has no means of forcing the government to comply.
The UK rejects Argentina’s sovereignty claim, arguing that the islanders have the right to determine their own future and develop their natural resources. In a referendum in 2013, residents of the Falklands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory. Argentina says the islands were populated illegally.
Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno praised Milei’s move as “a historic and unprecedented step” in Argentina’s nearly two-century campaign to secure sovereignty over the archipelago.
“Whoever explores or exploits our natural resources in the Malvinas without Argentine authorization must face the consequences,” he wrote on X, using Argentina’s name for the islands.
Milei, a self-described “anarcho-capitalist," initially drew scorn from his nationalist opponents for his conciliatory stance toward Britain and professed admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the wartime prime minister loathed in Argentina for ordering the islands’ recapture. The brief but bloody war, which erupted when the Argentine military dictatorship invaded the archipelago in 1982, killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders.
But Milei has taken an increasingly confrontational stance as oil production near the islands approaches its anticipated start in 2028 and U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of the Argentine leader, suggests he could reconsider Washington’s long-standing neutrality in the dispute.
Last week, Milei dedicated much of his UN General Assembly speech to Argentina’s sovereignty claim, accusing the international body of neglecting the Falklands dispute and denouncing the oil project as an illegal exploitation of Argentine resources.
He has threatened sanctions that would bar companies drilling around the Falklands from operating in Argentina’s booming oil and mining sectors. His government has sent Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization and extending penalties to fishing, the bedrock of the islands’ economy. Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations. An Argentine judge this month also ordered a halt to work on Sea Lion pending an environmental review.
Critics accuse Milei of using the sovereignty claim — one of the few causes in Argentina that cuts across the country’s stark political lines — to bolster flagging public support ahead of next year’s presidential election as the economy falters.

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
A Haitian-American pastor accused of helping to plan the July 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise went on trial Monday in Miami, Florida.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces eight charges, including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the US.
US prosecutors allege that Sanon helped finance the conspiracy and arranged travel and lodging for himself and others involved in the plot.
The alleged plan began in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and US businesspeople, according to the indictment.
Moise was killed on July 7, 2021 when armed men entered his home in Port-au-Prince and shot him. His wife, Martine Moise, was wounded in the attack.
The assassination was followed by an expansion of armed gang control across large parts of Haiti.
More than 40 people have been charged in the US in connection with the assassination, while 12 have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences, US authorities said.
The US case expanded this year after authorities charged 30 additional suspects and transferred 18 defendants from Haitian custody to the US.
The group includes Joseph Felix Badio, a former Haitian government official accused of involvement in the assassination, and 17 former Colombian soldiers accused of participating in the operation.
Proceedings in Haiti have faced repeated delays, with judges resigning from the case over security concerns. Armed gangs also seized control of the courthouse in downtown Port-au-Prince.
Haiti has not had an elected president since Moise's assassination and is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for December.
The country continues to face widespread gang violence, with thousands killed and more than 1 million people displaced in recent years.

‘Children are dying’: Fiji hopes declaring an HIV emergency will help it tackle crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:12:49 UTC
10:12:49 KST

On a recent Friday night, Dr Kesaia Tuidraki’s medical team parked its mobile clinic outside McDonald’s in downtown Suva, Fiji, and grabbed any kid they could to be tested for HIV. Of the 97 people screened, mostly teenagers – some on their way to get a burger, others to buy drugs – one in six tested positive.
“Children are suffering, children are dying, and if that doesn’t move you I don’t know what will,” Tuidraki, country director of Medical Services Pacific, tells the Guardian.
Fijian authorities this month called a national health emergency to deal with surging HIV cases, with an estimated one in 60 adults now living with the virus. It comes as new infections surge, with 2,016 new cases diagnosed in 2025 – rising by 27% in a year, and representing a 12-fold increase since 2010, according to UNAids. In a close-knit island nation of about 930,000 people, an estimated 9,100 are now living with the virus.
But only a fraction of those are tested and access treatment, prompting the government to scale up its pandemic announcement – first made in February 2025 – and mobilise urgent measures to prevent its spread. Dr Jason Mitchell, the head of Fiji’s HIV epidemic response, said it could take between five and 10 years to get a handle on the virus, and in the meantime he would expect numbers to rise.
Critics say moves to stem the spread of a disease that is being driven by cases in the young, with new diagnoses highest in those aged between 15 and 34, has been too slow. The crisis is complex and inextricably linked to the drug epidemic – more than 42% of new cases in 2025 were due to sharing contaminated needles or equipment.
Health advocates and social workers say primary school-age children are among those injecting themselves and friends are using the same contaminated needle, a problem raised by advocates as far back as 2019.
“I know these young boys, they ask me for syringes,” injecting drug user Rochelle*, who is living with HIV, tells the Guardian. “Whenever I have them I give them out. Someone has to give them, they’re already accessing the drugs.”
Rochelle, 38, says she tries to tell the boys not to share. Sometimes the kids listen – but not always.
Under current law, giving out syringes is technically considered aiding and abetting drug use. A concern among some politicians and medical professionals is that providing needles would encourage drug use – despite evidence from UNAids that this is not the case –and advocates are urging the government to let them distribute thousands of needles and syringes sitting untouched in a Suva warehouse.
“It’s really sad, honestly. We can’t wait any more, there are boxes and boxes already here,” Tuidraki says.
Mitchell says he expects a change to the HIV Act to be passed within the next two weeks, allowing public health workers to distribute needles. He adds that the government has been “cautious” in announcing the emergency, which his unit had been asking for since June.
Those leading the response say increased powers arising from the emergency declaration will help to quell the rapid spread of HIV, including to vulnerable populations like mothers and babies, at an estimated extra cost of $23m FJD (US$10.2m) a year.
“The immediate crisis right now is the spread of HIV, which is why the needle and syringe programme is critical,” UNAids, the UN agency that fights HIV and Aids, regional director Eamonn Murphy said.
‘People are scared’
The epidemic is complex but heavily linked to methamphetamine use. Fiji is a drug-running hub in the Pacific for methamphetamine bound for Australian and New Zealand markets, but use escalated during Covid when borders were closed and it began circulating domestically.
While Fijians want the crisis addressed, there has also been a backlash. Only 39% of those living with HIV in Fiji know their status, according to UNAids, and some of those spoken to by the Guardian continued to live in denial or refuse testing.
“There are people blaming the [queer] community, blaming women as irresponsible people, there’s a lot of cyberbullying. Minorities are being attacked online,” Mark Shaheel Lal, an advocate who lives with HIV, says. “Now it’s more like a scandal and people are scared.”
UNAids is also concerned about the spread of the virus to the Pacific, with rising cases seen in Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea. In November, Australia’s minister for foreign affairs, Penny Wong, announced A$48m for Pacific countries to fight HIV/Aids, while New Zealand committed NZ$4.2m to Fiji in July.
The introduction of PreP – or pre-exposure prophylaxis – an HIV prevention drug, would be a “gamechanger,” says Mitchell, who adds that one injection could be offered every six months for those at higher risk.
It would be especially important for women who are not able to push for safe sex practices with partners. Two in every 100 pregnant women now have HIV. “You can’t hide a bottle of pills, but you can get an injection,” says Michell.
For now, women are already being offered three HIV tests during pregnancy and sexual reproductive hubs are operating at the three main hospitals.
________
“There’s no miracles in the HIV response, it does not happen overnight. Unfortunately people are thinking this is like Covid, it’s very much not,” Mitchell says.
His team plans to open new clinics, integrate testing and treatment into GP services, work on harm reduction, and hire at least 100 more staff. He says that the increase in cases means more people are getting tested, which is a positive.
“Burnout is a major concern – we didn’t just start working yesterday, we’ve been working for 21 months. It’s difficult, and the difficulty is that all of it is preventable. It should not be happening.”
But in many areas, including rural localities, access to treatment continues to lag. Drug Free World Fiji founder and campaigner Kalesi Volatabu is still haunted by the 15-year-old girl she met when she started pushing for a safe needle programme six years ago. A drug mule who smuggled methamphetamine to New Zealand and Australia, she had names for the three main veins on the back of her hand; breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
“We had no idea of the severity, of the depth of the drug trade in this country, of the HIV crisis. Even I was naive, at the beginning, and everything was unreported for the longest time. We failed to act then – will we now?”

H1N1 dominates flu cases in India, found in 3 of 4 positive samples: WHO
NEW DELHI: H1N1 is the dominant flu strain detected in India, accounting for three out of every four influenza-positive samples reported in the latest surveillance data, according to World Health Organization (WHO).The finding is from WHO's surveillance data for weeks 36 and 37 of 2026, covering Sept 1 to 14 and updated on Sept 21. Across the South-East Asia region, 817 of 3,632 samples tested positive for influenza, giving an overall positivity rate of 22%.
India stood out for a high share of H1N1 among its positive samples. The A(H1N1)pdm09 accounted for 75% of influenza-positive samples in India, compared with 50% across the region. It was also the dominant strain in Bhutan and Thailand, where it accounted for 97% and74% respectively.Dr Rommel Tickoo, senior director, internal medicine, Max hospital, said H1N1 remains a seasonal strain, with higher complication risks for older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with underlying illnesses. He advised vaccination, respiratory hygiene, early testing where appropriate and timely antiviral treatment for high-risk patients.

Israel's Netanyahu holds secret meeting with UAE president
September 29, 2026
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly met with the president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, both governments confirmed late on Monday.
"The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them," read an Emirati statement.
Netanyahu's office said the visit "focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges."
The secret trip came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the UAE president had warned Netanyahu about an imminent threat from the Palestinian militant group Hamas ahead of the deadly attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 — a warning which the Israeli premier allegedly failed to pass on to security services.
Indeed, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Monday that the purpose of Netanyahu's visit had been to request that Sheikh Mohamed deny having given such a warning.
Netanyahu's office denied that the prime minister had made any such request, just as it had also denied the original report.
Netanyahu files complaint against Israeli broadcaster
Earlier on Monday, before the confirmation of Netanyahu's trip, Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet filed a complaint against Channel 12, accusing it of violating censorship rules by reporting the visit before the prime minister had returned to Israel.
"This evening, Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation," read a statement from Netanyahu's office.
It noted that the report had been made public while the premier's plane was still outside Israeli airspace and therefore "endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad" spy agency and other top security officials.
Israel and the UAE: diplomatic relations
Sheikh Mohamed's hosting of Netanyahu was a significant development at a time when the Israeli leader is seen by many across the Middle East as the chief propagator of the war in Gaza, which has seen over 70,000 Palestinians killed — many of them civilians.
It is also the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leaders after denying reports of a previous Netanyahu trip in May.
The UAE is one of only a handful of Arab nations which maintain official diplomatic ties with Israel after signing the Abraham Accords during US President Donald Trump's first term in 2020.
The UAE condemned the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 as a "serious and grave escalation" and said it was "appalled" by reports of Israeli citizens being taken hostage.
But relations have also been strained by Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, with the UAE denouncing "ongoing Israeli violations" in the Palestinian enclave.
Nevertheless, Israel reportedly deployed Iron Dome air defense systems, together with personnel to operate them, to the UAE during the war against Iran, as the Gulf state faced retaliatory attacks from Tehran.

Nothing’s New Headphone (1) Pro Are Made for the Studio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

The Headphone (1) Pro is Nothing's newest pair of cans, the company announced on Monday at an evening event in New York City. The headphones resemble Nothing’s first-ever over-ear headphones that debuted last summer, though the design and fit have been refined. The key change, though, is audio quality.
Instead of a single dynamic driver producing the sound in each earcup, Nothing has outfitted the Headphone (1) Pro with three drivers for each ear. Most headphones use a single 40-mm dynamic driver, so a single speaker ends up handling the bass, mids, and treble of your tracks. That can cause some muddiness and distortion. Adding more drivers—one for each specific frequency spectrum—gives the sound more room to stretch out and sparkle.
There’s a 40-mm bass dynamic driver to handle the low end. Then there’s a precision dynamic driver to tackle the midrange sounds like vocals, pianos, and guitars. The company says this driver will render those “S” and “T” sounds with more detail. Finally, there's the treble driver for the highs. Nothing’s driver uses xMEMS technology, which relies on a silicon diaphragm that should make transients—sharp bursts like a cymbal hit or a spiky synth stab—sound clearer.
All of these drivers working together should produce richer sound that’s more detailed overall. Every headphone maker claims their gadget produces the best sound on the market, but at least Nothing has attempted some technical feats here to try to convince you.
What's neat is you can see elements of the triple-driver architecture on the sides of the headphones—Nothing has added a couple of 9H Panda glass panels so you can peep the tech inside. The rest of the headphones are largely aluminum with titanium accents.
You'll no doubt worry about cracking that glass; Nothing claims that it is “shatter- and scratch-resistant," but Philipp Von Lintel, associate principal industrial designer at Nothing, says the glass had to survive durability tests 18 times from a drop of more than 1 meter. Also, the glass construction shouldn't affect repairability much—repair technicians can heat the glass from the outside to remove it and access the internal chamber for fixes. “Even if you crack it, there's a plastic film that keeps the chamber still working,” Von Lintel tells WIRED.
The Headphone (1) Pro is slightly lighter (by 2 grams) than the Headphone (1), with a wider headband and thicker padding, though battery life isn't as long, down to 68 hours with active noise canceling turned off versus 80. It has an IP52 dust- and water-resistance rating, so keep the hood of your rain jacket raised on rainy days.
Almost every gadget maker tosses the “Pro” moniker in the product name to justify a few extra features and a price bump. Yes, the Headphone (1) Pro cost $399, a $100 bump over the standard Headphone (1), but Nothing claims it is specifically catering to not just the average consumer who wants better sound, but also recording artists and audio professionals who work in the studio.
The company is including a feature that activates a flat equalization (EQ) mode—something mix engineers and audio producers prefer when they’re working—that’s triggered by a physical button on the headphones. Nothing collaborated with Metropolis Studio, a pro recording studio, to make the EQ features. There's even a “Studio B” Dynamic Spatial Audio mode that simulates Metropolis' mixing room, and four other Custom EQ profiles, like Concert Hall or Club. And yes, there’s a 3.5-mm jack so you can plug in (or stick with hi-res wireless or USB-C).
Charlie Smith, Nothing’s chief brand officer, says people will want these headphones for their commute to work. “That's fine, but people are making music on the go and need studio-level sound wherever they are," he says.
Nothing also claims the headphones have the best active noise cancellation it’s ever shipped, thanks to the use of 10 microphones to filter out ambient sounds. (Apple's AirPods Max, for comparison, use eight.)
“To us, this is a flagship product where we're able to showcase what we can do," Smith says. “It also helps elevate us as a brand.”
Sadly, they don’t fold up. Instead, Nothing is following Apple’s lead by including a bra-like carry case to keep the cans protected.
They'll officially hit store shelves on September 29—not only on Nothing's online store and Amazon, but also nationwide in Best Buy stores across North America.
