Choose what information you see below by using filters
Key Event
Is another rate hike actually going to work or will it just hurt borrowers?
That was a question a journalist asked Michele Bullock.
She noted that for those who have mortgages, "yes, this clearly impacts them and it hurts them".
"They've got less cash flow and they've got less money to spend on things," she said.
"But that's not the only way monetary policy works through the system."
Rate hikes also encourage greater saving and bring down asset prices.
"So if it impacts, for example, housing prices, which we think part of the downturn in the housing market has been related to interest rates, that sort of affects people's wealth," she said.
Higher interest rates also impact import prices.
"It makes imports cheaper, encourages people to spend more on imports rather than domestically produced goods," she said.
"So it again, it alters the supply-demand equation.
"So I guess my response would be I understand why the people who are impacted by this very directly in terms of loans feel that they are carrying the burden, but actually the interest rate increase gets into all sorts of cracks."
Key Event
Would a pullback in the bond market be risky?
ABC's Ian Verrender asked RBA Governor Michele Bullock whether bond markets, which are aggressively pushing interest rates higher across the globe, will force the central bank to a point where it is forced to raise rates to a point beyond which the board is comfortable with.
She said: "That's not worrying me at the moment".
She said while there's increased demand for funding, "I think the bond markets are reacting in an orderly way."
"Bond yields are rising quite quickly, but there doesn't seem to be anything disorderly about it. There's no liquidity issues that we can see. Having said that, we are watching it quite closely".
The RBA's financial stability review comes out on Thursday.
"It will talk a little bit about the vulnerabilities of having some of these asset prices really high and the risks that might be associated with a pullback in the bond market," Ms Bullock said.
Key Event
Falling house prices caused the RBA to think and pause before it raised rates
RBA Governor Michele Bullock said "there are a couple of downside risks" that caused the RBA to pause and consider whether it should raise interest rates to its highest level in 15 years.
"[The] housing market is one of them at least I think," she said.
"But I think what we've sort of discussed was the fact that there [are] three issues that we identified as risks on the upside and the skewed risks to the upside that we talked about last time.
"One was the Middle East conflict going on for longer and fuel prices rising again. Second was the AI boom. And the third risk was that in fact, capacity pressures were a bit stronger, a bit higher than we thought they were."
Key Event
Can we blame the war in the Middle East for rising interest rates: Not totally Bullock says
Asked to what degree has the worsening of the Middle East conflict led to today's rate hike decision, RBA Governor Michele Bullock responded: "the Middle East conflict has been a big shock and it's made us all poorer in this country".
"You will all recall that when the Middle East conflict first started, everyone was sort of thinking, 'oh, it'll probably not last very long'. Well, that's clearly not true. It's lasted, and there doesn't seem to be any end to it.
"That means that fuel prices, fertiliser prices, transport prices, all these things now are permanently higher. So this idea that they would go up and then come down again, it just hasn't happened.
She said the longer the war drags on, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases.
"So I think it's not the only reason for the decision today. I want to make that I want to make that clear. This isn't all about the Middle East conflict. It is making things much worse.
"And the longer it goes on, I think the more challenging it is to keep inflation expectations grounded at a level lower than what inflation is at the moment."
RBA considered keeping cash rate on hold
RBA Governor Michele Bullock has told reporters that the board considered both keeping the cash rate on hold and hiking it by 25 basis points in September's meeting.
"The holding, if you like, was domestic capacity pressures.
"This is a very difficult area. It's difficult to estimate output gaps and how tight the labour market is.
"Usually the evidence comes up in inflation numbers and unit Labor costs, those sorts of things. So we're still alert to that."
Key Event
Is there nothing the RBA can do about productivity?
RBA Governor Michele Bullock had earlier in the press conference noted that "productivity is important if we want the economy to be able to grow and create jobs. So I think again, it seems there's nothing we can do about productivity."
When asked later whether there was really nothing that the RBA could do, she responded that it was "incumbent upon businesses to take opportunities to improve productivity".
"We're not experts in individual productivity sort measures, but our research does suggest that we are a little bit further from the ... dynamic frontier than other countries are in some of these. So businesses need to step up to the plate as well," she says.
"All I'm saying is that individual productivity policies are not my or the Reserve Bank's bailiwick and monetary policy can't do anything about productivity.
"The best thing we can do for productivity is get inflation low and stable. So businesses and households can spend and invest in an environment where they're not worried about cost of living."
Key Event
Will the cash rate hit above 5pc by May?
RBA governor Michele Bullock was asked this and whether that is a level the economy could withstand.
She responded: "I know that's what the markets are expecting. What the markets are expecting is based on how they're interpreting the data and how they think we will interpret the data.
"The evidence has been that inflation has been a bit more elevated than we're expecting in underlying terms. So we're trying to strip out some of the supply shock.
"But in underlying terms market services, groceries, consumer durables, all these things inflation is just elevated. So that's the sort of information we'll be looking at.
"If it turns out that the restrictiveness that we've introduced by these interest rate rises is enough to bring some of those inflationary pressures back then maybe there doesn't need to be any more interest rate rises. And I would expect the markets will adjust as the data comes out."
Are we drifting towards the 1990s with interest rates in the double digits?
Anyone who is old enough to remember will know that interest rates back in the 1990s was in double digits.
RBA governor Michele Bullock was asked by a reporter if that's where we are drifting.
She said currently inflation is not in double digits like it was back then.
"Inflation is about 3.5%, it's a percentage point above our target. That is true, but it is nowhere near what it was in the 1990s. So I think we're in a good position at the moment."
Key Event
If underlying inflation comes in at 3.6 per cent in August is that unacceptably high?
Ms Bullock was asked about this and noted that such a rate "will mean that inflation, the underlying inflation rate has been about 3.5 per cent for the past six months".
"What we're trying to do is make sure that we have financial conditions tight enough so that looking forward, that inflation pressure eases," she said.
"We're not going to put a lot of emphasis necessarily on one number, but it is a consistent pattern."
She said the RBA raised interest rates three times earlier in the year and that "a lot of that effect is still to flow through".
"This is one more. And so what we are predicting, what is the hope here, is that this will be restrictive enough."
The latest CPI inflation data comes out tomorrow.
Key Event
Is there a greater chance of a recession? Bullock says that's not the RBA's 'base case'
RBA governor Michele Bullock was asked by a reporter whether the chance of a recession is now higher.
Ms Bullock said: "That is not our central base case at this point."
She noted that the unemployment rate "is still quite low historically and we still think the labour market is a little bit tight".
"So that's not actually sort of circumstances unlike some of our peer economies — for example, New Zealand and Canada — when they raised interest rates they raised them a lot higher. And they've now got unemployment rates which are much higher than ours."
She said to bring inflation down, "demand has to grow more slowly than supply for a period".
"That's a fact. That's why we've got these inflationary pressures. And still the aim is to, as I said, bring that excess demand down so that we can preserve as many of the gains in the labour market as possible".

It will take time to turn 'weak' productivity growth around: Chalmers
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says it's going to take a while for Australia to turn the corner on productivity.
The Reserve Bank declared Australia's weak productivity growth remains a constraint on the economy.
Chalmers says it's been a focus of the government but concedes there's more work to do.
"You don't turn around a productivity challenge which has been entrenched for so long quickly in a couple of months. Certainly not in a couple of years either. We've had this challenge for a couple of decades now," he says.
Chalmers takes responsibility for ‘our part of fight against inflation'
Jim Chalmers is taking questions from reporters in Brisbane now.
The treasurer is again defending his economic track record, placing the blame for the inflation challenge on the Middle East war.
While he acknowledged it wasn't the "only factor" he dismissed criticism that government spending was a key driver of inflation.
"We take responsibility for our part of the fight against inflation. That's why we've been managing the budget responsibility," he says.
"It's why we've made sure that public demand in our economy has slowed, rather than gathered pace.
"If you look at public demand in our economy versus private demand over the last year or so, for every $5 of demand in our economy, four of those have been private demand, one has been public demand."
Aussie dollar up after RBA hikes cash rate
The Australian dollar rose 1% to 70.18 US cents after the Reserve Bank's decision to hike the cash rate to a 15-year-high at 4.6%.
Australians paying price for Middle East war: Chalmers
Australians are paying a "hefty price" for the protracted conflict in the Middle East, Treasurer Jim Chalmers says following the RBA's rates decision.
The treasurer says while today's decision was anticipated, it doesn't make it any easier for households and stressed it was a problem not just for Australia but for "every major advanced economy".
"Australian workers didn't choose this war, but they are paying a hefty price for it. The war has been a disaster for the global economy," he says.
"As the RBA’s statement made clear, the conflict in the Middle East is broadening and pushing up energy prices and inflation around the world.
"Inflation is much lower than its peak, but it is higher than we would like, and the conflict in the Middle East is making inflation linger for longer."
Chalmers also notes that the RBA's statement highlighted the impact of AI-related demand on global prices for technology-related goods.
Key Event
Macquarie Bank lifts home loan rates
Macquarie Bank has announced it will lift variable home loan reference rates by 0.25% per annum effective from October 15, 2026.
This follows the Reserve Bank’s decision to increase Australia’s official cash rate to 4.6%.
The bank will also increase the ongoing variable interest rates paid on its transaction and savings accounts from the same day.
Macquarie's head of personal banking, Ben Perham, has encouraged any customers concerned about making their home loan repayments to get in touch, as financial assistance may be available.
Key Event
How AI is also driving inflation
The vast amounts of money being pumped into artificial intelligence is also pushing up inflation, the RBA says.
At its meeting today, the Board decided to increase the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60 per cent — its highest level in 15 years.
"AI-related demand is driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods," the RBA said in its statement explaining the decision.
It said its liaison with businesses indicates that "firms are experiencing cost pressures and are either increasing the prices of their goods and services or looking to do so".
"Short-term measures of inflation expectations remain elevated. And recent inflation outcomes in Australia were stronger than expected at the previous meeting," the RBA said.
Key Event
RBA notes slow growth, lower house prices
The RBA pointed to a continuing picture of slow growth and high inflation in its decision to raise interest rates to their highest level in 15 years.
"Growth in output has slowed but, at the margin, was stronger than expected in the June quarter," the RBA statement accompanying its decision said.
"There are signs that growth in consumer spending is easing gradually as expected, although housing prices have fallen in most capital cities and new housing loans have declined noticeably."
It was also keeping an eye on the jobs market. While the RBA's mandate is to keep inflation between 2 to 3 per cent, it also needs to ensure as many people have jobs as possible without causing high inflation.
It noted: "Labour market conditions have eased broadly as expected in recent months, and labour market leading indicators are broadly stable."
"Meanwhile, growth in business investment and debt is strong."
Key Event
The RBA says higher fuel prices as a result of war are feeding wider inflation
The RBA says since the previous meeting last month, "some of the upside risks to inflation are materialising".
At its meeting today, the Board decided to increase the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60 per cent.
It notes "the conflict in the Middle East has broadened and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts".
"There have been further disruptions to global oil supply and recent data suggest that growth and inflation in Australia have been higher than expected," it said in its statement explaining the decision.
"Higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to prices of other goods and services. This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy."
Key Event
RBA says decision was 'unanimous' and it will keep lifting rates to fight inflation
Explaining its decision to raise interest rates to its highest level in 15 years, the RBA said in its statement that "the Board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded" and it would need to "bring inflation back to target".
The RBA's target is for consumer price inflation to remain between 2 to 3 per cent.
"The three increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial conditions and the economy appears to be slowing," the RBA said.
"But inflation is still too high and the Board judged that, in light of recent developments, a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support a return of inflation to target in a reasonable period.
"The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed."
It sad today's policy decision was "unanimous".

Air Force, Industry Fear Continuing Resolution Could Hinder CCA Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:22:36 UTC
06:22:36 KST

The Air Force’s emerging Collaborative Combat Aircraft program would suffer delays if Congress fails to pass a budget before the end of this calendar year, a top service official said Sept. 28.
Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, said the program is ready for production, but advancing to that next stage requires a new budget. “You can’t go do production without production funding,” he said during a Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies appearance. “So that does provide limitations on what we can execute.”
CCAs are the semi-autonomous drone fighters the Air Force believes can bolster its manned fighter force. The first two models—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Systems’ FQ-44A Fury—are designed for air-to-air strike missions. The objective is for the compact uncrewed CCAs to cost less than $20 million apiece for the airframe, and to rapidly grow the force to include at least 500 in 2032, on its way to at least 1,000 later on.
Fiscal 2027 starts Oct. 1, but Congress failed to pass a budget before taking its recess, instead passing a funding measure that extends appropriations at 2026 levels until Dec. 11. Under such a continuing resolution, new programs, such as CCA production, are not authorized. If Congress fails to pass a budget the government could be forced to shut down. Congress could also vote to extend the CR for a month or more at that time.
Helfrich’s comments echoed concerns raised by Anduril officials at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference in National Harbor, Md., Sept. 14.
Erin Simpson, Anduril’s vice president of strategy execution for air dominance and strike, told reporters in a briefing that the company has worked to get a head start on procurement, including by building a new Arsenal-1 factory in Columbus, Ohio, buying parts in advance, and producing prototype Fury CCAs.
“We will not have a cold start to [launch] production in ’27,” Simpson said. “We will have assets rolling through. That said, even a company like ours can only do so much without procurement dollars.”
When asked about the CR’s potential effect on General Atomics’ production, a company spokesman pointed to a Sept. 21 release that said it is taking on risk by self-funding some of the first FQ-42s, to keep the program moving forward while the Pentagon’s funding is worked out.
“Production of FQ-42 Vengeance is underway on company investment as government funding plans mature, with GA-ASI continuing its longstanding tradition of working at-risk with its own funds to support U.S. procurement planning and prevent delays in delivery,” General Atomics’ statement said. GA-ASI plans to build multiple fighters for its own company aircraft fleet, to invest in inventing new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities for its global customers.”
Helfrich said the Air Force’s upcoming Emerald Flag exercise in December at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., will be a significant demonstration of how far CCAs have come. And it will further the work done by the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit to figure out how best to use CCAs in operational environments, and how to operate it under the Agile Combat Employment construct of flying aircraft out of dispersed, small and rough airfields in a future conflict.
“Setting up for Emerald Flag, it’s all hands on deck, but the EOU is central to making that happen,” Helfrich said. “They’re at the heart of taking a capability and making it into something that we can actually integrate into the Air Force.”
Both initial CCA models will fly at Emerald Flag alongside different manned fighters, he said, possibly with multiple CCAs flying at once.
The Air Force announced in July that Anduril’s Fury CCA had fired its first live missile in a test. General Atomics’ Vengeance will soon follow, Helfrich said. Helfrich indicated that test fire would likely happen before Emerald Flag.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to say exactly when the first FQ-42A live-fire test may take place, saying only that it would happen by the end of the year.
Helfrich said the FQ-42A’s live-fire test will focus on more than just launching the missile, and will be a test run of the entire process for firing weapons with an autonomous system, while still keeping a human “on the loop.”
“The human has to make the decision to use lethal force, and then go and engage on that target,” Helfrich said. “So we’re talking more like. Kill chain than we are about [a standard weapon firing] exercise.”

Trump announces plan for $15 billion steel plant, would be largest in U.S. history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:20:00 UTC
06:20:00 KST

President Donald Trump on Monday announced a steel-making company's plan to invest about $15 billion to build what would be the largest plant of its kind in U.S. history.
The Oval Office announcement with Mesabi Metallics came just weeks before the November midterm election, which is poised to be shaped by Americans' increasingly sour views of Trump's handling of the economy.
The steel plant is planned to be built in Iowa and aims to begin production in 2030, a White House official told CNBC on condition of anonymity ahead of the Oval Office event.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement earlier Monday morning.
Mesabi Metallics, based in Nashwauk, Minnesota, told CNBC the project will deliver "100% American steel: mined, melted and poured in Minnesota and Iowa."
The steel plant will use iron ore from Mesabi's mine on Minnesota's Iron Range, a more than $2.5 billion project that is just beginning production after roughly two decades in development. That project was beset by controversies and setbacks, including Essar Steel Minnesota filing for bankruptcy in 2016. Mesabi is part of the Essar Group, an Indian conglomerate.
The first phase of the Iowa steel plant is estimated to produce some 7.5 million tons per year, supporting up to 6,000 construction jobs, according to the White House. It is slated to eventually ramp up to 10 million tons annually and support at least 1,750 permanent jobs, the official told CNBC. The Minnesota mine project has reportedly created 200 full-time jobs out of an anticipated 350 total, according to Minnesota Public Radio.
Trump was joined in the Oval Office by Mesabi Metallics' CEO Joe Broking and Chairman Rewant Ruia, as well as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Export-Import Bank Chairman John Jovanovic and a number of Iowa elected officials.
Trump slapped 25% tariffs on steel and aluminum imports near the start of his second term, and then doubled them to 50%. The president, who strongly dislikes trade deficits and has criticized free-trade deals, has doled out a variety of heavy import duties as he seeks to boost domestic manufacturing.
Critics say the tariffs have played a major role in raising U.S. steel prices, which have recently hit multi-year highs.
But numerous steel trade groups on Friday sent a letter to Trump, crediting his steel tariffs with driving $47 billion in "announced and underway investment." They urged him not to weaken those tariffs, arguing that doing so would "put that progress at risk."
Lutnick said in the Oval Office that the plan is a "done deal." But complex, long-term construction projects can change drastically, or face insurmountable roadblocks, over their development cycles.
Construction on the Minnesota iron mine, for instance, was supposed to finish by 2016, prior to the company behind the project filing for bankruptcy, Minnesota Public Radio reported.
As president, Trump has previously touted projects that did not live up to their initial hype.
In his first term, Trump attended Taiwan electronics manufacturer Foxconn's groundbreaking for a planned $10 billion factory in Wisconsin, and praised the project as "the eighth wonder of the world." But in 2021, Foxconn reduced its planned investment to $672 million and cut the number of new jobs down to 1,454 from 13,000.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CNBC in a statement on Monday's factory announcement, "President Trump is delivering on his promise to rebuild American industry, reshore manufacturing, and create new jobs."
"Today's announcement underscores the President's historic efforts to revitalize the U.S. steel industry —supporting local communities, strengthening supply chains, and protecting our national security," Rogers said. "After decades of decline, this President is restoring America's industrial competitiveness and securing trillions of dollars in new investment."

Ukraine trains military orphans to ‘replace fallen fathers’ – WaPo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:17:13 UTC

Ukraine trains military orphans to ‘replace fallen fathers’ – WaPo
The Ukrainian government has set up five boarding schools for children whose parents were killed, went missing, or were left disabled in the conflict with Russia, preparing them for careers in the country’s military, The Washington Post has reported.
The newspaper gained access to one of the institutions for a report published on Monday, describing the two-year boarding schools as “part grief counseling and part boot camp,” effectively sealing the fate of the vulnerable children.
“[The] school puts them into a funnel toward the Ukrainian security services that are desperate for recruits, along with hundreds of other cadets at new government academies devoted to the still-young children of fallen fighters,” the article reads.
The children are also being prepared for “university entrance exams in their second year” and are required to complete a degree even if they choose to enter service. School staff insisted that “no pressure” be put on the cadets to pursue such careers, the Post noted.
The Ukrainian military needs some 30,000 fresh recruits per month just to maintain its current force size, the Post noted, citing Ukrainian officials. “Officially, Ukraine reports that about 55,000 have been killed in the war and about 114,000 are missing. But aid providers say those figures don’t begin to reflect the number of children who have lost at least one parent,” the article reads.
Independent casualty estimates, however, differ drastically from the official Ukrainian figures, with the US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating that Ukrainian forces have suffered between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and missing.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently said that the Ukrainian military was suffering 27,000 casualties a month.
Kiev has long struggled to replenish its ranks through forced conscription, with its mobilization effort growing increasingly chaotic and violent over the course of the conflict.
The mobilization campaign, dubbed ‘busification,’ has often involved draft officers ambushing military-age men on the streets, at workplaces, and outside their homes, using violence against those resisting or attempting to flee. The draft has sparked several protests and riots across the country, which the authorities have dismissed as “helping the enemy.”
The involvement of children in paramilitary training has been on the rise in Ukraine since the 2014 Western-backed Euromaidan coup, with the process accelerating further in the wake of the full-blown conflict with Russia.
The idea of lowering age thresholds for such training and, potentially, for active service has been repeatedly floated by various public figures. Moreover, boot camps for children have frequently been set up by openly neo-Nazi groups, with basic training going hand in hand with hateful indoctrination at such facilities.

Burnham’s EU push reopens Labour’s Brexit divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:10:36 UTC
06:10:36 KST

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham attends day two of the Labour Party Conference at Liverpool Experience Campus on September 28, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images
LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham is planning to go big on Brexit. For his party, the question is: How big?
The U.K. prime minister is now widely expected to use his annual speech to Labour’s party conference in Liverpool on Tuesday to talk up closer ties with the EU.
But Burnham will have to strike a delicate balance between those in his party who want to walk back Brexit — and those who want to make peace with it.
Advertisement
Hours ahead of Burnham’s speech, cabinet members were far from speaking with one voice on the issue.
Lucy Powell, Labour’s deputy leader, said at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the conference that going beyond EU plans inherited from Keir Starmer for a reset of relations was “not possible nor desirable.”
“I think there are ways we can improve our links on defense and security, but beyond that, I’m not going to speculate,” she added.
Her comments came after Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on Sunday warned that “constitutional questions” around Britain's EU relationship were causing “uncertainty” for business.
Also speaking at the POLITICO Pub, he warned against moves to join the customs union — which he said would involve the U.K. having to “accept a whole range of alignment on regulatory issues.”
Yet Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told delegates from the main Labour conference stage that the U.K’s future lay in a “deeper” partnership with the EU.
Advertisement
“Europe is not just our geography, but so much more,” he said. “It is how we pursue our values from climate to the Middle East. It's how we pursue our interests from trade to defense. It's where we build and protect our alliances … I say to this conference, our future lies in a stronger, deeper partnership with the European Union.”
Mayor of London Sadiq Khan, meanwhile, said the U.K.’s return to the EU is inevitable and that Burnham should start preparing the British public for that reality.
Further and faster
Burnham’s recently appointed EU Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told Labour conference delegates on Monday that the prime minister wanted to go “further and faster” than his predecessor.
Falconer, a former hostage negotiator who served in Britain’s diplomatic corps before being elected to parliament in 2024, confirmed the public would “hear a bit from the prime minister” on the EU.
At a packed rally of Labour activists on Sunday, Stella Creasy, the MP who chairs the Labour Movement for Europe caucus urged Burnham to drop Keir Starmer’s “red lines” in negotiations with the bloc.
Starmer's manifesto pledges rule out membership of the single market, customs union and free movement — and make a much closer deal with Brussels all-but impossible.
Advertisement
“Who starts a negotiation with a list of what you don’t want — apart from a toddler?” Creasy told her audience to rapturous applause — urging the government to instead draw up a “list of common goals” with the EU: “Let us say it proudly and clearly: drop the red lines now.”
Speaking at another event on Monday as news that Burnham was likely to address the issue filtered through conference, Creasy said that “what comes out tomorrow” should “set a plan of action” and amount to “more than warm words.”
Question of strategy
The divide is partly a disagreement over political strategy.
Labour figures disagree on whether relitigating Brexit is a good use of their political time. Proponents of a closer relationship say the issue is well-placed to enthuse and win back defectors to the Greens and Liberal Democrats. Skeptics say it will do more to turn off voters wary of well-worn debates and prime proponents of Brexit to accuse politicians of betraying the will of the people.
There are genuine economic disagreements, too. Whether the U.K. could prosper as a rule-taker inside the single market but outside the EU and whether its independent trade policy is worth sacrificing for a customs union are genuine matters of debate in the party.
Question marks also hang over how straightforward rejoining the bloc wholesale would be and whether the U.K. could get its old deal back.
Advertisement
Yet even if Burnham does stand up on Tuesday and promise a closer relationship with Europe, it could be easier said than done.
Current talks on Starmer’s relatively modest “reset” over an agriculture and food trade deal, youth visas, and coordination on emissions have proved harder to seal than anticipated.
A summit scheduled for July and postponed when Burnham took over is yet to get a new date, despite him having a sit-down meeting with the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the United Nations General Assembly last week.
An ever-expanding set of issues
The scope of talks has started to creep ever larger. London wants Brussels to give guarantees British businesses won’t be hit by new Made in Europe rules — while Brussels says it can’t be done.
“In the short term I’m quite gloomy. I think the summit which was supposed to happen in November may not happen at all,” Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think-tank told a fringe event. “Unless someone is willing to compromise there may not be a summit at all this year, I hope I’m wrong on that.”
Jukka Salovaara, the EU’s recently-appointed ambassador in London stuck a more optimistic tone. “My own expectation is for a summit to happen in November,” he said.
“True that there are many issues that need to be solved but that’s why we are working on them and making sure that we take a step forward. Summits are never an end in itself, it’s always about what we achieve together and where we can go.”

Airmen, Guardians Told to Select Religion Code from New Consolidated List
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:06:40 UTC
06:06:40 KST

Active-Duty Airmen and Guardians have until mid-October to update their personnel records with their religious preference using the Pentagon’s new consolidated list of Religious Affiliation Codes, according to a recent Department of the Air Force announcement.
The new list of codes—ordered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—slashed the number of religions specified in the Pentagon’s HR systems from more than 200 to roughly 30. Officials said in June that the consolidation was necessary to streamline the number of religious preferences for service members and shape the chaplain corps to support them.
The consolidation process collapsed roughly 170 denominations of Christianity down to 21 and includes widespread non-Christian religions such as Buddhism, Hindu, Islam, and Judaism, among other faiths. It removes Wicca, paganism, and other nontraditional faiths from the list, replacing them with an “Other Religious” category.
The department directs all Active-Duty members of the Air Force and Space Force to select their new Religious Affiliation Code in the Virtual Military Personnel Flight system and certify their record of emergency data is accurate by Oct. 16, the announcement states. Members of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard have until Nov. 9 to update their records.
“Transitioning to these standardized codes ensures our chaplain corps has the accurate demographic data they need to provide tailored resources and support to our service members, while continuing to respect their individual convictions,” Richard Anderson, assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs, said in the announcement.
Airmen and Guardians who fail to update their RAC before the deadline will have their records automatically updated to a selection that aligns with the new RAC list. For example, paganism would likely fall under the “Other Religions” category, according to an Air Force official.
Individual Airmen and Guardians, however, will not be limited by the new RAC list for the purposes of identifying their religious preference on the ID tags or “dog tags” they wear around their necks. The tags can be vital for helping chaplains determine the religious needs of service members wounded in battle.
Hegseth announced the effort to consolidate the list of religious preferences in a March 24 video on social media, calling the older list of Faith and Belief Codes “impractical and unusable.” Hegseth also directed chaplains to replace their rank insignia with their appropriate religious affiliation insignia in an effort to make them more approachable to younger service members. The announcement came six months after Hegseth singled out paganism in September 2025 because some troops have petitioned for religious exemptions so they could grow beards.
“If you want a beard, you can join Special Forces,” Heseth told hundreds of general officers at Quantico, Va., last Sept. 30. “If not, then shave. We don’t have a military full of Nordic pagans, but unfortunately, we have had leaders who either refuse to call BS and enforce standards, or leaders who felt like they were not allowed to enforce standards.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell has argued the new consolidated RAC list is not intended to provide a list of “officially approved” religions. Rather it is “designed to allow chaplains to quickly look at the religious composition of their units and determine how they structure resources to best provide for warfighters of all faith groups,” Parnell wrote in a June 5 social media post.

Space Force Interested in Commercial Antennas to Control Satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:04:22 UTC
06:04:22 KST

The Space Force is starting a new competition to bolster its network of antennas that track and manage Pentagon and other U.S. government satellites—and this time, acquisition officials are open to leasing commercial systems or even paying for commercial antennas as a service.
In a Sept. 24 notice, the Space Force and the Missile Defense Agency announced they are resetting the Satellite Communications Augmentation Resource program with a “Commercial Solutions Opening.” Instead of providing a list of detailed requirements, these openings define “areas of interest,” inviting vendors to pitch ideas based on commercially available technology.
The SCAR program is the Space Force’s effort to “revitalize” its Cold War-era Satellite Control Network, a collection of 19 antennas dispersed around the globe that track and maneuver satellites and collect data about their health and status. The service awarded and later canceled a $1.4 billion contract for Blue Halo, now part of AeroVironment, to build and deliver 12 multibeam, phased-array antennas for SCAR.
After cancelling that deal in March, officials explained they wanted to leverage commercial technology rather than acquire a bespoke, Space Force-centric design. This latest announcement offers more details on the approch, detailing three “areas of interest” for the SCAR program:
- A government-owned, contractor-operated model using commercial systems
- Long-term, exclusive government leases of commercially owned and operated systems
- “Antenna as a Service” giving the government access to commercial systems that could also be used by other customers
Each area of interest has benefits and drawbacks, the announcement states. Government-owned often means “bespoke technical solutions, Government-led maintenance,” and limited funding, officials wrote. Leasing or antenna-as-a-service carries security concerns, including “cyber risks that must be mitigated, such as multi-tenant data leakage, scheduling conflicts, and software interoperability bottlenecks.”
But the announcement lays out why Space Force leaders are eager to avoid rerunning the usual acquisition playbook.
“Space operations demand global, high-frequency satellite passes, yet owning and operating a globally distributed physical network is financially burdensome,” the announcement states. “Shifting to commercial ‘shared’ networks alleviates the need to establish dozens of Government-owned sites or dedicated leases.”
The current Satellite Control Network antennas can maintain contact with only one satellite at a time and not for very long. The network’s capacity is under strain as the Pentagon and other government agencies put up more and more spacecraft. According to a 2023 Government Accountability Office report, utilization rates have already been higher than the industry standard for the past decade, and Space Force leaders are expecting the number of satellites on orbit to greatly expand in the coming years.
Companies interested in SCAR have until Oct. 15 to submit white papers. The program office will then select one or more to move to a second phase of consideration.

RAF Fairford: AI-enhanced photos of suspects fuel false claims about their religion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

RAF Fairford: AI-enhanced photos of suspects fuel false claims about their religion
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as investigations continue. Meanwhile, AI-enhanced images purporting to show their faces have gone viral, with some users claiming it ‘proves’ the men are Muslim. SynthID confirms the sharpened images were created using OpenAI tools, meaning the AI has suggested different facial features. UK police have not disclosed any names or religion, only that the men are all British nationals. Vedika Bahl explains.
Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire have been released on bail as the investigation continues.
The arrests sparked a wave of speculation online, fuelled by images purporting to show the suspects’ faces at the time of their arrest. But the images circulating on social media have been enhanced using artificial intelligence.
The men, who were arrested on suspicion of terror offences, were photographed being apprehended near the base. The original image is grainy and blurry, with the men shirtless and handcuffed though no faces are clearly disce. Several social media users have since shared sharpened versions of the photograph, claiming the images reveal the men’s faces.
However, the sharpened, refined photo contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that the image was modified using OpenAI tools.
A second AI-enhanced image showing the men being detained has also circulated online. The two versions show noticeably different facial features, and lighting highlighting the limitations of using AI to enhance blurry photographs.
Despite this, the altered images have been widely shared. Two posts on X containing one of the images have amassed almost two million views, with some users falsely presenting it as evidence that the five men are Muslim.
In reality, there is currently no publicly available information about the suspects’ religion. Authorities have identified the five men as British nationals from London, aged between 23 and 25.
AI image-enhancement tools can generate details that are not present in the original image. Whilst internet users may have tried to refine the grainy image to see the men's faces more clearly, AI does not know what the original face looks like, leaving it to effectively guess or invent facial characteristics that do not actually exist.

For First Time, US F-35s Will Join Exercise in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:54:46 UTC
05:54:46 KST

Six U.S. Air Force F-35A fighters and 200-plus Airmen deployed to India on Sept. 26 for their first appearance in a large-scale exercise on Indian soil.
Exercise Tarang Shakti will run from Sept. 26 to Oct. 12, according to the Indian Air Force, with eight countries contributing aircraft. First held in 2024, the exercise is India’s largest multinational aerial training event.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Pacific Air Forces confirmed the arrival of the F-35s and released images of them at Jodhpur Air Force Station. The aircraft are from the 13th Fighter Squadron at Misawa Air Base, Japan.
This is the first time the USAF has deployed F-35s for an exercise in India, although USAF did previously display the Lightning II at Aero India, a large-scale air show. In 2024, the Air Force sent A-10s to Tarang Shakti in 2024, and USAF has sent F-15s and F-16s to participate in previous editions of Cope India, a major joint air combat exercise.
The U.S. and Indian air forces have built up their interaction in recent years. A B-1 bomber landed in India for the first time for Aero India in 2021, then returned for its first exercise at Cope India 2023. Last year, President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. might eventually sell F-35s to India, but little has been said on that topic since.
On the flip side of U.S.-India relations, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also worked to build ties with Russia and China. Modi met with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping earlier this month at the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) summit, at which he stressed better relations with both Russia and China.
The Indian Air Force has an eclectic mix of aircraft, including indigenous HAL Tejas light combat aircraft, Russian Su-30s, French Rafales and Mirage 2000s, American C-17s, and more. Russia has also pitched its new Su-57 fighter to India—the Su-57 and F-35 were both at Aero India in 2025.

In France, the largest forest fire since 1949 was completely extinguished after two months

In France, the largest forest fire since 1949 was completely extinguished after two months
Kyiv • UNN
The fire in southwestern France destroyed 37,296 hectares and forced 224,000 people to evacuate. More than 3,300 firefighters fought it.
A massive forest fire in southwestern France, which broke out in July and became the largest in the country since 1949, has been fully extinguished. Yle reports this, citing AFP, writes UNN.
Details
The fire was brought under control as early as August 1, but it continued to smolder underground for several weeks. More than 3,300 firefighters were involved in fighting the blaze.
According to the French authorities, the firefighting operation was the largest in the modern history of the country's civil protection service. The fire destroyed 37,296 hectares of land, while the total area affected by the blaze reached approximately 42,000 hectares.
More than 200,000 people evacuated
The fire broke out near the village of Saumos in the Gironde department. The blaze threatened the Cap Ferret peninsula, popular with tourists, and the areas surrounding Bordeaux.
Because of the fire, approximately 224,000 people were forced to evacuate. Despite the scale of the disaster, there were no fatalities.
The last time France experienced a larger forest fire was in 1949, when approximately 50,000 hectares burned in the same region. According to preliminary data, fires have already destroyed approximately 98,000 hectares in France this year—the highest figure since 1976.

NASA announces plans to revive Boeing’s troubled Starliner spacecraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:43:23 UTC
05:43:23 KST

After a failed maiden crewed voyage, Boeing’s Starliner is getting another shot at flying NASA’s astronauts to space.
At a press conference on Monday NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the space capsule will head to the International Space Station (ISS) on an uncrewed test flight as soon as December—a technical step back for the multi-billion-dollar initiative.
The troubled Starliner hasn’t flown since its unsuccessful crewed mission in 2024. In that test, after several scrubbed launches, the vessel, named Calypso, carried astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams to the ISS for what was supposed to be an eight-day stay. But helium leaks and malfunctioning thrusters raised safety concerns, leading NASA to decide Williams and Wilmore could not return to Earth onboard Calypso.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The empty spacecraft did eventually make it back to Earth in one piece. Wilmore and Williams, however, ended up spending 286 days on the ISS before they returned in a SpaceX Dragon capsule.
In a report released in February, NASA said the botched mission resulted from several failures. There were issues with the ship’s design and engineering, particularly with the thrusters, but the report concluded that the biggest cause was lax NASA oversight of Boeing, a lack of data transparency with vital personnel and poor decision-making.
A number of changes have been made to Starliner’s design in the wake of Calypso, including alterations to seal designs, as well as the thruster system. Those changes will be put through their paces during the upcoming uncrewed mission, and data will be collected to “validate the recent remediation efforts,” Isaacman said on Monday. If that goes well, a Starliner vehicle could carry out a crewed mission sometime in 2028 under the command of NASA astronaut Woody Hoburg.
“He’s an absolutely brilliant guy who’s helping on a lot of our ignition priorities, and I am confident his experience will serve this mission incredibly well,” Isaacman said of Hoburg.
Another major change will be the rocket that will loft Starliner to space. Starliner originally flew onboard United Launch Alliance’s (ULA’s) Atlas V rocket, but the vehicle is no longer in production. Instead, Isaacman said, NASA plans to use ULA’s Vulcan Centaur heavy-lift rocket for future Starliner missions.
As things stand, NASA wants Starliner to work. Isaacman and other NASA officials at the press conference emphasized the fact that there is only one operational crew capsule, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon, that can ferry NASA astronauts to and from orbit. Elon Musk’s firm hasn’t been shy about wanting to sunset the Falcon 9 rocket that launches Crew Dragon, as well as the capsule, in favor of developing its Starship megarockets. At the same time, Isaacman said, having some redundancy and more options available for crewed missions is preferable when considering the needs of a thriving space economy.
Isaacman stressed that, at this point, there are no other contenders to supply capsules for missions to the ISS and that SpaceX and Boeing will be the only options for the foreseeable future.
“One of them is serving our needs very well,” Isaacman said. “The other one we’ve been committed to getting operational.”

peripheral vision and artwork that exceeds the eye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:35:43 UTC
05:35:43 KST

This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.
peripheral vision and artwork that exceeds the eye
these artists make seeing everything at once impossible, and use that limit as material.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
when an artwork becomes too large for the eye
There is a familiar way of looking at art. Most of us tend to stand back, face the work, and take in the whole image. We can see it happen at any museum. There have been, however, some fascinating experiments across twentieth-century art and exhibition design which begin by making that position fail.
Mark Rothko enlarged fields of color until they could exceed the viewer’s central field of vision. Herbert Bayer mapped images above and around the eye. The Eameses arrayed thousands of photographs across seven screens at once, and Lina Bo Bardi pulled paintings away from the wall altogether. Across very different media, the same question still stands: what does art become when there is more to see than one viewpoint can contain?
Peripheral vision marks the edge of attention. We perceive color and movement beyond our line of sight, but detail begins to fall away. An artwork that extends into and beyond this territory behaves in a way that’s unique. Its edges become harder to hold at once, or other images enter behind it. Looking becomes physical, and involves distance, turning, and movement through space. The artwork can remain completely still while the viewer becomes active.
rothko makes scale intimate
Mark Rothko understood scale through proximity. His large canvases were never intended simply as monumental pictures to admire from across a gallery. Writing in 1949, he explained that he painted large because he wanted the experience to remain ‘very intimate and human.’ A small picture could be surveyed from outside, he argued, while a larger one places the viewer within the experience. ‘However you paint the larger picture, you are in it,‘ he wrote.
The idea becomes physical once we stand close to one of the large dark red canvases of the Seagram Murals, for instance. A wash of color extends far beyond our field of vision and we become immersed in a new, atmospheric world of total red. Rothko even specified that his largest pictures should be encountered at close range. The scale works through a strange inversion: the painting grows enormous so the distance between object and viewer can shrink.
barnett newman asks the viewer to come closer
Barnett Newman’s Vir Heroicus Sublimis, painted in 1950–51, stretches nearly eighteen feet across. Five narrow vertical bands, which Newman called ‘zips,’ interrupt an expanse of red. From across the room, the painting resolves fairly easily into a rectangle with a compositional structure. Newman wanted another encounter. He hoped viewers would approach the canvas closely enough for the red field to take over their vision.
At that distance, the painting becomes hard to see all at once. One zip appears clearly while another sits farther out toward the edge of vision. The perimeter of the canvas loses some of its authority. MoMA describes the effect as an ‘engulfing environment,’ though the canvas itself stays resolutely flat against the wall.
The spatial experience comes from the viewer standing too close for conventional looking to work. Newman compared the encounter to meeting another person, something understood physically before it can be surveyed from a safe distance.
herbert bayer draws the field of vision
Earlier in the 20th century, Herbert Bayer turned this problem into a diagram. His Diagram of the Field of Vision, first developed for the 1930 Deutscher Werkbund exhibition in Paris and reworked in 1935, places an eye at the center of an expanding field of images. Pictures occupy positions overhead and below the conventional eye line. The viewer faces several directions at once. Bayer described the arrangement as an ‘inclusive picture’ of possible viewpoints, with exhibition material extending beyond the frontal wall.
The drawing is almost funny in its bluntness. Exhibition design becomes a geometry problem built around a human head. Instead of assuming that vision travels straight ahead toward a wall, Bayer works with everything the eye can potentially register around it. The diagram also exposes something museums tend to conceal: every display already contains an idea of where the viewer should stand. Bayer just drew that relationship out in full.
the eameses give the eye too much
For Glimpses of the U.S.A., produced for the 1959 American National Exhibition in Moscow, Charles and Ray Eames projected 2,200 still and moving images across seven screens, each measuring twenty by thirty feet. Photographs of homes, highways, supermarkets, newspapers, and other fragments of postwar American culture appeared in rapid combinations across the enormous array.
Nobody in the audience could inspect all seven screens simultaneously. Looking meant choosing, even when the choice lasted only a second. One image sat at the center of attention while another registered somewhere beside it. Charles Eames later explained that the multiple projection system was meant to engage the viewer’s senses through reinforcement across images.
The installation turns visual excess into an organizational tool. Where Rothko stretches one image beyond comfortable viewing distance, the Eameses multiply images until attention itself becomes the scarce resource.
Charles and Ray Eames, Glimpses of the U.S.A., 1959 | video © Eames Office
lina bo bardi removes the wall
At the Museu de Arte de São Paulo, Lina Bo Bardi’s glass easels lift paintings onto transparent panes set into heavy concrete bases. The works stand throughout the open gallery instead of forming a procession along its perimeter. MASP describes the arrangement as a ‘forest’ of artworks, with visitors free to move among paintings that appear suspended in space.
The effect comes from overlap. Look at one painting and another may appear beyond its edge. Walk sideways and the composition of the room changes. Turn around and the back of a canvas enters view, complete with its label and support. A work that would usually claim an isolated patch of wall now shares the field of vision with other paintings and other people. Bo Bardi leaves each artwork intact while removing the architectural device that normally tells us how to approach it.
the viewer becomes part of the display system
Taken together, these works make the viewer unusually aware of the act of looking. Rothko uses distance. Newman uses scale. Bayer works through orientation, while the Eameses overload attention and Bo Bardi uses position. The work exceeds the easy frontal view in a different way each time. A visitor has to move, turn, choose a focus, or accept that part of the visual field will remain unresolved.
This is where the idea separates from the contemporary language of ‘immersive’ art. Filling every surface with imagery can create a powerful environment, although visual saturation alone says little about how a viewer is being asked to see.
The earlier experiments are compelling because their techniques remain exposed. Bayer literally diagrams the apparatus. The Eameses leave seven screens hanging above the audience. Bo Bardi forces you to view a massive collection of layered imagery at once. The experience comes from understanding that your own body occupies a specific position within a larger visual system.

Your exclusive invitation to steelman religion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:21:42 UTC
05:21:42 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello friends,
I want to share some backstage gossip with you that may or may not get me fired. But I do think it ultimately reflects well on the company.
Before we send any of our quarterly magazines to the printer, and then to members, the team will read every article a few times over, and then we’ll discuss them. Normally, it’s fairly easygoing. “Yeah, I loved all of these,” or “I think this one was my favorite.”
But recently, there was a furor. A good-spirited, intellectual roundtable.
About one article, the question was raised: “Is this narrative too simplistic?” Some said yes, some said no. The dialectic swayed for several hours, and Plato would have been happy.
You see, Big Think prides itself on bringing depth to the debate. And there are many ways to do this. We can line up and juxtapose a variety of sides. We can call upon oodles of empirical research and analyze the data. But first, and most importantly, we can try to “steelman” an argument wherever we can.
If you want to build a good argument, do not create a caricature or one-dimensional strawman to knock down. Lay out the best version you can of a position and then critique it if you will. Disagree, but disagree properly.
One area crammed with strawmen is debates about religion. It’s nearly impossible to have a debate about religion without it degrading into either a mudslinging battle of egos or embarrassing misrepresentations.
“Christians just worship a bearded man in the sky! It’s primitive!”
“Islam is a structurally violent religion. It’s incompatible with the West!”
“Wait, so if I’m rude to you, does that mean I’ll be reincarnated as a tapir?”
It’s often little more than a debate about faith conducted in bad faith. People are talking past each other, and there’s no hope of any progress or growth in the meeting. But we can do better. So, if you want to join me — and join Big Think’s mission to do better — you can hear me in a live conversation with the YouTuber and scholar of religion, Andrew Henry, about “What people get wrong about religion.”
Sign up on Big Think and get your questions ready.
Go well,
Jonny
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

British police release five men on bail after airbase incident

British police release five men on bail after airbase incident
FAIRFORD, England – The British police said on Sept 28 that five men arrested near an airbase used by the US were released on bail, as Washington asserted a “foreign actor” was involved in the suspected bomb plot.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, said he was “surprised that they released them”, adding, “I wouldn’t have done that”.
The release of the five – all London-based Britons in their mid-20s – came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have “the full picture”.
Earlier, Iran had denied involvement in any plot to target the Royal Air Force Fairford base in Gloucestershire, south-west England, following the security scare there early on Sept 27.
Counter-terror probe
British counter-terror police are leading the investigation after the authorities received reports on Sept 27 of three “suspicious” white vans near the airbase, which the US has used to bomb Iran.
The police said in their latest update on Sept 28 that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, had been released on bail.
“This does not mean the investigation is over,” Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding that the five would be subject to “stringent” bail conditions.
He said officers were “considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”.
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and “preparation of a terrorist act” under British anti-terrorism laws, according to the police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to “extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts”.
Bomb-disposal team
The authorities have not confirmed any details of the threat, but bomb-disposal experts were seen working at the scene.
The Daily Mail and Press Association both reported late on Sept 28, citing sources, that tests on materials in the back of the vans established that they were “not viable explosives”.
A farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase said she rang the police after seeing the vans blocking a road and a group of masked men.
The anonymous woman told the media on Sept 28 that she believed the police had “dropped the ball” on the threat.
But British Defence Minister Wes Streeting said the woman only had a “partial picture”.
Iran denies involvement
Trump, on Sept 27, said Britain and the US had the suspects “under investigation” for a while and alleged that “they were looking to do big damage to our fort”.
After hearing news of their bail, Trump said on Sept 28 that the case “might be” linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.
Trump’s top diplomat Marco Rubio said the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor”, without giving further details.
Iran’s Embassy in London said on social media platform X that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved.
It criticised “the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran” to the incident.
US used base
In March, Britain gave the US permission to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran” to destroy Iranian missiles at the source.
Since then, US bombers and other planes have been seen taking off and landing at the base – the only one on the British mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, has seen increased activity and security in recent months.
The authorities evacuated around 85 households from the village early on Sept 27, and they were allowed to return home the next day.
Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the US in operations against Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused London of “putting British lives in danger” by allowing the bases to be used “for aggression against Iran”. AFP

Boeing 737 Max 10 certification delayed by software issue, FAA says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:16:04 UTC
05:16:04 KST

The head of the Federal Aviation Administration said a software problem will delay its certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10 as the agency assesses whether it poses a safety issue, a potential setback for the manufacturer as it seeks to complete government approval of its best-selling family of aircraft.
Boeing had expected to receive a green light from its regulator on the years-delayed planes "very soon," CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month. But Boeing said Saturday that last month it flagged a software glitch on some 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures.
"We haven't concluded whether this is a safety-of-flight issue or not, but we will be delaying the 10 ... until we're satisfied that we don't have an issue here," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference on air traffic modernization in Washington, D.C., on Monday.
The FAA said in a statement that "safety dictates the certification timeline." It added that the agency was "following our safety review process to investigate this software glitch and won't hesitate to take action if needed."
Boeing shares extended earlier losses after Bedford's comments, shedding nearly 7% Monday, as investors assessed another delay after years of setbacks for the aircraft.
"We continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process," Boeing said in a statement.
Boeing said over the weekend that the issue could occur with a vertical navigation system after an aircraft misses an approach and has to go around and line up to land again, such as in situations when there is an obstruction on the runway, for example. Both the company and Bedford said pilots are trained for those circumstances.
"The pilots remain in control of the airliner, train for these scenarios," Bedford said Monday. "The issue that we're looking at right now is the workload component."
The FAA certified the Max 7, the smallest of the family, last month. Those planes have the most updated version of the software, which the FAA is evaluating. It isn't clear how that could affect deliveries of those planes to customers like Southwest Airlines.
U.S. airlines said they don't have any Max aircraft with the issue, in part because they are allowed to revert to older software on those models, if needed, not the newer version that has the potential issue.
Bedford said Boeing had fixed a previous bug in the system but "unexpectedly ... introduced a new bug."
Boeing has been trying to move on from years of safety crises, including two crashes of the Max 8 in 2018 and 2019. A flight control system was implicated in those crashes.
Bedford added on Monday that unlike that system, this "doesn't take control away from the pilots."
The company had originally planned to start delivering the Max 10 in 2020 before those safety concerns and other problems delayed the plane. It is the last of the Max family waiting to be certified.

Anyone attempting to illegally enter the United States will be apprehended, prosecuted, and removed from the country.”

Supreme Court Justice Alito will not participate in big climate change case next week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:13:00 UTC
05:13:00 KST

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, in a surprising reversal, has recused himself from participating in a major climate-change case the Supreme Court is set to hear next week, which involves the oil companies Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy.
Environmental groups had called on Alito, one of the court's six conservative justices, to not participate in the case because of his holdings of stock in oil and gas companies. Alito does not hold stock in Exxon Mobil or Suncor Energy, according to his most recent financial disclosure for 2025.
Alito previously refused to step off the case after the Supreme Court accepted it for consideration earlier this year. However, in 2023, he did not participate in the court's decision not to consider jurisdictional questions raised by the companies in the same case.
The case, known as Suncor Energy (USA) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, is focused on the question of whether federal law precludes claims made under state law seeking damages for injuries allegedly caused by climate change to greenhouse gas emissions.
The case is set to be argued on Oct. 5.
"I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case," Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, wrote lawyers for the parties in the case, on Monday.
Alito's sudden recusal sets up the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling on the Supreme Court in the case. A tie in a Supreme Court decision leaves in place the lower-court decision that was being appealed.
The case involves a lawsuit by the city of Boulder, Colorado, and its surrounding county, that seeks damages for alleged harms from the effects of global climate change. A trial court denied a motion to dismiss that was filed by Suncor and Exxon, and the Colorado state Supreme Court affirmed that ruling, allowing the suit to head to trial.
If the Supreme Court rules against the oil companies, the case would proceed toward trial.
In May, a Supreme Court spokeswoman told NBC News that Alito would not step aside from the case.
"Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party" involved in the case, the spokeswoman told NBC News at the time.
She added that the Supreme Court's legal counsel had advised Alito that "his recusal is not required," according to NBC.

The turret houses 12 anti-aircraft guided missiles with an independent elevation mechanism, while close-in air defense is provided by two 30-mm six-barrel cannons.

Senate tees up college sports bill aimed at regulating NIL deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:05:55 UTC
05:05:55 KST

The Senate on Monday voted 77-22 in favor of a bill to create a national framework for name, image and likeness deals in college sports as one of its last acts before the chamber gears up to leave town later this week ahead of the 2026 midterm election.
The legislation, which would codify athletes' rights to earn NIL money and grant the NCAA, conferences and schools a controversial antitrust exemption to enforce certain rules, is the latest step in a multi-year effort to regulate money in college sports.
Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Republican and Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, led the bill, dubbed the Protect College Sports Act. It now passes to the House, where its fate remains uncertain amid opposition from the Congressional Black Caucus and outside groups, including the NAACP.
President Donald Trump called the bill's passage a "really big deal" in a Truth Social post. "It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves," Trump said.
The legislation would tighten transfer rules, allowing players to switch schools once without a penalty; cap eligibility at five years; and increase the revenue-sharing pool schools can use to pay athletes directly, including up to $5 million that could go to women's sports and Olympic sports, which tend to bring less revenue than men's football and basketball to schools.
Cruz said it was a "monumental day" for college sports. "The United States Senate voted to protect the hundreds of thousands of student athletes currently competing in college sports, the millions who will follow in their footsteps, and every college sports fan who wants to preserve this great American tradition for generations to come."
Members of Congress have introduced a flurry of bills and held numerous hearings in the roughly five years since a series of legal rulings led the NCAA to suspend its longstanding prohibition on students being compensated and loosen its rules around transferring. The moves ushered in a new era of college sports in which top athletes — particularly in football and basketball — could switch schools freely and secure million-dollar NIL deals.
But these new rules came with downsides, as smaller schools, women and Olympic athletes, fans and coaches complained about power conferences consolidating power. Lawmakers have scrambled to respond, but earlier attempts repeatedly fell short.
Earlier, a similar bill, dubbed the SCORE Act, was pulled from consideration in the House due to opposition from the Congressional Black Caucus.
The CBC, which has more than 50 members across the House and Senate, said it could not support legislation that would benefit "major athletic institutions that continue to remain silent while Black voting rights and Black political power are being systematically dismantled across the South." The statement came out in the immediate aftermath of a Supreme Court decision that hollowed out portions of the Voting Rights Act.
The CBC also opposes the Protect College Sports Act, and other detractors, including Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., have argued it would give too much power to the NCAA and conferences at the expense of players.
"What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation. This bill protects the billions of dollars that coaches and sports industry executives are making over the suppression of compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world," Murphy said earlier this month at a virtual press conference. "This bill seeks to give an unprecedented antitrust exemption to an industry that is violating the law every single day."
With Senate passage of the bill before midterms, it's unlikely the House would take it up until the lame duck period after the Nov. 3 election. Cruz on Monday said he's been in contact with House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and thinks Johnson will call the House back to vote on the measure.
A House source familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, said the House returning to take up the college sports bill is "highly unlikely."
