Russian dictator tests NATO in the Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:22:46 UTC
22:22:46 KST

For decades, polar bears posed the greatest threat to Svalbard’s small population, but Russia’s encroaching activities in the Arctic are now raising increasingly serious concerns, reports Politico.
Fears are mounting that Russia might use the Arctic archipelago—part of Norwegian territory—to test NATO at a time when US commitment to European defense remains uncertain. Allies suspect Moscow of snooping around undersea cables near Svalbard and planning military operations to probe the legal framework governing its presence in the Arctic region. As Russia expands hybrid attacks across Europe, Oslo is rushing to bolster its naval and surveillance capabilities to protect NATO’s northern flank, while local authorities in Svalbard are investing in critical infrastructure and have developed an evacuation plan.
Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik told Politico that tensions are rising in the Arctic and the north, affecting Svalbard as well. Norwegians are aware that Russia employs a range of tactics to provoke and find ways to create hybrid threats. Despite the fact that the Svalbard archipelago belongs to Norway, a Russian town is located on its main island, Spitsbergen. Moscow and Oslo have long sought to avoid an escalation of tension, but this fragile balance is increasingly under threat. Western nations are concerned about Russian hybrid attacks in Europe and have warned that, by the end of the decade, Russia could attempt a limited incursion into NATO territory. Kari Aga Myklebost, a professor of Russian history at the Arctic University of Norway and an expert on Svalbard affairs, stated that Russian leaders are unpredictable and increasingly prone to taking risks; she does not rule out any scenario regarding the Kremlin’s willingness to confront NATO.
Svalbard has long symbolized Norway’s efforts to foster cooperation among Arctic nations, including Russia. Beyond its remote location—more than 900 kilometers from the Norwegian mainland—and its frigid temperatures, the archipelago is also distinguished by its unique status. Under a 1920 international agreement, signatory nations recognized Oslo’s sovereignty over the archipelago while gaining the right to explore and extract natural resources there. Shortly thereafter, the Soviet Union acquired Barentsburg to begin coal mining operations.
The agreement prohibited the use of Svalbard for military purposes—including the construction of naval bases
and military fortifications—though Norway is permitted to visit the archipelago with coast guard and military vessels.
At the height of the Cold War, 2,400 Soviet citizens lived on Spitsbergen—the archipelago’s only permanently inhabited island—comprising 70% of its population. Moscow has shown no inclination to break the agreement, as doing so would run counter to its interests. Russia’s Kola Peninsula, home to two-thirds of its nuclear submarines, lies approximately 1,000 kilometers away, and Myklebost noted that Russia has thus far sought to avoid escalating the situation. The area is also strategically significant for NATO; in the event of a military conflict, Russian submarines would transit through this region into the North Atlantic and dive to great depths, posing a threat to NATO and the United States.
However, tensions have risen following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Since 2022, local Russian officials have faced criticism for hosting a youth organization indirectly linked to the navy, announcing missile drills, and organizing annual military parades—one of which even included helicopter flyovers. In 2024, Moscow also launched direct shipping routes from Russia and, last year, established a branch of the Russian Geographical Society—led by former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu—in Spitsbergen. Myklebost described this as a “gray-zone provocation.” It is a cost-effective way to establish a Russian presence and challenge Norwegian jurisdiction. Consequently, Norwegian intelligence services warned this year that the Kremlin is seeking to expand Russian capabilities in Svalbard.
This spring, British, American, and Norwegian forces detected Russian vessels testing a secret weapon
designed to sever undersea cables off the coast of Svalbard.
Although coal reserves in Barentsburg are dwindling, Moscow has not abandoned the town. In 2025, the Russian state-owned company Trust Arktikugol, which manages Barentsburg, received 20 million euros in subsidies. Russia’s Ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, told Politico that he wanted to see a shift in economic activity from coal mining to service provision, with Trust Arktikugol investing in the town’s upkeep.
Many of Barentsburg’s Soviet-era buildings are surrounded by cranes and scaffolding, signaling continued Russian interest. However, Korchunov insisted that Russia does not question Norway’s sovereignty, emphasizing instead the need to adhere to the terms of the Svalbard Treaty. He accused Oslo of aligning with a negative NATO trend toward militarizing the entire Baltic and Arctic regions.
Vice Admiral Rune Andersen of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters stated that his priority is to strike a balance between deterrence and maintaining stability in Svalbard, while preserving peace in the face of hybrid threats. Nevertheless, given the risk of escalation, the military is investing in enhanced surveillance capabilities, with three new maritime mapping satellites set to become operational next year. The navy and coast guard are also being upgraded to ensure a constant presence. Meanwhile, the local strategy relies on keeping tensions within certain limits. Katharina Rise, Deputy Governor of Svalbard, stated that her office meets with the Russian consulate four times a year, and that the dialogue is good and constructive.
She noted that ensuring stability and low tension is their responsibility.
Terje Aunevik, mayor of Longyearbyen—the largest Norwegian settlement on Spitsbergen—said that authorities have a plan for the rapid evacuation of the town should tensions suddenly escalate sharply. The town relies on imports and is served by two undersea internet cables, an airport, a water reservoir, and a diesel-powered power plant; however, Aunevik noted that substantial investments are planned. Two new water reservoirs are scheduled to be built by 2029.
Barentsburg does not look particularly menacing. A few locals walk among dozens of dilapidated buildings. Smoke rises from the coal power plant’s chimney, and a solitary flag bearing the hammer and sickle flutters in the wind. Barentsburg resembles a relic of a bygone era. Even some recent “hybrid activities” might stem more from a local desire to be noticed and secure funding for the town’s upkeep.
However, Putin’s unpredictability and US President Donald Trump’s wavering attitude toward his country’s NATO obligations are variables that could play out in various ways. Given the acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, and airspace violations across Europe, fears are mounting that Putin could escalate the situation further.
Anxiety is palpable in Spitsbergen, too.
A waitress in Barentsburg—who had arrived from St. Petersburg and wished to remain anonymous—admitted that locals fear a potential war between Russia and NATO. Guide Jonatan Svensson, who has lived in Longyearbyen for five years, said there is constant talk that the Russian government wants to pressure NATO, and that Svalbard is the place where this will happen. Two anonymous NATO officials stated that, to alleviate these fears, NATO should consider air patrols over Svalbard, relocate air defense systems to northern mainland Norway, and conduct joint exercises nearby—provided Oslo agrees and the requirements of the Svalbard Treaty are respected. However, NATO currently has no plans to increase its naval or air presence in the region, though some worry that the current stance will not be enough to deter Russia.
Ståle Ulriksen, a lecturer at the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, said that, theoretically, it would be easy for Russia to occupy Svalbard by flying in special forces from northern Russia and seizing the airport. He noted, however, that such a scenario is unlikely.
Russia would not necessarily need to carry out a full-scale occupation. According to Myklebost, Russia could manufacture an emergency situation affecting local Russians and dispatch crisis management forces; this would not constitute clear grounds for invoking NATO’s Article 5. She stated that the worst-case scenario is one in which Moscow sees an opportunity to test NATO’s unity. It is possible that Norway might ask for help, while Trump declares that Americans will not jeopardize good deals with Russia over a tiny island.

The 3rd Army Corps liberated the settlements of Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk region. In addition, the Defense Forces regained control of Karpivka and Novomykhailivka.
Thanks to the successful completion of the third phase of Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainian forces regained control of another 51 km² of territory, reported Brigadier General Andriy Biletskyi, commander of the corps and the army group Center.
During the fighting, the Russian invaders suffered losses of approximately 2,000 personnel, and more than 250 Russian servicemen were taken prisoner.

During the breakthrough of enemy defenses, Ukrainian troops deployed remotely controlled BTR-60s. Converted into armored robotic kamikaze systems, these vehicles were used to destroy the enemy’s most fortified positions and firing points.
Soldiers of the 3rd Assault Brigade made a key contribution to the operation.
Meanwhile, soldiers of the 3rd Border Guard Detachment named after Hero of Ukraine Colonel Yevhen Pikus regained control of Ridkodub and secured their positions on new lines. Units of the 10th DOZOR Mobile Border Guard Detachment also participated in the assault operations.
During the first phase of Vivaldi, Ukrainian fighters cleared the settlements of Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, and the outskirts of Korovyi Yar. In addition, Ukrainian forces completely liberated the village of Seredne.
During the second phase, they liberated Shandryholove and Derylove and established full control over Drobyshev.

Tehran gallery traces capital’s past, explores future of smart tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:21:27 UTC
22:21:27 KST

Tehran gallery traces capital’s past, explores future of smart tourism
TEHRAN – A new gallery in Tehran is taking visitors on a journey through the capital’s political, social, cultural and artistic history while using digital technology and artificial intelligence to offer a glimpse of how tourism in the city could evolve in the future.
The “Stories of Tehran” gallery opened at the Kushk-e Bagh-e Honar cultural complex in the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone on Sunday, coinciding with World Tourism Day and Tehran Week. The exhibition runs from September 27 to October 8 under this year’s World Tourism Day theme, “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Redesign Tourism.”
The gallery brings together historical maps, illustrated timelines, infographics, photographs and interactive features, to name a few, to present different chapters of Tehran’s history, from its early development and eventual selection as Iran’s capital to its political and social transformations in the modern era.
Among the subjects presented are some of the city’s earliest known developments, its old plane trees, food culture, historic buildings and major political and cultural events. A section also documents damage inflicted on historic buildings and cultural spaces during the recent war with the US and the Israeli regime.
Seyyed Mohammad-Hossein Hejazi, managing director of the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, said the event was designed to introduce Tehran’s tourism attractions and present the city through its past and future.
“Unfortunately, Tehran has mostly been viewed as a transit city in recent years rather than a final destination for tourists,” he told reporters.
Hejazi said the exhibition was part of broader efforts to introduce the capital’s attractions from different perspectives and strengthen its position as a tourism destination.
Digitalization is also being incorporated into plans for tourism services in the Abbasabad zone. Hejazi said Tehran Municipality’s “Shahrzad” application had been linked to a planned tourism card for the Abbasabad area.
The card, which has not yet been launched, is modeled partly on systems such as the Istanbulkart and Dubai Pass, he said. It is expected to eventually provide access to a range of services, including public transportation, museums, recreational facilities and tourism and leisure attractions.
Hejazi said the Abbasabad area had been selected as a pilot site for the initiative and that a trial could potentially begin in the coming months.
The “Stories of Tehran” concept itself dates back to the COVID-19 pandemic, when international tourism came to a halt. According to Alireza Moghaddam-Nia, director of tourism at the Abbasabad zone, the area at the time sought to provide virtual journeys through Tehran by drawing on the knowledge and experiences of tour guides, tourism businesses and other industry stakeholders.
The exhibition’s central timeline stretches across the gallery walls and traces major events in Tehran from the Safavid and Qajar periods to contemporary history. Historical maps of the old city are also eye-catching.
Visitors can hear stories about the city and interact with replicas and toys associated with old Tehran. The exhibition also incorporates elements of the city’s natural heritage, including its long-lived trees, rather than focusing solely on monuments and historical events.
One of the main features is the use of artificial intelligence and digital technology to create interactive tourism experiences. Visitors can take virtual tours of countless locations across Tehran and use a QR-code-based service to create photographs of themselves against images of the city from different periods.
The organizers say the idea is to combine digital tools with physical and immersive experiences rather than allow technology to replace direct engagement with destinations.
“The technology can facilitate tourism services and the travel experience, but it should not replace the tourist’s real experience,” Sara Mirzaei, deputy head of tourism and recreation at the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, said.
She cited emerging tools such as smart glasses capable of translation and content generation as examples of technologies that could make travel easier.
The exhibition also looks at the history of the 560-hectare Abbasabad area, which today contains a number of Tehran’s major cultural, tourism and recreational facilities, including the Tabiat Bridge, Ab-o-Atash Park, Mina Dome, Bagh-e Honar, Book Garden and the Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Sacred Defense.
According to Mirzaei, the transformation of the area into a cultural and tourism zone followed years of planning and efforts to determine an appropriate future for the site. The exhibition traces that history and highlights how the area eventually developed into one of Tehran’s major cultural and recreational destinations.
The organizers say the gallery is partly intended to challenge the perception of Tehran as merely a transit point for tourists.
The exhibition also contains a distinctive element looking far beyond the present: a mailbox for letters addressed to Tehran’s mayor in the year 1450 in the Iranian calendar, equivalent to 2071–72.
Visitors are invited to write down their hopes, expectations and ideas for the future of Tehran and place them in the mailbox. The box will be sealed after the exhibition and preserved for opening in 1450.
Mirzaei described the idea as a paradox of the digital age. At a time when physical correspondence has largely given way to email and messaging applications, visitors are being invited to put their thoughts on paper and entrust them to the future.
The juxtaposition is deliberate: an exhibition centered on artificial intelligence and digital tourism has created space for one of the oldest forms of communication, a handwritten letter.
The broader program accompanying the exhibition includes educational panels, specialist workshops and film screenings focusing on smart tourism, tourism platforms, historical urban landscapes, safe travel and new technologies. Other programs comprise a screening of a documentary about the Omidvar brothers, the famed Iranian globetrotters, a workshop on rediscovering Iran and sessions on the role of emerging tourism technologies in developing smart urban economies.
The Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, described by its organizers as a major green and recreational hub in the capital, is also seeking to strengthen its international tourism profile.

Hong Kong checkpoints to handle 7.44 million passenger trips for National Day break
Immigration Department says figure includes inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors using sea, land and air control points
Hong Kong’s checkpoints are expected to handle about 7.44 million passenger trips over mainland China’s National Day “golden week” break, while people movements are anticipated to peak this weekend.
The Immigration Department said on Monday that the figure would include inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors travelling via the city’s sea, land and air control points between October 1 and 7.
The department also said it anticipated that the most popular control points would be those at Lo Wu, the Lok Ma Chau Spur line and Shenzhen Bay, but added that none of the city’s checkpoints would have their service hours extended.
Authorities earlier said they expected the city would welcome 1.29 million mainland visitors over the break. Last year’s figure reached 1.4 million thanks to a longer holiday period of eight days that included the Mid-Autumn Festival.

Nvidia said Monday it has authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program, taking its total to $235 billion, amid record spending on artificial intelligence.
The chip giant said it marks the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It expects to complete the total remaining buyback program through fiscal 2028.
Nvidia produces the most advanced chips used for AI and has been a huge beneficiary of the boom in spending on the infrastructure needed to power the tech.
Nvidia's shares have climbed 24% over the past 12 months, lifting the company's market cap to $5.42 trillion. The stock was up 2.8% on Monday.

Combined hyperscaler capital expenditure is projected to exceed $1.3 trillion by 2027, S&P Global Ratings said in August, as companies race to build AI infrastructure including data centers.
Huang earlier this month said Nvidia would double the number of chips it sells in 2027.
Alongside making the leading chips for AI — graphics processing units — including its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, the company produces a variety of additional semiconductors. That includes central processors, or CPUs, switch chips, chips for optical networking, chips for laptops, Jetson chips for robots and cars, and the chip inside Nintendo's Switch 2 gaming console.
"I think we're going through the largest infrastructure build-out in human history, and we have the benefit of being a very central part of that," Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years, and every single year, as we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders," he said.

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:07:02 CST
22:07:02 KST

ZAGREB, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Croatian government on Monday announced new fuel prices, raising the price of Eurosuper while lowering the price of diesel.
Eurosuper 95 will rise by 2 cents to 1.76 euros (about 2.01 U.S. dollars) per liter, while the price of Eurodiesel will drop by 5 cents to 1.86 euros (about 2.11 U.S. dollars) per liter. Blue diesel for farmers and fishermen will also drop and will cost 1.42 euros (about 1.62 U.S. dollars) per liter.
The new prices include government subsidies. Without them, they would be higher.
Under Croatia's fuel price system, the government sets temporary ceilings on retail prices, and stations cannot charge more than the limit. The caps are revised every week to follow changes in the global oil market, with the aim of protecting consumers and the wider economy from sudden price spikes.
Global oil prices have fluctuated in recent months amid the crisis in the Middle East, raising concerns over supply and pushing up energy costs worldwide.
The price of blue diesel in Croatia has almost doubled since the beginning of the year, putting additional pressure on farmers and fishermen. Rising fuel prices have also pushed up inflation in Croatia. According to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, annual inflation stood at 4.2 percent in August. Energy prices rose 17.6 percent year-on-year. ■

DR Congo Ebola cases top 8,000 as WHO warns outbreak still expanding
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:06:57 CST
22:06:57 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have surpassed 8,000, the DRC health authorities said Monday, as the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that the outbreak remains large, geographically expanding and marked by sustained transmission.
As of Saturday, the country had recorded 8,067 confirmed cases, including 3,901 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 48.4 percent, according to the latest government situation report released on Monday. A total of 2,070 patients have recovered.
In its latest Disease Outbreak News published Friday, the WHO said the number of new cases reported each day remained high, while transmission intensity varied considerably across affected provinces and health zones.
"The continuously high case fatality ratio, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care," the WHO said.
Ituri Province remains the epicenter of the outbreak, but transmission patterns continue to diverge. Incidence in Ituri had declined gradually from a mid-August peak, while North Kivu Province saw a substantial rise that reached its highest reported level in mid-September, according to the WHO. Sustained transmission also continues in Haut-Uele Province, while renewed transmission activity has been reported in Tshopo Province.
The outbreak has now affected 63 health zones across seven provinces. The WHO said the latest geographic expansion, including newly affected areas in Sud-Ubangi and Haut-Uele, had increased the risk of cross-border transmission.
Since it was declared in May, the outbreak has evolved into the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- A three-day regional capacity-building workshop on Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS) in Africa opened in Johannesburg on Monday, aiming to raise awareness and strengthen agricultural heritage management across the continent.
The workshop brings together government officials, national focal points, site representatives, experts from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations, research institutions, and civil society organizations from English-speaking African countries.
Funded by the FAO-China South-South Cooperation Program, the event provides participants with technical knowledge and practical tools to develop GIAHS proposals and access funding opportunities. A similar workshop will be conducted for French-speaking African nations.

Asia leads the world with 65 sites, with China holding the largest share.
Mbairamadji commended China's consistent support for capacity building and technical skill transfers, noting that China organizes annual high-level training programs, invites international participants for exchange visits, and supports the GIAHS Secretariat in disseminating best practices.
Du Lei, counselor at the Chinese Embassy in South Africa, reiterated China's commitment to partnering with FAO to assist African nations in achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Morongoa Leseke, chief director at South Africa's Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, welcomed the initiative as South Africa advances its national tree-planting program. She emphasized the value of learning from China's advanced agricultural technology and expressed hopes of collaborating with FAO to train local communities in agroforestry. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- A senior Communist Party of China (CPC) official on Monday called on the China Overseas Friendship Association to actively support compatriots from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, as well as overseas Chinese, in contributing to Chinese modernization.

The China Overseas Friendship Association was founded in 1997 to step up contacts between people in the Chinese mainland and those living in Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan and abroad.
It is a non-profit social organization voluntarily formed by representatives from various sectors and relevant organizations in the mainland, compatriots from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, and prominent figures among overseas Chinese.
Li noted progress made by the association over the past year in uniting the Chinese people at home and abroad and promoting exchanges and cooperation with Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan compatriots and overseas Chinese, stressing the need to make winning hearts and rallying strength a priority in its work.
Efforts should focus on advancing the successful practice of the "one country, two systems" principle, and playing an active role in driving economic development, fostering social harmony and enhancing effective governance in Hong Kong and Macao, Li said.
He also underscored the need to safeguard and promote national reunification, firmly oppose separatist activities by "Taiwan independence" forces, and promote exchanges and cooperation between China and other countries. ■

HELSINKI, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Andreas Norlen of the Moderate Party was re-elected speaker of parliament on Monday as the newly elected Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, convened for the first time following this month's general elections.
Norlen won 200 votes in a secret ballot, defeating the Social Democratic Party's candidate Johanna Haraldsson, who received 146 votes.
The Moderate Party had nominated Norlen for another term, with the Sweden Democrats, the Christian Democrats and the Liberal Party backing his candidacy. The Left Party also announced ahead of the vote that it would support Norlen, citing his experience as speaker and in overseeing government-formation talks.
The Social Democratic Party requested a secret ballot and nominated Haraldsson, a lawmaker from southern Sweden's Jonkoping County, as their candidate.
Norlen, who has served as speaker since 2018, will now continue to oversee the process of forming Sweden's next government.
Earlier on Monday, the Social Democratic Party leader and former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson announced that she would return the exploratory mandate she received from Norlen on Sept. 18 to explore the possibility of forming a new government.
Andersson said the Left Party's decision to support Norlen had created what she described as a new parliamentary constellation and that she currently saw no conditions for forming a government herself.
The Left Party rejected the suggestion that its support for Norlen amounted to a political alliance with the Moderate Party, saying the decision was based on his experience as speaker.
Sweden held its parliamentary election on Sept. 13. The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Centre Party won a combined 176 seats in the 349-seat parliament, while the Moderate Party, Sweden Democrats, Christian Democrats and the Liberal Party secured 173 seats.
Outgoing Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson tendered his resignation following the election. Under Sweden's constitutional system, the speaker consults the parties and proposes a candidate for prime minister. ■

====================================================================================================

SpaceX’s Starship lifts off in make-or-break orbital test flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:06:27 UTC
22:06:27 KST

SpaceX’s Starship is on a mission to prove itself. The largest rocket ever built lifted off from the company’s Starbase facility in South Texas on Monday at 8:49 A.M. EDT, soaring toward space atop its giant Super Heavy booster. This test flight—the 14th fully integrated launch—was more than just another Starship shakedown: it marked the first time the enormous spacecraft has propelled itself into orbit around Earth.
The first orbital flight puts Starship over its biggest hurdle yet in SpaceX’s race to make the vehicle its new workhorse for space launches, replacing the wildly successful Falcon 9. Yet issues along the way—the flight was meant to last hours longer than it did—served as a potent reminder of just how audacious SpaceX’s hopes for Starship really are—and how far the company must go to build a robust, reliable orbital transportation system.
Flight 14’s vehicle is the third-generation version of Starship, standing about 124 meters (407 feet) tall when stacked with its Super Heavy booster. That first stage, Booster 21, powered the vehicle upward using 33 Raptor 3 engines. After stage separation, Booster 21 performed a controlled return and splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meanwhile, Starship accelerated toward orbit. About 25 minutes after liftoff, it reignited one of its three sea-level Raptor engines to raise and circularize its trajectory. (The ship also carries three vacuum-rated Raptor engines for in-space maneuvers.) Incredibly, SpaceX seemed unsure as to whether to push ahead to orbit, calling off that part of the test for a brief moment before deciding to go for orbit minutes later.
At that point, Starship became an orbital spacecraft. The vehicle reached an altitude of roughly 275 kilometers. Along the way, it deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites—the first operational payloads to be carried to orbit by Starship. Three of those satellites also beamed back imagery of Starship’s heat shield, which must remain intact to ensure the spacecraft doesn’t break apart and burn up during reentry.
SpaceX had originally planned a 10-hour mission that would see Starship orbit the globe at least six times, but a little over an hour and a half into the flight, SpaceX made the call to bring Starship back to Earth early. Starship performed a deorbit burn at approximately 11 A.M. EDT and re-entered Earth’s atmosphere at around 11:40 A.M. The ship performed a controlled splashdown in the Pacific Ocean at 11:58 A.M.
A test of SpaceX’s grand vision
Starship occupies an unusual place in the history of rocketry. Unlike all previous launch systems, it’s designed to be fully reusable: both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft would be recovered and flown repeatedly in normal operations.
Intended to carry both crew and cargo, Starship is the linchpin of SpaceX’s grand vision of launching a million data center satellites into orbit and separately sending astronauts to the moon and, eventually, to Mars.
That radical vision has depended on a chain of technological achievements: entering orbit, deploying payloads, surviving reentry, making pinpoint landings and achieving smooth recoveries—and then repeating the sequence flawlessly, again and again, to reach the frequency of flights necessary to make Starship’s economics work.
Today’s flight did not prove all of those things—and nor was it supposed to. Neither the Starship or booster attempted a tower catch (that may happen during the next test flight, according to SpaceX), and Flight 14 didn’t demonstrate any of the daunting orbital propellant transfers required for missions to the moon or Mars.
For more than three years, Starship’s development has been defined by a series of spectacular successes and failures, accruing incremental progress in between. The fourth flight, in 2024, demonstrated controlled splashdowns of both stages. Flight 5 saw the first-ever tower catch—a dramatic recovery of a Super Heavy booster using the launch tower’s mechanical arms. Later launches introduced major vehicle upgrades, including the current third-generation Starship. Flights 12 and 13 successfully tested this new generation, although the booster on Flight 13 was lost during landing.
A major failure during Flight 14 wouldn’t have doomed SpaceX’s plans for Starship—but it would have complicated them. The company uses a “test to failure” philosophy, pushing its systems to their limits to identify problems. Flight 14 didn’t deliver on all its aims—it was supposed to orbit Earth at least six times—but the fact that it deployed its payload and got in and out of orbit safely nonetheless could minimize any tinkering before the next test.
To the moon and beyond
Of all Starship’s promises, the most notable may be the vehicle’s role in NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the moon. The space agency has selected a version of Starship as one of two potential Human Landing Systems (HLS) for Artemis. Under the current plan, SpaceX is developing Starship HLS for Artemis III—a low-Earth orbit test mission in 2027—and for a crewed lunar landing, the Artemis IV mission, in 2028.
That version of Starship must be refueled in Earth orbit via a succession of tanker flights by other Starships before heading to the moon. The Starship would then depart Earth orbit, travel to lunar orbit and rendezvous with astronauts there for a down-and-back foray to the moon’s surface. NASA’s inspector general has said this will require more than 10 tanker flights, with the first refueling beginning more than 200 days before the crewed mission.
That is a wildly ambitious plan. And it means the largely successful nature of today’s orbital test is not merely be good news for SpaceX. It could also reduce one of the fundamental uncertainties hanging over NASA’s lunar plans, adding credibility to the space agency’s controversial Artemis architecture.
NASA’s inspector general also concluded earlier this year that Starship HLS is behind schedule for future Artemis missions, warning that further technical problems could spiral into greater delays for the entire program. This no doubt contributed to NASA’s decision to shift an actual crewed landing from Artemis III to Artemis IV, and it reinforces the space agency’s choice to also pursue Blue Origin’s Blue Moon vehicle as another Human Landing System, creating some redundancy in the lunar architecture.
But after Blue Moon’s ride to space, Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, suffered a catastrophic explosion on the launch pad during preflight testing in late May of this year, the status of this second option for Artemis lunar missions is also in question.
This makes it hard to understate NASA’s reliance on Starship—and hence on a successful Flight 14—for keeping Artemis on schedule.

====================================================================================================

SpaceX's Starship launches on 14th flight, first headed to orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:03:05 UTC
22:03:05 KST

SpaceX’s Starship makes orbital debut deploying Starlinks before early ending
TEXAS - SpaceX’s giant Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time on Sept 28 and deployed the new Starlink satellites, achieving milestones in its 14th test flight despite an engine failure and a decision to cut the mission short.
The uncrewed mission was scheduled to last 10 hours, but was reduced to three after one of Starship’s three main engines shut down prematurely following separation from the spacecraft’s lower-stage Super Heavy booster rocket.
It is unclear how much of a setback the engine failure on Sept 28, the latest glitch since Starship test flights began in 2023, will pose for the goal of Elon Musk’s newly public company to put the powerful spacecraft into routine service later in 2026.
Unlike past Starship flights, the mission on Sept 28 was both a high-stakes test of the next-generation rocket and an operational endeavour carrying millions of dollars’ worth of Starlink satellites to orbit, representing Starship’s first revenue-generating mission, even though its final design is still under development.
SpaceX shares fell 2% on Sept 28.
Much of SpaceX’s market worth and continued investor confidence in the company – valued at US$2 trillion as of Sept 25’s close – ride on the success of Starship, which was designed as the world’s first fully reusable spacecraft.
The 40-story-tall vehicle, consisting of a Super Heavy booster rocket topped by the main upper-stage Starship vessel, launched from SpaceX’s Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville.
The Super Heavy booster lofted the Starship upper stage into space before returning itself to Gulf waters for an engine-controlled splashdown, following hard landings for the booster on two previous missions.
Some engines on that booster stopped working during its descent, SpaceX said.
Upon reaching space, one of Starship’s three main engines shut down prematurely, a development that led SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot to announce on the company’s live stream of the mission that the craft would be unable to reach orbit.
“The team has made the call not to commit to orbit,” Huot said.
But Huot reversed course minutes later after an update from engineers confirmed that the craft could still attempt to fire other onboard engines that would boost it into orbit, which Starship successfully did minutes later.
Satellites deployed
Once in orbit, Starship began deploying 26 next-generation Starlink satellites one by one at a planned altitude of roughly 269 km, marking the ship’s first orbital deployments.
“All 26 Starlink V3 operational satellites deployed and operating nominally,” Musk wrote on X.
“Deploying all 26 Starlink V3 satellites into target orbit is a huge win, especially since this marks Starship’s very first revenue-generating commercial flight,” said Dean Sladen, quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components.
“But from an engineering perspective, the real story was how the team handled that engine failure during ascent.”
Engine issues have popped up on some of Starship’s previous suborbital flights in space, a lingering challenge for the programme in an area crucial to the rocket’s ability to maneuver in space.
While that function is less critical for low-orbiting Starlink deployments, it is crucial for Starship’s future assignments of taking NASA astronauts to the moon.
NASA administrator Jared Isaacman, writing on X, congratulated SpaceX on “getting Ship to orbit and managing every step in a safe, responsible, and especially inspirational way”.
Starship’s controlled descent into the Pacific culminated with a thruster maneuver that flipped the vehicle vertically so that it hit the sea in a nose-up position.
Fire engulfed the base of the rocket as it touched down on the ocean surface before tipping on its side, followed by a large fireball.
The company had not planned to recover and reuse the spacecraft from the sea following the mission.
Test mission with real payload
Starship was built to launch SpaceX’s Starlink satellites more frequently and carry future NASA missions to the moon.
Reaching orbit, a primary benchmark for any new rocket designed to deliver payloads to space, has been a long-delayed feat for Starship, which Musk once predicted would be achieved in 2022, to be followed by satellite deployments in 2023.
All 13 of Starship’s previous test flights since 2023 were limited to suborbital space in a nearly decade-long development campaign that has cost SpaceX more than US$15 billion to date.
Musk has said he envisions ultimately flying hundreds or thousands of Starship missions a year, a launch pace unprecedented in the space industry.
“Starship is 2 to 3 years away from hourly flights,” Musk wrote on X on Sept 27.
Analysts estimate the launch on Sept 28 of SpaceX’s new V3 Starlink satellites equals hundreds of millions of dollars in projected revenue for the company’s Starlink unit, based on the network's added customer capacity - underscoring Starship's fundamental role in serving the company's profit nucleus.
According to SpaceX, the V3 Starlink satellites on the mission on Sept 28 can handle 10 times more data than their predecessor V2 mini-sats that the company has been launching 20 or 30 at a time on its workhorse Falcon 9 rockets.
Seeking to build out his broadband satellite constellation at a faster pace, Musk wants to launch the higher-capacity V3s in batches of 60 per launch once Starship goes into routine operation.
Starship’s orbital debut also comes three months after SpaceX went public with a record-shattering IPO in June that made it the sixth-biggest US company by value and turned Musk, who founded the company in 2002, into the world's first trillionaire.
Much of SpaceX’s market worth and continued investor confidence in the company — valued at $2 trillion as of Sept 25's close — rides on the success of Starship, which was designed as the world's first fully reusable spacecraft.
The silver-coloured, multi-finned rocket ship will be key to achieving Musk’s ambitions of slashing launch costs, vastly expanding his Starlink business and deploying thousands of orbital AI data centres to space.
Starship is also set to play a pivotal role in NASA’s Artemis programme, which aims to return astronauts to the moon’s surface for the first time since 1972 and build a long-term lunar presence as a stepping stone to eventual human exploration of Mars.
As a measure of Starship’s integral place in SpaceX’s corporate future, investors wiped roughly US$100 billion off SpaceX’s market value after test flight 13 was aborted at the last second in July. The flight ultimately got off the ground five days later.
Surviving the return to Earth
One critical objective for Starship’s 14th outing will be surviving its return flight to Earth, starting with the deorbital firing of one Raptor engine while in space and precisely angling the vehicle for atmospheric re-entry.
The spacecraft’s final controlled descent is designed to culminate with a thruster manoeuvre to flip the vehicle vertically so that it hits the sea in a nose-up position. While future missions call for Starship to execute a similar touchdown on land back in Texas, no recovery of the spacecraft is planned for its latest flight, contrary to Musk’s previous hopes. REUTERS

In run for Brazil's presidency, Flavio Bolsonaro tests staying power of his father's legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:02:36 UTC
22:02:36 KST

In run for Brazil's presidency, Flavio Bolsonaro tests staying power of his father's legacy
SAO PAULO, Sept 28 - From the bare-walled, 12-square-meter cell where he was serving a 27-year sentence for a failed coup plot, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro passed his most prized asset to his eldest son: his blessing to follow in his political footsteps in 2026.
"Let's go, it's you," Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the main right-wing candidate in the October 4 presidential election, remembers his father telling him in late 2025, over the rattle of the cell's air-conditioning unit.
The younger Bolsonaro immediately accepted the mission: "He was humiliated and convicted because the system did not want him in public life," he told Reuters last December, soon after announcing his candidacy for the presidency.
The two men now have a chance to exact revenge on the politicians, judges and special interests they blame for driving Jair Bolsonaro from public life and ending his far-right, populist makeover of Latin America's largest economy.
The 45-year-old senator is polling neck and neck with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has long been one of the region's most powerful figures and is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term.
The strength of Bolsonaro's bid, and the loyalty of the right-wing electorate to the former president, have turned Brazil into a test case for a belief embraced by many on the left around the world: that prosecuting and imprisoning a populist leader can contain the movement he or she built.
Carlos Melo, a professor of politics at Sao Paulo's Insper institution, said that former President Bolsonaro may be the most vocal figurehead of a movement that has long existed in Brazil and worldwide.
"The far-right goes beyond Bolsonaro," he added.
'IT HAD TO BE A BOLSONARO'
The competitiveness of the younger Bolsonaro's bid for power came as a surprise to many.
Unlike his brothers, he had faced corruption allegations, including leading an alleged kickback scheme that prosecutors said benefited relatives of Adriano da Nobrega, a former police officer accused of heading a gang of hired killers.
Of the former president's three eldest sons, the senator was also the least combative, softening the edge that was central to his father's rise and presenting himself as a "more centered Bolsonaro."
The announcement of his candidacy rattled markets, with bankers alternating between high-level meetings and cautious distance for much of the campaign.
Other conservative parties were skeptical, too, with some right-wing candidates announcing their own bids for the presidency.
For months, Flavio Bolsonaro tried and failed to convince others to join his ticket, ultimately settling on a little-known lawmaker from his own Liberal Party as his running mate.
"There was an initial lack of communication, owing perhaps to Flavio's first presidential run," said conservative Senator Tereza Cristina, a prominent agribusiness leader who was prevented from accepting the role of Bolsonaro's running mate by her party's leadership.
Still, Liberal Party loyalists seemed confident of their choice.
"It had to be a Bolsonaro," Valdemar Costa Neto, the head of the Liberal Party, told Reuters.
GLOBAL CONSERVATIVE EMBRACE
Despite the initial sour welcome at home, Senator Bolsonaro's bid was quickly embraced by the global conservative movement, which is eager to see Brazil join the regional right-wing wave that has brought Argentina's Javier Milei, El Salvador's Nayib Bukele and Ecuador's Daniel Noboa to power.
Senator Bolsonaro has followed the same playbook as many of those Latin American right-wing populists, uniting conservative factions around Christian traditionalism, free-market economics, and a fierce hostility to the left.
He is pledging to cut taxes and embark on an aggressive fiscal adjustment to lower long-term borrowing costs in Brazil. The platform has pleased the business community and investors, though economists say the proposals are short on specifics.
"Flavio sees a broader global realignment at stake and wants to be part of it," said Paulo Kramer, a political scientist and former campaign adviser to Jair Bolsonaro.
With the help of his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who was removed from his position as a member of the Brazilian Congress after he moved to the US, Flavio Bolsonaro managed at the end of May to get a meeting with US President Donald Trump, who described him as "a smart young man who loves his country, Brazil, very much!"
During his first term in the White House, Trump established a close political and personal friendship with Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio Bolsonaro's attempt to rekindle that alliance, however, has left many Brazilians cold.
His meeting with Trump was preceded by Washington's announcement of steep tariffs on Brazilian imports, giving Lula an opportunity to brand Flavio and Eduardo Bolsonaro as "traitors."
Polls showed Brazilians blamed the Bolsonaros more than Lula for the tariffs, which were imposed in July.
"I don't think President Trump has helped Flavio at all," said Thomas Shannon, who served as a U.S. ambassador to Brazil during the Obama administration. "I think that was more harmful to Flavio."
DARK HORSE
Having overcome the initial skepticism over his candidacy, Senator Bolsonaro's campaign faced its biggest blow in May, after an investigation revealed he had asked a disgraced banker, who was accused of leading a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme, for money to fund a Hollywood biopic of Jair Bolsonaro.
Production contracts outlined $12 million in transfers from a fund connected to the banker, Daniel Vorcaro, to a U.S. fund managed by an attorney representing Eduardo Bolsonaro.
After first denying involvement, Flavio Bolsonaro admitted that the banker had funded the movie, but maintained there was no wrongdoing, merely "a private sponsorship, with no strings attached."
The revelation, however, triggered swift backlash. The senator saw his support drop in polls and some of his allies turned openly critical. Romeu Zema, a businessman who is also running for the presidency, called it "a slap in the face."
Newly unsealed court records revealed that the Federal Police in July had opened an investigation into Flavio Bolsonaro for corruption, money laundering, and illicit capital flight linked to the movie project.
He dismissed the probe as a "political hit job" and has since recovered in the polls with less than two weeks to go before the first round of voting. A second round will be held on October 25 if no candidate wins a simple majority. If Bolsonaro wins, he would be sworn in some four years after thousands of supporters of his father rampaged through Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential offices, smashing windows, furniture and artwork in the worst attack on state institutions since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s.
The prospect of a Bolsonaro returning to the Planalto Palace in Brasilia where presidents carry out their duties is raising the possibility of fresh institutional clashes.
If elected, Flavio Bolsonaro would likely move quickly to undo two legal blows to his family: his father's house arrest in Brasilia and Eduardo Bolsonaro's conviction for coercion related to a U.S. lobbying campaign that prosecutors said sought to pressure Brazilian Supreme Court justices not to convict the former president.
Freeing his father is Flavio Bolsonaro's main goal, something the presidential candidate alluded to during an Independence Day rally earlier this month.
"I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest," he said. REUTERS

How adults feel about their ADHD depends heavily on their specific symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

A new study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders suggests that how adults feel about their attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder depends on their specific symptoms. Researchers found that individuals with higher levels of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms tend to view their condition more positively, while those with primarily inattentive symptoms are less likely to see their diagnosis as an advantage. These findings highlight the diverse ways people experience and interpret their neurodevelopmental differences.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a condition that begins in childhood and often continues into adulthood. The diagnosis is based on two main categories of symptoms. The first is inattention, which involves difficulty focusing, sustaining attention, or staying organized. The second category is hyperactivity and impulsivity, characterized by excessive physical movement, restlessness, or acting without thinking. For many years, medical and psychological research focused heavily on the negative impacts of these symptoms, such as difficulties in school, struggles with emotional regulation, and challenges in relationships.
Recently, the rise of the neurodiversity movement has encouraged scientists to look at the other side of the coin. Earlier qualitative studies gathered personal stories showing that people with ADHD often identify real strengths and silver linings in their condition. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that adults diagnosed with ADHD reported experiencing notable personal strengths, identifying positive themes like high energy, unconventional thinking, and a drive for novelty. Similarly, a 2018 interview-based study revealed that many adults with ADHD identify distinct personal strengths and resilience linked directly to their diagnosis.
This qualitative foundation sparked recent efforts to study these positives numerically. A 2024 study took early steps to measure these strengths, finding that people with more ADHD traits in the general population also scored higher on traits like cognitive flexibility and sensory processing sensitivity. The new research, led by Gili Katabi of Tel-Aviv University, builds on this momentum by creating a formal scale to measure positive attitudes toward ADHD. The authors wanted to test whether these positive feelings depend on whether someone’s symptoms are mostly hyperactive or mostly inattentive.
To explore this, the researchers developed the Positive Attitudes Toward ADHD Scale. This questionnaire was designed to capture how individuals perceive the positive aspects of their own condition, based on themes from previous interviews like creativity, dynamic energy, and resilience. Participants rated their agreement with various statements on a five-point scale. The team then recruited three distinct groups of adults with ADHD to test the scale and see how scores related to symptom types.
The first sample included 84 young adults in Israel with formal ADHD diagnoses who completed the questionnaires in a laboratory setting. This initial group helped the researchers confirm that the new scale was reliable and captured a wide range of attitudes. The second sample involved 125 adults in Israel who also participated in the lab. For this group, the researchers conducted structured clinical interviews by phone to verify that the participants still met the criteria for ADHD at the time of testing, while excluding those with heavy alcohol or cannabis use.
The third sample was an online group of 126 English-speaking adults residing in 24 different countries. These participants provided detailed written information about their diagnosis and treatment history to confirm their status. Across all three groups, participants filled out the new attitude scale alongside a widely used checklist that measures the frequency of their inattentive and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms over the past six months.
When analyzing the results, the researchers found that more frequent ADHD symptoms overall were associated with more favorable attitudes toward the condition. However, breaking the symptoms down into the two main categories painted a more detailed picture. Across all three samples, a higher frequency of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms strongly predicted more positive attitudes toward having ADHD.
In contrast, inattention symptoms showed a very different pattern. Higher levels of inattention tended to associate with less positive attitudes toward the condition, though this negative association was not statistically significant across every sample. The researchers also ran a follow-up test with 35 participants from the second sample to measure their general life satisfaction. They found that the link between hyperactive symptoms and positive attitudes remained distinct, indicating that the new scale was capturing specific feelings about ADHD rather than just a generally happy outlook on life.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that young adult hyperactivity and impulsivity predicted higher relationship and job satisfaction later in life. Together, this body of research suggests that the physical and mental energy associated with hyperactivity might foster traits like curiosity and enthusiasm that people learn to appreciate over time.
There are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The new scale relies entirely on self-reporting, meaning it captures how people feel about their own condition, not objective measurements of their abilities. Endorsing statements about creativity or flexibility does not necessarily mean a person would score higher on a behavioral test of divergent thinking. The study focuses on subjective opinions, which are important for understanding self-esteem and coping, but are separate from observable advantages.
Another detail to consider is the potential for reporting biases based on how society views different symptoms. Hyperactive and impulsive traits might be easier to reframe in a positive light, such as viewing restlessness as boundless energy. Inattentive traits, like spacing out or forgetting things, might feel less socially acceptable and harder to spin positively. Additionally, the researchers noted that their scale did not include questions about hyperfocus, a common experience where people with ADHD become intensely absorbed in tasks they find interesting, which might have skewed the results away from the inattentive dimension.
Future studies could incorporate reports from friends or family members to provide a more rounded view of how these traits manifest in daily life. Scientists might also test whether these contrasting attitudes exist in children and adolescents, or if they are unique to adults who have had more time to adapt to their neurodevelopmental differences.
The study, “ADHD Individuals’ Positivity About Their Condition Varies by Their Levels of Hyperactivity/Impulsivity Versus Inattention Symptoms,” was authored by Gili Katabi, Merav Huss, Steve Lukito, Tycho J. Dekkers, Edmund Sonuga-Barke, and Nitzan Shahar.

Peru’s penguins are on the brink. A super El Niño could make it worse.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Peru’s penguins are on the brink. A super El Niño could make it worse.
Scientists running a ‘living laboratory’ are preparing for the birds’ eventual return
The first time I was in Punta San Juan, the desert was flooded with birds. It was 2012, and I was making a short documentary film about the cormorants, pelicans and penguins that made this arid peninsula in southern Peru one of the largest gatherings of seabirds on Earth.
At the time, this 133-acre reserve — a patch of rock and sand jutting into the frigid waters of the Pacific Ocean — was home to more than a quarter million seabirds, including 300,000 Guanay cormorants (Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum) and some 3,000 Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti).
One of the few species of desert penguin, the Humboldt live along the arid coast of Peru and Chile, where they nest in burrows dug into guano deposits or small cliff caves. Punta San Juan was home to the largest colony in Peru.
By 2025, there were fewer than 500 penguins left. Avian flu had spread through the reserve in 2022 and 2023, crashing seabird populations and spreading to marine mammals such as sea lions and seals. El Niño struck next. The climate pattern is characterized by months of warmer than usual sea surface temperatures in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Those warm waters pushed anchovy — the penguins’ main food source — deeper and farther out to sea. Industrial fishing operations put even more pressure on the surviving animals.
Ecologist Susana Cárdenas-Alayza, who has run the Punta San Juan Program in partnership with Cayetano Heredia University, the Peruvian government and American zoos for more than 20 years, is increasingly alarmed. As a scientist, Cárdenas-Alayza says, she is used to dealing with numbers and controlled variables, “but diseases and climate events escape my control.”
Now, the reserve is facing a new threat: a potential “super” El Niño. Soaring sea surface temperatures are disrupting the cold, fish-rich waters of the Humboldt Current, which flows past the peninsula. When I returned in July, much had changed from my first trip, when streams of penguins lined the cliffs of the reserve. This time I saw only five penguins — and several abandoned nests with cold eggs. When food is scarce, penguins either stop reproducing or leave their nests altogether to search for a more favorable habitat, Cárdenas-Alayza says. They often starve along the way.
The destruction has also been hard on the reserve’s volunteers, who protect the penguins in what Cárdenas-Alayza calls a “living laboratory.” For decades, volunteers from around Peru and the rest of the world have counted birds, recorded their diets and built artificial nests to keep penguin chicks safe. In the summer of 2025, they even launched a “penguin patrol” to safeguard the Humboldts from workers harvesting guano, nitrogen-rich bird droppings essential for agriculture. Wanting to pitch in, the workers built a temporary, half-kilometer-long wall out of sacks of guano to shield the penguins on their daily walk to the sea.
Keeping research going — and morale high — in the emptying ecosystem has been one of the biggest challenges of Cárdenas-Alayza’s career. No one knows how long the current El Niño will last — or when the fish will return.
Nevertheless, Cárdenas-Alayza says she still has hope. Many species in Punta San Juan are philopatric, or loyal to their territory. That means that even when they leave in search of food or other resources, they eventually come back.
Biologist Patricia Majluf, who founded the Punta San Juan Program in 1979, shares one example of resilience: The El Niño event of 1997–98 decimated the reserve’s sea lions and seals. Penguin numbers dropped into the low hundreds. But the animals eventually mounted a remarkable recovery, helped by a major reduction in anchovy fishing quotas in 2006.
Scientists are busy preparing Punta San Juan for the animals’ return. Cárdenas-Alayza briefed incoming members of Peru’s Congress on the situation in July, and she and her fellow researchers are lobbying hard for stricter fishing quotas. They are also championing a new ecosystem restoration strategy, a collaborative framework that engages fishing communities, companies, students and even local chefs to help the reserve’s animals recover.
Back in Punta San Juan, Cárdenas-Alayza’s team is pressuring the government to reinforce a protective concrete wall around the reserve. In the meantime, they are trapping invasive species that prey on young birds, such as foxes and rats. They are also developing AI tools to speed data analysis from remote cameras monitoring breeding among the surviving Humboldt penguins.
As I prepared to leave, Cárdenas-Alayza, Majluf and I shared a meal of chifa, a Peruvian-Chinese cuisine that is a traditional Sunday dinner for Peruvian families. The three of us talked about our experiences teaching and people we had known at the reserve — and Cárdenas-Alayza teased Majluf, saying she was her “conservation mom.” It was at that moment that I realized what kept drawing me back to the reserve. I had come to document the region’s desert penguins, but I had learned so much more: Conservation isn’t just about science; it’s about relationships. At the end of the meal, we all opened our fortune cookies. Cárdenas-Alayza laughed when she saw hers: “Mountains are meant to be climbed.”
Anna Elisa Sotelo’s work on this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

Bose Launches New Wired Earbuds After More Than a Decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Bose used to make lots of wired headphones. But it’s been a minute. Specifically, it’s been 11 years. Since then, wired headphones entered 2026 having a serious moment, with sales up for the first time in five years—10 percent in the back half of 2025 and 20 percent at the start of 2026. Young people are driving the trend, including celebrities sporting wired earbuds and literally writing songs about them.
Bose president of consumer audio Raza Haider (among others at the company) noticed. He dropped off his teen at college last year and saw wired earbuds left and right. A return to wired earbuds seems to be a national trend—it’s certainly popular among the Gen Z and Gen A of New York City, and the teenage kids of WIRED staffers too.
The new $99 Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds come to the market just in time to capitalize on this trend. Launching them, from idea to final product, took the company around eight or nine months, said Haider. This is much faster than most audio releases I’m familiar with. Haider explained that Bose has been working toward enabling faster, more efficient production to accelerate new product launches, revisions, and collaborations.
Testing the Bose Wired Earbuds: Are They Any Good?
I was one of a few reviewers to get these earbuds ahead of launch. I’ve had them for only four days, and they’re technically a late-stage prototype, not the final product, so this is more of an impression than a full review. But so far, so good.
As with any wired headphones, the simplicity is a big part of the appeal. There’s no battery to charge, no app to download, no Bluetooth to fiddle with, and no latency to ruin your TV show or video game.
Already, the Bose earbuds leapfrog cheaper wired pairs (like Apple EarPods) in sound quality and active noise canceling (ANC). They have clear detail across lows, mids, and highs, especially for something at this price point. More importantly, the noise canceling is a godsend. I can listen to music at more comfortable levels, even during a commute or café stop.
What I don’t love: The central control panel is a little heavy. It has a volume up and volume down, as well as a play/pause/noise-canceling mode switch button, but it weighs down the cable. It’s pretty flush against my torso, which is nice, but it also weighs down the earbuds in my ears. The cable tension it adds is annoying, especially compared to the tension-free experience of using wireless earbuds. The cable is thick and premium-feeling, but it inevitably ends up tangled inside of the included soft pouch.
The earbuds have (removable) silicone wing-tip stabilizers, and the box comes with extra ear tip and stabilizer sizes to find your best fit. The buds come in black, white, and a limited-edition mint color, and they start shipping October 15. You can preorder starting today at Bose and Best Buy.
While Bose's return to wired headphones feels significant, wired earbuds never truly went away. Here are some of WIRED's favorites that are currently available to buy.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hires Wall Street economist David Zervos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:53:03 UTC
21:53:03 KST

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has hired veteran Wall Street economist David Zervos, the longtime chief market strategist at Jefferies, as a counselor in the Treasury Department. Zervos was a CNBC contributor.
Bessent announced the hire Monday in a statement obtained first by CNBC. Zervos will serve in a broad advisory capacity and is expected to begin immediately.
He has backed Bessent's recent decision to increase buybacks of some long-term Treasury debt and has called for lower interest rates from the Federal Reserve.
Zervos in a brief interview called himself a "Wall Street geek" and said he was excited for his third stint in government. Bessent "has done an incredible job in this administration at guiding the economy through a lot of tumultuous periods," Zervos said.
"Whether it's trade, whether it's war, he's stepped up," he said of Bessent.
Zervos will add intellectual firepower to the Treasury after a series of staff departures that have drawn some attention. Seven of the department's 16 Senate-confirmed appointees had left the department as of mid-August, the Washington Sun reported. Bessent is on his third chief of staff since becoming Treasury secretary in January 2025.
Fellow Wall Street economist Joseph Lavorgna of SMBC Nikko served in a similar role as counselor to Bessent before leaving in March. The position doesn't require Senate confirmation.
Bessent handles an especially broad portfolio for a Treasury secretary. He has been effectively President Donald Trump's top negotiator on China and has been closely involved in policy debates about artificial intelligence, although Trump on Friday said Bessent would not add a role as the administration's top AI advisor.
Zervos was considered by Trump to run the Federal Reserve, though the president ultimately chose Kevin Warsh for the job in January.
Zervos has worked at Jefferies, a New York-based investment bank, since 2010.
Zervos has a doctorate in economics and has worked twice for the Fed. The first time was at the start of his career, in the early 1990s, when he did technical economics and interest rate research. He left for the private sector and returned to the Fed in 2009 as a visiting advisor in the wake of the financial crisis. Warsh was a governor at the Fed then, though it isn't clear if he and Zervos worked together directly at the time.
Zervos will serve as a special government employee, he said in an email to his clients. That status allows him to avoid some often-onerous divestiture requirements that come with other federal appointments, but it restricts how long he can hold the position. Zervos said he expects his term to end in April 2027.
Zervos said last year he believed interest rates should be "much lower." Since Warsh took the job, Zervos has said he thinks Warsh can make room for lower interest rates by cutting the Fed's balance sheet. Those reductions are one of Warsh's top priorities.
The Fed raised interest rates earlier this month for the first time since 2023. That decision prompted frustration from some economists in the Trump administration, but Bessent has been more circumspect. He said Sunday in an appearance on Fox News that the Fed "should have an open mind" about how to manage the economy.
Bessent has intervened in Treasury markets as interest rates have continued to rise. The 10-year Treasury hit 5.2% on Friday, a level last seen in 2007, powered by a strong economy, competition for capital from the artificial intelligence build-out and concerns about inflation as the Iran war continues.
Zervos, in a CNBC appearance last month, backed Bessent's decision to increase buybacks of some long-term Treasury debt, a move that may have eased pressure on some Treasury yields. Some on Wall Street had criticized the buybacks, but Zervos said he supported them.
"I don't see how you could fight this when the firepower and the cards are all sitting in the Treasury Department," Zervos said.

U.S. Embassy Issues Security Alert to Citizens in U.K. Amid Suspected Terror Plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:50:40 UTC
21:50:40 KST

The U.S. embassy in London has issued a security alert for American citizens in the U.K. following a suspected terror plot near an RAF airbase used by the U.S. military, which led to the arrests of five men who have since been released on bail.
“U.S. citizens are encouraged to exercise caution and be mindful of personal security,” read the notice responding to the Sunday incident near RAF Fairford. “U.S.-associated facilities, gatherings, and organizations may be at heightened risk. U.S. citizens are advised to follow instructions of local authorities for their personal safety and security.”
The alert reminded Americans that the U.K. in April raised its national terrorism threat level to “severe” from “substantial,” a decision made after an antisemitic attack in London was declared a terrorist incident by police. The “severe” level, according to the Metropolitan Police, means “an attack is highly likely.”
The warning came after British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after they were detained near RAF Fairford in southwest England, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran, in the early hours of Sunday. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base, which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) previously said could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military.
The U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) confirmed in a statement to TIME that the five arrestees were British nationals in their 20s who live in London. They were all released on bail Monday afternoon, local time. "They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," according to the CTP.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme early Monday that it is too soon to speculate over the motives during a live investigation. Questioned about a potential Iran link, he said: "We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies."
CTP’s deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans said she was “very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised,” but stressed more time is needed to work through the case.
Additionally, the head of CTP Laurence Taylor emphasized his officers are considering this case from "every possible angle," including the potential that this "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. "The circulation of such fabricated speculations... will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the U.K.," it said Monday.
What we know about the arrests at RAF Fairford
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. It has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
Gloucestershire Police, the local authority responsible for the area, received a call from a concerned resident at 12:45 a.m. local time on Sunday, regarding three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airbase.
The local resident, a farmer, told police she had found the road blocked by three white vans. “I saw a large group of hooded and masked men. When they saw me, they ran ahead of me… I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place,” she later told the BBC.
Armed officers responded to the call and five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act, as well as section 5 of the Terrorism Act.
Police evacuated residents from around 85 nearby households and put a cordon in place while the British Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team examined the vehicles.
While the farmer who alerted police has been hailed for their actions, Streeting has indicated they only had a “partial picture” of the matter and appeared to suggest U.K. security forces had been aware of a suspected plot involving RAF Fairford.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday claimed the suspects had been “under view for a long time.”
"Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great… and we got them,” Trump told reporters.
When asked if Trump had been correct, Streeting did not reject the assertion.
“Our security services and our police, they don’t ask for praise, but I think it was a proud moment yesterday to see the President of the United States recognize the extraordinary work that our police and our security and intelligence services do every day throughout the year and throughout the world to keep us safe,” he said. “That’s all I want to say this morning on that.”
TIME has asked the Ministry of Defense and Downing Street whether the British authorities were already investigating a potential plot.
Speaking at the Labour Party conference later Monday morning, Streeting celebrated the U.K. and U.S. alliance as “the closest of any two nations on Earth” and vowed the two countries “will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.”
British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband, meanwhile, referred to the incident near RAF Fairford as a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”
The U.K. must be prepared to “confront” all the security threats facing Europe and the world, he told conference attendees, adding that “we will act against the proxies of Iran.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham referred to the seemingly foiled terror plot as "deeply concerning," ahead of holding a COBRA meeting (a session of the government’s emergencies committee) to discuss the incident with top advisers Monday afternoon.
Concerns over the risk Iran poses to the U.K.
The U.K. government gave authorization in March for the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The base’s role in the U.S. military’s seven-month operation against Iran may have made the site a target.
While British police and lawmakers have said it's too early to determine who was behind the suspected terror plot, the U.K. government has repeatedly issued stern warnings regarding the threat the Iranian regime poses to the U.K.
On Feb. 28, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer addressed the nation, explaining the U.K. had no involvement in the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran, but emphasizing the government’s belief that Iran cannot be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon.
“Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community,” he said. “Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil."
In March, four men were arrested on suspicion of conducting surveillance of locations and individuals linked to the Jewish community in London to assist Iran. One man was an Iranian national and the other three were British-Iranian nationals. The CTP said the arrests were “part of a long-running investigation and part of our ongoing work to disrupt malign activity where we suspect it.”
A separate investigation resulted in a man being charged in May with assisting a foreign intelligence service relating to Iran.
Earlier this month, a man and woman were arrested in London as part of National Security Act investigation. They were apprehended on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service. Again, the country to which the investigation was linked was Iran.
The IRGC was designated a threat to national security in the U.K. under new powers in July, after a series of antisemitic attacks across England., including arson offenses against Jewish ambulance services.
“These new powers will make it easier to prosecute and lock up anyone carrying out [Iran’s] dirty work here in Britain,” said Starmer at the time.
