Full text: Address by Chinese Vice President Han Zheng at general debate of 81st session of UN General Assembly
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:41:04 CST
18:41:04 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng delivered a speech on Saturday at the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
The following is the full text of the speech:
Statement by H.E. Han Zheng
Vice President of the People's Republic of China
At the General Debate of the 81st Session of
The United Nations General Assembly
New York, September 26, 2026
Mr. President,
Colleagues,
The world is witnessing intertwined changes and turbulence, protracted geopolitical conflicts, widening development gaps and a growing number of global challenges. Five years ago, at the 76th Session of the UN General Assembly, President Xi Jinping put forward the Global Development Initiative. Since then, he has proposed the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative. These initiatives provide strategic guidance for building a community with a shared future for humanity. At a time when countries of the world find their future so closely linked, more and more of them want to join hands to shoulder the historic mission of addressing difficulties and challenges, and advancing the well-being of all humanity. With this in mind, I propose that we take the following four steps.
First, we should safeguard the postwar international order and foster lasting peace based on common security. The world wants peace, not war. The international system centered on the UN and the international order underpinned by international law that emerged after World War II must be upheld. We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation. We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorization. Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with rules, upholding rule of law and doing what's right.
China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East including the Gulf should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded. China calls for advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza in accordance with the principle of the Palestinians governing Palestine. It also calls for bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date. On Ukraine, President Xi Jinping has put forward four points on what must be done, which are the fundamental guidance for China in playing a continued, constructive role in its own way for achieving a political settlement of the crisis. China urges the relevant country to immediately stop using threat of force against Cuba and immediately and completely lift the blockade and sanctions against Cuba.
Second, we should address the global development predicament and promote prosperity for all through openness and cooperation. We should keep development at the center of the international agenda, and jointly forge a global development partnership based on unity and equality and that is balanced and inclusive. It is important to give priority to key areas including poverty reduction, food security and energy transition, step up resource input, and increase support for countries in the Global South. Developed countries should honor their commitment to development financing and climate financing. The international community should also build consensus and pool strengths to formulate the post-2030 global development agenda. Facing a new scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation, especially the dynamic development of artificial intelligence, we should take a people-centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide, and promote development that is universally beneficial.
Both history and reality prove that countries can hardly achieve development without an open and cooperative international environment. Protectionism produces no winners; building walls, erecting barriers, decoupling and cutting off supply chains disrupt global industrial and supply chains and harm the interests of all parties. We must firmly safeguard the WTO-centered, rules-based multilateral trading system, build an open world economy, jointly foster and strengthen new growth drivers, and see that economic globalization is inclusive and delivers benefits to all.
Third, we should advance exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations and rebuild unity and mutual trust through communication and dialogue. Diversity has created splendor in the world. Condescension and a self-centered mindset have no place in the interactions among different cultures. Promoting mutual respect, solidarity and harmonious coexistence is the right approach to take. We need to use the UN platform to boost international people-to-people exchanges, and take the celebration of the International Day for Dialogue Among Civilizations as an occasion to promote mutual understanding and amity among all peoples and the common development of diverse civilizations. We should reject ideological prejudice, and respect the development paths and social systems decided on independently by the people of all countries. We should deepen the sharing of governance practices and jointly explore ways to tackle challenges facing our times.
Fourth, we should stay committed to multilateralism and take steps to safeguard fairness and justice. Multilateralism is the choice made by humanity after going through scourges, and fairness and justice are the joint pursuit of the people of all countries. China holds that all countries, big or small, are equal members of the international community, and that world affairs should be handled by all through consultation, and rule of law, fairness and justice in international affairs should be jointly upheld. Countries should join forces and act together to safeguard the UN and make it stronger. China supports the UN in reforming and improving itself. It should advance the UN 80 Initiative and enhance the performance of its bodies rather than merely cut its budgets and mandates. It should effectively address global challenges including climate change and public health security, improve governance rules in such areas as cyberspace, outer space and polar regions, and truly increase the representation and voice of the Global South.
China pays high tribute to Secretary General Antonio Guterres who will complete his term soon. China supports the election, in accordance with the UN Charter, of a new secretary general who honors the UN Charter, has exceptional capability, upholds integrity and fairness, and demonstrates courage and dedication.
Mr. President,
Colleagues,
On October 25, 1971, right here in this august hall, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 at its 26th Session with an overwhelming majority, by which the UNGA decided to restore all the rights of the People's Republic of China in the UN and recognize the representatives of the Government of the People's Republic of China as the only legitimate representatives of China to the UN. This is of profound and far-reaching significance for both China and the world.
Over the past 55 years, China has been a stabilizing force in times of volatility. China is firmly committed to pursuing peaceful development, and has the best track record on peace and security among major countries. It is the largest contributor of peacekeepers among the permanent members of the UN Security Council. It also took the initiative that led to the issuance of the first joint statement of the leaders of the five nuclear-weapon states on preventing nuclear war. China has been a main engine driving common development. China has created two miracles at home, namely, fast economic growth and long-term social stability, and it has, over many years, contributed around 30 percent to global growth. China has joined hands with more than three fourths of the countries in the world in pursuing high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, it has mobilized over 23 billion U.S. dollars and carried out more than 2,000 projects under the Global Development Initiative, and it has granted zero-tariff status to all the African countries and least developed countries having diplomatic relations with it to empower the Global South in pursuing modernization. China has been a progressive force in an era of change. China has always spoken up for the Global South, stood up for the legitimate rights and interests of developing countries, and continued to work toward a more just and equitable global governance system. In October, China will host the Global Governance Forum in the Xiong'an New Area. You are welcome to attend the forum and join the discussion about the way forward in global governance.
Mr. President,
Colleagues,
No matter how the international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice, and in its commitment to multilateralism. China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity and make the world a better place for all of us. Thank you. ■

Interview: China-U.S. innovation cooperation creates shared opportunities -- Silicon Valley entrepreneur

Unknown Publisher

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Steve Hoffman, CEO of Silicon Valley-based startup incubator Founders Space, said he remains optimistic about China-U.S. economic and trade cooperation, citing the two economies' complementary strengths and broad potential for collaboration in artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Hoffman said he sees particularly strong potential for cooperation in AI.
During Chinese President Xi Jinping's just-concluded state visit to the United States, the two sides agreed to establish China-U.S. AI dialogue to exchange views on AI-related risks and benefits, with the next round to be held in November. A communication channel for AI-related incidents will also be set up.
"As CEO of Founders Space and someone deeply involved in AI, I see President Xi Jinping's visit as an important step forward," Hoffman said. "I was encouraged that AI was discussed at the presidential level."
"At Founders Space, I have always believed that cross-border collaboration drives the most transformative breakthroughs, and the progress made between the United States and China on AI is a vital step forward," he said.
"Establishing formal channels to manage high-stakes risks proves both nations recognize AI safety as a shared global responsibility rather than a zero-sum game," he added.
Hoffman noted that competition between China and the United States does not have to preclude cooperation, adding that the two countries could work together in areas such as AI safety, scientific research, open-source AI and responsible AI deployment.
"The United States and China will have a major role in shaping the future of technology, so continued dialogue and cooperation are important," Hoffman said.
He also pointed to the potential for cooperation between Chinese and American entrepreneurs, saying their different strengths can create opportunities that would be difficult to develop within either market alone and lead to "genuine win-win outcomes."
"The most successful collaborations are never one-sided," Hoffman said. "They happen when each side understands what the other side needs and then finds a structure where both can succeed."
"Innovation is increasingly global," he said. "Trying to force innovation back inside national borders would be extremely difficult and, in many cases, counterproductive."
In his work advising large companies on AI strategy, Hoffman said he has seen some companies turn to Chinese open-source models to maintain greater control over their data.
"Open models also allow entrepreneurs, researchers, and smaller companies to participate in the AI revolution," he said.
Looking ahead, Hoffman said China and the United States could continue working together in areas of shared interest, including AI safety, scientific research, climate change and global economic stability.
"That is ultimately what I want to see more of: practical cooperation that turns differences into new opportunities for both sides," Hoffman said. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: French scholar in pursuit of century-old cultural imprints in coconut carvings
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:54 CST
18:40:54 KST

HAIKOU, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Roland Bourdeix, a French researcher devoted to coconut genetics for over two decades, has chosen to bring his cherished collections back to China for restoration, seeking the origins of the century-old cultural exchanges centered on coconut carvings.
The scholar has visited more than 40 tropical countries for his research. He regards the coconut tree as the "tree of life" and believes that coconut shell carving stands out as one of the most exquisite forms among the material and symbolic cultures derived from it.
Aiming to build a coconut-themed ecological museum, Bourdeix has collected a large number of rare ancient coconut carvings from around the world over the past 25 years, including a batch of Chinese coconut carvings dating back to the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) that were exported to Europe about a century ago.
Since the 19th century, Chinese coconut carvings have been sold to Europe and Southeast Asia as souvenirs or diplomatic gifts via southern Chinese cities of Guangzhou and Macao. Some of these works were subsequently passed down through generations in European families.
When Bourdeix discovered that some of the collections had cracked or been damaged over time, he decided to bring them back to south China's Hainan Province for restoration rather than having them repaired locally in Europe.
He explained that this is not merely about restoring the artifacts, but also a cultural journey back to their origin, expecting his efforts to draw greater public attention to the culture of coconut carving.
A traditional carving art using coconut shells, coconut wood and other materials, coconut carving is mainly practiced in Hainan. Records of Hainan coconut carvings date back to as early as the Tang Dynasty (618-907), and the carvings were presented as treasures to the imperial court during the Ming and Qing dynasties.
Hainan coconut carving was included in the national intangible cultural heritage list in 2008.
In 2025, the province launched a three-year action plan to systematically promote the inheritance and innovation of coconut carvings.
Coordinated by the provincial coconut industry association, Qiongtai Normal University in the province undertook the restoration.
Wu Mingju, a national intangible cultural heritage inheritor of coconut carving and a teacher of coconut carving courses at the university, immediately identified the works' age and craftsmanship features upon seeing them.
"Most of them feature Chinese mythological figures, and although the appearance is flawed, the complete lineage of traditional craftsmanship is still evident," he said.
Zhang Bidi, a coconut carving artist with the industry association, introduced a comprehensive restoration plan: bonding broken parts with epoxy resin, meticulously repairing and carving along the original grain with chisels, and grinding and filling damaged fragments with coconut material of the same type.
The artisans consulted with Bourdeix and confirmed every detail of the restoration. A shared understanding of craftsmanship that transcended language and culture soon established full mutual trust between the two sides.
Recalling his encounter with Wu, the Frenchman said that despite their different cultural backgrounds, he regarded Wu as a brother, and that both were driven by the same passion, curiosity and love for multiculturalism.
They discussed restoration techniques, their personal collections and ways to promote coconut carving, and agreed to co-author academic papers and jointly participate in the museum's construction that Bourdeix is preparing in France.
"The coconut carvings' journey witnessed another reconnection of a cultural bond that transcends remote mountains and seas," said Gao Yiping, a professor at the university's school of fine arts.
In recent years, cultural and creative products that integrate coconut carvings with trendy brands have repeatedly won popularity in the domestic market, showcasing the strong vitality of traditional craftsmanship in modern times, according to the professor.
Bourdeix believes the open platform of the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP) is providing a broader space for coconut carvings to reach the global stage.
He expects Chinese coconut-carving culture to reach more parts of the world and for the country's coconut research resources to be further integrated into the international academic network.
Hainan FTP began island-wide special customs operations on Dec. 18, 2025. In the first half of 2026, Hainan recorded 1.603 million inbound and outbound passenger trips, including 883,000 by foreign nationals. ■

High-speed rail line through mountainous central China region opens to traffic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:53 CST
18:40:53 KST

The first train of Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, G6888, is pictured ahead of its departure from Xingshan Railway Station in Xingshan County, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 28, 2026. The 101-kilometer Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway officially entered service on Monday. The railway, with a designed speed of 350 kilometers per hour, is an important part of the country's high-speed rail network. (Xinhua/Wang Zichen)
WUHAN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway line in central China's Hubei Province began service on Monday, facilitating tourism, industrial development and rural revitalization in the mountainous region, according to China Railway Wuhan Bureau Group Co., Ltd., its operator.
Traversing the Daba Mountains, the 101-km line with a design speed of 350 km per hour connects China's two major high-speed railway arteries, namely the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu line and the Zhengzhou-Chongqing line.
Shang Zejin, chief designer of the railway, said the construction process faced multiple challenges posed by complex geological conditions, including deep-buried tunnels, high in-situ stress, high gas concentrations and karst formations.
Designers and constructors applied numerous new technologies and construction techniques to tackle these problems. Of the total length, bridges and tunnels account for more than 94 percent of the line, Shang said.
Opened shortly before China's National Day holiday, the railway is expected to boost tourist flows between major cities including Wuhan, Zhengzhou and Chongqing, as well as iconic attractions such as the Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River, unleashing renewed economic momentum for the central region.
Ma Rong, deputy director of the passenger transport department of China Railway Wuhan Bureau Group Co., Ltd., said the railway line will cut travel time and improve services, providing solid support for high-quality development in adjacent regions.
China has built the world's largest high-speed railway network. By the end of 2025, the total length of operating railways in the country had reached 165,000 km, including over 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to reach 70,000 km by 2035. ■

Asian Games | China takes two diving golds as Lin, Wang claim 1m titles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:29 CST
18:40:29 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China maintained its dominance in diving at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by winning both 1m springboard gold medals here on Monday.
Lin Shan and Long Yiping finished 1-2 in the women's 1m springboard. Li scored 263.05 points for gold, while Long finished second with 254.25. South Korea's Kim Su-ji took bronze with 245.05.
Although Lin remained consistent throughout the five rounds, she said she was not fully satisfied with her performance.
"Although the result is quite good, I am not very satisfied with the process," Lin said. "I didn't show my strengths. Each dive was stable, but not elegant or refined enough."
Lin said her strengths usually lie in her lines and entries, but neither had been perfectly executed on Monday.
"I have to set high standards for myself. If I don't demand enough of myself, I can't reach the world's top level," she said.
Lin, who won silver at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, said reaching the top of the podium after several years of hard work gave her further motivation. "After all these years, I've come this far, and my results have improved. I need to be more determined and keep moving forward," she said.
For Long, who was making her Asian Games debut, a mistake on her fourth dive cost her valuable points. Her 107C earned only 33.00 points, leaving her eighth in that round.
"It was more regret than disappointment, because I lost too many points on that dive," Long said. "But this is something I can adjust in training. That dive has already passed, so I was more focused on doing the upcoming one well."
Long bounced back with a strong final dive, scoring 57.20 points for her 5333D.
"I was very excited to take part in the Asian Games. The venue and environment here are excellent. As for my performance, I still have some shortcomings that give me more areas to improve in training," she said.
Long said she hopes to compete at more international events and work toward the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.
In the men's 1m springboard, Wang Zongyuan added another gold for China with 442.75 points, well ahead of South Korea's Kim Yeong-nam, who scored 373.30. China's Liu Chengzan took bronze with 361.45.
Wang led from the opening dive and topped the standings in four of the six rounds. His highest score came on his fourth dive, a 405B, which earned 81.60 points.
Despite successfully defending his title, Wang said there was still room for improvement.
"I'm very happy to stand on the top of the podium and successfully defend my title from the Hangzhou Asian Games," Wang said. "But there were still many shortcomings throughout the competition, and I'll work on them in training."
Wang said he had not fully settled into his competition rhythm in the opening rounds.
"Maybe it was the first two dives. I didn't immediately enter the competition mode or reach the right level of excitement. I was distracted a little," he said. "Fortunately, I gradually found my competition rhythm in the later rounds."
Liu, making his Asian Games debut, made a costly mistake on his third dive, a 205C, scoring just 36.00 points and dropping to fourth after the round. He recovered with 73.60 points on his fourth dive and eventually secured bronze.
"I'm definitely not satisfied. To be honest, today's performance was quite far from the level I showed in training," Liu said.
After the mistake, Liu said he tried not to dwell on it. "Once I made the mistake, I told myself not to think about that dive anymore and to focus on the dives ahead. There were still opportunities, so I just wanted to slowly make up the points," he said.
Looking ahead to Tuesday's 3m springboard competition, Wang said he would focus on himself.
"My goal hasn't changed. I hope to do my best tomorrow," he said. "The biggest challenge is still myself." ■

It was completely illegal because they picked us up from private property. We don't call this detention; we call it kidnapping,” he said.
“When we asked the police on what grounds we were detained, their only reply was, 'Sir, we have orders from above, so we arrested you, detained you.' The condition of schools here is very poor, especially in the remote areas where most schools don't even have their own buildings,” he said.“A complete facade has been created in the name of development, but we want the country to see the reality of that development,” Ranka added. But as I've been released, Abhijit is not coming. A glimpse of Yuanyang Hani Terraces in SW China's Yunnan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:16 CST
18:40:16 KST

Villagers harvest rice in Aichun Village of Yuanyang County in Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Sept. 21, 2026.
Listed as a World Cultural Heritage Site, a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System, and a World Heritage Irrigation Structure, the Yuanyang Hani Terraces vividly demonstrate China's ecological wisdom of "harmonious coexistence between humans and nature." Today, the millennia-old mountain farming in the terraced fields is taking on a new look.
The terraces are nestled in the Ailao Mountains along the southern bank of the Red River in Yunnan. For centuries, fragmented plots, steep slopes and narrow paths had forced farmers to carry rice sacks on their backs or with horses. Today, drones can transport grain directly from paddy edges to village rooftops, reducing transport costs and shortening the transport time from 40 minutes to less than 10 minutes.
New planting technologies are also easing farmers' workloads. A degradable paper-film embedded seeding and fixed-point planting technology developed by the School of Agriculture of Yunnan University has been applied in Niujiaozhai Town of Yuanyang County, allowing farmers to complete a full day's transplanting work in two to three hours. Local agricultural authorities have also improved rice varieties and introduced rice-fish-duck farming to raise household incomes.
While new technologies support farming, the ancient terraces still rely on the participation of local people, who maintain and repair ditches to keep water supplies stable and prevent terraces from being abandoned.
To protect the terraces, it is critical to let farmers share the fruits of economic development. Cooperatives here have boosted sales of local red rice via e-commerce and distributed profit dividends to farmers. Azheke Village, nestled in the heart of the terraces, has embraced a unique approach to tourism development. Villagers have contributed resources such as terraces, houses and traditional ways of life, creating a model of collective participation and shared prosperity.
The improved livelihoods have drawn young rural migrants back home. In Duoyishu Village alone, over 80 homestays are now in operation, with more than 100 returning youths working in tourism, catering and transport sectors.
In Yuanyang, the annual rice harvest now means far more than a good crop. It embodies a dynamic balance between ancient heritage protection and modern development, ensuring that the millennia-old terraces stay cultivated, local communities stay prosperous, and the unique farming legacy endures for generations. Economic Watch: China's industrial profits retain double-digit growth via high-tech, new growth drivers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:16 CST
18:40:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's industrial profits maintained double-digit growth in the first eight months of 2026, driven by rapid expansion of high-tech manufacturing and new growth drivers, official figures showed on Monday.
Profits of industrial firms above designated size increased 15.7 percent year on year during the first eight months of 2026, according to National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data.
These industrial firms with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.97 million U.S. dollars) saw their combined profits reach 5.27 trillion yuan in the January-August period.
In August alone, profits of major industrial firms grew 4.2 percent year on year, the NBS noted.
Yu Weining, an NBS statistician, attributed this relatively fast profit growth to the steady advance of industrial production and a widened increase in industrial product prices.
Earlier data revealed that the country's industrial output rose 5.3 percent in the first eight months of the year, while the producer price index, which measures costs of goods at the factory gate, climbed 3.8 percent year on year in August.
Yu highlighted the electronic sector as the main pillar supporting industrial growth, with profits surging 110 percent year on year, contributing 62 percent to the overall profit growth of industrial firms.
"The accelerated expansion of new technology applications, represented by artificial intelligence, has driven the expansion of demand in related fields, propelling swift profit growth in the electronics industry," Yu said.
Yu noted that rising chip demand driven by emerging scenarios such as new energy vehicles, the Internet of Things and computing power centers had boosted profits in the optoelectronic device manufacturing and semiconductor discrete device manufacturing industries by 72 percent and 51.8 percent, respectively.
High-tech manufacturing played a prominent role in driving growth. During the January-August period, profits of high-tech manufacturing firms above designated size soared 54.7 percent year on year, 39 percentage points higher than the overall growth rate.
Profits of raw material manufacturing jumped 47.3 percent year on year in the January-August period, contributing 6.2 percentage points to the overall profit growth. Higher international crude oil and non-ferrous metals prices, meanwhile, helped lift chemical and non-ferrous metals profits in this period, while petroleum processing recovered from making losses to generating profits.
Industrial firms' unit costs continued to decline in the January-August period, with cost per 100 yuan of operating revenue down 0.41 yuan year on year, while the profit margin on operating revenue rose 0.44 percentage points to 5.66 percent, reflecting improved cost control and profitability.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) highlights the development of a modern industrial system anchored by advanced manufacturing. The country will move to upgrade traditional sectors to the mid-to-high end of the value chain, nurture emerging industries, and make forward-looking plans for industries of the future, according to this development blueprint.
Looking ahead, Yu said efforts should be made to expand domestic demand, optimize supply, accelerate the shift from old growth drivers to new ones, and promote the sustained development of the industrial economy with new and improved quality. ■

SC extends Class VII-VIII relaxations to Class VI (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the CBSE to extend to Class VI students the same exemptions and relaxations available to students of Classes VII and VIII under its newly introduced three-language scheme.Under the order, Class VI students will have to study the newly mandated third language, but they will not have to appear for a CBSE Board examination in that language when they reach Class X. The exemption is currently available to students who are in Classes VII and VIII.
The Supreme Court has also extended another relaxation to Class VI students. Those already studying two non-native languages will be allowed to continue with the same combination and take one additional Bharatiya Bhasha as their third language.This means such students will not have to drop or change either of their existing languages to accommodate the two regional languages required under the new language scheme.
The directions bring Class VI students on par with the current Classes VII and VIII batches in terms of the exemptions and flexibility available under the CBSE's three-language policy.

Solving Math’s Greatest Problems Was an Art Form. Then Came AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

From Suno composing uncanny elevator music to Tilly Norwood delivering customer-service-inflected one-liners, artificial intelligence has rattled creative industries. You can add math to the list after OpenAI said that, using thousands of agents, it had solved a decades-old puzzle known as the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem.
“The artists and the musicians have already gone through this,” says Juspreet Singh Sandhu, a mathematician at Colorado State University.
Despite what timed high school exams might have you believe, mathematicians aren’t focused on getting the right answer as fast as possible. In fact, contrary to math’s image as a practical subject, the development of new mathematical ideas often resembles artistic exploration, akin to inventing a game or puzzle. Mathematicians typically follow a thoughtful, deliberate process to develop their ideas. In contrast, OpenAI approached the proof with brute force, which shortcut the process in a way that threatens to undermine human understanding.
“A mathematician, like a painter or poet, is a maker of patterns,” wrote the English mathematician G. H. Hardy in his 1940 essay, A Mathematician’s Apology. As Hardy describes it, a painter uses shapes and colors, and a poet uses words, while a mathematician constructs patterns out of ideas.
A pacifist, Hardy wrote the essay during World War II to argue that people should pursue mathematics for its own sake, separate from applications, particularly wartime ones. His essay promotes “useless” mathematics. He cites famed mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss’ oft-quoted statement about number theory, the subfield of math which involves the study of integers, as the epitome of beautiful, useless math. While Hardy’s comparison of math to art holds up, he would turn out to be wrong on some of the specifics: After being useless for centuries, number theory would prove valuable for encryption protocols widely used today to secure your emails and bank accounts.
At this point, though, useless is exactly what OpenAI’s proof is. The puzzle it solves is simply one that’s been interesting to mathematicians for decades.
Its name comes from the Navier-Stokes equations, which 19th-century scientists developed to describe the flow of viscous fluids. Engineers use the equations to model airflow for airplane design. But mathematicians became enamored with the equations themselves, not their applications.
“Mathematicians’ main interest in the equations was certainly not engineering,” says Jared Speck, a mathematician at Vanderbilt University. They pursued answers to the problem, he says, because of the “mathematical richness, the puzzle aspect of it.” The puzzle’s solution will not help anybody design a more aerodynamic airplane wing. Put another way: Many cakes are cylindrical, but studying the equations that describe a cylinder won’t necessarily help you bake a better cake.
“When problems resist solution, they take on a bit of lore,” says Speck. The draw of Navier-Stokes is similar to why people play Sudoku or chess, both of which have no utility other than being fun and intellectually stimulating. The equations describe fluid flow, approximately, in the world we live in. But mathematicians imagined how the equations would apply in a fringe, almost sci-fi context, just because it intrigued them. They formulated a puzzle: They wanted to know whether the equations implied that in unrealistic conditions, a fluid could explode for no physical reason.
Mathematicians expect approximate equations like Navier-Stokes to imply such nonsensical situations, which they find particularly interesting because sometimes they can lead to brand-new mathematical ideas. For years the community had been developing “a deep and beautiful theory” around the equations, says Speck. They were on the verge of cracking the problem before OpenAI’s proof found that yes, the Navier-Stokes equations did imply a sci-fi fluid explosion.
While people do perform results-oriented math, such as to design new cryptography protocols or optimization algorithms for robotics, the mathematics community is by and large “interested in more than just a yes or no answer to a problem,” says Speck.
There’s also the problem of understanding the final answer itself. When humans write proofs, they organize their arguments based on previous research, which they cite. They spend months, if not years, writing and communicating the steps of their proofs to try to convince colleagues of their insights. Consider it akin to workshopping a poem, but with logic instead of emotion.
That didn’t happen with OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof. LLMs don’t reliably cite their work, and they don’t explain themselves clearly to humans. The 166-page proof remains under peer review, and experts have not yet had time to confirm its validity. Mathematicians have criticized the company's lack of transparency in how it arrived at the solution, and Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, has suggested that OpenAI may have used his and others’ work without proper attribution.
“We don't even know how autonomous it was, or how much human expertise is necessary to scaffold the process,” says Sandhu.
Because of these and other factors, “basically nobody in my community really understands what's going on,” says Speck. “In fact, the proof was done in a very unfamiliar order. First, the result was given to us by the computer, and now people are like, ‘Let's try to understand what's going on.’ We're at the very beginning of that.”
Sandhu has signed an online declaration titled “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics,” which says mass-producing proofs “could destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas.” The declaration’s initial signatories were 25 winners of the Fields Medal, often called the Nobel Prize in mathematics. The declaration is not against the use of AI, says Sandhu, who, like many mathematicians, already uses AI in his work. To Sandhu, the declaration states that “mathematical culture values understanding,” and that the speed through which LLMs tear through proofs could mean that “we will have solved without understanding.”
In response to the declaration, OpenAI this week formed an advisory group of mathematicians to guide the company’s use of AI. “We believe those criticisms [in the declaration] highlight the need for thoughtful engagement between AI companies and the math community,” an OpenAI spokesperson writes in an email, adding that the company wants “mathematicians to have a meaningful voice” in how AI is used.
However they’re used, the speed of LLMs may hinder human creativity. The models, while still error-prone, can churn through long calculations that human mathematicians find unpleasant. But mathematicians may miss valuable insights by outsourcing all these calculations, says Lorenzo Gavassino, a theoretical physicist at the University of Cambridge in the UK. “When a calculation turns out to be harder than expected, to the point of it being discouraging, that is when the greatest progress is possible,” he says. The struggle inspires mathematicians to invent new concepts.
Gavassino gives the invention of the imaginary number, i, which is the square root of –1, as an example. Mathematicians invented i in the 16th century after generations of trying to solve cubic equations, expressions that contain an x3 term and no higher exponents. This new concept gave birth to an entirely new subfield of math, known as complex analysis. Centuries later, physicists would use imaginary numbers in the equations for describing quantum mechanics, and they were able to use mathematicians’ theorems about i to build their understanding of electrons, atoms, and, now, quantum computers.
Like many mathematical concepts, the imaginary number was initially mostly useless. Often, a mathematical concept’s practical success unfolds over generations. First, mathematicians noodle extensively over the logic behind the concept. After the field develops a solid understanding of the ideas, people find applications in contexts their inventors never intended.
Mathematicians have a saying, Gavassino tells me: “Good mathematicians prove theorems; great mathematicians propose conjectures; the greatest of all provide definitions.” He explains what it means using an analogy that compares the mathematical process to a game. Good mathematicians win a game; great mathematicians propose ways to win a game; the greatest of all invent the game in the first place. In the case of Navier-Stokes and other areas where AI systems have come up with proofs, the LLM demonstrated how to win a game, but Gavassino thinks the technology is still far from being able to invent new ones.
Gavassino isn’t afraid that LLMs will do math better than he can. He thinks of LLMs as just another tool—one with the reliability, currently, of a “drunk guy”—and that it’s possible to use them responsibly and creatively. But he distrusts how leaders may exploit inflated ideas of their performance for political purposes. “I am afraid, instead, that certain people with not great intentions may start to say, ‘You know what? There is no need to finance research. We can let AI do the discovery in place of the researchers,’” says Gavassino.
Notably, OpenAI also spent millions—equivalent to the annual pay of dozens of academic mathematicians—on computational power to generate the proof. A similar sum could fund dozens of graduate students, all with the potential to unlock new creative solutions and puzzles.
The mathematical community has long relied on a teacher-apprentice structure to discover new ideas sustainably over generations. “When I was starting out, I was given problems that people senior to me probably could have solved more easily themselves, or at least done more quickly,” says Speck. “But they were investing in me. They were giving me an opportunity to develop.”
Now, AI seems to be capable of picking math’s lowest-hanging fruit, and thereby threatening to scoop younger researchers and deprive students of training opportunities. That in turn could turn off the spigot of human creativity that’s built the entire field—and led to far-flung advances some mathematicians may never have even considered. “Trying to answer big questions in general forces us to develop new ideas, techniques, strategies, and languages that then become useful elsewhere,” says Gavassino.
That creative process gave rise to LLMs themselves. The study of differential equations and complex analysis has enabled the invention of the lasers for etching the computer chips where the models reside. The software itself consists of neural networks, which crunch numbers using the tools of linear algebra, a mathematical field at least as old as the 17th century. AI companies have fattened their models with generations of human insight.
Now that the models are fed, and trillion-dollar valuations must be sought, the companies may very well trample the community that created their product in the first place.

Lai said drone production reached NT$12.9 billion in 2025, more than 2.5 times the 2024 level, with more than 267 firms involved in systems integration and component manufacturing. He also asked the Legislative Yuan to support the Ministry of National Defense's proposed supplemental budget of nearly NT$60 billion.

Taiwan’s history of trapping invaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:23:37 UTC
18:23:37 KST

The Chinese idiom “closing the door to beat the dog” (關門打狗) has evolved from a rural proverb into a polarizing strategic metaphor.
While modern Taiwanese leaders reject its derogatory language, the core tactic — luring an enemy into enclosed terrain, sealing escape routes, and launching an inescapable attack — is deeply woven into Taiwan’s legacy of resistance. Over centuries, local forces have repeatedly used geography and strategic choke points to resist stronger adversaries.
The folk and architectural blueprint
In traditional courtyards, catching an aggressive dog required shutting the main gate first to trap the animal. This found a physical manifestation in traditional East Asian military architecture through the wengcheng (甕城), or barbican system — walled enclosures built outside fortress gates that trapped invading forces inside a lethal bottleneck.
In 1948, Mao Zedong formalized a similar concept into military doctrine during the Liaoshen Campaign to isolate Nationalist forces at the Jinzhou railway junction.
However, long before and after Mao’s maneuvers, people in Taiwan adapted similar forms of entrapment as tools for survival.
Pre-Japanese and colonial resistance
Because Taiwan’s geography consists of dense forests, mountains, and narrow valleys, local resistance forces often relied on terrain to neutralize better-equipped conventional armies.
During the Lin Shuang-wen Rebellion of 1787–1788, Lin’s rebel forces faced Qing troops sent to suppress the uprising. According to accounts of the campaign, rebel forces exploited difficult terrain and fortified mountain positions while resisting Qing advances.
During the 1895 Japanese invasion, local Hakka and Hoklo volunteer militias under Wu Tang-hsing used the rugged terrain around Baguashan in Changhua while confronting advancing Japanese forces.
The battle became one of the largest engagements of the 1895 resistance and a defining example of how terrain shaped the fighting.
The 1930 Wushe Rebellion offers another example. Seediq Indigenous fighters under Mona Rudao used the difficult Mahebo terrain, including narrow mountain routes and suspension bridges, against Japanese forces.
Resistance fighters cut at least one important suspension bridge during the uprising to slow the Japanese advance. Japanese forces eventually responded with overwhelming military force, including aircraft.
The authoritarian reversal and postwar defense
During the 228 Incident and subsequent White Terror era, the logic of containment was tragically turned inward by the KMT authoritarian state.
Security forces used martial law, arrests, searches, port controls, and large-scale security operations to suppress dissidents, intellectuals, activists, and others deemed threats to the regime.
Two years later, however, geographic containment played a very different role during the Battle of Guningtou on Kinmen.
Former Japanese Imperial Army General Nemoto Hiroshi secretly traveled to assist KMT forces fighting the Chinese Communists and later advised Taiwan’s military leadership.
During the battle, PLA troops landed on Kinmen but became separated from reinforcements as Taiwan’s defenders used armor, artillery, air power, and coastal defenses to destroy or disable landing craft and isolate the invading force.
After approximately three days of fighting, the PLA landing force was defeated. The battle halted the immediate Communist advance on Kinmen and became one of the defining military encounters of the early cross-strait confrontation.
Modern cross-strait rhetoric
Today, Beijing has revived the idiom during military encirclement exercises around Taiwan.
Chinese state media and military commentators have used “closing the door to beat the dog” to describe scenarios in which PLA forces seek to cut Taiwan off from external support while preventing forces on Taiwan from escaping.
Taiwanese commentators have also used the phrase in a different context to warn taishang against moving manufacturing operations to China, where attractive incentives can later give way to regulatory pressure or restrictions once businesses are deeply invested.
The phrase remains potent enough to trigger domestic controversy.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, then-Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) used “closing the door to beat the dog” to describe his containment strategy during a major outbreak associated with Huannan Market.
Ko said the strategy involved concentrating screening and vaccination efforts among the highly mobile market population. His choice of language nevertheless drew criticism for its blunt and dehumanizing imagery.
The modern Western reversal
More recently, the metaphor has been applied to US-China diplomacy.
A Liberty Times analysis published after the September Trump-Xi summit argued that Western democracies — particularly the United States under President Donald Trump — had effectively turned the concept back against Beijing.
Unlike the psychological deception of the classic “Empty Fort Stratagem” (空城計), which relies on bluffing an opponent, the article portrayed the summit as a structural form of containment.
Washington offered Xi Jinping a lavish welcome and the prestige of a White House state visit while continuing to maintain extensive economic and technological restrictions on China.
The underlying argument is that ceremonial engagement does not necessarily translate into strategic concession. Washington can offer diplomatic theater while continuing to constrain Beijing in areas such as advanced technology, trade, and artificial intelligence.
Taiwanese agency
Crucially, this geopolitical contest is not merely a game played between superpowers. Taiwan possesses its own historical and contemporary agency and continues to use asymmetric defense and strategic maneuvering to secure its sovereignty.
Today, one source of Taiwan’s leverage lies in its “silicon shield” — its central position in advanced semiconductor manufacturing through TSMC.
In a conflict, this technological dominance would not function as an absolute barrier. Instead, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry acts as a major global economic tripwire.
Any blockade or occupation that disrupted advanced chip production would impose enormous costs not only on Taiwan, but on China and the wider global economy.
Taiwan also faces genuine vulnerabilities in energy resilience and maritime supply lines. Its agency therefore lies in raising the economic, military, and political costs of coercion.
By modernizing asymmetric military capabilities, reinforcing civic infrastructure, and deepening global economic interdependence, Taiwan can make aggression increasingly costly while strengthening its own resilience.
The goal is not to recreate an ancient battlefield trap. It is to ensure that coercion or invasion presents Beijing with costs that outweigh any conceivable benefit, preserving Taiwan’s freedom and democratic system.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US Ambassador to China David Perdue said President Donald Trump once asked Chinese leader Xi Jinping whether China wanted to buy American weapons while discussing Washington’s arms sales to Taiwan, the Financial Times reported Monday.
Perdue made the disclosure when asked about reports that Trump had delayed a proposed NT$439 billion (US$14 billion) arms package for Taiwan to avoid upsetting Xi. Perdue said Trump had noted that the US sells weapons to countries around the world and “at one point” asked Xi whether China wanted to buy some.
Perdue did not say when Trump made the remark or provide further details. The White House also did not say how Xi responded.
A US official told the Financial Times that Washington had no plans to sell weapons to China. The State Department subsequently said US law prohibits such sales and that there was no offer or plan to provide weapons to Beijing.
The Trump administration has also raised concerns about Beijing providing Iran with dual-use technology that could have military applications, per ABC News.
Perdue rejected suggestions that the status of the Taiwan package reflected an effort to avoid harming relations with Beijing. He said US policy toward Taiwan had not changed and discussions over the proposed sale were continuing.
Taiwan Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大㵢) said the US remains Taiwan’s main weapons supplier. He said Taiwan hoped to receive the proposed package “as soon as possible.”

Acer celebrates 50th anniversary with musical
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:22:50 UTC
18:22:50 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Acer is celebrating its 50th anniversary with “Smile for Half a Century,” a musical created in collaboration with Cloud Gate Dance Theatre, OneSong Orchestra, and Story Works.
The production tells the story of Acer’s five-decade journey, bringing the company’s history to the stage while inviting employees, partners, and other stakeholders to celebrate the milestone together. Acer founder Stan Shih (施振榮) served as co-producer of the musical, which premiered Monday and was streamed online for audiences worldwide, per UDN.
The production features employees and colleagues from Acer and affiliated companies, including AUO, Qisda, and Wistron, along with contributions from overseas colleagues and behind-the-scenes footage. Combining music, theater, dance, and technology, the musical presents Acer’s corporate history through the experiences of the people who contributed to its development.
Shih said that when a group of young entrepreneurs founded Acer 50 years ago with limited resources and ambitious ideas, he never imagined that the company's entrepreneurial journey would eventually be brought to the stage as a musical. He said the production was not intended to celebrate a single individual but rather to reflect on the challenges and bottlenecks the company has overcome, per UDN.
Shih said the production also allowed him to reconsider Acer's legacy. Companies, he said, should not measure their achievements solely through tangible, immediate, and directly measurable results. Intangible assets such as talent, culture, trust, brand reputation, and shared experiences can become some of the most valuable legacies accumulated over decades.

Over 39% of South Koreans say they believe reunification with North Korea is impossible, the highest number since Seoul National University’s Institute for Peace and Unification Studies began its annual poll in 2007.
The results of the institute’s poll released Monday showed respondents who believe reunification is impossible rose 3.5 percentage points from the previous year. The July 1 to 26 poll interviewed 1,200 adults aged 19 to 74 and had a margin of error of 2.8%.
Of the over 60% of respondents who believed reunification was possible, 27.5% said they expected it would take at least 30 years; 16.1%

Ukrainian forces advance in key eastern battlefield, senior commander says
KYIV, Sept 28 - Ukraine's military has recaptured more territory from Russian forces in the north of the Donetsk region, a senior military commander said on Monday, in an operation aimed at complicating Moscow's assault on Ukraine's key eastern strongholds.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps recaptured an area of 51 square kilometres (20 square miles), said Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi, who has commanded operations in the area since last month.
In total, the operation called "Vivaldi" has recaptured 176 sq km in the north of Donetsk, has freed three more villages and has restored Ukrainian control over two more villages, Biletskyi said.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington-based think tank, has said the operation has achieved the "operationally-significant" goal of disrupting Moscow's effort to conduct a wide encirclement of the "fortress belt" of Ukrainian cities.
Russia's overall frontline advances have slowed this year but its forces have been bearing down on the cities from the south and infiltrating deeper into the eastern city of Kostiantynivka.
The Donetsk region has seen most of the fiercest battles of the war.
Ukraine still holds about 20% of Donetsk while Russia wants to control all of it — Moscow's main territorial demand at negotiations that have so far stalled but which the US wants to restart.
The reported gains in the Donetsk region would add to Ukraine's push earlier this year in the southeast, where Kyiv said it clawed back more than 700 sq km of territory during a months-long counterattack. REUTERS

Live Updates: Iran says Trump must choose between war or diplomacy as talks resume
What to know about the Iran war today:
- President Trump confirmed that American and Iranian negotiators exchanged messages through mediators on Monday. He didn't share any details on the talks, but said, "We're going to win."
- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran is "fully prepared for the war to be resumed," and also for the possibility of renewed diplomacy aimed at ending the seven-month conflict. It's "up to President Trump to choose," he said.
- Last week, Iran proposed a seven-day ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, contingent upon the U.S. meeting conditions laid out in the mid-June memorandum of understanding, which fell apart after several weeks. Mr. Trump publicly rejected the new Iranian proposal last week, and Iran has insisted it will not change its demands.
Iran says it expects an answer today from U.S. on proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he expected a formal answer on Tuesday from the United States to Tehran's proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.
Qatari intermediaries "presented ideas, and we discussed them; they are set to raise the matter with the American side once more, after which the final U.S. response will be conveyed to us", Araghchi said late Monday.
Iran's top diplomat, who is in New York for the U.N. General Assembly, said "the Qataris hope this will be done by tomorrow".
On Iran talks, Trump says "I offered them NOTHING"
President Trump denied that he has offered to relieve Iran of some sanctions and unfreeze its funds, writing on Truth Social: "I offered them NOTHING!"
The president was reacting to an Axios story that said Mr. Trump is open to granting sanctions relief in exchange for progress on Iran's nuclear program.
A U.S. official also told CBS News on Monday that Mr. Trump is willing to grant Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if progress is made on the nuclear issue.
Trump confirms U.S. spoke to Iranian negotiators through mediators today
President Trump confirmed to reporters that American and Iranian negotiators exchanged messages through mediators on Monday.
He did not share any details on the talks, saying, "We're going to win."
CBS News reported earlier Monday that indirect U.S.-Iran talks began in the morning. A U.S. official said Mr. Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on Iran's nuclear program, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, and the two sides remain apart on the timing of commitments.
An Iranian diplomatic source told CBS News the primary issue is that the U.S. president does not seem to have a clear position on what he wants from negotiations, making it difficult to move from discussions to a concrete agreement.
Uncertainty about Strait of Hormuz weighs on U.S. bond market
Yields in the U.S. bond market cranked higher Monday and again reached their highest levels in roughly two decades, which knocked U.S. stocks further from their record high.
Monday's rise in yields followed the latest swings for oil prices, which have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide.
The latest turns came after President Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
Gas prices could soar if the U.S. bans diesel exports, economists say
A move by the U.S. to temporarily halt diesel exports amid record-high prices would initially lower costs, but a prolonged ban could drive up domestic gasoline prices, according to Goldman Sachs.
President Trump on Sunday told reporters his administration is "very seriously" considering a ban on diesel exports. Calls to restrict exports of U.S.-refined diesel have picked up in recent weeks, mostly from Republican lawmakers, as a lever they believe will help lower prices. Diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, and has only eased slightly since then, slipping to $6.45 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA data.
The war with Iran is pushing up oil and gas prices, creating widespread financial strain on U.S. motorists, food delivery drivers and farmers.

Yemen says it launched over 350 strikes against Houthi targets
Yemen's defense ministry said it carried out 356 strikes against Houthi military targets over the past 24 hours, killing or wounding an estimated 476 fighters.
Video posted by the Yemeni military showed strikes on various Houthi positions across several front lines.
Military spokesman Col. Majed al-Nazili said the strikes targeted Houthi command centers, weapons depots, artillery positions, vehicles and other military equipment.
 
U.S. official: Talks ongoing through mediators, but no deal unless nuclear issue addressed
The U.S. and Iran are continuing to have discussions, viewed as positive and constructive, through mediators, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, according to a U.S. official.
President Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on nuclear issues, the official said. Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, but the two sides still remain apart on the timing of commitments and who takes which steps first.
The official said the U.S. is skeptical of Iran's promises after it broke the memorandum of understanding by firing on commercial vessels, and is looking for assurances that Iran is serious.
Iranians face arduous journeys as U.S. sanctions ground planes
Flying out of Iran has long required patience in the face of restrictions and delays, but new U.S. sanctions have grounded flights on short notice and left war-weary travelers feeling trapped as they try to leave the country.
Passengers who booked tickets out of Iran to Middle Eastern destinations like the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, Oman and Turkey have faced short-notice cancellations as the latest sanctions bite.
Among those scrambling for a way out is Mitra, a 49-year-old woman who had planned to travel to Paris via Istanbul along with her brother, but who now faces a long journey by road to get to Turkey.
"Some airlines are still selling tickets, but they keep getting canceled. It honestly makes us feel completely trapped," she told an AFP journalist in Paris, using a pseudonym for fear of retribution by authorities.
"When we were told that flights had been suspended, we decided to travel to Istanbul by land instead," she said.
Mitra described paying around $75 to book a flight to the Iranian city of Tabriz, from where she will travel by road for several hours to reach the border.
In Van in Turkey, they will stay at a hotel, because the wait at the border can be long and chaotic.
"At this point, we're just hoping that we can actually get out. They might even close the land border," she fears.
Israel releases on bail U.S.-Palestinian reporter accused of working for Iran
An Israeli court on Monday released on bail a Palestinian-American journalist who had been detained for nearly two weeks on charges including working for Iran, her lawyer told the AFP news agency.
An AFP journalist saw Naqaa Hamed, who has contributed to Iran's state-run Press TV, being released at a checkpoint near Jenin in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Hamed's lawyer Khaled Mahajneh told AFP that an Israeli military court released her on bail of 8,000 shekels — about $2,600 — and on condition she comply with future summons for questioning.
Mahajneh said Hamed spent "two weeks of detention under difficult conditions at Damon prison" in the northern Israeli city of Haifa.
The Israeli military arrested Hamed on Sept. 15 at a checkpoint near Bethlehem as she was returning from a reporting assignment for Turkish broadcaster TRT, according to her family and a journalist who was accompanying her at the time.
Press TV, which is owned by the Iranian state, reported on her arrest and release and described her as its West Bank correspondent.
Colleagues said Hamed, who holds U.S. citizenship, had stopped working with Press TV about a month earlier and had become a freelance journalist.
The Israeli government considers Press TV a propaganda arm of Iran's government.
Israel is currently holding 36 journalists in its prisons, according to the Palestinian Prisoners' Club, an NGO working for prisoners' rights.
Rising oil prices push U.S. stock values down as Trump rejects Iran's latest offer
Rising oil prices are knocking the U.S. stock market further from its record high on Monday, while building pressure even higher within the U.S. bond market.
The S&P 500 fell 0.8% and gave back most of its gains from last week, which had brought it to the brink of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 372 points, or 0.7%, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1% lower.
Most of the U.S. stock market sank under the weight of a 2.8% rise for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude oil to $100.19 per barrel. That overshadowed a gain for Wall Street's most influential stock, Nvidia, after it announced a historic funneling of cash to its investors through a buyback of its shares.
Oil prices have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide. The latest turns came after President Donald Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
"I'd like to make a deal, too," Mr. Trump said Saturday. "But that deal would not be acceptable."
Brent climbed above $101 per barrel Monday morning, before the U.S. stock market opened for trading, but it pared its gains as U.S. officials said mediators were still working with Iran and the United States on a deal to end the fighting and open the strait.
For all its ups and downs, a barrel of Brent remains much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. That has helped worsen inflation, and the average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is up to nearly $4.48 from $3.13 a year ago, according to AAA.
Iranian foreign minister to meet mediators in New York over potential renewal of talks with U.S.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is scheduled to meet mediators in New York on Monday morning to discuss the latest proposals and efforts to revive negotiations with the United States, Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency reported.
According to ISNA, Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz as part of a deal to end the war, in exchange for the release of Iranian funds and assets that Tehran says have been unlawfully blocked.
The proposal was conveyed to the U.S. through mediators in New York. Although President Trump rejected the offer over the weekend, Iranian officials say indirect contacts and mediation efforts continue.
Araghchi said Iran is awaiting a response via the mediators before deciding its next steps. He reiterated that any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz would depend on Iran's conditions being met, saying Tehran would not back down from its conditions.
"We are waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators and we will make a decision based on that," ISNA quoted Araghchi as saying.
No representatives from the U.S. side will be attending Monday's meeting, the report said.

U.K. police release on bail 5 men arrested near air base used by U.S. for Iran strikes
British counter terror police released on bail five British men arrested over the weekend near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. forces to launch strikes on Iran.
Metropolitan Police Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said the men were being released following "extensive interviews," adding that the investigation was not over and they remained "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others."
Referring to reports that British authorities were investigating a possible link to Iran, he said: "I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident."
"At this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation … be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Iran said Monday that it "categorically denies" any involvement in the incident.
Iran "categorically rejects" involvement in suspected terror plot on military base hosting U.S. aircraft
Iran "categorically rejects" claims that it was involved in a suspected terror plot on a British military base hosting U.S. aircraft, its embassy in London said Monday.
British counterterrorism police were leading an investigation Monday after five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act in an English village near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. bombers.
The Associated Press reported that British authorities are investigating the possibility of a link between Iran and the arrests near RAF Fairford, but that as of Monday there had been no conclusions reached about whether the apparent plot against the base could have been state-backed.
This year, groups with purported links to Iran have carried out several attacks on U.K. soil, primarily targeting the Jewish community in north London.
U.S. and Iran expected to continue talking this week through mediators, official tells Reuters
The U.S. and Iran are expected to have separate talks with mediators on Monday or Tuesday, an official with knowledge of the negotiations told the Reuters news agency.
With Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the U.S., as well as Qatari mediators, the talks are set to focus on an updated version of the seven-day proposal Iran gave to U.S. counterparts last week during the United Nations General Assembly, the official told Reuters.
President Trump said Sunday that he expected talks with Iran to resume in the coming days, a day after he rejected a new proposal put forward by Tehran last week for a seven-day ceasefire and phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Saudi Arabia's strategic East-West Crude Oil Pipeline operational again, Bloomberg says
Saudi Arabia has resumed exporting oil using its crucial East-West Crude Oil Pipeline after drone strikes earlier this month forced it shut, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter quoted by Bloomberg.
Saudi Arabia had been using the pipeline to transport oil from its eastern production hubs to its Red Sea ports for export — a vital alternative route as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has remained severely disrupted by the U.S.-Iran war.
The pipeline was shut down earlier this month after a series of drone attacks that Saudi authorities blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
The state-run energy giant Saudi Aramco, which operates the kingdom's oil infrastructure, tested the pipeline last week and has now resumed overseas shipments via the Red Sea route, a source familiar with the operation told Bloomberg.
Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have vowed to impose a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports and against Saudi ships, and they have targeted several vessels in the region.
Iran lodges complaint with U.N. over U.S. sanctions on its aviation industry
Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over U.S. sanctions against its aviation sector, which have forced the cancellation of many flights across the region, state media reported Monday.
The U.S. imposed restrictions this month on the entire Iranian aviation industry and vowed to take a hard line against any companies or countries that continue to assist it.
As the sanctions took effect last Wednesday, some major airlines were forced to cancel international flights as several nations in the region implemented bans.
"To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)," said civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.

Ayatollah Khamenei says U.S. forces will soon be pushed back
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.
In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah — who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began — said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."
He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.
U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.
The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.
Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.
The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.
Value of Iran's currency falls to all-time low against the dollar
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.
Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.
Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center.
Iran's U.N. delegation has no plans to negotiate directly with the U.S.
Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side ... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Since the outbreak of the war in February, negotiations between Tehran and Washington have occurred largely through mediators.
CBS/AFP
British police investigating possible Iranian links to suspected terrorist plot against U.K. air base used by U.S.
U.K. police said five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran were being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
RAF Fairford, a U.K. Royal Air Force base about 85 miles west of London in rural Gloucestershire, has been used by American bombers to conduct strikes against Iranian missile sites. The British government, under an agreement made under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, granted the U.S. permission to use Farford and other key U.K. bases provided it was only for strikes defined as defensive in nature.
Authorities are investigating a link between the arrests in Fairford and Iran as one possibility. Iranian authorities have declared all bases used to attack Iranian territory as legitimate targets.
President Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests.
"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."
Iran says it is ready for either diplomacy, or a return to fighting as war reaches 7-month mark
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.
"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."
"At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.
President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.
Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.
Trump expects talks with Iran to resume this week
President Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after he rejected a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to the U.S. to reopen the Strait of Hormuz over seven days, but Mr. Trump asserted that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly."
"They overplayed their hand," Mr. Trump told Axios.
The president said resuming strikes on Iran was not off the table, adding: "I am always thinking about it."

Sen. Kennedy says Iran's plan was "not a serious offer"
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said Iran's proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks was "not a serious offer."
"The president's not Bambi's baby brother. He turned it down," Kennedy said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"We need to continue doing what we're doing — the sanctions, the blockade," said Kennedy.
"Now there's just one problem: The strait is at least partially closed, and it's affected the price of oil. And oil's in everything, including gasoline, and it's painful as hell," he said, adding: "We've got to either figure out a way to settle this thing, to get the strait open, or to escalate."
Kennedy said he would not support sending U.S. ground troops into Iran, however.

What is known about arrests at US airbase in Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
