18:12:34 KST

Suspected plot to attack UK's Fairford airbase, used by US: What do we know?
LONDON, Sept 28 - British police said on Monday they were investigating whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved in an apparent plot to attack an airbase used by the United States, but said five men they had arrested would be released on bail.
Below is what is known so far about the incident at RAF Fairford:
WHAT HAPPENED AT FAIRFORD?
Police were called to the airbase, 90 miles (145 km) west of London, early on Sunday morning by a local farmer who said she had seen three large white vans parked near the base and a group of "hooded and masked men" running into a field nearby.
Armed officers from the local force, Gloucestershire Police, responded and arrested five men in the Whelford area, about a mile from the base.
The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of offences under the explosives act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act after counter-terrorism police took over the investigation.
About 85 households were evacuated from properties near where the three vehicles were found and a 400-metre cordon was put in place around them.
WHY WERE THE MEN RELEASED?
The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said on Monday afternoon the men were being released after "extensive interviews and inquiries" and that they remained under investigation.
"They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others," he said.
He later said the incident was being considered from all angles, including whether offences had been committed "by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT THE MEN WHO WERE ARRESTED?
The five men detained were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 who lived in London, police said.
An image on social media purported to show some of the suspects, seated shirtless with hands behind their backs, after their arrest. Reuters was unable to independently locate and verify the source of the photograph.
WHY WOULD FAIRFORD BE A TARGET?
Fairford, which opened in 1944 and was used by allied troops for the D-Day invasion of Normandy, has this year been used by US forces for strikes on Iran.
It is one of the US Air Force's only European airfields suitable for heavy bombers, and played a key role in both the first Gulf War in 1991 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect Fairford after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. The Guards said any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
Over the last six weeks there has been increased surveillance in the area after a specific threat from the Iranians, according to a local councillor.
WHAT HAVE PEOPLE SAID SO FAR ABOUT THE INCIDENT?
The farmer, who has not been named, told British media she saw eight to 10 men running from the vans with their faces covered and that they got within about 100 metres of the perimeter fence of the airbase.
"I just can't process how that base was on such high alert, and that the men were even there," she said, adding that a blockade had focused only on the main entrance.
"I'm really glad they ran away."
British Defence Minister Wes Streeting told BBC TV he was grateful to the witness but that she only had a "partial picture" of what had happened after she said she was "staggered" it had been left to a member of the public to report them despite the heightened threat.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday the group had been under investigation as part of a long-running investigation. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding that the suspects intended "big damage" to the base.
Iran's embassy in London said in a statement on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" about Tehran's possible involvement in the incident. REUTERS

The Next Evolution of AI Is Learning From Your Dodgy Gaming Skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

With the twirl of a thumbstick, squeeze of a trigger, and press of a few buttons, even an unskilled player can dance their way through a 3D video game environment. A British startup is wagering that straightforward sequences like these contain a trove of information that can be used to train new artificial intelligence models.
There is a growing belief in corners of the AI industry that large language models will ultimately be limited by their inability to navigate the physical world. Trained only on words, LLMs are perhaps ill-equipped to pilot autonomous vehicles, steer robotic arms, or perform any other action that requires finesse and precision. To remedy that shortcoming, a crop of celebrated researchers including Fei-Fei Li and Yann LeCun are focusing their efforts on a different class of AI: world models.
To become fluent in real-world physics, world models need to be trained on a combination of visual and action data. Before it can deftly maneuver a robotic arm, a model might need to be trained on video footage of the factory floor, coupled with information about how firmly an object should be gripped, with what torque it’s manipulated, and so on. But unlike LLMs, trained on oceans of text, there is no similar corpus of material available to world model labs.
“For world models, you need cause and consequence,” says Xiatian Zhu, an associate professor specializing in AI at the University of Surrey. “On the internet, we have very little of this type of data.”
Worldmodeldata, a British startup advised by LeCun, is aiming to solve that problem by packaging controller inputs and other data collected by video game studios—an exhaust product available in massive quantities—into training datasets for world models. Some companies, like General Intuition and Niantic, are already collecting video game data from their own platforms to build models. But Worldmodeldata pitches itself as a broker that curates and organizes data, saving labs from striking individual agreements with tons of game studios.
“There are millions of great games, and they are more and more similar to the real world,” Rhea Loucas, CEO of Worldmodeldata, tells WIRED. “Why don’t we take the vast, abundant, diverse experiences from video games, and teach AI?”
Though the hypothesis is yet to be fully tested, researchers are broadly working under the assumption that the performance of world models will improve in line with the size of their training datasets, in a similar way to LLMs. That means the shortage of suitable training data is one of the largest bottlenecks to progress.
Some labs have tried to manually generate their own data by attaching sensors to humans and robots in testing environments. But that approach yields only a small amount of data, and it doesn’t account for the fringe scenarios a model might encounter in the wild.
“You can pay people to demonstrate pick-and-place tasks. But repetition alone won’t capture the disorder of the world you’re asking a machine to operate in,” says Nicole Fraenkel, a partner at VC firm Khosla Ventures, which has invested in General Intuition.
Worldmodeldata’s theory is that data collected from video game environments—visual representations of a 3D space paired with actions taken by the player—is both available in the necessary quantities and sufficiently varied to capture all-important corner cases.
“The corner cases are the ones to actually get right,” says Fraenkel. “The cost of error with a car, plane, drone, factory forklift, or autonomous quadruped is very high.”
Worldmodeldata says it has licensed almost 1 million hours' worth of data from studios behind various popular video games, though Loucas declined to name them. In the future, the startup is aiming to create avenues for individual players to be compensated, too.
Loucas believes that video game data will ultimately make up the majority of the training material for world models, which will later be optimized using data specific to a given real-world environment or task. “This could well lead to the GPT moment for world models—making them really useful,” Loucas claims.
Not everybody shares the same optimism about video game data, though. Nvidia, which publishes a family of world models optimized to run on its chips, prefers to use a custom engine it devised specifically to replicate real-world physics as the backbone for its AI.
Ming-Yu Liu, who leads world model development at Nvidia, says that models trained on video game inputs are unlikely to fare well with tasks that require fine-grained motor control, like the careful manipulation of objects. That’s because video game physics is often eccentric, and developers take shortcuts to create the illusion of realism—a character dips a hand to collect an apple from the table—without coding in the details: the pressure applied by each finger to prevent the apple slipping from their grasp.
“I would be more conservative on using video game data for manipulation,” Liu says. “The physics for manipulation is much more involved.” Training on video game data is better reserved, he says, for world models meant for generating hyperrealistic video or 3D environments.
Zhu, the academic from the University of Surrey, has similar concerns. “Video games are, in essence, simulators. They do have some degree of physical grounding,” he says. “But they are very coarse, approximate.”
But until world models reach their ChatGPT moment, all kinds of ideas for getting them there remain on the table. “There are many paths to the promised land,” says Fraenkel. “The truth is, the jury is still out on which one is going to work best.”

====================================================================================================

Nvidia’s Answer to Rogue Agents Is an Open-Source AI Security System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Amidst ongoing reports of AI agents wreaking havoc on online infrastructure, chipmaker Nvidia is rallying tech companies to use its new open-source tool for AI security.
Over the last few months, frontier AI labs have disclosed multiple incidents in which AI agents have hacked into other companies or, in more recent examples, probed official US and Australian government websites. While Nvidia has already taken a leading role in rallying the AI industry around open source security, it’s now introducing one new software security platform and making an agentic AI sandbox more broadly available.
OpenShell, one of the Nvidia’s recently launched security sandboxes for AI agents, is now entering general release for all users. OpenShell was first announced at Nvidia’s annual GTC Conference in March; it’s a framework for containing agents as they carry out tasks and isolating their activity in the operating system kernel, the foundational program that has access to virtually all parts of a computer system in order to coordinate hardware and software.
Nvidia’s launch materials indicate that it has AI safety and security collaborations with dozens of other tech companies, including Anthropic, Cisco, CoreWeave, CrowdStrike, Dell Technologies, Hugging Face, JPMorganChase, Mistral, Microsoft, and Palantir. Nvidia says SpaceXAI is using the Open Agent Safety Platform for its Cursor agents and Grok models. The company also says Anthropic and Nvidia are “building security into Claude Managed Agents.” Salesforce, Scale AI, and SAP are all confirmed to be integrating OpenShell to some degree. However, it is unclear whether OpenShell has been adopted by Nvidia’s full list of partners, or whether Nvidia is gesturing broadly.
One notable name is missing entirely from Nvidia’s list: OpenAI. Both companies indicated that OpenAI is a part of Nvidia’s OpenShell effort, though both declined to comment directly on why the AI lab was excluded from the announcement.
Security engineers and AI safety experts have considered the need to isolate and monitor agentic AI since well before the recent revelations of rogue agent hacking. Nvidia’s own OpenShell announcement in March noted that the framework would add “privacy and security controls to make self-evolving, autonomous AI agents, or claws, more trustworthy, scalable and accessible,” months before OpenAI disclosed that its AI agents had hacked the open source AI company Hugging Face. (Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face earlier this month for $12.9 billion.)
The chip giant has also developed a new software platform called Sentry, an isolated security domain for chips that’s supposed to continuously monitor long-running AI agents. While Sentry is technically a software tool, it’s meant to be implemented on Bluefield, Nvidia’s line of programmable data processing units (DPUs). The idea is that in addition to the restrictions imposed by OpenShell, Sentry can act as a separate, independent mechanism that can “quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their boundaries.”
Sentry is another way for Nvidia customers and open-source users to actually implement security policies through OpenShell, says Justin Boitano, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of enterprise computing. While traditional sandboxes are built for “application-level isolation,” people now want to run fleets of agents, which demands a “collective policy across all of those agents,” he says.
“Agents are very creative at finding ways to achieve the goals that they’re given,” Boitano says. “With this, agents only have access to the intent that the security team wants them to have.”
Boitano adds that Nvidia is working with both Arm and Intel to create a version of Sentry that works on the x86 chip architecture. “Once it runs on those instruction-set architectures, it can run on any architecture,” he says.
Nvidia is positioning all of this as part of a new open-source framework called the Open Agent Safety Platform, which now encompasses OpenShell and Sentry as well.
In July Nvidia launched an industry-wide AI safety coalition that now comprises more than 120 companies. The coalition’s stated goal was to reduce AI risks, particularly through a program called the Shared AI Findings Exchange (SAFE). Last month, Boitano said that SAFE was designed to be “governed independently, with no single company or industry segment controlling its findings.”
But one company keeps appearing at the center of these industry-wide, open-source AI initiatives, and that company is Nvidia. The world’s most valuable company, on which most of the tech industry depends on for the most performant chips, appears to be positioning itself to deepen its influence and set standards at varying levels of the AI technology stack, from silicon to security software.
Though efforts to contain and control agents are already in progress throughout the industry, recent rogue agent behavior suggests a need to raise awareness about long-standing, core security practices—even, apparently, within trillion-dollar frontier labs. Some experts say that this also gets to the heart of the question about what it really means for an autonomous piece of software to “go rogue.”
“Anything that makes it easy for companies to deploy agents in a way that has more guardrails and more safety should be applauded,” says longtime security engineer and researcher Niels Provos, speaking generally about tools geared toward containing and monitoring agents. Provos himself launched an open source framework in February focused on these issues. “If nothing else, these types of tools help to dispel the myth that agents can’t be controlled.”

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Japan claimed both BMX racing gold medals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Monday, with Sae Hatakeyama winning the women's final and Asuma Nakai retaining his men's title.
China's Lin Haochao edged Indonesia's Fasya Ahsana Rifki by 0.033 seconds to secure men's bronze.
Racing took place in light rain at the Nagoya Velodrome BMX Race Course. Each category featured three preliminary runs, with the top four riders from each heat advancing to an eight-rider final decided over a single race.
Liao finished second in all three of her preliminary runs, while teammate Wang Mengyao won the first two runs in her heat. In the women's final, Hatakeyama crossed the line in 33.401 seconds, with Liao second in 34.500 and Indonesia's Jasmine Azzahra Setyobudi third in 34.932. Wang was relegated to eighth in the official results.
Competing at her first Asian Games, Liao said nerves had affected her since the previous evening and through the preliminaries. In the final, she concentrated on her start, acceleration and the sections ahead.
"I performed above my usual level today," she said, also praising Wang for assisting her through the turns.
The Chinese team had trained in Linyi, Shandong Province, for more than a month but had only three one-hour sessions on the Nagoya course. The rain added another challenge, as Liao had never raced in wet conditions before.
"I'm quite satisfied," Liao said of her silver medal, adding that she hoped the team could build on this performance at next year's Asian championships.
In the men's final, Nakai, the Hangzhou 2022 champion, finished in 30.103 seconds. Fellow Japanese rider Hyoga Kiuchi took silver in 30.583. Lin crossed the line in 32.947, just ahead of Indonesia's Fasya Ahsana Rifki in 32.980. China's Chen Yucheng placed fifth in 33.466.
"I just wanted to give everything and sprint for the line," said Lin, who finished fourth at the previous Asian Games.
Peng Haibo, deputy secretary-general of the Chinese Cycling Association, said the team was satisfied with its performance. China had set out to challenge for women's gold and reach the men's final, and came away with medals in both events.
Peng described the Games as an opportunity to test the team's preparation in a major competition and said riders and coaches would apply the lessons learned as they continue training with an eye on Olympic qualification and the Los Angeles 2028 Games.
BMX racing made its Olympic debut at Beijing 2008 and was introduced to the Asian Games program at Guangzhou 2010. ■

Raccoons cause growing trouble in Japan's rural, urban areas
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:47:52 CST
17:47:52 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Damage from raccoons is mounting across Japan as the invasive species expands its habitat from rural areas into cities, Kyodo News reported Monday.
Japanese official data showed that nationwide agricultural crop losses caused by raccoons reached 693 million yen (around 4.4 million U.S. dollars) in fiscal 2024, more than double the amount recorded a decade earlier.
In particular, raccoon damage has become increasingly noticeable in urban areas in recent years. In the western city of Osaka, for example, complaints from residents about raccoons have steadily grown, from 161 in fiscal 2023 to 332 in fiscal 2024 and 397 in fiscal 2025, the report said.
Among the complaints were reports of goldfish being eaten from garden ponds and the animals breaking into attics.
Raccoons also ranked first among wildlife species causing agricultural damage in Osaka Prefecture, accounting for over 40 percent of the total, with crop losses of 84.06 million yen in fiscal 2024, twice the amount recorded the previous year.
Osaka prefectural authorities believe the animals are settling in residential areas in search of food and have urged residents not to approach or feed them.
More places where raccoons can breed, such as vacant houses, may have also helped expand their habitat, the report said, citing an official from the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries.
Hokkaido in the north is facing a similar problem, with raccoons spreading to nearly the entire prefecture by the end of January this year.
Local officials said raccoon numbers are increasing so quickly that it has become an endless battle.
Nevertheless, experts said continued efforts, such as setting traps, are needed to reduce the animal's population and limit the damage they cause. ■

Feature: Shanghai brings Chinese rhythms to Barcelona's La Merce
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:47:22 CST
17:47:22 KST

BARCELONA, Spain, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Music flowed into squares, dancers and street performers filled public spaces, and fireworks lit up Barcelona's waterfront as the city celebrated La Merce, one of its most important annual festivals, from Sept. 23 to 27.
This year, the familiar festival rhythm carried a distinctive Chinese note. As 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of the sister-city relationship between Shanghai and Barcelona, Shanghai became the first Asian city to serve as La Merce's guest city. More than 100 artists delivered 14 performances spanning acrobatics, dance, jazz, and traditional Chinese music.
The Fengxian rolling lantern performance was among the opening-night highlights. After traditional Catalan giant figures performed at Sant Jaume Square on Sept. 23, artists from Shanghai's Fengxian District took the stage with large golden lanterns, lifting and rolling them through a series of demanding moves. Near the end, sparks burst from the lanterns, echoing an earlier traditional Catalan dragon that sprayed sparks into the night and drawing cheers from thousands of spectators.
Esteve Carames, director of cultural programs at the Barcelona Institute of Culture, said the Fengxian rolling lanterns were chosen for the opening ceremony because of their distinctive regional character and connection with coastal life.
"Barcelona is also a coastal city," he told Xinhua. "We blended Barcelona's distinctive traditions with those of Shanghai."
Similar cross-cultural touches ran through Shanghai's guest-city program.
Later that evening, at Doctor Pla i Armengol Gardens, the Shanghai Conservatory of Music Jazz Ensemble incorporated the suona, a traditional Chinese wind instrument, into contemporary jazz arrangements. Its bright, piercing sound mingled with trumpet and percussion as audience members danced along.
Two nights later at Barcelona's Cathedral Square, the Shanghai Chinese Orchestra presented the AI-composed concert "Zero/One: Colors of China," featuring Shanghai-style traditional music as well as an adaptation of the Spanish flamenco work "Gitana Hechicera."
"One of the most attractive things about Shanghai is the way tradition is combined with highly innovative projects, and that is very similar to Barcelona's understanding of culture," Carames said.
That cultural dialogue was also visible onstage.
Castells, or human towers, are among Catalonia's best-known folk traditions, with participants climbing onto one another's shoulders to build towers several levels high.
Echoing that tradition, the Fengxian performers added a "stacked rolling lantern" sequence, lifting the lanterns layer by layer.
Beyond the stage, the program invited local residents to take part.
At Estacio del Nord Park, a Chinese games corner organized by the Confucius Institute Foundation of Barcelona drew more than 6,000 participants. Visitors learned Chinese numbers and simple greetings through games and joined handicraft activities.
Wang Jinwei, co-director of the Confucius Institute Foundation of Barcelona, said such activities had no clear boundary between performers and spectators, allowing children and parents to experience Chinese culture through play.
After a performance by the Shanghai Dance School in the same park, one Barcelona resident asked a Xinhua reporter whether there would be another show. "I want to come back during the holiday and bring my family with me," he said.
The Chinese presence also took to the sky.
On Sept. 24, 750 drones rose into the night sky above the Barceloneta waterfront to mark the 25th anniversary of the sister-city relationship. The drones formed images including the Monkey King and the Oriental Pearl Tower alongside familiar Barcelona landmarks such as the Sagrada Familia.
Tens of thousands of residents and tourists gathered along the waterfront, cheering as new images took shape in the sky.
Videos of the drone show later spread across Chinese social media. On Xiaohongshu, a video captioned "Seeing Shanghai's skyline in Barcelona" drew thousands of likes and comments. One Shanghai user wrote: "Wishing my family in Barcelona good health and all the best." The video was posted on the Mid-Autumn Festival, a traditional occasion for family reunions in China.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni said at the opening ceremony that the 25-year relationship between Barcelona and Shanghai is not only a link between municipal governments, but also a human bond built day by day by Barcelona's Chinese community.
Xavier Marce, Barcelona city councilor for culture and creative industries, said the events had opened a door to further exchanges.
"This is only the beginning," he said. "We are very confident that, taking this event in Barcelona as a starting point, there will be more exchanges and cooperation between Barcelona and Shanghai in the coming years." ■

Daphne Cousins: Musicality in Light
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:38:55 UTC
17:38:55 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
People find abstract art difficult. There seems to be nothing to look at. There’s no recognisable subject to anchor the gaze and set out a thought or emotion. Paintings built from shape and colour can feel arbitrary, as if made up as the artist went along.
But consider another abstract artform you’re already very familiar with, that you likely enjoy every day: music.
The abstract paintings of Daphne Cousins (1946–2025) offer a direct way past the difficulties that may prevent you from understanding — less still enjoying — abstract painting. She saw music in her mind, and painted what she saw.
Cousins was synaesthetic — a rare condition in which two or more sensory pathways are bridged. To Cousins, sound and vision were conjoined. Different types of music conjured different kinds of visions in the minds eye.
My hope in this article is that we come to grasp not only a basic taste for abstraction, but also an appreciation that abstract art can offer a deeply personal response to an artist’s experiences that gives rise to a shared pleasure that is both sensual and reflective.
Brazilian Rhythm
Let’s start simply. We’ll take a basic two-tone example of what we’re about to explore.
Take a look at the picture above. To a casual glance, this image looks severe, perhaps austere: straight-edged, pristine black shapes against stark white.
There’s no loose gesture or indulgence, not so much as a fleck out of place. It’s hard to believe it was painted. But sit a moment in the presence of this image and they begin to move.
The forms pulse in relation, in weight, measure, and repetition. They slide and lean in various cadences. This is an abstraction that’s ostensibly “geometric” and still, but movement is insistent in the form.
You realise this here is the parsimony of rhythm in black and white. Music is expressed as musicality in shape and colour, the forms echo notation but aren’t passive, they animate themselves.
Our eyes perceive a strident rhythm, the blocks of black assemble like punctuation, and silent pulses of white space assert themselves as fully and insistently.
These images resist resolution into pattern — “the grid”, as an ordering substrate, is ever-present in the uniform relations of shape and colour, but the forms are rendered as a unity on the surface. There is no implied continuity beyond the picture’s edge.
This is one of two stark images are called “Brazilian Rhythm 1 and 2”. It’s confounding — of all kinds of music, who’d be daring enough to render such a thing into black and white? The musical creole of far-flung cultures brought together, in the grain of maracas, the stride of piano, the dancing guitar?
You could gather guesses about the source of these structures — from syncopated samba to the languid legato of bossa nova. Regardless, there’s a quiet thrill in the audacity of the stark black and white. It’s an exercise, of some sort, in reduction.
I had the pleasure of researching Cousins’ body of work for a new exhibition. You can see Cousins’ paintings at Experiencing Together — A retrospective, 29th September — 4th October 2026 at the Peggy Jay Gallery, Burgh House in Hampstead, London. Visit daphnecousins.com for more info.
Cousins’ work evolved early on as an investigation into her subjective experience of sound. The Brazilian rhythms, in her words, were devised to “optically simulate the energy and contrapuntal vitality of the sound.”
These were minor works — studies in gouache — that epitomised a grand ambition: to transmute a sensation that was personal in essence to a public medium.
Early in her career, the sensation of this synthesis of sound and colour was put to paper and canvas systematically — a colour was intuitively assigned to each tone on the scale.
Such a practice deepened Cousins’ appreciation for music, particularly classical music — Bach and Bartók were twin passions.
Concerts and listening sessions transported her into a state of awe and wonder, no doubt arising from the eccentric synthesis of colour, tone, shape, contrast, timbre and rhythm happening within.
To capture such a thing, if possible, became a lifelong creative preoccupation.
Colourscape, Silence and Sound
In works dating from the late 1960s to early 1970s, Cousins gave life to synaesthetic sensation at scale, producing spectral apparitions that spread across the surfaces of paper and canvas — loose grids of tonal blocks wavering against expanses of black.
Like the music itself, there is a continuity of tones and the measured silences between them.
In art appreciation and analysis, there’s a time-honoured distinction between “figure” — the things our attention is drawn to; and “ground” — the backdrop against which figures play out some kind of drama.
It’s hard to describe these as forms — as if they are figures against a ground. We ought to think — or see, rather — in terms of “colourscape”. These span the paintings horizontally from edge to edge, wavering vertically in a way that resembles the oscillations of sound waves.
In the 1970s we see more emphasis on composition, on reconciling independent forms, and a more refined and muted palette of colours.
One composition is anchored in 45-degree diagonals of grey bands fringed with tonally equivalent hues of blue and red that fold over themselves. Among these bands, vertical columns of horizontal stripes in varying tones convey subtle rhythms.
The bands’ folds and their interplay with the vertical columns hold a tension between flatness and the illusion of three dimensions. Like the earlier works, there is movement, but the movement is steady with an absence of momentum.
The painting is a knot of judgements — edges pause, planes overlap, lines intersect, and colours modulate form. Coherence is achieved not by fusion but by coexistence, much as two melodies coexist within a single passage of music.
The banding and stripe motif continued to be explored throughout the 1970s and 1980s, but in progressively wider colour ranges of lush and bright varieties. In one series, tone seems to be explored systematically through the striped-column or band motif; in others, rhythm animates shape.
Some works are saturated edge-to-edge with rhythm and colour, such as the pastel rainbow series; others opt for large colour fields rendered either by vigorous gesture or with a machine-like precision.
The “Auditory Space-Field”
The works of the 1990s are more pared back. Diagonal and horizontal lines are the principal motifs, and emerging more clearly here is what Cousins called “the auditory space-field” — an enveloping ground into which the pulses of rhythm pass in lines. The presentation is so crisp in these works it resembles print. It brings to mind Cousins’ transitional statement:
“I am now working with sound concepts, (moving away from the immediate stimulus) dealing with specific qualities and situations inherent in sound […] One has become concerned with defining the interaction between sound and mind in visual terms.”
The effect is for those who are not synaesthetic to re-present the beauty of music as concrete form. It’s impossible to be literal about this. In her Master’s thesis, Cousins wrote, “the aim is not to replicate synaesthetic experience but to explore intense creative ideas implicated by it.”
Cousins considered developing a system of representing music. In such a system, what would the work of different composers look like? How would duration in time be expressed? How and where does music exist when we hear it? How is loudness, pitch, rhythm and timbre expressed?
To even come close to answering these questions, Cousins had to generate the visual equivalent of the “auditory space-field” — a topology, if that’s even possible, where sound/forms structure themselves.
Her experiments in translating bars of the works of Bach, Mozart, Britten, and Bartók into a uniform 12-colour scale and duration-to-length ratio were interesting but unsatisfactory. It was, in her words, a “limiting paradigm […] bound by the strictures of another’s creativity.”
In her postgraduate research, Cousins struggled with how exactly to render music in space. She soon resolved the problem by inverting the auditory space-field. So, instead of rendering the sound within a void, the void was situated in the inner area of the painting, and the sound/colour was rendered on the outer edges in block-like forms.
When set against a white ground, the interplay of colour flowing out from a void into the whiteness became a more satisfactory expression of music in light and colour.
The paintings grew wider — up to eleven feet in fact — as they traced time in space from left to right. The colours bled around the edges of the canvases, giving the paintings more of an object-like appearance, bringing the musicality of colour into the space of the room.
We can see two longstanding threads through Cousins’ career — the experimental ambition to systematise the “simulation” of music in visual form, and the continual investigations into form and shape inflected by the bridging of auditory and visual senses.
In every case, forms are divested of any semblance of nature. But that’s not to say they are unnatural: each image summons a sense, at least, of the deepest, most fundamental structures of thought ensconced in the mind. These images are echoes of the inner sanctum of subjective experience — to behold them is to feel the connection that Cousins sought.
You can see Cousins’ work at a new exhibtion, Experiencing Together — A retrospective, 29th September — 4th October 2026 at the Peggy Jay Gallery, Burgh House in Hampstead, London. Visit daphnecousins.com for more info.

Taiwan envoy says US policy unchanged after Trump-Xi summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:37:17 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Representative to the US Alexander Yui Tah-ray (俞大㵢) said Sunday that he believes US policy toward Taiwan remains unchanged following US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Yui made the comments during an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” where he discussed the Trump-Xi summit, Taiwan-US relations, and competing interpretations of World War II history.
Asked about Trump’s comments that Taiwan came up during his meeting with Xi but was not a major topic, Yui said Taiwan was mentioned but did not appear in the official statements issued by either side following the meeting. Yui noted that Taiwan did not appear in either side’s statements about the summit’s results, according to the show's transcript.
Yui acknowledged that the Chinese side described Taiwan as a “foundational” issue but said Washington did not endorse Beijing’s position. He pointed to a meeting before Xi’s visit between US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of Japan and South Korea on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Yui said the three countries reaffirmed their support for peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and opposed coercion, while also supporting Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations. He said there had been no change in the US position toward Taiwan.
Yui was also asked about Trump’s comments in May that he wanted to speak with President Lai Ching-te (賴清德). He did not confirm that a call between Trump and Lai had taken place, saying instead that communication between Taiwan and the US remained “open,” “regular,” and “very, very close” at different levels.
The interview also turned to historical references made by Trump and Xi during Xi’s visit to Washington. Yui said Trump had highlighted the role of the US Flying Tigers, while Xi had referred to the Chinese Communist Party's role in fighting Japan during World War II.
“That’s not correct,” Yui said, displaying historical material concerning the Flying Tigers. He also argued that the People's Republic of China was not established until 1949 and therefore could not have been the government fighting alongside the US during the war.
Yui contrasted that history with the Korean War, in which forces of the newly established People's Republic of China fought US-led United Nations forces after Chinese troops entered the conflict in 1950. He said the historical record should be viewed in its proper context when discussing current US-China relations and Taiwan.
Yui also rejected the suggestion that Taiwan and US allies such as Japan were responsible for creating tensions in the region. He said Taiwan wanted peace and stability and argued that Beijing was responsible for creating much of the current tension.
The CBS interview came days after Trump and Xi met at the White House. Trump said afterward that Taiwan had been discussed but that the two leaders did not spend much time talking about it. Yui's comments followed similar statements from Taiwan officials that they had received assurances that US policy toward Taiwan had not changed after the summit.

Resetting the body clock could help the brain recover after stroke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:35:12 UTC
17:35:12 KST

Resetting the body clock could help the brain recover after stroke
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Rochester Medical Center
- Summary:
- Strengthening the body’s natural daily rhythms helped mice recover after stroke by improving the brain’s waste-clearing system and reducing lingering inflammation. The approach worked even when treatment began three days after the stroke, suggesting circadian-based therapies could eventually offer a new way to support long-term recovery.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Rochester Medicine have found that strengthening the body's natural daily rhythms to improve sleep may help the brain recover after a stroke. The work points to a possible new way to support brain waste clearance and improve recovery well after the initial injury.
Published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, the study showed that interventions designed to reinforce circadian rhythms improved recovery in mouse models of stroke. These improvements were accompanied by stronger activity in the glymphatic system, the brain's waste-clearing network, along with lower levels of inflammatory molecules that can persist after a stroke.
How the Brain Clears Waste
The findings build on more than a decade of research led by URochester Medicine neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard, MD, DMSc. Her laboratory discovered the glymphatic system in 2012.
This system moves cerebrospinal fluid through the brain, helping remove waste products and other debris. Later studies found that glymphatic activity is especially strong during sleep and plays an important role in maintaining brain health.
Neuroscientist Lauren Hablitz, PhD, later helped show that glymphatic activity is influenced not only by sleep, but also by circadian rhythms, the body's internal 24-hour clock. In a landmark 2020 study, Hablitz, Nedergaard, and colleagues demonstrated that glymphatic function follows daily cycles even independently of sleep, establishing a direct link between circadian biology and the brain's waste-clearing system.
Stroke May Disrupt the Brain's Timing
"The discussion of stroke recovery really starts with the idea that stroke is not just a vascular event, but also a disorder of timing," said Hablitz, lead author of the new study.
Scientists have long known that strokes tend to follow distinct time-of-day patterns. They occur more often during the morning and are frequently more severe near the end of the sleep period.
After a stroke, many patients also develop disrupted sleep-wake cycles. Those disturbances have been linked with worse recovery, depression, and reduced quality of life.
"That led us to ask a simple question," said Hablitz. "If timing is broken after a stroke, can we improve recovery by reinforcing the biological clock?"
When the Brain's Cleanup System Slows Down
In a healthy brain, the glymphatic system carries cerebrospinal fluid along blood vessels and through brain tissue. This process delivers nutrients while helping remove waste products and inflammatory signals.
Earlier research has shown that glymphatic function becomes impaired after stroke. That disruption may reduce the brain's ability to clear harmful molecules that accumulate during recovery.
Stroke research has traditionally focused on separating beneficial inflammation from harmful inflammation and finding ways to suppress the damaging forms. Hablitz and her colleagues suggest that another part of the problem may be that the brain is no longer clearing inflammatory signals effectively.
"We think part of the problem may be a failure of cleaning," she said. "If the system responsible for clearing signaling molecules isn't working properly, everything builds up."
Under this model, stroke damages both brain tissue and the pathways responsible for removing inflammatory signals. As those molecules accumulate, they may contribute to continued damage and slower recovery.
Resetting the Body Clock
To test whether stronger circadian rhythms could improve recovery, the researchers examined several interventions known to affect the body's internal clock. These included timed light exposure, melatonin, a clock-targeting drug called KL001, and time-restricted feeding.
The team first showed that each of these interventions could improve glymphatic function in healthy animals. They then selected the most promising strategies, KL001 and time-restricted feeding, and tested them in mouse models of stroke.
Treatment did not begin until three days after the stroke, far beyond the narrow window used for clot-busting drugs and other acute stroke treatments.
Even with that delay, mice that received either intervention showed better motor recovery, smaller lesion volumes, improved glymphatic flow, and lower levels of inflammatory cytokines in the brain.
"All of the cytokines moved in the same direction," Hablitz said. "That suggests we may not be targeting one specific inflammatory pathway. Instead, we may be helping the brain clear inflammatory signals more effectively."
A Strategy That Could Be Easier to Use
One of the most promising approaches was time-restricted feeding, a behavioral intervention that is already being investigated for obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other conditions.
That could make the findings especially relevant for stroke rehabilitation because such an approach might eventually be easier to use outside specialized medical settings.
"One of the exciting aspects of this work is that we're studying interventions that could potentially be implemented not only in hospitals but also at home," Hablitz said.
What Researchers Need to Test Next
The researchers emphasize that the findings so far are limited to animal models. More studies will be needed to determine exactly how circadian rhythms, glymphatic function, and inflammation influence one another after stroke.
Future work will also examine whether improved glymphatic flow directly causes better recovery and whether circadian-based interventions can eventually be tested in clinical trials.
More broadly, the study reflects a growing view in neuroscience that sleep, circadian rhythms, and fluid movement through the brain are central to brain health.
By learning more about how the brain's internal clock regulates the glymphatic system, researchers hope to uncover new ways to improve recovery not only after stroke, but also in other neurological conditions involving inflammation and poor waste clearance.
"Understanding how circadian regulation shapes glymphatic clearance will help us develop more targeted therapies," said Hablitz. "Ultimately, our goal is to find ways to improve the brain's ability to clear waste, reduce inflammation, and recover after injury."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Rochester Medical Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Emma Waight, Yuxi Zhu, Ashley Caudell, Velia S. Vizcarra, Evan Newbold, Michael J. Giannetto, Evalien Duyvestyn, Estephanie Balbuena, Wei Song, Tanzil M. Arefin, Yuki Mori, Maiken Nedergaard, Lauren M. Hablitz. Chronotherapy to reinforce circadian rhythms improves poststroke outcomes and glymphatic function in mice. Journal of Clinical Investigation, 2026; 136 (12) DOI: 10.1172/JCI201800

South Korea eyes Turkish engines for its drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:32:02 UTC
17:32:02 KST

- South Korea's Defense Acquisition Program Administration asked TAI about buying TEI's PD170 drone engine, which powers Türkiye's Anka and Aksungur drones.
- The inquiry follows two failed Korean military drone demonstrations in August and September, including kamikaze drones that crashed seconds after launch.
South Korea’s arms procurement agency has asked Türkiye whether it can buy the Turkish PD170 drone engine, a powerplant already flying on some of the world’s most combat-tested drones, as Korean military drone programs suffer a string of public crashes.
Turkish Aerospace Industries, or TAI, recently received an inquiry from South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration about buying the PD170 turbodiesel engine built by its subsidiary TEI, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported Sept. 27. A TAI official told Yonhap the company views potential cooperation with South Korea broadly and hopes joint engineering projects could lay the groundwork for long-term industrial partnerships and new aerospace programs.
Neither side has said which Korean drone program the engines would power, how many Seoul wants or what a deal might be worth. An official at Türkiye’s defense procurement agency, SSB, told Yonhap he could not comment on specific engine models and that a statement would come only after the necessary procedures and negotiations are finished.
The PD170 is a 170-horsepower turbodiesel built for medium-altitude, long-endurance drones, the fixed-wing aircraft that fly for a day or more to watch or strike targets. It powers TAI’s Anka and Aksungur drones and, according to Yonhap, Baykar’s Bayraktar TB2 and TB3. TAI said an Aksungur fitted with the engine stayed aloft for 45 hours and reached 42,000 feet (12,800 m). TEI says the design draws on experience from building engines for U.S.-designed F-16 fighter jets under license in Türkiye.
Turkish drones have been used in combat in Ukraine and across the Middle East, and Türkiye’s defense exports passed $10 billion last year. TAI has also been pushing into more advanced designs. Last month, it said its Anka-3 stealth drone launched two Süper Şimşek jet-powered drones from under its wings during a test flight. Yonhap reported the idea is for the small drones to mimic larger aircraft, draw fire from enemy air defenses and expose their radars, which the Anka-3 could then attack. The Anka-3 originally flew with a Ukrainian engine, and TEI’s own TF6000 turbofan is now being integrated into the aircraft.
South Korea has become one of the world’s fastest-growing arms exporters, with Chunmoo rocket launchers sold to Croatia, K2 tanks certified under NATO’s quality assurance system and rising Middle Eastern interest in its Cheongung-II air defense missiles. Its military drones have had a harder year.
On Sept. 16, at the Ministry of National Defense’s 2026 defense drone technology exhibition, a jet-powered drone developed by Korea Aerospace Industries nosedived into the ground right after takeoff. On Aug. 25, the South Korean Navy and the Agency for Defense Development tried to launch medium-size kamikaze drones from the 14,500-ton amphibious assault ship ROKS Marado in waters south of Busan. Both drones flew for only a few seconds before falling into the sea, and the planned strike on an uncrewed surface vessel never happened. The Navy said it would keep testing the drones’ performance at sea.
Yonhap described the engine inquiry as linked to assessments that South Korea lags behind in drone technology, though neither Seoul nor Ankara has said that directly.

The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.

The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. Taiwan builds drone industry park to shed Chinese supply chain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:20:09 UTC
17:20:09 KST

- Taiwan broke ground on an aerospace and drone industrial park in Chiayi on Sept. 28 and opened a new NCSIST drone research campus.
- The park aims to build a drone supply chain free of Chinese components and is planned to host about 100 companies.
Taiwan broke ground Monday on an aerospace and drone industrial park in the southern county of Chiayi, where the island’s main military research institute wants to build a drone supply chain free of Chinese parts.
President Lai Ching-te led the Sept. 28 ceremony, which also opened a new Minxiong campus for the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, known as NCSIST, the state-run institute that develops most of Taiwan’s homegrown missiles and military drones. The institute did not say at the ceremony how much the new park will cost, how many companies have signed up or when it will open.
The Minxiong campus took three years to build. It includes a research building, hangars, laboratories and facilities for integration testing, and NCSIST says engineers there can work on every stage of a drone’s development, from designing the airframe to building the propulsion and flight-control systems and testing the finished aircraft. The campus also uses digital twin technology, which creates a virtual copy of an aircraft that can be tested in simulation before a real one flies, along with artificial intelligence and virtual reality tools.
The industrial park going up next door is meant to bring manufacturers, government agencies, universities and researchers together around shared computing power and digital engineering tools. NCSIST describes the goal as a “non-red supply chain,” the term Taiwan uses for components and systems that do not come from China. Chiayi County Magistrate Weng Chang-liang said in August that the park is planned to hold about 100 companies.
Taiwan’s push for its own drones picked up after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, where both sides used drones on a massive scale and Ukraine initially relied heavily on Chinese-made DJI models. Concerns that Chinese drones and parts could be tracked or cut off have pushed Taiwan to require that drones bought by public agencies come from non-Chinese supply chains.
The new park builds on the Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center, which opened in August 2022 in Puzi City, also in Chiayi County, on a site that had sat empty for years. The center now hosts more than 50 drone companies and institutions, and Weng said in August that demand has outgrown its space, with another 40 to 50 firms waiting to move in.
The industry has grown quickly. Taiwan’s drone output reached NT$12.9 billion ($407 million) in 2025, about 2.5 times the 2024 figure, and exports totaled NT$2.95 billion ($93 million), according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs. In October 2025, the Executive Yuan, Taiwan’s cabinet, launched a six-year, NT$44.2 billion ($1.39 billion) program to develop the uncrewed vehicle industry, with a goal of pushing annual drone output above NT$40 billion ($1.26 billion) by 2030.
That spending has faced political resistance. In July, the Ministry of Economic Affairs warned that cuts proposed by the opposition Kuomintang, which controls the legislature, would hurt the industry. Weng has also pressed lawmakers to approve more than NT$40 billion ($1.26 billion) in drone-related procurement funding.
Taiwan’s drone strategy relies on three tiers: buying larger military drones from the United States, having NCSIST develop mid-size military drones, and buying small dual-use drones from Taiwan’s private sector. The Minxiong site is designed to link the institute’s military work with those private companies.

bottega veneta crumples cardboard boxes into sculptural stools for summer 2027 show

illya goldman gubin embraces cardboard boxes, shaping them into stools for bottega veneta
the ukrainian artist shapes each box through direct physical contact, leaving its folds, creases, and irregularities visible in a series of individually formed seats.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
Illya Goldman Gubin shapes cardboard through an embrace
For Bottega Veneta’s Summer 2027 show, Ukrainian artist Illya Goldman Gubin turns cardboard boxes into stools through an unusually physical process, embracing and crumpling each box with his body before reinforcing it with resin and fiberglass. Each stool begins as an individual box, with its folds and interlocking flaps retained in the final form, recalling the interwoven leather fettucce of Bottega Veneta’s Intreccio. Goldman Gubin uses his own body to give each piece its final form, leaving the marks of that encounter visible on the finished seats.
Bottega Veneta’s Intreccio inspires the folded structure
Cardboard has been a recurring material in Goldman Gubin’s work, from sculptures and installations to furniture. For these stools, he starts with the box as it is, folding and crumpling it by hand so that each form develops through the pressure of his body. The resulting creases, dents, and uneven surfaces remain visible once the cardboard is reinforced with resin and fiberglass, making each stool slightly different from the next.
A cardboard box is made to carry something before it is usually thrown away, but Goldman Gubin gives the same material another purpose by turning it into a seat. The box that once carried an object can now carry a person, while its folded flaps are worked into one another to recall the interwoven leather fettucce of Bottega Veneta’s Intreccio. Goldman Gubin uses the existing structure of the box to create the interlocking effect. The process leaves the making visible in the finished stools, with the original material still legible beneath the hardened surface. What begins as an ordinary cardboard container is reshaped through direct physical contact into a piece of furniture, retaining the folds and irregularities produced along the way.

A local lawmaker warned of "profound" consequences if the parade did not proceed in the next two days.
About 2,000 protesters including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill and Claire Hanna, the leader of Irish nationalist party SDLP, blocked the route on Sunday. This led to a standoff, with both sides declining to disperse and police between them.
The attempt to hold the parade from Portadown to the nearby hamlet of Drumcree followed Friday's lifting of an almost 30-year ban on the route. The parade had triggered unrest across British-run Northern Ireland in the run-up to a 1998 peace deal.
The head of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition told protesters late on Sunday that he would meet Northern Ireland Minister Chris Bryant and the chief of police after receiving commitments that the march would not proceed overnight.
He asked that a small number of volunteers remain on the road through the night to ensure the commitments were not broken, the BBC reported.
"We've stopped them once, the process now is to stop them permanently," Breandán Mac Cionnaith told the protesters.
Northern Ireland's Parades Commission, set up during the original Drumcree dispute to regulate marches, permitted a smaller-than-usual parade after its initial decision to continue the ban was quashed by the High Court in August over a procedural error.
EFFORTS TO REDUCE TENSION
Bryant has the power to revoke the Parades Commission's ruling at the request of Northern Ireland's police, but said he had received no such request.
"I've made it very clear that I think it's important that we get to a resolution and we need to find some kind of compromise. Nobody wants to perpetuate this tension and this anger," Bryant told reporters after meeting political parties on Sunday night.
The dispute has created new tension in Northern Ireland's compulsory power-sharing devolved government led by Sinn Fein and pro-British rivals, the Democratic Unionist Party. The DUP says the parade must go ahead.
"He (Bryant) has 24 to 48 hours to ensure the rule of law is upheld and the parade proceeds," DUP lawmaker Carla Lockhart wrote on social media after the party met the minister.
"If that does not happen, the consequences will be profound. Mob rule cannot defeat the rule of law." REUTERS

China's deep-sea drilling capacity reaches 5,000-meter level
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:00:39 CST
17:00:39 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on July 28, 2026 shows China's ocean drilling vessel Mengxiang conducting an operation at night. China's Mengxiang ocean drilling vessel has set a national record for deep-sea drilling, elevating its capability to the 5,000-meter level, after obtaining basalt samples from the South China Sea basin, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Monday. This marks China's entry into international advanced ranks in deep-sea drilling operation capacity, according to the ministry. (Photo by Zhang Fatao/Xinhua)
GUANGZHOU, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's Mengxiang, meaning Dream, ocean drilling vessel has set a national record for deep-sea drilling, elevating its capability to the 5,000-meter level, after obtaining basalt samples from the South China Sea basin, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Monday.
This marks China's entry into international advanced ranks in deep-sea drilling operation capacity, according to the ministry.
A 4.27-meter basalt sample was extracted during the voyage via a self-developed drill, which made China the third country after the United States and Japan to obtain hard rock samples from a deep ocean basin using drilling vessels.
The research team conducted a long-term and high-intensity operation of shipborne remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), deploying two ROVs to operate for over 358 hours in total at a depth of 4,000 meters, with a single continuous operation lasting up to 103 hours, reaching internationally advanced levels, said Sun Zhen, a researcher at the Guangzhou Marine Geological Survey (GMGS) in south China.
Following the standards of the International Ocean Discovery Program for the first time, researchers also completed on-site multi-parameter processing and analysis of the samples, including cataloging, cutting, scanning, testing and storage, thereby mastering full-process operational capabilities for ultra-deep water ocean scientific drilling.
The samples and data obtained during the voyage provide crucial empirical evidence for addressing core scientific issues such as the expansion of the South China Sea. They are also of great significance for studying the evolution of the ancient marine environment in the sea and for the exploration and development of ultra-deep water energy resources, researchers noted.
A total of 170 researchers from nine institutions participated in the voyage, which was organized by the China Geological Survey and implemented by the GMGS.
China's first domestically-built ocean drilling vessel, Mengxiang, was officially commissioned in 2024. ■

====================================================================================================

Column: A miner's leave slip that debunks Japan's "benevolent colonialism"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:00:23 CST
17:00:23 KST

by Zhou Yaxin
In the winter of 1943, at the Xi'an Coal Mine in what was then the Japanese puppet regime of "Manchukuo" in China's northeast, a miner named Li Xingyu submitted a leave application.
Written in simple, broken words, the slip reads: "My name is Li Xingyu. My three sons are all dead. I am heartbroken ... My mother is over seventy and blind ... I have nowhere else to turn. I beg the director to have mercy and give me a certificate so that I may return home to visit my mother. I worked shifts with my sons, never missing a single day ... Of my five children, four are dead. I have no heart left to work ..."
This leave application was never approved.
Today, it is preserved at the Exhibition Hall of the Liaoyuan Miners' Tomb from the Period of Japanese Occupation in Northeast China. Also on display are the largely intact remains of 197 miners, along with more than 20 sets of scattered remains. Some skulls bear knife marks, and some leg bones are severed. The youngest victim was merely 12 years old. A local ballad from the era captured the horror: "Electric fences stretch high, watchtowers stand tall; miners are locked up like prisoners in a cell. Entering the mine was like stepping through hell's gate; to stay alive was harder than death itself."
These are stark reminders of the colonial expansion and resource plundering carried out by Japanese militarism in northeast China, deeply rooted in history and etched in memories that remain searing to this day.
After the Meiji Restoration, Japan embarked on a path of military expansion in Asia. China's northeast, with its abundant resources and unique geostrategic position, became a primary target.
On Sept. 18, 1931, the Japanese Kwantung Army deliberately staged the September 18th Incident. Within less than half a year, China's three northeastern provinces fell under Japanese occupation.
The crimes committed by Japanese militarism during its 14-year colonial rule in the region will never be forgotten. The lie of "benevolent colonialism" repeatedly peddled by Japan's right wing will collapse under its own weight.
Plundering resources and monopolizing the economy -- Japan pursued a colonial economic model of "Japan being the industrial hub and China's northeast the raw material base." It set up over 200 entities, including major railway, power and coal companies, and used them to seize control of northeast China's economic lifelines. According to incomplete statistics, between 1932 and 1945, Japan extracted 223 million tons of coal and 120 million tons of grain, along with other resources, from northeast China to fuel its war machine. Japan also profited enormously from opium smuggling in the region.
Enslaving education and colonial indoctrination -- The Japanese invaders adhered to the principle that "To subjugate a nation, first erase its history." After the establishment of the puppet "Manchukuo" in 1932, Japan started to replace Chinese language with Japanese in schools, attempting to make Chinese children forget their own history and identity. The puppet regime revised middle school textbooks, removing content on traditional Chinese culture and history to promote the narrative that "Manchukuo" was an "independent state."
Brutal exploitation and disregard for human life -- Across coal mines, the Japanese military enforced a policy that treated human lives as expendable in the pursuit of coal. Countless laborers starved, died from disease, were beaten to death or burned alive in mines where basic safety measures were virtually nonexistent. According to the Japanese puppet regime's coal production cost data, Chinese laborers were listed alongside explosives and detonators, treated as little more than inputs in the production process.
During the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, Japan forcibly recruited over 10 million Chinese laborers across the country. In northeast China alone, 2 million died from abuse. Unit 731 of the Kwantung Army built the world's largest germ warfare base in Harbin, where it experimented on imprisoned civilians and prisoners of war -- subjecting them to frostbite, poison gas and low-pressure tests, and deliberately infecting them with plague, anthrax and cholera. During Japan's invasion of China, an estimated 650,000 Chinese died as a result of Japanese biological warfare.
Yet even today, some right-wing forces in Japan not only refuse to reflect on their history of colonial aggression, but also deliberately distort historical facts.
They portray the war of aggression as an effort to "liberate Asia from Western colonial rule," and claim that Japan accelerated the "modernization" of some Asian countries and regions through infrastructure construction and "good governance" during its colonial rule.
The historical record tells a different story.
The infrastructure built by Japan in occupied territories was designed primarily to serve its own war needs. The systematic extraction of resources and the atrocities committed under Japanese militarism left local people in abject poverty, severely disrupted the economic and social development of Asian nations, and impeded the progress of colonized countries. The so-called "good governance" practices are in fact evidence of crimes, scars of suffering, and engines of death. The much-vaunted "Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere" was in reality a "Greater East Asia Aggression Sphere." Tens of millions of soldiers and civilians died under Japanese militarism -- hardly a record of "co-prosperity."
Ninety-five years on, some right-wing forces in Japan still show no remorse or repentance for the September 18th Incident. They even attempt to tamper with historical facts and whitewash their record, seeking to turn the page on all their crimes of aggression and colonization in Asia. The Chinese people will never accept this, nor will the peoples of other Asian countries that suffered Japanese aggression.
History cannot be falsified. Conscience and justice will endure. Miner Li Xingyu's leave application is an irrefutable evidence, as are the miners' remains on display and the records left behind by the puppet regime.
The alarm bell of the September 18th continues to ring -- not to perpetuate hatred, but to ensure that these pieces of evidence are seen, remembered and passed on from one generation to the next.
As long as these records endure, the historical truth will endure, and the Japanese right wing's plot to peddle the myth of "benevolent colonialism" will never succeed.
Editor's note: The author is an international affairs observer.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

"After facing each other in the team event over the past couple of days, both of us made more targeted preparations," Wang said.
"I think I was able to gain and learn a lot from today's match," she added.
China's losses to An and Yamaguchi ended its hopes of singles gold at the Games. Earlier, Chinese men's singles stars Li Shifeng and Shi Yuqi, the Hangzhou champion and runner-up respectively, had exited in the round of 32 and round of 16.
In the men's singles semifinals, Thailand's Kunlavut Vitidsarn defeated Indonesia's Alwi Farhan 21-13, 21-15, while Singapore's Loh Kean Yew beat South Korea's Yoo Tae-bin 21-19, 19-21, 21-12.
There was an upset in the mixed doubles, where China's world No. 1 pair and title favorites Feng Yanzhe and Huang Dongping fell 21-12, 21-14 to Indonesia's Amri Syahnawi and Nita Violina Marwah.
"We don't look like we have solutions and we seem to always be playing to our opponents' rhythm," Huang said. "The male player is not very tall, but he's so fast. If we can't keep up with him, then it will be quite hard for us to attack."
China's other mixed doubles pair, Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin, reached the final with a 21-13, 21-9 win over Chinese Taipei's Ye Hong-wei and Nicole Gonzales Chan.
In the men's doubles semifinals, China's Liang Weikeng and Wang Chang battled for an hour to overcome Indonesia's Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri 21-17, 13-21, 21-9, while Indonesia's Leo Rolly Carnando and Daniel Marthin upset South Korea's top pair Kim Won-ho and Seo Seung-jae 21-11, 21-14.
In the women's doubles, China's Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning came from a game down to beat Malaysia's Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan 16-21, 22-20, 21-12.
The Chinese pair will face Baek Ha-na and Lee So-hee in the final after the South Korean duo eliminated Japan's Rin Iwanaga and Kie Nakanishi 21-13, 21-9.
All five individual gold medals will be decided on Tuesday. ■

Sweden faces political deadlock after Andersson gives up attempt to form government
STOCKHOLM, Sept 28 - Attempts to form a new government in Sweden hit the buffers on Monday after Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson said she was unable to secure enough support, despite the centre-left bloc winning a narrow majority in this month's election.
"I can conclude that there is currently no possibility for me to form a government," Andersson said at a press conference, saying she had lost the support of Sweden's Left Party.
The speaker of Sweden's parliament, Andreas Norlen, told reporters he will meet each party leader one-on-one on Wednesday before announcing who will have the next go at exploring the formation of a government.
One likely option would be Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, whose Moderates are the next biggest party after the Social Democrats.
The general election on September 13 saw the centre-left opposition taking 176 seats in parliament, just beating the centre-right's 173.
The result was driven by a decline in support for the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, bucking a Europe-wide trend of gains for the far right.
Despite the centre-left's victory, the vote, widely seen as a referendum on Kristersson's promise to bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into a ruling coalition, has left forming a stable government fraught with difficulties.
Andersson said she had given up trying to form a government after the Left Party, one of the parties she needed to form a majority, said it would support a candidate from the centre-right as speaker of parliament.
The Left Party has said previously it will only support Andersson as prime minister.
Andersson would likely get another shot at trying to form a government if any centre-right attempt fails.
The speaker can put four candidates forward to parliament for approval, but if each is rejected, Sweden will hold a new election.
Casting a further cloud over the process, police said on Friday they had started preliminary investigations into five complaints of election fraud around Stockholm.
The probes come days after prosecutors opened a separate investigation into suspected fraud in the central Swedish town of Borlange, a case that could put 11 parliamentary seats in play if the Election Review Board orders a re-run of the vote there.
In 2018, Social Democrat Stefan Lofven took 134 days to form a new government. REUTERS

U.S. Navy’s newest destroyer arrives in Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:56:20 UTC
16:56:20 KST

- The future USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), a Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, arrived in Whittier, Alaska, on Sept. 27, 2026.
- The U.S. Navy will commission the ship there on Oct. 3, the first Navy commissioning in Alaska since 2013.
The U.S. Navy’s newest destroyer, the future USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), arrived in Whittier, Alaska, on Sept. 27, less than a week before it is due to be formally commissioned there in a ceremony the state has not hosted in more than a decade.
The Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer will be commissioned Oct. 3, 2026, in the small port town on Prince William Sound, the U.S. Navy said. Commissioning is the ceremony at which a ship officially joins the fleet and the crew takes charge of it. The last Navy ship commissioned in Alaska was the amphibious transport dock USS Anchorage (LPD 23), in Anchorage on May 4, 2013.
The ship is named for Ted Stevens, a decorated World War II Army Air Corps pilot who went on to represent Alaska in the U.S. Senate for four decades and became a leading voice on defense spending. It is the first Navy warship to carry his name. Alaska’s congressional delegation and state officials pushed to hold the ceremony in the state, and then-Secretary of the Navy John Phelan approved Whittier as the location in March.
After the ceremony, the destroyer will not stay in Alaska. Its homeport is Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, where it arrived in May after delivery trials.
Ted Stevens was built by Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Ingalls Shipbuilding division in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and delivered to the U.S. Navy in December 2025. It is one of the Flight III ships, the latest version of the Arleigh Burke design, which has been in production since the 1980s and makes up the backbone of the U.S. Navy’s surface fleet.
The main change in Flight III is the AN/SPY-6(V)1 air and missile defense radar, which can detect and track aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles at longer range than the SPY-1 radar on earlier Arleigh Burke destroyers. The ship also carries the Aegis Baseline 10 combat system and has more electrical power and cooling capacity to run its newer sensors and weapons. The destroyer displaces about 9,700 tons and can carry out air defense, ballistic missile defense, anti-submarine and surface warfare missions.
Holding the ceremony in Alaska ties the ship to the U.S. Navy’s growing presence in the far north. The Navy said it maintains a persistent operational presence in Alaska, including high-latitude maritime security operations, and the state sits along the northern Pacific and Arctic sea lanes that link North America with Asia.
Ted Stevens is part of a steady stream of new Flight III destroyers entering the fleet from Ingalls and from General Dynamics’ Bath Iron Works in Maine. The U.S. Navy has not said where the ship will make its first deployment or when it will join a carrier strike group.
The commissioning ceremony is scheduled for Oct. 3 in Whittier.

Protesters demand Spanish government limit evictions after pensioner forced out
MADRID, Sept 28 - Protesters camped outside the Madrid regional government's headquarters for a third day on Monday to object to the eviction of an octogenarian and demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.
Protests boiled over last week after police evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal on a stretcher from her Madrid home of more than seven decades because of an eviction order secured by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Hundreds of people outside her building clashed with police, while the Socialist-led central government condemned the centre-right regional administration for not preventing the eviction.
By Monday, hundreds of tents filled the central Puerta del Sol square, echoing the protests of 2011 when it was occupied for a month by activists demonstrating against austerity measures adopted during the global financial crisis.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Sunday the government was working to enact a housing decree in parliament by Tuesday that would bring immediate relief for tenants.
Unlike in the financial crisis, when many evictions were linked to mortgage defaults after a property bubble burst, a growing share are now related to rent disputes, reflecting a shortage of properties. Rents have on average doubled over the past decade, far outpacing salaries.
TENS OF THOUSANDS MARCH THROUGH MADRID
On Saturday, some 30,000 people marched through Madrid to object to the treatment of Abascal and others forced from their homes by investment funds.
Marchers shook keys and bore banners with slogans including "Speculators go home" and "Housing is for living".
As night fell on Puerta del Sol, home to the office of Isabel Diaz Ayuso, centre-right president of the Madrid region, dozens of activists put up tents, and their number has steadily grown since.
Blanca, a student, said young Spaniards were struggling to move out of their parents' homes.

Further protests were set to take place across Spain on Monday, according to the Tenants' Union, which has been co-ordinating the protests.
From her hospital bed in Madrid, Abascal said she could not join the demonstration and urged protesters to keep fighting.
"Be brave, fight, defend what is yours and, please, take care of yourselves; keep camping there for as long as your bodies can hold out and as long as you wish to. Let’s hope all this comes to a successful conclusion tomorrow," she said in a video distributed by the Tenants' Union.
Spain has a deficit of 750,000 homes, according to the central bank, which has said that figure could rise to over 1 million by 2028. Only about 120,000 are built each year, a sixth of the rate before the 2008 financial crisis.
Ayuso said the protests were an attempt to "change the rules of the game" on existing contracts and asked whether the activists thought there should be age limit for paying rent. REUTERS
